sec.title: Background
sec.p: In this book we have attempted to collect most of the consequences of the axiom of choice that have been discovered during the past 90 years. Our goal is to present these statements and the relationships between them in an easily accessible format. Since 1904, when Zermelo introduced the axiom of choice, hundreds of its consequences have appeared in articles by almost as many authors. These articles have explored the complicated pattern of implications between the various consequences. With the introduction of independence proofs by Fraenkel, Mostowski, Specker and Cohen, the pattern of relationships became still more intricate. The results in this area are scattered over a wide spectrum of journals and books. As a result a particular theorem may be proved and reproved by several different authors. For example, Shannon [1988] asked whether or not the axiom of choice for countable families of countable sets implies the countable union theorem. In Howard [1992] Shannon’s question was answered in the negative. Shortly afterward Norbert Brunner, in his review of Howard [1992], pointed out that the result had already been obtained by Felgner in [1974]. This book was begun with the primary purpose of preventing such occurrences. We hope it will also serve as a reference for non-set theorist who need to know the strength of some particular statement relative to the axiom of choice and its consequences.

In some ways our work is similar to that of Herman and Jean Rubin (Rubin/Rubin [1985]) which contains equivalents of the axiom of choice. However, our task is complicated by the fact that the statements we consider are not, in general, equivalent. We are concerned with sentences in the language of set theory which can be proved using the axiom of choice but which are not theorems of set theory with that axiom omitted (with the exception of form 0 described below). We call these sentences forms of the axiom of choice. The forms are numbered starting with form 0. Form 1 is the axiom of choice and form 0 is 0=0, provable in set theory without any form of the axiom of choice. The remaining forms are numbered in the order we encountered them as we reviewed the literature.

We consider two versions of set theory. The first is Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory which we denote by \mathrm{ZF}. For our purposes any one of the axiomatizations of the theory \mathrm{ZF} will be satisfactory. To be specific we shall use the one given in Jech [1973b], page 35. The second version of set theory is denoted by \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. The theory \mathrm{ZF}^{0} is the following modification of \mathrm{ZF}. A constant symbol \emptyset is added to the language together with the axiom ( orall x)(x
ot \in \emptyset ). In addition the axioms of extensionality (A1 in Jech [1973b]) and foundation (or regularity) (A8 in Jech [1973b]) are modified to allow the existence of atoms (or urelements). Each atom a has the property that a
eq \emptyset and 
eg (\exists x)(x\in a). Let set(x) be the formula x=\emptyset \vee (\exists y)(y\in x). Then the modified version of the extensionality axiom mentioned above is
The modified version of the axiom of regularity is

Corresponding to these two theories are two types of models: Cohen models of \mathrm{ZF} which use forcing to extend a model of \mathrm{ZF} in which the axiom of choice holds to a model in which it fails and Fraenkel-Mostowski (FM) permutation models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. Starting with a model of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} in which the axiom of choice is true, and in which the class of atoms is non-empty, \mathrm{FM} models use permutations of the atoms to obtain a submodel in which the axiom of choice is false. Both types of models are described in more detail in part III of the book.

Our policy on notation and terminology is (for the most part) to use that of the original articles and books, or standard terminology. However, we are careful to distinguish between the terms “denumerable” and “countable”. We use the term “denumerable” to mean “countably infinite”. A set x is denumerable or countably infinite if x\approx (\omega ), and a set is countable if it is either finite or denumerable.

sec.title: Description of the parts of the book
sec.p: This book is divided into seven parts
Part I is the numerical list of forms. For example, the listing for form 3 is
FORM 3. 2m=m: For all infinite cardinals m,\,2m=m. Tarski [1954a].
[3 A] For all cardinals m and n,\,n\leq m and m infinite \rightarrow m+n=m. Halpern/Howard [1970].
[3 B] \aleph _{0}\cdot m=m: For all infinite cardinals m,\,\aleph _{0}\cdot m=m. Halpern/Howard [1970].

[3 C] Definability of cardinal addition as the least upper bound: (For all cardinals x,\,y and z) (x+y=z iff (x\leq z and y\leq z and (\forall u)(x, y\leq u\rightarrow z\leq u)). Häussler [1983] and Tarski [1949a].

[3 D] Every pair of cardinals has a least upper bound in the usual cardinal ordering and for all cardinals \kappa and \gamma , if n\kappa \leq \gamma for all n\in \omega , then \aleph _{0}\kappa \leq \gamma . Hickman [1979b].
[3 E] E(IV, V): For all infinite cardinals m,\,m+1=m implies 2m=m. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[3 F] E(III, V): For every set X, if \mathcal{P}(X) is Dedekind infinite then 2|X|=|X|. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[3 G] E(II, V): For every set X, if there is a non-empty family of subsets of X which is linearly ordered by \subseteq and has no maximal element then 2|X|=|X|. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[3 H] E(Ia, V): For every set X, if 2|X|>|X| then X is amorphous. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.

In most cases a form’s listing contains its number, a name for the form, a precise statement of the form and a reference to the bibliography. Following each form in part I is a list of statements known to be equivalent to the form. We also refer to these statements as forms. In the example given above, forms [3 A] through [3 H] are all equivalent to form 3. The listing of each equivalent form ends with a reference to an article (or note) where the proof of equivalence can be found.

Part II is the topical list of forms. This listing of the forms by subject matter is the part of the book which is most similar to H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985]. The listing of each form in part II contains the same information as its listing in part I. One difference between part I and part II is that in part II a form and its equivalents need not occur together. For example, form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) is in the section of algebraic forms while its equivalent form [14 P] (Alaoglu’s Theorem) is in the section of forms from analysis.

Part III, titled “Models”, contains a brief description of each model of set theory. These descriptions include the forms that have been proved true in the model and the forms that have been proved false together with a reference to the proof. Each description ends with a list of all forms known to be true in the model and all forms known to be false. For example, in model \mathcal{M}1 form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) was proved to be true in Halpern/Levy [1971]. These facts are included in the description of \mathcal{M}1. Since form 14 implies form 30 (the Ordering principle), form 30 is also true in the model and therefore form 30 occurs in the final list of forms which are true in the model. There are two sections in part III. Section 1 contains Cohen models for \mathrm{ZF}. In most cases the models are denoted by \mathcal{M}k, where k is a positive integer. Section 2 contains models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. Our notation for these models is \mathcal{N}k, where k is a positive integer.

Part IV, titled “Notes”, is a collection of notes which are referred to in other parts of the book. Whenever we consider notation or terminology to be nonstandard we add a note explaining it. Our policy on proofs is to omit them if they are readily available in the literature. However, if a proof is not, in our judgement, readily available, we have included it in a note. Other notes include a survey of the relationships between the (infinitely many) versions of the axiom of choice for sets of n element sets, n a positive integer (note 15), a brief exposition of the transfer theorems of Jech/Sochor and Pincus (note 103), and various properties of and relations between forms (notes 18 and 120).
Part V is called “References for Relationships Between Forms”. To explain part V it is helpful to consider an example. A typical line from part V is below.

The first two numbers are form numbers. The third number which occurs in parentheses is a code number for the status of the implication “form 43 implies form 63”. The number 3 is the code for “not provable in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory”. The other code numbers that we use are

def.p: for “The status of the implication is unknown.”
for “The implication is provable.”
for “The implication is provable and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1.”
for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}.”
for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF} and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1 or 3.”
for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.”
for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are odd.”
for “The status of the implication is unknown and we have found the question asked somewhere in the literature.”

sec.p: In part V the implication codes are odd numbers for the most part. Following the code number in a typical line of part V is a reference to a bibliography item and possibly a note and, in the case of a non-implication, a model number. In the example, Felgner [1971a] refers to a bibliography item in part VI and M2 refers to the model \mathcal{M}2 from part III.
Part VI, our bibliography, is a listing of all articles and books we have used arranged alphabetically by author.
Part VII consists of two (n+1) by (n+1) matrices where n is the last form number. (Currently n=383.) We refer to these matrices as table 1 and table 2.

Printed copies of table 1 and table 2 are not included. They may be accessed using the software that is included. In addition the program maketex.c in the software package will create TeX files containing copies of table 1 and table 2 which may then be printed. Tables 1 and 2 are also available at either of the authors’ web sites: http://www.math.purdue.edu/~jer/ or http://www.emunix.emich.edu/~phoward/

The natural numbers 0 through n are the row and column headings in both table 1 and table 2 and are to be thought of as form numbers. Each entry in the body of table 1 is one of the code numbers 0 through 7 used in part V. The code number in row n and column k of table 1 describes the status of the implication “form n implies form k”. Odd entries (1, 3, 5 or 7) mean that the implication or non-implication (or open problem) has a reference listed in part V. For example, the entry in row 43, column 39 of table 1 is 3. This means that form 43 does not imply form 39 in \mathrm{ZF} and there is a reference in part V to this result. The entry in table 1 at position 8, 40 (that is, row 8, column 40) is 4. This means that form 8 does not imply form 40 in \mathrm{ZF} and this non-implication follows from implications and non-implications that have references in part V.

When an even entry is encountered in table 1 it is possible, by studying table 1, to find implications and non-implications from which this even entry follows and which are referenced in part V. For example, an examination of table 1 reveals that the entries at positions 43, 8 and 40, 39 are both 1 and that (as noted earlier) the entry at position 43, 39 is a 3. This means that form 43 implies form 8, form 40 implies form 39 and form 43 does not imply form 39 in \mathrm{ZF}. Further all these results are referenced in part V. It follows from these three results that form 8 does not imply form 40 and hence we have “reduced” the non-implication “form 8 does not imply form 40” to results that have references in part V.

The purpose of table 2 is to provide a direct path to this reduction. In table 2 the non-zero entries are form numbers. These non-zero entries occur only in positions where the corresponding entry in table 1 is 2, 4, or 6. If the table 1 entry at position m,\,k is 2, then the entry in table 2 is a form number j such that form m implies form j and form j implies form k. Thus the implication “form m implies form k” is “reduced” to the implications “form m implies form j ” and “form j implies form k”. If the table 1 entries at positions m,\,j and j,\,k are both 1’s then the original implication (“form m implies form k”) has been reduced to implications with references in part V. If either of the table 1 entries at positions m,\,j or j,\,k is a 2 then the implication corresponding to the 2 can be reduced again using table 2. Similarly, if the entry at position m,\,k of table 1 is a 4 or a 6, the table 2 entry at position m,\, k will be a form number j of a form such that one of two things happens: Either form j implies form m and form j does not imply form k or form k implies form j and form m does not imply form j. These two possibilities are illustrated in the diagram below.

In either case the non-implication “form m does not imply form k” has been “reduced”. Using this method with the 4 at position 8, 40 in table 1 we see that the table 2 entry at position 8, 40 is 231. Referring back to table 1, we see that the entry in position 8, 231 is a 3 and the entry at position 40, 231 is a 1. The non-implication “form 8 does not imply form 40” has been reduced to the two facts “ form 8 does not imply form 231” and “form 40 implies form 231” both of which have references in part V.

sec.title: Software
sec.p: This section contains a description of the software. The next section contains detailed instructions for its use. All programs and computer files mentioned in this section are on the diskette enclosed inside the back cover. Using the software that is included will eliminate the need for calculations using table 2. The enclosed diskette contains two data files: rfb1.tex and models.dat. The purpose of these files is described later in this section.

The software also includes several programs each of which is described below. There are two versions of each program: A source file with extension .c suitable for compiling on any machine with a c compiler and an executable version with extension .exe which can be run directly on any \mathrm{PC} which runs MS DOS. Here are the descriptions of the c programs

def.p: mk_book.c – This program must be run before any of the others. (From the file rfb1.tex it creates two matrices of size 384 by 384 (which are versions of table 1 and table 2) and stores them in the two files book1 and book2. These files (book1 and book2) are used by the other c programs to extract information about implications among the forms. Each of book1 and book2 uses about .5 megabytes of memory.

p.bold: AFTER RUNNING mk-book.c ANY OF THE FOLLOWING CAN BE USED:

def.p: weakac.c – This is the main program for obtaining information about the relationships between forms. When you run the program the data files book1 and book2 will be read into memory and then the main menu will appear on the screen. Then menu is show below.

MAIN MENU1.
see the meanings of the implication codes
type 1 <enter>2.
see what is known about the implication ¡form n implies form k¿ for any two form numbers n and k
type 2 <enter>3.
get information about a single form
type 3 <enter>4.
see table 1 restricted to any subset of the forms
type 4 <enter>5.
see a submatrix of table 1 consisting of consecutive rows and columns
type 5 <enter>6.
see how an implication or non-implication follows from those with a reference in part V
type 6 <enter>7.
see the models in which a form is true and those in which it is false
type 7 <enter>8.
exit the program
type 8 <enter>
In order for option 7 to work the file models.dat must be present.
maketex.c – A program which will create TeX files for table 1 and table 2 from book1 and book2 if you want a hard copy of either of these.

sec.title: Using the Software
sec.p: The Setup. There are three steps in the setup procedure:

def.p: Copy the files from the floppy disk to your computer’s memory.

Compile the c programs using a c language compiler. (This step is not necessary if you are working on a computer running MS DOS. We have included complied executable DOS files for each of the c programs.)
Run the program mk_book. This program creates the data files used by the other programs.

sec.p: The program mk_book takes between 5 and 10 minutes to run. It creates the data files book1 and book2 from the file rfb1.tex. The files copied from the floppy disk together with the data files book1 and book2 occupy about 2.3 megabytes of memory.

To carry out the setup procedure on a DOS machine, put the floppy disk in the disk drive. Assuming that this is drive a:, the following instructions given at the DOS prompt (\mathrm{C}:\backslash >) will create a directory called weakac and copy the files from the disk into that directory.
md \mathrm{c}:\backslash weakac
copy \mathrm{a}:^{\ast }\cdot ^{\ast }\mathrm{c}:\backslash weakac
To complete the setup on a DOS machine change to the weakac directory and run mk_book with the following two commands.
cd c:\backslash weakac
mk_book
Answer y to the question “Do you want to continue?”.
On a non-DOS machine a c language compiler is required. You must compile the c language programs mk_book.c, weakac.c, and maketex.c. On a UNIX machine, for example, the command
cc -o mk_book mk_book.c
will compile the c program mk_book.c and store the executable program in the file mk_book. The other programs should be compiled similarly. To complete the setup type
mk_book
at the UNIX prompt to run the program mk_book.

Running the Other Programs. The program weakac is the program that is used for getting information about the relationships between the various consequences of \mathrm{AC}. It is described in the previous section. To run it type
weakac
at the DOS or UNIX prompt. Follow the instructions on the screen. In particular you are offered the option of writing the program’s output in a file.
The program maketex will create TeX files for either table 1 or table 2. At the DOS or UNIX prompt type
maketex
You will be prompted with the lines:
“Enter the mane of the file to be converted to
TeX. This will usually be book1 or book2.”
To make a TeX file for table 1 type book1. To make a TeX file for table 2 type book2. You will then be prompted with the question:
“To what file name should the TeX file be
written? Must be different from the input file.”

At this point you choose the name for the output file. It may be any valid file name other that book1 or book2. For example table1.tex or table2.tex are suitable. A few more lines appear on the screen and you are prompted with the question “Today’s date?” Enter the date in any format. For example 8/10/97 or August 10, 1997 are suitable responses. The final question is
“Will the output be table 1 or table 2?
respond 1 or 2.”
Make the appropriate response and the TeX file for table 1 or table 2 will be created. When processed by a TeX program and printed, each of these tables is 144 pages long.

sec.title: Acknowledgements
sec.p: We have received many helpful suggestions and comments from colleagues. In particular we thank Andreas Blass, Norbert Brunner, Robert Cowen, Kyriakos Keremedis, Marianne Morillon, David Pincus, Herman and Arthur Rubin, Eric Schechter and John Truss. We would also like to thank the referee whose report we found extremely helpful. Our thanks also to Andrew Smith. His translations of several articles into English made life much easier for us. We are grateful to Leonard Lipshitz and the Mathematics Department at Purdue University for providing an opportunity for the authors to work side by side during the Fall 1994 semester. The publishers representatives, Sarah Donnelly and Sergei Gelfand, were very helpful. We should also like to thank Betty Gick, a secretary in the Purdue Mathematics Department, who helped us with TeX. Finally we are grateful to our spouses Herman Rubin and Gale Howard for their patience and encouragement.

sec.title: Final Note
sec.p: We have tried to give the original sources of the results. However, this is not always possible. When we give references like Jech [1973b], Mathias [1979], G. Moore [1982], H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], etc., it means that information about the results can be found there. It does not necessarily mean that it is the original source. We have also made an effort to check the accuracy of our results, especially when the source is a preprint. As far as we can tell, our results are consistent. However, because of the amount of data that we have, it is virtually impossible to prevent some error from sneaking in. We just hope the errors are not serious and we encourage readers to contact us when they encounter errors or software problems. We would also appreciate hearing of new results in this area. We shall add all additions and corrections to our web pages.

[\boldsymbol{0} B] If X is finite then X^{\omega } is compact. Brunner [1984b].
[\boldsymbol{0} C] Closed subspaces of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b].
[\boldsymbol{0} D] Products of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b]

[\boldsymbol{0} E] The box product of a well ordered family of limited amorphous spaces is limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b] and note 52.

[\boldsymbol{0} F] Cancellation for surjective cardinal equivalence: For every k\in \omega -\{0\},\,(\forall x\forall y)(kx=^{\ast } ky implies x=^{\ast }y) (The expression x=^{\ast }y means that there is a function f from x onto y and a function g from y onto x.) Truss [1984].

[\boldsymbol{0} G] Cancellation for injective cardinal inequality: For every k\in \omega -\{0\},\,(\forall x\forall y)(kx\leq ky implies x\leq y) (\leq is the usual (injective) cardinal ordering.) Lindenbaum/Tarski [1926].
[\boldsymbol{0} H] F. Riesz Theorem: A Hilbert space is finite dimensional iff its closed unit ball is compact. Brunner [1983a].

(a) The closed unit ball is sequentially compact.
(b) Each unconditionally convergent series converges absolutely.
(c) Each ortho-normal system is Dedekind finite.
Brunner [1983a] and note 94.

[\boldsymbol{0} J] Zermelo’s Fixed Point Theorem: For every partially ordered set (X, \leq ), if every well ordered subset has a least upper bound then every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988], Zermelo [1908b] and Abian [1980].

[\boldsymbol{0} K] For all partially ordered sets (X, \leq ), if there is a \displaystyle \sup function \sigma on the well ordered subsets of X then every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988] and note 38.

[\boldsymbol{0} L] Caristi’s Fixed Point Theorem: If (X, \rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi : X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering (x\leq y iff \rho (x, y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)) every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t \leq f(t) has a fixed point. Caristi [1976], Manka [1988], and note 38.
[\boldsymbol{0} M] A T_{1} topological space is Dedekind finite if and only if every subspace has a dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[\boldsymbol{0} N] If X and Y are topological spaces with dense Dedekind finite subsets so is X\times Y. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[\boldsymbol{0} O] A Lindelöf space with a dense, Dedekind finite subset is compact. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[\boldsymbol{0} P] A Lindelöf space with a Dedekind finite basis is compact. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[\boldsymbol{0} Q] For all cardinal numbers m and n and Dedekind finite cardinals p, if p+m=p+n then m=n. Tarski [1949b] and note 94

[\boldsymbol{0} AL] For every set A, there is an \aleph which cannot be covered by fewer than |A| sets each of cardinality <|A|. Note 131.

[\boldsymbol{0} AM] Assume V is a separable vector space, D is a countable dense subset of V, and p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R} satisfies p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y), and (\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx) =tp(x)). Also assume that p satisfies the following condition:

Moreover, if f is a linear function from a subspace S of V into \mathbb{R} which satisfies (\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x)), then f can be extended to f^{\ast }:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R} so that f^{\ast } is linear and (\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast }(x)\leq p(x)). Note 143.
FORM 1. C(\infty , \infty ): The Axiom of Choice: Every set of non-empty sets has a choice function.
[1 A] In every vector space, every generating set contains a basis. Halpern [1966].
[1 B] Every commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Hodges [1979].

[1C] For all infinite cardinals m,\,UT(m, m, m): If every member of an infinite set A has power |A| then |\bigcup A|=|A|. (Note that [1 C] implies m^{2}=m for all infinite cardinals m.) Howard [1994].
[1 D] Cardinal successors 3: For every cardinal m there is a cardinal n such that m<n and (\forall p)(m<p\rightarrow n\leq p). Tarski [1954a] and Jech [1966a].
[1 E] K(0): For every set S there is an ordinal \alpha and a one to one function f:S\rightarrow \alpha . (See form 81(n)).

[1 F] For all ordinals \alpha ,\,DC(\aleph _{\alpha }): Given a relation R such that for every subset Y of a set X with |Y|<\aleph _{\alpha }, there is an x\in X with Y\ R\,x, then there is a function f:\aleph _{\alpha }\rightarrow X such that \forall \beta <\aleph _{\alpha },\, \{f(\gamma ):\gamma <\beta \}\,R\,f(\beta ).) Levy [1964] and note 133.
[1 G] Form 163 + form 8. Brunner [1982a] and note 94.
[1 H] Form 164 + form 67. Brunner [1982a] and note 94.
[1 I] In every metric space (X,\,d) there is an \epsilon -lattice for some \epsilon >0 which is not a strict upper bound of d. Brunner [1984e] and note 17.
[1 J] Form 49 + form 51. Morris [1969] and note 121.
[1 K] Form 133 + form 64. Clear

[1 L] Hajnal’s Free Set Principle: For every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{<\lambda } where \lambda is a well orderable cardinal and \lambda <|X| there is a free set of cardinality |X|.\, ([X]^{<\lambda } is the set of subsets of X of cardinality <\lambda . Brunner [1989] and note 22.

[1 M] The ramification Lemma: If S:X^{\leq \theta }\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E) is a ramification system, then for each g\in E there is an f which is maximal (with respect to inclusion) in \{h\in X^{\leq \theta }:g\in S(h)\}. Brunner [1989] and note 22.

[1 N] For every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{WO} (well ordered subsets of X) there is a co-well-orderable free subset H. (H is co-well-orderable if X\,\backslash \, H is well orderable). Brunner [1989] and note 22.

[1 O] A(D1, C): For every T_{2} topological space (X, T), if X is covered by a well ordered family of closed, discrete sets then each family U\subseteq T of pairwise disjoint sets is well ordered. Brunner [1983a] and note 26.
[1 P] A(P): (Depends on P for P\in \{W1, W2, B1, L1, L2, S, C, H1, A1\}) Every T_{2} topological space has property P. Brunner [1983a] and note 26.
[1 Q] For any partial order (X, \leq ) there is a sup function on the bounded (above), well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988] and note 38.
[1 R] For any partial order (X, \leq ) there is a sup function on the bounded subsets of X. Manka [1988] and note 38.
[1 S] For any partial order (X, \leq ) if every well ordered subset of X is bounded then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988] and note 38.
[1 T] For every directed partial order (X,\, \leq ) there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988] and note 38.
[1 U] For every directed partial order, if every well ordered subset of X is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988] and note 38.

[1 V] For every partially ordered set (X, \leq ), if every well ordered subset is bounded above then every function f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988] and Abian [1980].
[1 W] Form 133 + form 88. Brunner [1982a].
[1 X] Form 15 + form 91. Brunner [1982a].

[1 Y] Refined Dual Cantor-Bernstein Theorem: If f:X\rightarrow Y and g:Y\rightarrow X are onto then there is a bijection h:X\rightarrow Y such that h\subseteq f \cup g^{-1}. Banaschewski/Moore [1990].
[1 Z] If (P, \leq ) is a quasi-order and P\neq \emptyset and every antichain is finite, then there is a P generic filter which is well orderable. Shannon [1990] and note 47.
[1 AA] Assume f:S\rightarrow R where f is surjective and R\subseteq S. Then every mapping g of S into R has the form g=f\circ h for some h:S\rightarrow S. Smith [1982].

[1 AB] Assume f:S\rightarrow R where f is surjective and R\subseteq S. Then the mappings of S onto R are precisely the mappings of the form f\circ h where h:S\rightarrow S and (\forall y\in R)(\exists x\in S)(h(x)\in f^{-1}(\{y\})). Smith [1982].

[1 AC] Assume f:S\rightarrow R where R\subseteq S. Then the retractions of S onto R (that is, the mappings g : S\rightarrow R which are the identity on R) are precisely the mappings f\circ h where h:S\rightarrow S and (\forall y\in R)(h(y)\in f^{-1}(\{y\})). Smith [1982].

[1 AD] For every class K of similar algebras SP^{g}K \supseteq P^{g}S\,K. (For any class K of similar algebras, S\,K is the class of all subalgebras of elements of K (not closed under isomorphism) and P^{g}K is the class of direct products of elements of K not closed under isomorphism). Andreka/Nemeti [1980].
[1 AE] There is a set S such that SVC holds with S and such that \mathcal{P}(S)-\{\emptyset \} has a choice function. Blass [1979] and note 59. Also see form 191.
[1 AF] Form 191 + form 8 + form 193. Blass [1979] and note 60.
[1 AG] Form 192 + form 191. Blass [1979] and note 60.
[1 AH] E(V, VI): For all infinite cardinals m,\,2m=m implies m^{2}=m. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[1 AI] E(VI, VII): For all infinite cardinals m,\,m^{2}=m implies there is an ordinal \alpha such that m=\aleph _{\alpha }. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.

[1 AJ] Let \mathcal{F} be a family of mappings of a poset (X, \leq ) into itself such that \forall f\in \mathcal{F},\,\forall x\in X,\,f(x)\leq x. If for some element e of X each chain in X containing e has a lower bound, then the family \mathcal{F} has a common fixed point. Kasahara [1976].
[1 AK] There is an ordinal \beta such that for all cardinals x,\,\alpha (x+\aleph (x), x\cdot \aleph (x))< \beta . Truss [1973b] and note 98.
[1 AL] There is an ordinal \beta such that for all cardinals x,\,\alpha (x, x^{2})<\beta . Truss [1973b] and note 98.

[1 AM] There is an ordinal \beta such that for no cardinal x is there a strictly increasing sequence of cardinals \{y_{\gamma }:\gamma <\beta \} such that y_{\gamma }^{2}=x. Truss [1973b] and note 98.

[1 AN] Every lattice (L, \cap ,\,\cup , \subseteq \rangle of sets (that is, L is a family of sets and \cap ,\,\cup and \subseteq are the usual operations) with a greatest element has a maximal, proper ideal. Bell/Fremlin [1972a].
[1 AO] Any continuous surjection between compact spaces, where the range space is Hausdorff, has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell [1988] and note 114.
[1 AP] For any type \tau of the form \tau =(M), every homomorphism of an algebra of type \tau is closed. Diener [1989] and note 115.
[1 AQ] For any type \tau of the form \tau =(M), every homomorphism of an algebra A of type \tau into an algebra B of type \tau maps A onto a subalgebra of B. Diener [1989] and note 105.

[1 AR] Let S be any family of disjoint non-empty sets and let \tau =(\bigcup S), then any homomorphism from \mathfrak{P}(\tau ;\bigcup S) into \mathfrak{P}(\tau ;S) maps \mathfrak{P}(\tau ;\bigcup S) onto a subalgebra of \mathfrak{P}(\tau ;S). Diener [1989] and note 115.
[1 AS] Turinici’s Fixed Point Theorem: If (X, \leq ) is a directed, partially ordered set and \tau is a topology on X such that
(a) (X, \leq ) is upper semicontinuous with respect to \tau ,
(b) Every well ordered subset of (X, \leq ) is convergent as a net, then every function f:X\rightarrow X such that \forall x\in X,\,x\leq f(x) has a fixed point. Manka [1988] and note 38.

[1 AT] For all cardinal numbers \kappa _{1} and \kappa _{2}, if a graph is both \kappa _{1} and \kappa _{2} colorable then it is also \kappa colorable for some \kappa such that \kappa \leq ^{\ast }\kappa _{1} and \kappa \leq ^{\ast }\kappa _{2}. (\leq ^{\ast } is the surjective cardinal ordering). Galvin/Komjáth [1991] and note 118.
[1 AU] Every graph has an irreducible, good coloring. Galvin/Komjáth [1991] and note 118.
[1 AV] Every graph of the form G(A, H(A)) has an irreducible, good coloring. (H is the Hartogs aleph function.) Galvin/Komjáth [1991] and note 118.
[1 AW] Every graph has a chromatic number. Galvin/Komjáth [1991] and note 118.
[1 AX] Birkhoff Representation Theorem: Every algebra is isomorphic to a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible algebras. Birkhoff [1944], Grätzer [1979] and [1986].

[1 AY] For each \lambda \in \Lambda let S_{\lambda } be a subset of some topological space X_{\lambda }. Then \mathrm{cl}(\prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }S_{\lambda })=\prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }\mathrm{cl}\,(S_{\lambda }), where the first “cl” is closure in the product topology and the second “cl” is closure in X_{\lambda }. Schechter [1992].

[1 AZ] For each \lambda \in \Lambda , let X_{\lambda } be a complete uniform space. Then, the product \prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }X_{\lambda } equipped with the product uniform structure, is also complete. (See, for example, Kelley [1955] pp 176ff for definitions.) Schechter [1992].
[1 BA] (Depends on the prime p) Every group has a maximal p-subgroup. Howard/Yorke [1987] and note 24.

[1 BB] Strong Nielsen-Schreier Theorem II: If G is a group which is freely generated by X and U is a subgroup of G, then there is a subset A of G which freely generates U and is level with respect to X. Howard [1985] and note 129.

[1 BC] Assume P is a partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound and f:P\rightarrow P satisfies \forall x\in f(P)\cup \{a\in P:a is an upper bound for some chain in f(P)\},\, x\leq f(f(x)). Then f has a fixed apex u (that is, there is some v\in P such that f(u)=v and f(v)=u.). Tasković [1988], [1992].

[1 BD] Let P be a partially ordered set in which every increasing sequence has an upper bound and f:P\rightarrow P satisfies x\leq f(f(x)) for all x\in f(P)\cup \{x\in P:x is an upper bound for some increasing sequence in f(P)\}. Then f has a fixed apex u (that is, \exists v\in P, such that f(u)=v and f(v)=u). (For purposes of [1 BD], “sequence” means a function whose domain is an ordinal.) Tasković [1992].
[1 BE] Every unique factorization domain can be mapped homomorphically onto a non-zero subdirectly irreducible ring. Rav [1988], Grätzer [1979] pp 122-124 and note 84.

[1 BF] (\mathrm{D}T_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is dense in X. (Y is dense in X if there is no non-empty open subset O\subseteq X such that O\cap Y=\emptyset .) McCarten [1988] and note 106.

[1 BG] (\mathrm{C}T_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is codense in X. (Y is codense in X if there is no non-empty closed subset C\subseteq X such that C\cap Y=\emptyset .) McCarten [1988] and note 106.

[1 BH] (\mathrm{T}T_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is thick in X. (Y is thick in X if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset H\subseteq X such that H\cap Y=\emptyset .) McCarten [1988] and note 106.
[1 BI] (\mathrm{M}T_{0}): Every topological space has a maximal T_{0} subspace. Schnare [1968] and note 106.
[1 BJ] In every vector space over the two element field, every generating set contains a basis. Keremedis [1996a].

[1 BK] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is pairwise disjoint. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997].
[1 BL] Every family of closed sets in a T_{2} topological space includes a maximal subfamily with the finite intersection property. Keremedis [1996b] and H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], p 60, M14.

[1 BM] For every family \{(X_{i}, T_{i}):i\in k\} of T_{1} topological spaces, the box topology contains an element \prod _{i\in k}O_{i}, such that \emptyset \neq O_{i} and O_{i}\neq X_{i} for all i\in k. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BN] For every family \{(X_{i}, T_{i}):i\in k\} of disjoint T_{1} topological spaces, the free union contains an open set O such that \emptyset \neq O\cap X_{i} and O\cap X_{i}\neq X_{i} for all i\in k. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.
[1 BO] For every T_{1} topological space (X, T) and every base (subbase) B for X there exists a \subseteq -maximal cellular family Q\subseteq B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.
[1 BP] For every dense in itself topological space (X, T) and every base B for X there exists a nest N included in B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.
[1 BQ] For every dense in itself topological space (X, T) and every base B for X there exists a tower R included in B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BR] For every T_{2} space (X, T) and every subbase \mathcal{B} for X, if \mathcal{C} and \mathcal{D} are cellular families of X included in \mathcal{B}, then there is a cellular family \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{B} such that \mathcal{C} and \mathcal{D} are equipollent to subsets of \mathcal{E}. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.
[1 BS] For every Abelian group (G, +), for every H\subseteq G, the infinite system of equations
has a solution in H iff each of its equations has a solution in H. Keremedis [1996].
[1 BT] For every Boolean ring (B, +, \cdot ) and every H\subseteq B which is closed under + there exists a \subseteq -maximal ideal Q\subseteq B such that H\cap Q=\{0\}. Keremedis [1996].
[1 BU] In every vector space over \mathbb{Q}, every generating set includes a basis. Blass [1984a] and note 137.

[1 BV] If (X, T) is a T_{4} topological space and G=\{G_{i}:i\in K\},\,|G_{i}|\geq 2, is a locally finite family of compact sets with non-empty pairwise disjoint interiors, then there is a continuous real valued function f on X which assumes at least two distinct values on each G_{i}. Keremedis [1995] and note 43.

[1 BW] If (X, T) is a T_{4} topological space and U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\},\,|U_{i}|\geq 2, is a locally finite family of open non-empty pairwise disjoint sets, then there is a continuous real valued function f on X which assumes at least two distinct values on each U_{i}. Keremedis [1995] and note 43.
[1 BX] For every Abelian group G and every subgroup H of G there exists a set of representatives for the quotient G/H. Keremedis [1996].

[1 BY] If x is a set of sets of cardinality at least 2, then there exists a function f such that for each u\in x,\,f(u) is a finite, non-empty, proper subset of u. (Form [1 BY] implies [62 E] (KW(\infty , <\aleph _{0})) and 67 (MC) and 62+67\rightarrow \mathrm{AC}.) Blass [1979].

[1 BZ] Vector Space Multiple Choice: For every family V=\{V_{i}:i\in K\} of non-trivial vector spaces there is a family F=\{F_{i}:i\in K\} such that for each i\in K,\,F_{i} is a non-empty, finite, independent subset of V_{i}. Note 127.

[1 CA] Strong Nielsen-Schreier Theorem I: If G is a group which is freely generated by X and U is a subgroup of G, then there is a subset A of G which freely generates U and has the Nielsen property with respect to X. Howard [1985] and note 129.

[1 CB] For every infinite cardinal \kappa , if (X, T) is a T_{2} space having a base B such that no Q\subseteq B,\,|Q|<\kappa , is a tower, then for every family \mathcal{D}=\{D_{i}:i\in \kappa \} of dense open sets of X there is a filter F\subseteq T such that for every i\in \kappa there is a b\in F with b\subseteq D_{i}. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 CC] PC(\aleph _{0}, \mathrm{odd}, \infty )\, +\,MC_{\omega ^{+}}. PC(\aleph _{0}, \mathrm{odd}, \infty ) is “Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.” and MC_{\omega ^{+}} is “For every natural number n\geq 1 and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function f such that for each u\in x,\,f(u) is a non-empty finite subset of u such that |f(u)| and n are relatively prime.” Note 133.
[1 CD] In a commutative ring, every proper ideal can be extended to a maximal ideal. Krull [1929]. ([1 CD] implies [1 B]).

[1 CE] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is discrete. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[1 CF] If a topological space is cwH, then it is cwH(B) for every basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.
[1 CG] The disjoint union of cwH spaces is cwH(B) for every basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.
[1 CH] If a topological space is cwN, then it is cwH(B) for any basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.
FORM 2. Existence of successor cardinals: For every cardinal m there is a cardinal n such that m<n and (\forall p<n)(p\leq m). Tarski [1954a].
FORM 3. 2m=m: For all infinite cardinals m,\,2m=m. Tarski [1954a].
[3 A] For all cardinals m and n,\,n\leq m and m infinite \rightarrow m+n=m. Halpern/Howard [1970].
[3 B] \aleph _{0}\cdot m=m: For all infinite cardinals m,\,\aleph _{0}\cdot m=m. Halpern/Howard [1970].

[3 C] Definability of cardinal addition as the least upper bound: (For all cardinals x,\,y and z) (x+y=z iff (x\leq z and y\leq z and (\forall u)(x, y\leq u\rightarrow z\leq u)). Häussler [1983] and Tarski [1949a].

[3 D] Every pair of cardinals has a least upper bound in the usual cardinal ordering and for all cardinals \kappa and \gamma , if n\kappa \leq \gamma for all n\in \omega , then \aleph _{0}\kappa \leq \gamma . Hickman [1979b].
[3 E] E(IV, V): For all infinite cardinals m,\,m+1=m implies 2m=m. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[3 F] E(III, V): For every set X, if \mathcal{P}(X) is Dedekind infinite then 2|X|=|X|. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[3 G] E(II, V): For every set X, if there is a non-empty family of subsets of X which is linearly ordered by \subseteq and has no maximal element then 2|X|=|X|. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[3 H] E(Ia, V): For every set X, if 2|X|>|X| then X is amorphous. Howard/Yorke [1989], notes 85(H) and 94.
FORM 4. Every infinite set is the union of some disjoint family of denumerable subsets. (Denumerable means \cong \aleph _{0}.) Whitehead [1902].
FORM 5. C(\aleph _{0}, \aleph _{0}, \mathbb{R}): Every denumerable set of non-empty denumerable subsets of \mathbb{R} has a choice function. Sageev [1975].
FORM 6. UT(\aleph _{0}, \aleph _{0}, \aleph _{0}, \mathbb{R}): The union of a denumerable family of denumerable subsets of \mathbb{R} is denumerable. G. Moore [1982] and note 3.
[6 A] Every uncountable subset of \mathbb{R} contains a condensation point. G. Moore [1982] p 205 and 324, Sierpiński [1918].
[6 B] Every uncountable subset of \mathbb{R} has two condensation points. G. Moore [1982] p 205 and 324, Sierpiński [1918].
FORM 7. There is no infinite decreasing sequence of cardinals. Schoenflies [1908].
FORM 8. C(\aleph _{0}, \infty ): Every denumerable family of non-empty sets has a choice function. Sierpiński [1918].
[8 A] PC(\infty , \infty , \infty ): Every infinite family of non-empty sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner [1983a].
[8 B] PC(\aleph _{0}, \infty , \infty ): Every denumerable family of non-empty sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Monro [1975].
[8 C] Every \sigma -compact space is Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.
[8 D] Every \sigma -compact, locally compact T_{2} space is weakly Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.
[8 E] In a metric space every sequentially continuous real valued function is continuous. Brunner [1982c].

[8 F] Martin’s Axiom (\aleph _{0}): Whenever (P\leq ) is a non-empty, ccc quasi-order (ccc means every anti-chain is countable) and \mathcal{D} is a family of \leq \aleph _{0} dense subsets of P, then there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter G in P. Kunen [1980], Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[8 G] Let R be a relation and R^{\ast }, the transitive closure of R. (x\,R^{\ast }\,y iff there exists a finite ascending R-chain connecting x to y.) If every ascending R-chain is finite, then every ascending R^{\ast }-chain is finite. Diener [1994].
[8 H] A disjoint union of a countable set of compact T_{2} spaces is Lindelöf. Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 I] A disjoint union of a countable set of Lindelöf T_{2} spaces is Lindelöf. Keremedis [1996] and note 132.

[8 J] Hemicompact T_{2} spaces are Lindelöf. (A hemicompact space is a space (X, T) that can be written as a disjoint union \bigcup \{K_{n}:n\in \omega \} such that (i) each K_{n} is a compact set in X; (ii) K_{N}\subseteq K_{n+1} for all n\in \omega ; and (iii) for every compact set K in X, there is an n\in \omega such that K\subseteq K_{n}.) Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 K] Hemilindelöf T_{2} spaces are Lindelöf. (In [8 J], in the definition of hemicompact replace “compact” by “Lindelöf” to get the definition of hemilindelöf.) Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 L] Every second countable topological space is separable. Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 M] Form 131+ form 32. Keremedis [1996] and note 132.

[8 N] DP: If (X, T) is a topological space having a countable \pi -base, then for every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open sets of X, there is a countable dense set S\subseteq X such that for all i\in \omega and for all but finitely many s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}. Keremedis [1996] and note 132.

[8 O] DUCCC + form 131. DUCCC is “If X is a denumerable family of disjoint topological spaces each having the ccc property, then the disjoint union of the spaces in X has the ccc property.” (Y has the ccc property if every collection of disjoint open sets is countable.) Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 P] DUSS + form 131. DUSS is “The disjoint union of a denumerable family of separable topological spaces is separable.” Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 Q] DUSC + form 131. DUSC is “The disjoint union of a denumerable family of second countable topological spaces is second countable.” Keremedis [1996] and note 132.
[8 R] SCDUL + form 131. SCDUL is “The denumerable disjoint union of second countable spaces is Lindelöf.” Keremedis [1996] and note 132.

[8 S] PC(WO, \infty , \infty ): Every infinite well ordered set of non-empty sets has an infinite subset with a choice function. ([8\ \mathrm{A}]\rightarrow [8\ \mathrm{S}]\rightarrow [8\ \mathrm{B}])

[8 T] PUT(\aleph _{0}, \infty , \aleph _{0}): The union of a denumerable set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets has a denumerable subset. ([8\ \mathrm{A}]\rightarrow [8\ \mathrm{T}]\rightarrow [8\ \mathrm{B}])
[8 U] PUT(WO, \infty , WO): The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets has an infinite well ordered subset. ([8\ \mathrm{U}]\leftrightarrow [8\ \mathrm{T}])
FORM 9. Finite \Leftrightarrow Dedekind finite: W_{\aleph _{0}} (Jech [1973b]): E(I, IV) (Howard/Yorke [1989]): Every Dedekind finite set is finite. Dedekind [1888] and note 94.
[9 A] For all infinite x, if x is Dedekind finite, then \mathcal{P}(x) is is Dedekind finite). Notes 8 and 94.
[9 B] E(II, IV) (Howard/Yorke [1989]): (\forall x)(x is T-finite if and only if x is Dedekind finite). Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[9 C] The image of a Dedekind finite set is Dedekind finite. Jech [1973b] p 161 prob 11.2, notes 11 and 94.
[9 D] The union of a Dedekind finite family of finite sets is Dedekind finite. Jech [1973b] p 161 prob 11.4, notes 12 and 94.
[9 E] No Dedekind finite set can be mapped onto \aleph _{0}. (See form 160.) Monro [1975] and note 94.

[9 F] There is no subset A of the class of Dedekind finite cardinals such that A under the usual cardinal ordering is order isomorphic to \langle \mathbb{R},\,\leq \rangle . Tarski [1965], Jech [1973b] p 161 prob 6, and note 94.
[9 G] Every infinite set has a denumerable subset. Cantor [1895] and G. Moore [1982] p 9.
[9 H] If A is Dedekind finite and B is Dedekind infinite, then A\precsim B. G. Moore [1982] p 28 and note 94.
[9 I] If \emptyset \in K and for all A\in K and for all b\not \in A,\,A\, \cup \,\{b\}\in K, then every Dedekind finite set is in K. G. Moore [1982] p 28 and note 94.
[9 J] The union of a Dedekind infinite family of non-empty sets is Dedekind infinite. G. Moore [1982] p 130 and note 94.
[9 K] If A is uncountable and B is countable, then |A-B|=|A|. G. Moore [1982] p 201.
[9 L] If A is uncountable and B is countable, then |A\cup B|=|A|. G. Moore [1982] p 202.
[9 M] If \aleph _{0}<|A| and \aleph _{0}=|B|, then \aleph _{0}<|A-B|. G. Moore [1982] p 202.
[9 N] If \aleph _{0}\leq ^{\ast }m, then \aleph _{0}\leq m. Lindenbaum/Tarski [1926], G. Moore [1982] p 216, and note 69.
[9 O] m\leq \aleph _{0} or \aleph _{0}\leq m. Lindenbaum/Tarski [1926] and G. Moore [1982] p 216.
[9 P] If m+\aleph _{0}<n+\aleph _{0}, then m<n. Lindenbaum/Tarski [1926] and G. Moore [1982] p 216.
[9 Q] If m+\aleph _{0}=n+\aleph _{0}, then m=n or m,\,n\leq \aleph _{0}. Lindenbaum/Tarski [1926] and G. Moore [1982] p 216.
[9 R] E(III, IV): Every Dedekind finite set has a Dedekind finite power set. Howard/Yorke [1989] and note 94.
[9 S] E(Ia, IV): Every Dedekind finite set is amorphous. Howard/Yorke [1989], notes 57 and 94.
[9 T] Restricted Choice: For every infinite set X there is an infinite Y\subseteq X such that the collection of non-empty subsets of Y has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco [1996].
FORM 10. C(\aleph _{0}, <\aleph _{0}): Every denumerable family of non-empty finite sets has a choice function.
[10 A] UT(\aleph _{0}, <\aleph _{0}, \aleph _{0}): The union of denumerably many pairwise disjoint finite sets is denumerable. Shannon [1988] p 569.
[10 B] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countable Families of Finite T_{2} Spaces: The product of a countable family of finite T_{2} spaces is compact. Krom [1981].
[10 C] Every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{WO} on a Dedekind finite, infinite set X has arbitrarily large, finite free subsets. Brunner [1989], notes 22 and 94.
[10 D] In every Hilbert space with a Dedekind finite orthonormal basis, the closed unit ball is sequentially compact. Brunner [1983a] and note 94.
[10 E] PC(\aleph _{0}, <\aleph _{0}, \infty ): Every denumerable family of finite sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner [1983a].
[10 F] König’s Lemma: Every \omega tree has an infinite chain. Pincus [1972], note 21, and note 35.

[10 G] For all metric spaces X and Y and continuous functions f from X onto Y such that f^{-1}(y) is finite for all y\in Y, if X has a dense Dedekind finite subset, then so does Y. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[10 H] \sigma -compact, paracompact T_{2} spaces are weakly Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.

[10 I] Assume (P, \leq ) is a partial order such that P is a denumerable union of finite sets and contains a non-empty subset Q relative to which depths are defined for all x\in \mathrm{P}. If all Q-strong antichains of P are finite then for each denumerable family \mathcal{D} of dense sets there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter. Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[10 J] Let S be a denumerable set of propositional sentences over an infinite set of propositional letters (in a propositional language where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences). Then S has a model if and only if every finite subset of S has a model. Lolli [1977].

[10 K] Let S be a consistent denumerable set of sentences in a first order language (where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences). Then S has a model. Note 19.

[10 L] Let S be a denumerable set of sentences in a first order language (where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences) such that every finite subset has a model. Then S has a model. Note 19.
[10 M] PUT(\aleph _{0}, <\aleph _{0}, \aleph _{0}): The union of denumerably many pairwise disjoint finite sets has a denumerable subset.
[10 N] PUT(WO, <\aleph _{0}, WO): The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint finite sets has an infinite well ordered subset.
[10 O] PC(WO, <\aleph _{0}, \infty ): Every infinite well ordered family of finite sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.
FORM 11. \mathbb{R} is hereditarily Lindelöf. Lindelöf [1905].
FORM 12. \mathbb{R} is Lindelöf. Young [1903].
FORM 13. Every Dedekind finite subset of \mathbb{R} is finite. G. Moore [1982] and note 94.
[13 A] \mathbb{R} has no dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[13 B] There is a separable topological space X and a set A\subseteq \mathbb{R} such that X^{A\times \omega } has no dense, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
FORM 14. BPI: Every Boolean algebra has a prime ideal. M. Stone [1936].
[14 A] Ultrafilter Theorem: Every proper filter over a set S (in \mathcal{P}(S)) can be extended to an ultrafilter. Jech [1973b] p 17.
[14 B] Stone Representation Theorem: Every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to a set algebra. Jech [1973b] p 27 prob 2.12 and M. Stone [1936].
[14 C] Every commutative ring with unit has a prime ideal. Scott [1954].

[14 D] Every ring with unit has a (two sided) prime ideal. (An ideal P in a ring R is prime if P\neq R and for any ideals A and B in R, if AB\subseteq P then A\subseteq P or B\subseteq P.) Blass [1986] and Banaschewski [1985].

[14 E] Almost Maximal Ideal Theorem: Every bounded, non-trivial, distributive lattice has an almost maximal ideal. (Definitions: If D is a bounded non-trivial distributive lattice, I(D) is the lattice of ideals of D. An almost maximal ideal in D is an ideal P of D such that s(P)=P where s is the operation on I(D) defined as follows: If e is the unit of I(D), (i) For a\in I(D) we say x\in I(D) is a-small if x\vee b=e implies a\vee b=e for all b\in I(D). (ii) For any a\in I(D), s(a) is the join of all a-small elements of I(D)). Banaschewski/Harting [1985] and Blass [1986].
[14 F] Every non-trivial complete distributive lattice with compact unit has a prime ideal. Banaschewski [1985] and note 29.
[14 G(n)] (n\in \omega , n\geq 3)\,P_{n}: For every graph G if every finite subgraph of G is n-colorable then G is n-colorable. Läuchli [1971] and note 117.

[14 H] Compactness Theorem for First Order Logic: If \Sigma is a set of formulas in a first order language such that every finite subset of \Sigma has a model then \Sigma has a model. Henkin [1954a] and Jech [1973b] p 17.
[14 I] Consistency Principle: For every binary mess M on a set S there is a function f on S which is consistent with M. Jech [1973b] p 17 and note 109.

[14 J] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: The product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact. (For many compactness theorems T, it is clear that [14 J] implies T implies [14 K].) Łoś/Ryll-Nardzewski [1954] and Rubin/Scott [1954].

[14 K] Compactness of the Generalized Cantor Space: \{0,1\}^{I} is compact for any I. (For many compactness theorems T, it is clear that [14 J] implies T implies [14 K].) Jech [1973b] p 28, prob 17 and Mycielski [1964].

[14 L] Stone-Čech Compactification Theorem: For every topological space X there is a pair (Y, j) such that Y is a compact topological space and j is a continuous surjection from X onto Y such that for all topological spaces Z such that Z is compact and completely regular and for all continuous f:X\rightarrow Z, there is a unique continuous h:Y\rightarrow Z such that f=h\circ j. Rubin/Scott [1954] and note 71.

[14 M] R. Cowen’s Generalization of Konig’s Lemma: Let T be a collection of locally finite trees such that for any finite set of levels of T, there is a consistent set of vertices piercing those levels. Then there is a consistent set of vertices piercing the entire set of levels of T. Cowen [1977b] and note 21.
[14 N(n)] (n\in \omega ,\,n\geq 2) [14 M] restricted to families of trees where no tree in the family has a vertex with more than n successors. Cowen [1977b], Howard [1984a], and note 21.

[14 O] Let \{A(i):i\in I\} be a collection of finite sets and R a symmetric binary relation on \bigcup _{i\in I}A(i). Suppose that for every finite W\subseteq I, there is an R-consistent choice function for \{A(i):i\in W\}. Then there is an R-consistent choice function for \{A(i):i\in I\}. Łoś/Ryll-Nardzewski [1951] and note 109.
[14 P(n)] (For n\geq 3) [14 O] restricted to \{A(i):i\in I\} such that for all i\in I,\,|A(i)|\leq n. Cowen [1977b] and note 109. (For n=2 see form 141.)
[14 Q] Alaoglu’s Theorem: The unit ball is compact in the weak^{\ast } topology in the dual of a Banach space. (See [52 E].) Johnstone [1984] and note 23.
[14 R] Every coherent local lattice is spatial. Banaschewski [1981] and note 29.
[14 S] Every compact, regular local lattice is spatial. Banaschewski [1981] and note 29.
[14 T] Every regular commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Banaschewski [1983] and note 29.
[14 U] Every closed proper ideal in a Gelfand algebra is contained in some maximal ideal. Banaschewski [1983] and note 29.
[14 V] FIP Extension Principle: Let \mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{X} have the finite intersection property, then \mathcal{F}\subseteq U for some ultrafilter U on X. Schechter [1996a].
[14 W] Universal Subnet Theorem: Any net has a universal subnet. Schechter [1996a] and note 31.
[14 X] Cowen-Engler Lemma: Let \Lambda and X be sets. Let \Phi be a family of functions from subsets of \Lambda into X. Assume

def.p: \Phi (\lambda )=\{f(\lambda ):f\in \Phi and \lambda \in dom f\} is finite for each \lambda \in \Lambda ,
each finite S\subseteq \Lambda is the domain of at least one f\in \Phi , and
\Phi has finite character, (that is, a function f from a subset of \Lambda into X is in \Phi if and only if every finite subset of f is in \Phi ).

sec.p: Then at least one f\in \Phi has domain \Lambda . Schechter [1996a]. (See [14 I].)
[14 Y] Form 99 + Form 62. Note 33.

[14 Z] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Families of Finite Spaces: If \{X_{i}:i\in I\} is a family of finite topological spaces, then \prod _{i\in I}X_{i} is compact. (Cleary [14 Z] implies [14 K] and is implied by [14 J].) Jech [1973b] p 28 prob 17, A.A. Lewis [1983], and Wolk [1967].

[14 AA] Alexander’s Subbase Lemma: A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase S for the topology such that every cover by elements of S has a finite subcover. Kelley [1955] p 143, A.A. Lewis [1983], Wolk [1967], and note 34.
[14 AB] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Sober Spaces: A product of compact, sober topological spaces is compact. Blass [1986], Johnstone [1984] and note 37.

[14 AC] (Depends on k, n\in \omega with k\geq 2,\,n\geq 2 and n+k\geq 5.) P(k, n): If X is a set and P is a property of subsets of X of n character (that is, \forall y\subseteq X(P(y) iff \forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq n\rightarrow P(z)))), then if every finite subset of X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets (that is, sets z such that P(z)), then X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets. Cowen [1982].

[14 AD] (Depends on k\in \omega , k\geq 2)\ P(k): If X is a set and P is a property of subsets of X of finite character (that is, \forall y\subseteq X(P(y) iff \forall z\subseteq y(z finite \rightarrow P(z)))), then if every finite subset of X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets (that is, sets z such that P(z)), then X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets. Cowen [1982].
[14 AE] For any distributive lattice D with zero and unit, any ideal J\subseteq D and a\not \in J, there is a prime filter F such that a\in F and F\cap J=\emptyset . Banaschewski [1981].

[14 AF] Disjoint Transversal axiom (2,3): If X is a set, \mathcal{U} is a subset of \{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 2\} and \mathcal{V} is a subset of \{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 3\} and if for each two finite subsets \mathcal{U}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{V} there are transversals Y_{1} and Y_{2} for \mathcal{U}_{0} and \mathcal{V}_{0} respectively such that Y_{1}\cap Y_{2}=\emptyset , then there are disjoint transversals X_{1} and X_{2} for \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V} respectively. (Y\subseteq X is a transversal for \mathcal{U} if for all y\in \mathcal{U},\, y\cap Y\neq (\emptyset .) Schrijver [1978].

[14 AG] Topological Rado Lemma: Let \{T_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of compact Hausdorff spaces and suppose for each finite F\subseteq I, there is a set \Phi (F) of partial choice functions on I whose domains include F and such that (a) F_{1}\subseteq F_{2} implies \Phi (F_{2})\subseteq \Phi (F_{1}) and (b) the set \{\phi |F:\phi \in \Phi (F)\} is closed in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in F\} in the product topology. Then there is a choice function f on I satisfying for any finite F\subseteq I,\,\exists \phi \in \Phi (F) such that f and \phi coincide on F. Rav [1977].

[14 AH] Principle of Consistent Choices: Let \{T_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of compact Hausdorf spaces and suppose R is a symmetric binary relation defined for all pairs of elements belonging to distinct T_{i} and such that for all i
eq j in I, the set E(i, j)=\{(x, y):x\ R\ y and x\in T_{i} and y\in T_{j}\} is closed in T_{i}	imes T_{j}. Furthermore suppose that for every finite subset F\subseteq I, with at least two elements, \exists \phi \in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in F\} such that \phi (i)\ R\ \phi (j) for all i
eq j in F. Then \exists f\in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in I\} such that f(i)\ R\ f(j) for all i
eq j in I. Rav [1977].
[14 AI] Engelers Lemma: Let \mathcal{E} be a family of functions whose domains are subsets of a set S with range \subseteq \{0,1\} and such that

def.p: For every finite F\subseteq S,\,\exists \phi \in \mathcal{E} with domain F.
The restriction of any function in \mathcal{E} to any subset of its domain is in \mathcal{E}.
If \phi is any function with domain \phi \subseteq S such that the restriction of \phi to any finite subset of its domain is in \mathcal{E} then \phi \in \mathcal{E}.

sec.p: Then \exists f\in \mathcal{E} whose domain is S. Rav [1977].

[14 AJ] Robinson’s Valuation Lemma: Let \{\phi _{x}:x\in X\} be a family of partial valuations on a set S. (\phi is a partial valuation on S if the domain of \phi \subseteq S and the range of \phi \subseteq \{0,1\}.) Suppose \mathfrak{B} is a filter base on X such that for every finite F\subseteq S and for every B\in \mathfrak{B} there is x\in B such that F\subseteq dom \phi _{x}. Then there is a total valuation f on S (that is, dom f=S) such that for all finite F\subseteq S and all B\in \mathfrak{B},\,\exists x\in B such that F\subseteq dom \phi _{x} and f|F=\phi _{x}|F. (\mathfrak{B} is a filter base means \forall B_{1},\,B_{2}\in \mathfrak{B},\,\exists B_{3}\in \mathfrak{B} such that B_{3}\subseteq B_{1}\cap B_{2}.) Rav [1977] and Cowen [1973]. Compare with [14 I].

[14 AK] Let X be a set and \mathcal{D}=\{Y_{i}:i\in I\} a family of finite pairwise disjoint subsets of \mathcal{P}(X). Suppose for every finite subset \{a, b, \ldots , k\} of I,\,\exists s\in I such that Y_{s}\subseteq Y_{a}\wedge Y_{b}\wedge \ldots \wedge Y_{k} (If Y and Z are finite pairwise disjoint sets then Y\wedge Z= \{A \cap B:A\in Y and B\in Z and A \cap B\neq \emptyset \}.) Then there is a choice function \mu whose domain includes \mathcal{D} such that the family \{\mu (Y_{i}):i\in I\} (where \mu (Y_{i})\in Y_{i}) of subsets of X is closed under finite intersections. Rav [1977].

[14 AL] The radical of a proper ideal A in a commutative ring R with identity is the intersection of all prime ideals in R containing A. (The radical of A= \{x\in R: for some m\in \omega ,\, x^{m}\in A\}.) Rav [1977] and note 80.
[14 AM] Let A be a subring of a commutative ring R and p a prime ideal in A such that p=Rp\cap A. Then there is a prime ideal J in R such that p=J\cap A. Rav [1977] and note 80.
[14 AN] In every commutative ring with identity, every proper ideal is included in some prime ideal. Rav [1977].

[14 AO] Suppose R is a commutative ring, A is a proper ideal in R, and S is a multiplicative semigroup in R not meeting A. Then there is a prime ideal p in R such that A\subseteq p and p\cap S=\emptyset . Rav [1977] and note 80.

[14 AP] Suppose to each finite subset F of a set I there corresponds a set \Phi (F) of functions whose domains are subsets of I including F and such that (a) F_{1}\subseteq F_{2} implies \Phi (F_{2})\subseteq \Phi (F_{2}) and (b) \forall i\in I,\,\big \{\phi (i):\phi \in \bigcup \{\Phi (F):F finite and F\subseteq I\}\big \} is finite. Then there is a function f with domain I such that for all finite F\subseteq I,\,\exists \phi \in \Phi (F) such that \phi and f coincide on F. Rav [1977], Cowen [1973] and note 80.
[14 AQ] Strong Rado Lemma 1: Let T be a family of finite sets and let \mathcal{F} be a collection of finite subsets of T satisfying
(1) (\forall K\in T)(\exists S\in \mathcal{F})(K\in S)
(2) (\forall S_{1}, S_{2}\in \mathcal{F})(\exists S_{3}\in \mathcal{F})(S_{1}\cup S_{2}\subseteq S_{3})

Assume there is a function \phi with domain \mathcal{F} such that for each S\in \mathcal{F},\,\phi (S)= \phi _{S} is a function with domain S and satisfies (\forall K\in S)(\phi _{S}(K)\in K). Then there is a function f with domain T and with the following property: For all S\in \mathcal{F} there is an S^{\prime }\in \mathcal{F} such that S\subseteq S^{\prime } and f and \phi _{S^{\prime }} agree on S. Howard [1993].

[14 AR] Patching Lemma: Let L be a local system of S (that is, L\subseteq \mathcal{P}(S) and for each finite E\subseteq S, there exists H\in L such that E\subseteq H). Let F be a set and n a positive integer. Suppose that for each H\in L, there is a function f_{H}:H^{n}\rightarrow F and \{f_{H}(x):H\in L\} is finite for each x\in S^{n}. Then there is a function f:S^{n}\rightarrow F such that for any finite subset K\subseteq S^{n}, there is an H\in L with K\subseteq H^{n} and f and f_{H} agree on K. Hickin/Plotkin [1976] and note 83.

[14 AS] Let \mathfrak{A} and \mathfrak{B} be (universal) algebras of type r where \mathfrak{A} and \mathfrak{B} have underlying sets A and B respectively and B is finite. Suppose for every finite C\subseteq A there is a partial r homomorphism from \mathfrak{A} into \mathfrak{B} with domain C. Then there is an r homomorphism from \mathfrak{A} into \mathfrak{B} . van Benthem [1975].

[14 AT] Assume D and E are sets and for all d\in D,\,d is finite. Suppose that for every finite F\subseteq D, there is an S such that (\forall f\in F)(f\cap S\in E). Then there is an S such that (\forall d\in D)(d\cap S\in E). van Benthem [1975].

[14 AU] If Z is a real vector lattice with order unit 1 then the set of all positive linear functionals u on Z with u(1)=1 is a convex set that has an extreme point. See H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], pages 177 and 182 for definitions. Also see Gardiner [1974].
[14 AV] Every Boolean algebra has a 2-valued measure. Pincus [1972] and note 147.

[14 AW] The Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic: If \Sigma is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of \Sigma is satisfiable, then \Sigma is satisfiable. Henkin [1954b].

[14 AX] Structural Completeness Theorem for Propositional Logic: Assume At is a set of propositional variables and S is the set of propositional formulas generated by At. Assume X\subseteq S and a\in S satisfy the following: For any function e:At\rightarrow S if Cn(\{b[e]:b\in X\})\subseteq Cn(\emptyset ) then a[e]\in Cn(\emptyset ). Then a\in Cn(X). (Cn(Y) is the deductive closure of Y\ \cup all substitutions of axioms for the classical predicate calculus and for a\in S,\,a[e] is a with each propositional variable p replaced by e(p).) Pogorzelski/Prucnal [1974].

[14 AY] Let F be a class of partial functions on I of finite character such that (a) \{f(\nu ):f \in F\} is finite for each \nu \in I and (b) for each finite W \subseteq I, there exists f\in F with dom(f)=W. Then F contains a function with domain I. (F is of finite character means f\in F iff for all finite w\subseteq I, f|w\in F.) Cowen [1973].

[14 AZ] Let \Phi =\{\phi _{t}\}_{t\in T} be a set of partial valuations on a set S (that is, dom(\phi _{t})\subseteq S and range(\phi _{t})\subseteq \{0,1\}) such that for all finite U\subseteq S there is a t \in T for which U\subseteq dom(\phi _{t}). Then there is a valuation \Psi with dom(\Psi )=S and such that for every finite U\subseteq S, there is a t\in T with U\subseteq dom(\phi _{t}) and \Psi |U=\phi _{t}|U. Cowen [1973].

[14 BA] Monteiro’s Theorem for Complete Atomic Boolean Algebras: Let K be a complete atomic Boolean algebra, A a subalgebra of the Boolean algebra B and f a homomorphism from A to K. Let d be a semimorphism from B into K (that is, d:B\rightarrow K,\, d(0)=0,\,d(1)=1 and for all x,\,y\in B,\, d(x\vee y)=d(x)\vee d(y)\ ) with f(x)\leq d(x) for all x\in A. Then there is a homomorphism h from B to K such that h(x)\leq d(x) for all x\in B and h/A=f. Monteiro [1965] and Bacsich [1972a].

[14 BB] Fraïssé’s Theorem: Let \mathcal{E} be inductively ordered (that is, for any E,\,E^{\prime }\in \mathcal{E},\,\exists E^{\prime \prime }\in \mathcal{E} such that E\cup E^{\prime }\subseteq E^{\prime \prime }.) For any E\in \mathcal{E}, assume \mathcal{R}_{E} is a finite set of m-ary relations on E. If for any E,\,E^{\prime }\in \mathcal{E} with E\subseteq E^{\prime } we have \forall R\in \mathcal{R}_{E^{\prime }},\,R/E\in \mathcal{R}_{E} then there is an m-ary relation S on \bigcup \mathcal{E} such that S|E\in \mathcal{R}_{E} for any E\in \mathcal{E}. Bénéjam [1970]. See [14 Y].

[14 BC] If m_{0} is an additive, real valued measure on a subalgebra \mathcal{B}_{0} of a Boolean algebra \mathcal{B} then there exists a measure m on \mathcal{B} such that m=m_{0} on \mathcal{B}_{0} and the range of m is contained in the closure of the range of m_{0}. Tarski [1930] and note 147.
[14 BD] Let H be a hypergraph. If every finite subhypergraph has an independent vertex cover then H has an independent vertex cover. Cowen [1990] and note 117.
[14 BE] Let H be a hypergraph. If every finite subhypergraph is 2-colorable then H is 2-colorable. Cowen [1990] and note 117.

[14 BF] Let H be a hypergraph whose edges contain at most three vertices. If every finite subhypergraph of H has an independent vertex cover then H has an independent vertex cover. Cowen [1990] and note 117.
[14 BG] Let H be a hypergraph whose edges contain at most three vertices. If every finite subhypergraph of H is 2-colorable then H is 2-colorable. Cowen [1990] and note 117.
[14 BH] The sum of finite frames is a spatial frame. Paseka [1989] and note 29.
[14 BI] Every compact, conjunctive frame is spatial. Paseka [1989] and note 29.
[14 BJ] The sum of compact, regular frames is spatial. Paseka [1989] and note 29.
[14 BK] The sum of 4-element Boolean algebras is spatial. Paseka [1989] and note 29.
[14 BL] Every compact, 0 dimensional frame is spatial. Paseka [1989] and note 29.
[14 BM] A system of equations over a finite ring R has a solution in R if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in R. Abian [1972a] and note 30.
[14 BN] A system of equations over a finite field F has a solution in F if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in F. Cowen/Emerson [1995] and note 30.
[14 BO] A system of equations over a finite structure (A, +, \cdot ) has a solution in A, if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in A. note 30.
[14 BP] Every non-empty bounded distributive lattice has a prime ideal. Morillon [1988].
[14 BQ] Every proper ideal in a bounded distributive lattice is the intersection of the prime ideals containing it. Morillon [1988] and note 79. (Compare with [14 AE].)
[14 BR] Every \vee -compact non trivial lattice has a principal prime ideal. Morillon [1988], [1985] and note 71.
[14 BS] Every bounded distributive lattice has a prime ideal choice function. Morillon [1988], [1985] and note 71.

[14 BT] If (A_{i})_{i\in I} is a family of bounded, distributive, \vee -compact lattices and if (J_{i})_{i\in I} is a family such that for all i\in I,\,J_{i} is a proper ideal in A_{i} then there is a family (P_{i})_{i\in I} such that for all i\in I,\,P_{i} is a prime principal ideal in A_{i} containing J_{i}. Morillon [1985], [1988] and note 71.

[14 BU] If (A_{i})_{i\in I} is a family of distributive non trivial bounded lattices, then there is a family (f_{i})_{i\in I} such that each f_{i} is a prime ideal choice function on A_{i}. Morillon [1985], [1988] and note 71.
[14 BV] For every set E there is an effectively E-adequate ultrafilter. Morillon [1988], [1985] and note 71.
[14 BW] For every set E there is an ultrafilter choice function on E. Morillon [1985], [1988] and note 71.

[14 BX] If (E_{i})_{i\in I} is a family of sets and (F_{i})_{i\in I} is a family such that for each i,\,F_{i} is a filter in \mathcal{P}(E_{i}), then there is a family (U_{i})_{i\in I} such that for each i\in I,\,U_{i} is an ultrafilter in \mathcal{P}(E_{i}) containing F_{i}. Morillon [1985], [1988] and note 71.
[14 BY] For every topological space X, every proper ideal in the normed \mathbb{R}-algebra of continuous bounded functions from X into \mathbb{R} is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon [1988].
[14 BZ] Every proper ideal in a non-trivial normed \mathbb{R}-algebra or \mathbb{C}-algebra with identity is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon [1988].

[14 CA] If (A_{i})_{i\in I} is a family of non trivial commutative normed algebras with identity then there is a family (J_{i})_{i\in I} such that for each i\in I,\,J_{i} is a maximal ideal in A_{i}. Morillon [1988].

[14 CB] If X is a topological space and I is a proper ideal in the algebra of all bounded continuous functions from X to \mathbb{R} such that every function in I vanishes at at least one point of X then I is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon [1988].
[14 CC] A projective limit of compact topological spaces is compact. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[14 CD] A projective limit of a directed projective system of compact topological spaces is compact. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[14 CE] A projective limit of a directed projective system of compact nonempty topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[14 CF] A projective limit of a directed projective system of non-empty sets is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[14 CG] A projective limit of a directed projective system of finite sets is compact. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[14 CH] For every bounded, distributive lattice (A, \wedge , \vee ) in which 0 is \wedge -compact, for all a\in A,\,a\neq 0 and for all sequences (X_{n})_{n\in \omega } of subsets of A, there is a prime filter in A which contains a and respects each X_{n}. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[14 CI] 3-Sat: Restricted Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic II: If \Sigma is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of \Sigma is satisfiable and if every formula in \Sigma is a disjunction of at most three literals, then \Sigma is satisfiable. (A literal is a propositional variable or its negation.) Cowen [1990].
[14 CJ] The Completeness Theorem for Propositional Logic: Every consistent set of formulas is satisfiable. Henkin [1954a] and [1954b].
[14 CK] The Completeness Theorem for First Order Logic: Every consistent set of formulas is satisfiable. Henkin [1954a] and [1954b].
[14 CL] Gelfand Extreme Point Theorem: If A is a non-trivial Gelfand algebra then the closed unit ball in the dual of A has an extreme point e with e\neq 0. Morillon [1986], notes 23 and 29.

FORM 15. KW(\infty , \infty ) (KW), The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle: For every set M there is a function f such that for all A\in M, if |A|>1 then \emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A. (See form 81(n)). Kinna/Wagner [1955].
[15 A] K(1): (\forall M)(\exists \alpha an ordinal) (|M|=|A| for some A\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\alpha )). (See form 81(n).) Jech [1973b] p 53 prob 4.12 and Kinna/Wagner [1955].
[15 B] SDO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is a dense linear ordering of y. Pincus [1997].

[15 C] SUO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is an unbounded linear ordering of y. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].
[15 D] SDUO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is a dense unbounded linear ordering of y. Pincus [1997].
FORM 16. C(\aleph _{0}, \leq 2^{\aleph _{0}}): Every denumerable collection of non-empty sets each with power \leq 2^{\aleph _{0}} has a choice function. Sierpiński [1918].

FORM 17. Ramsey’s Theorem I: If A is an infinite set and the family of all 2 element subsets of A is partitioned into 2 sets X and Y, then there is an infinite subset B\subseteq A such that all 2 element subsets of B belong to X or all 2 element subsets of B belong to Y. (Also, see form 325.) Jech [1973b] p 164 prob 11.20 and Ramsey [1929].
FORM 18. PUT(\aleph _{0},2, \aleph _{0}): The union of a denumerable family of pairwise disjoint pairs has a denumerable subset. Brunner [1984f].
[18 A] PC(\aleph _{0},2, \infty ): Every denumerable set of pairs has an infinite subset with a choice function.
[18 B] The union of a denumerable family of pairs has a denumerable subset. Note 135.
[18 C] PC(WO, 2, \infty ): Every infinite well ordered set of pairs has an infinite subset with a choice function.
[18 D] PUT(WO, 2, WO): The union of an infinite well ordered family of pairwise disjoint pairs has an infinite well ordered subset. ([18D \leftrightarrow 18)
FORM 19. A real function is analytically representable if and only if it is in Baire’s classification. G. Moore [1982] (2.3.1).

FORM 20. If \{A_{x}:x\in S\} and \{B_{x}:x\in S\} are families of pairwise disjoint sets and |A_{x}|=|B_{x}| for all x\in S, then I\bigcup _{x\in S}A_{x}|=|\bigcup _{x\in S}B_{x}|. G. Moore [1982] (1.4.12 and 1.7.8).

FORM 21. If S is well ordered, \{A_{x}:x\in S\} and \{B_{x}:x\in S\} are families of pairwise disjoint sets, and |A_{x}|=|B_{x}| for all x\in S, then |\bigcup _{x\in S}A_{x}|=|\bigcup _{x\in S}B_{x}|. G. Moore [1982].

FORM 22. UT(2^{\aleph _{0}},2^{\aleph _{0}},2^{\aleph _{0}}): If every member of an infinite set of cardinality 2^{\aleph _{0}} has power 2^{\aleph _{0}}, then the union has power 2^{\aleph _{0}}. Borel [1898] and G. Moore [1982].

FORM 23. (\forall \alpha )(UT(\aleph _{\alpha }, \aleph _{\alpha }, \aleph _{\alpha })): For every ordinal \alpha , if A and every member of A has cardinality \aleph _{\alpha }, then |\bigcup A|=\aleph _{\alpha }. G. Moore [1982].
FORM 24. C(\aleph _{0},2^{(2^{\aleph _{0}})}): Every denumerable collection of non-empty sets each with power 2^{(2^{\aleph _{0}})} has a choice function. G. Moore [1982].
FORM 25. \aleph _{\beta +1} is regular for all ordinals \beta . Feferman/Levy [1963] and Gitik [1980].
FORM 26. UT(\aleph _{0},2^{\aleph _{0}},2^{\aleph _{0}}): The union of denumerably many sets each of power 2^{\aleph _{0}} has power 2^{\aleph _{0}}. Borel [1898].
