312. A subgroup of an amenable group is amenable. (G is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure \mu on \mathcal{P}(G) such that \mu (G)=1 and \forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu (gA)=\mu (A).) Wagon [1985].

313. \mathbb{Z} (the set of integers under addition) is amenable. (G is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure \mu on \mathcal{P}(G) such that \mu (G)=1 and \forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu (gA)=\mu (A).) Wagon [1985].

[370 A] Measured Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem: If \mathcal{B} is a Boolean algebra and there is a measure on \mathcal{B} then there is an ultrafilter on \mathcal{B}. Morillon [1989], [1990] and note 147.

sec.title: MISCELLANEOUS FORMS
sec.p: [\boldsymbol{0} T] If a set S is hereditarily countable (that is, every y\in TC(S) is countable) then the rank of S is <\omega _{2}. Jech [1982].

[\boldsymbol{0} AD] For all ordinals \beta , well ordered cardinals \gamma \geq 1 and all n\in \omega , there is a well ordered cardinal \kappa such that \kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{n}. Erdös/Rado [1952] and note 97.
[1 G] Form 163+ form 8. Brunner [1982a] and note 94.
[1 H] Form 164+ form 67. Brunner [1982a] and note 94.

[1 L] Hajrial’s Free Set Principle: For every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{<\lambda } where \lambda is a well orderable cardinal and \lambda <|X| there is a free set of cardinality |X|.\, ([X]^{<\lambda } is the set of subsets of X of cardinality <\lambda . Brunner [1989] and note 22.

[1 M] The ramification Lemma: If S:X^{\leq \theta }\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E) is a ramification system, then for each g\in E there is an f which is maximal (with respect to inclusion) in \{h\in X^{\leq \theta }:g\in S(h)\}. Brunner [1989] and note 22.

[1 N] For every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{WO} (well ordered subsets of X) there is a co-well-orderable free subset H. (H is co-well-orderable if X\backslash H is well orderable). Brunner [1989] and note 22.
[1 W] Form 133 + form 88. Brunner [1982a].
[1 X] Form 15 + form 91. Brunner [1982a].
[1 Y] Refined Dual Cantor-Bernstein Theorem: If f:X\rightarrow Y and g:Y\rightarrow X are onto then there is a bijection h:X\rightarrow Y such that h\subseteq f\cup g^{-1}. Banaschewski/Moore [1990].
[1 AA] Assume f:S\rightarrow R where f is surjective and R\subseteq S. Then every mapping g of S into R has the form g=f\circ h for some h:S\rightarrow S. Smith [1982].

[1 AB] Assume f:S\rightarrow R where f is surjective and R\subseteq S. Then the mappings of S onto R are precisely the mappings of the form f\circ h where h:S\rightarrow S and (\forall y\in R)(\exists x\in S)(h(x)\in f^{-1}(\{y\})). Smith [1982].

[1 AC] Assume f:S\rightarrow R where R\subseteq S. Then the retractions of S onto R (that is, the mappings g\,:\,S\rightarrow R which are the identity on R) are precisely the mappings f\circ h where h:S\rightarrow S and (\forall y\in R)(h(y)\in f^{-1}(\{y\})). Smith [1982].
[1 AE] There is a set S such that SVC holds with S and such that \mathcal{P}(S)-\{\emptyset \} has a choice function. Blass [1979] and note 59. Also see form 191.
[1 AF] Form 191 + form 8 + form 193. Blass [1979] and note 60.
[1 AG] Form 192 + form 191. Blass [1979] and note 60.
4. Every infinite set is the union of some disjoint family of denumerable subsets. (Denumerable means \cong \aleph _{0}.) Whitehead [1902].
[10 C] Every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{WO} on a Dedekind finite, infinite set X has arbitrarily large, finite free subsets. Brunner [1989], notes 22 and 94.
[14 I] Consistency Principle: For every binary mess M on a set S there is a function f on S which is consistent with M. Jech [1973b] p 17 and note 109.
[14 X] Cowen-Engler Lemma: Let \Lambda and X be sets. Let \Phi be a family of functions from subsets of \Lambda into X. Assume

def.p: \Phi (\lambda )=\{f(\lambda ): f\in \Phi \ \mathrm{and}\ \lambda \in \mathrm{dom}\ f\} is finite for each \lambda \in \Lambda ,
each finite S\subseteq \Lambda is the domain of at least one f\in \Phi , and
\Phi has finite character, (that is, a function f from a subset of \Lambda into X is in \Phi if and only if every finite subset of f is in \Phi ).

sec.p: Then at least one f\in \Phi has domain \Lambda . Schechter [1996a]. (See 14 I.)

[14 AC] (Depends on k,\,n\in \omega with k\geq 2,\,n\geq 2 and n+k\geq 5.) P(k,\,n): If X is a set and P is a property of subsets of X of n character (that is, \forall y\subseteq X(P(y) iff \forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq n\rightarrow P(z)))), then if every finite subset of X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets (that is, sets z such that P(z)) then X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets. Cowen [1982].

[14 AD] (Depends on k\in \omega ,\,k\geq 2) P(k): If X is a set and P is a property of subsets of X of finite character (that is, \forall y\subseteq X(P(y)\ \mathrm{iff}\ \forall z\subseteq y(z\ \mathrm{finite}\ \rightarrow P(z)))), then if every finite subset of X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets (that is, sets z such that P(z)), then X can be partitioned into k or fewer P-sets. Cowen [1982].

[14 AF] Disjoint Transversal axiom (2,3): If X is a set, \mathcal{U} is a subset of \{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 2\} and \mathcal{V} is a subset of \{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 3\} and if for each two finite subsets \mathcal{U}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{V} there are transversals Y_{1} and Y_{2} for \mathcal{U}_{0} and \mathcal{V}_{0} respectively such that Y_{1}\cap Y_{2}=\emptyset , then there are disjoint transversals X_{1} and X_{2} for \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V} respectively. (Y\subseteq X is a transversal for \mathcal{U} if for all y\in \mathcal{U},\, y\cap Y\neq \emptyset .) Schrijver [1978].

[14 AT] Assume D and E are sets and for all d\in D,\,d is finite. Suppose that for every finite F\subseteq D, there is an S such that (\forall f\in F)(f\cap \,S\in E). Then there is an S such that (\forall d\in D)(d\cap \,S\in E). van Benthem [1975].

[14 BB] Fraïssé’s Theorem: Let \mathcal{E} be inductively ordered (that is, for any E,\,E^{\prime }\in \mathcal{E},\,\exists E^{\prime \prime }\in \mathcal{E} such that E\cup E^{\prime }\subseteq E^{\prime \prime }.) For any E\in \mathcal{E}, assume \mathcal{R}_{E} is a finite set of m-ary relations on E. If for any E,\,E^{\prime }\in \mathcal{E} with E\subseteq E^{\prime } we have \forall R\in \mathcal{R}_{E^{\prime }},\,R/E\in \mathcal{R}_{E} then there is an m-ary relation S on \bigcup \mathcal{E} such that S|E\in \mathcal{R}_{E} for any E\in \mathcal{E}. Bénéjam [1970]. See [14 Y].
[14 CF] A projective limit of a directed projective system of non-empty sets is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

17. Ramsey’s Theorem I: If A is an infinite set and the family of all 2 element subsets of A is partitioned into 2 sets X and Y, then there is an infinite subset B\subseteq A such that all 2 element subsets of B belong to X or all 2 element subsets of B belong to Y. (Also, see form 325.) Jech [1973b] p 164 prob 11.20 and Ramsey [1929].
[34 A] \exists \alpha <\omega _{2} such that there are no hereditarily countable sets of rank \alpha . Jech [1982] and note 48.
[43 I] Form [106 A] + form 10. Blass [1979].
[43 P] The ultraproduct of a well founded structure by a countably complete ultrafilter is well founded. Spector [1980] and note 54.

[88 A] P(2,2): If X is a set and P is a property of subsets of X of 2 character (that is, \forall y\subseteq X(P(y)\ \mathrm{iff}\,\forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq 2\rightarrow P(z)))) then if every finite subset of X can be partitioned into two or fewer P-sets (that is, sets z such that P(z)) then X can be partitioned into two or fewer P-sets. Cowen [1982].
[126 F] Every denumerable family of sets having the sfip also has a pseudo-intersection. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.
[132 A] Every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{WO} (well orderable subsets of X) on a Dedekind finite, infinite set X has an infinite free subset. Brunner [1989]. notes 22 and 94.

137(k). Suppose k\in \omega -\{0\}. If f is a 1-1 map from k\times X into k\times Y then there are partitions X=\bigcup _{i<k}X_{i} and Y=\bigcup _{i<k}Y_{i} of X and Y such that f maps \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times X_{i})\ \mathrm{onto}\ \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times Y_{i}). Truss [1984].
[137 A(k)] For all X and Y\subseteq \mathbb{R} form 137(k) holds. Truss [1984]

138(k). Suppose k\in \omega . If f is a partial map from k\times Y onto k\times X (that is, the domain is a subset of k\times Y), then there are partitions X= \bigcup _{i<k}X_{i} and Y=\bigcup _{i<k}Y_{i} of X and Y such that f maps \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times Y_{i}) onto \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times X_{i}). Truss [1984].
[138 A(k)] For all standard X and Y, form 138(k) holds. Truss [1984]. This is equivalent to 138(k) in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

[140 A] (Form 137 with k=2): If f is a 1-1 map from 2\times X into 2\times Y then there are partitions X=X_{0}\cup X_{1} and Y=Y_{0}\cup Y_{1} of X and Y such that f maps (\{0\}\times X_{0})\cup (\{1\}\times X_{1}) onto (\{0\}\times Y_{0})\cup (\{1\}\times Y_{1}). Truss [1984].

152. D_{\aleph _{0}}: Every non-well-orderable set is the union of a pairwise disjoint, well orderable family of denumerable sets. Brunner/Howard [1992]. (See note 27 for D_{\kappa },\,\kappa a well ordered cardinal.)
172. For every infinite set S, if S is hereditarily countable (that is, every y\in TC(S) is countable) then |TC(S)|=\aleph _{0}. Jech [1982].
179(\epsilon ). Suppose \epsilon >0 is an ordinal. \forall x,\,x\in W(\epsilon ). David [1980] and note 25.
184. Existence of a double uniformization: For all X and Y, for all E\subseteq X\times Y, if there is an infinite cardinal \kappa satisfying:

def.p: \forall y_{0}\in Y,\,|\{(x,\,y_{0}):x\in X\}\cap E|=\kappa and
\forall x_{0}\in X,\,|\{(x_{0},\,y):y\in Y\}\cap E|=\kappa ,

sec.p: then \exists U\subseteq E such that for all (x,\,y)\in E,\,\exists !z\in X such that (z,\,y)\in U and \exists !z\in Y such that (x,\,z)\in U. (U is called a double uniformization of E.) Kaniewski/Rogers [1980].
191. SVC: There is a set S such that for every set a, there is an ordinal \alpha and a function from S\times \alpha onto a. Blass [1979].
192. EP sets: For every set A there is a projective set X and a function from X onto A. Blass [1979] and note 60.

[201 B] Disjoint Transversal axiom (2,2): If X is a set and \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V} are subsets of \{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 2\} and if for each two finite subsets \mathcal{U}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{V} there are transversals Y_{1} and Y_{2} for \mathcal{U}_{0} and \mathcal{V}_{0} respectively such that Y_{1}\cap Y_{2}=\emptyset , then there are disjoint transversals X_{1} and X_{2} for \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V} respectively (Y\subseteq X is a transversal for \mathcal{U} if for all y\in CalU,\, y\cap Y\neq \emptyset .) Schrijver [1978].
230. L^{1}=HOD. Szczepaniak [1977] and note 82.

234. There is a non-Ramsey set: There is a set A of infinite subsets of \omega such that for every infinite subset N of \omega ,\,N has a subset which is in A and a subset which is not in A. Prikry [1976] and Mathias [1968].
282. \omega {\not \rightarrow } (\omega )^{\omega }. Erdös/Rado [1952], Kleinberg/Seiferas [1973] and note 97.

309. The Banach-Tarski Paradox: There are three finite partitions \{P_{1},\,\ldots ,\,P_{n}\},\,\{Q_{1},\, \ldots ,\,Q_{r}\} and \{S_{1},\,\ldots ,\,S_{n},\,T_{1},\,\ldots ,\,T_{r}\} of B^{3}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|\leq 1\} such that P_{i} is congruent to S_{i} for 1\leq i\leq n and Q_{i} is congruent to T_{i} for 1\leq i\leq r. Banach/Tarski [1924].

325. Ramsey’s Theorem II: \forall n,\,m\in \omega , if A is an infinite set and the family of all m element subsets of A is partitioned into n sets S_{j},\,1\leq j\leq n, then there is an infinite subset B\subseteq A such that all m element subsets of B belong to the same S_{j}. (Also, see form 17.) Ramsey [1929].

sec.title: ORDERING PRINCIPLES INCLUDING PROPERTIES OF PARTIAL ORDERS
sec.p:
[ oldsymbol{0} Z] Suppose X and M are sets, F is a function from \mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset \} into M and G is a function on M such that  orall z\in \mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset \},\,G(F(z))\in \mathcal{P}(z)-\{\emptyset \}. Then there are unique W and R such that W\subseteq M,\,R\subseteq W	imes W and R is an irreflexive well ordering of W, the range of G|W is a partition of X, and  orall w\in W,\,w=F(X-\,( igcup \{G(
u )\,:
u \in W\,\mathrm{and}\,
u \,R\,w\})). Kruse [1974].
[\boldsymbol{0} AH] No infinite well orderable set is amorphous.
[1 J] Form 49 + form 51. Morris [1969] and note 121.
[1 K] Form 133 + form 64. Clear

[8 G] Let R be a relation and R^{\ast }, the transitive closure of R. (x\,R^{\ast }\,y iff there exists a finite ascending R-chain connecting x to y.) If every ascending R-chain is finite, then every ascending R^{\ast }-chain is finite. Diener [1994].
[15 B] SDO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is a dense linear ordering of y. Pincus [1997].

[15 C] SUO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is an unbounded linear ordering of y. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].
[15 D] SDUO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is a dense unbounded linear ordering of y. Pincus [1997].
30. Ordering Principle: Every set can be linearly ordered. Schröder [1988].
[30 A] If R is a partial ordering in which the set of predecessors of each element is linearly ordered, then there is a linear ordering extending R. Felgner [1969].

[30 B] ADO: Every infinite set differs finitely from a set with a dense linear ordering: for all infinite x, there is a y\subseteq x such that y has a dense linear ordering and x-y is finite. Pincus [1997].
[30 C] SADO: For every set F there is a function f with domain F such that for all x\in F,\, f(x)\subseteq x,\,f(x) has a dense linear ordering, and x-f(x) is finite, Pincus [1997].
[30 D] UO: There exists an unbounded linear ordering on every infinite set. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].
[30 E] ADUO: For all infinite x, there exists y\subseteq x such that y has a dense unbounded linear ordering and x-y is finite. Pincus [1997].
[30 F] SADUO: For every set F there is a function f with domain F such that for all x\in F,\, f(x)\subseteq x,\,f(x) has a dense unbounded linear ordering, and x-f(x) is finite. Pincus [1997].
49. Order Extension Principle: Every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering. Tarski [1924] p 78.
51. Cofinality Principle: Every linear ordering has a cofinal sub well ordering. Sierpiński [1918] p 117.
[51 A] For all linear orders (X,\,\leq ), there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.
[51 C] For every linearly ordered set (X,\,\leq ), if every well ordered subset of X is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.
[67 B] MW: Each set can be covered by a well ordered family of finite sets. Levy [1962].
77. A linear ordering of a set P is a well ordering if and only if P has no infinite descending sequences. Jech [1973b] p 23.
[77 A] If a linearly ordered set (X,\,\leq ) has no greatest element then it has a subset of order type \omega . Sierpiński [1918].
79. \mathbb{R} can be well ordered. Hilbert [1900] p 263.
90. LW: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered. Jech [1973b] p 133 and Felgner/Jech [1973].
91. PW: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered. Jech [1973b] p 133 and H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985].
103. If (P,\,<) is a linear ordering and |P|>\aleph _{1} then some initial segment of P is uncountable. Jech [1973b] p 164 prob 11.21.

[118 G] Each complete linear order admits an extreme choice, that is, if (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order then there is a choice function f on the set of non-empty open interval of X with the property that for all (a,\,b,\,c)\in X^{3} with a<b<c,\,f((a,\,c))\in \{f((a,\,b)),\,b,\,f((b,\,c))\}. Morillon [1991a].
[118 H] For each linear order (X,\,\leq ), there is an ordinal \alpha and a strictly increasing injective map j from (X,\,\leq ) to \{0,1\}^{\alpha } with the lexicographic order. Morillon [1987].
[118 I] Every linearly ordered set of linear orders each of which is non-empty and conditionally complete has a choice function. Morillon [1988], van Douwen [1985], and note 71.
[118 J] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear, complete order, then the order topology on X is hereditarily normal. Morillon [1988], van Douwen [1985], and note 71.
[118 K] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is highly separated. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[118 L] If X is a linear, complete order, then the order topology on X is highly separated. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 M] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the family \{A(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\} has a choice function. (A(a,\,b) denotes the set of continuous, order preserving functions from X into [0,1] such that f(a)=0 and f(b)=1.) Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 N] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the family \{A^{\prime }(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\} has a choice function. (A^{\prime }(a,\,b) denotes the set of continuous functions from X into [0,1] such that f(a)=0 and f(b)=1.) Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[118 O] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is effectively normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[118 P] If (X,\,\leq ) is a complete linear order, then the order topology on X is effectively normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[118 Q] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is hereditarily normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
[118 R] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is monotonely normal. Morillon [1987] and note 71.

[118 S] If (X,\,\leq ) is a complete linear order, then there is a choice function \ast for the family of non-empty open intervals of X such that if a,\,b,\,c\in X and either (a,\,b)\neq \emptyset or (b,\, c)\neq \emptyset , then \ast ((a,\,c))\in \{\ast ((a,\,b)),\,\ast ((b,\,c)),\,b,\,b^{+}\} (where b^{+} is the successor of b if it exists and b otherwise). Morillon [1987] and note 71.
[118 T] Every complete linear order has an increasing choice function. Morillon [1987] and note 71.

129. For every infinite set A,\,A admits a partition into sets of order type \omega ^{\ast }+\omega . (For every infinite A, there is a set \{\langle C_{j},\,<j\rangle :j\in J\} such that \{C_{j}:j\in J\} is a partition of A and for each j\in J, <j is an ordering of C_{j} of type \omega ^{\ast }+\omega .) Brunner [1984f].
130. \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) is well orderable. Brunner [1984f].
133. Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset. Brunner [1982a].
163. Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982a] and note 94.
164. Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite subset with a Dedekind finite power set. Brunner [1982a], notes 42 and 94.
[170 B] There is an uncountable, well orderable set of reals. Raisonnier [1982] and note 3.
185. Every linearly ordered Dedekind finite set is finite. Hickman [1979a] and note 94.
[185 A] If X is a linearly ordered set and there is neither an increasing nor a decreasing injection f:\omega \rightarrow X, then X is finite. Hickman [1979a].
198. For every set S, if the only linearly orderable subsets of S are the finite subsets of S, then either S is finite or S has an amorphous subset. Hickman [1978b] and note 57.
227. For all groups G, if every finite subgroup of G can be fully ordered then G can be fully ordered. Rav [1977] and note 79.
228. Every torsion free Abelian group can be fully ordered. Rav [1977] and note 79.

229. If (G,\,\circ ,\,\leq ) is a partially ordered group, then \leq can be extended to a linear order on G if and only if for every finite set \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}\subseteq G, with a_{i}\neq the identity for i=1 to n, the signs \epsilon _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\epsilon _{n}\,(\epsilon _{i}=\pm 1) can be chosen so that P\cap S(a_{1}^{\epsilon _{1}},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}^{\epsilon _{n}})=\emptyset (where S(b_{1},\,\ldots ,\, b_{n}) is the normal sub-semi-group of G generated by b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{n} and P=\{g\in G:e\leq g\} where e is the identity of G.) Rav [1977].
[231 A] Every almost well orderable set (W-set) is well orderable. Note 25.
293. For all sets x and y, if x can be linearly ordered and there is a mapping of x onto y, then y can be linearly ordered.
294. Every linearly ordered W-set is well orderable. Morris [1969] and note 25.
295. DO: Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering. Gonzalez [1995a].
[295 A] DUO: Every infinite set has a dense unbounded linear ordering. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].

316. If a linearly ordered set (A,\,\leq ) has the fixed point property then (A,\,\leq ) is complete. ((A,\,\leq ) has the fixed point property if every function f:A\rightarrow A satisfying (x\leq y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(y)) has a fixed point, and ((A,\,\leq ) is complete if every subset of A has a least upper bound.) Höft/Howard [1994].
377. Restricted Ordering Principle: For every infinite set X there is an infinite subset Y of X such that Y can be linearly ordered. De la Cruz/Di Prisco [1996].

sec.title: II. Versions Of Martin’s Axiom
sec.p: [\boldsymbol{0} S] If (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order such that P is non-empty, well orderable and every antichain is finite then there is a P-generic filter . Shannon [1990] and note 47.
[1 Z] If (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order and P\neq \emptyset and every antichain is finite, then there is a P generic filter which is well orderable. Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[8 F] Martin’s Axiom (\aleph _{0}): Whenever (P\leq ) is a non-empty, ccc quasi-order (ccc means every anti-chain is countable) and \mathcal{D} is a family of \leq \aleph _{0} dense subsets of P, then there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter G in P. Kunen [1980], Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[10 I] Assume (P,\,\leq ) is a partial order such that P is a denumerable union of finite sets and contains a non-empty subset Q relative to which depths are defined for all x\in \mathrm{P}. If all Q-strong antichains of P are finite then for each denumerable family \mathcal{D} of dense sets there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter. Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[43 C] Existence of a generic set: If \mathcal{D} is a denumerable collection of dense sets in a partial order (P,\,\leq ) then for all p\in P there is a \mathcal{D} generic G with p\in G. Goldblatt [1985] and note 47.

[43 D] If \mathcal{D} is a denumerable collection of dense subsets of a partial order (P,\,\leq ) then for all p\in P there is a sequence f:\omega \rightarrow P with f(0)=p and (\forall n\in \omega )(f(n)\geq f(n+1)) and range (f)\cap D\neq \emptyset for all D\in \mathcal{D}. Goldblatt [1985].

171. If (P,\,\leq ) is a partial order such that P is the denumerable union of finite sets and all antichains in P are finite then for each denumerable family \mathcal{D} of dense sets there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter. Shannon [1990] and note 47.
[10 F] König’s Lemma: Every \omega tree has an infinite chain. Pincus [1972c], note 21, and note 35.
[43 H] Every tree in which every element has at least one successor has a branch. Blass [1979] and note note 21.

[86 A(\alpha )] If (P,\,\leq ) is a tree of height \lambda \leq \aleph _{\alpha } which has fewer than \lambda branches of height <\lambda then one of the following holds for the upside down tree (P,\, \geq ):

def.p: There is a cardinal \mu <\lambda such that (P, \geq ) does not contain a strong antichain of cardinality \mu .
(P,\,\geq ) contains a strong antichain of cardinality \lambda .
(P,\,\geq ) contains a chain of cardinality \lambda .

sec.p: Shannon [1992] and note 119.

[106 A] DMC: Dependent Multiple Choice: Every tree in which every element has at least one immediate successor has a subtree whose levels are finite and in which every element has at least one immediate successor. Blass [1979], Brunner [1983c], Fossy/Morillon [1995] and note 21.
216. Every infinite tree has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Pincus [1972a] and note 21.
249. If T is an infinite tree in which every element has exactly 2 immediate successors then T has an infinite branch. Truss [1975], note 87 and note 21.

p.bold: IV. Other Partial Ordering Properties (See note 71.)

sec.p: [\boldsymbol{0} J] Zermelo’s Fixed Point Theorem: For every partially ordered set (X,\,\leq ), if every well ordered subset has a least upper bound then every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988a], Zermelo [1908b] and Abian [1980].

[\boldsymbol{0} K] For all partially ordered sets (X,\,\leq ), if there is a sup function \sigma on the well ordered subsets of X then every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[\boldsymbol{0} L] Caristi’s Fixed Point Theorem: If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi : X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)) every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t \leq f(t) has a fixed point. Caristi [1976], Manka [1988a], and note 38.
[1 Q] For any partial order (X,\,\leq ) there is a \sup function on the bounded (above), well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.
[1 R] For any partial order (X,\,\leq ) there is a \sup function on the bounded subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.
[1 S] For any partial order (X,\,\leq ) if every well ordered subset of X is bounded then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.
[1 T] For every directed partial order (X,\,\leq ) there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.
[1 U] For every directed partial order, if every well ordered subset of X is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[1 V] For every partially ordered set (X,\,\leq ), if every well ordered subset is bounded above then every function f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988a] and Abian [1980].

[1 AJ] Let \mathcal{F} be a family of mappings of a poset (X,\,\leq ) into itself such that \forall f\in \mathcal{F},\,\forall x\in X,\,f(x)\leq x. If for some element e of X each chain in X containing e has a lower bound, then the family \mathcal{F} has a common fixed point. Kasahara [1976].
[14 W] Universal Subnet Theorem: Any net has a universal subnet. Schechter [1996a] and note 31.
[43 K] Let M be a non-empty set partially ordered by < without <-minimal elements. Then there is a subset C of M which is linearly ordered by < such that C has no <-minimal element. Note 146.
[43 L] Z_{\omega }: If every chain in a partially ordered set P is finite, then P contains a maximal element. Tarski [1948], Wolk [1983], and note 54.

[43 M] If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering, (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)), there is a maximal element. Brunner [1987a] and note 38.

[43 Q] Matrix(\omega ): For every atomless poset (P,\,\leq ) and every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open subsets of P, there exists a matrix C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega \},\, |\bigcup C|=\omega of P for D. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[43 R] Any partial order (A,\,\leq ) with no infinite descending chains is well founded, (that is, for all X such that \emptyset \,\neq X\subseteq A,\,X has a minimal element.) Spector [1980] and note 54.

59(\leq ). If (A,\,\leq ) is a partial ordering that is not a well ordering, then there is no set B such that (B,\,\precsim ) (the usual injective cardinal ordering on B) is isomorphic to (A,\,\leq ). Mathias [1979] p 120.
[70 B] Weak Universal Net Theorem: There is a universal net in \omega which is not eventually constant. Schechter [1996a] and note 31.

[87 A(\alpha )] Z_{\aleph _{\alpha }}: Let P be a partially ordered set in which every well ordered chain has type <\aleph _{\alpha }. If every well ordered chain in P has an upper bound in P, then P contains a maximal element. Wolk [1983].

[87 B(\alpha )] Z_{\aleph _{\alpha }}^{\ast }: Let P be a well-founded partially ordered set, (that is, every chain in P is well ordered), in which every chain has type <\aleph _{\alpha }. If every chain in P has an upper bound in P, then P contains a maximal element. Wolk [1983].
89. Antichain Principle: Every partially ordered set has a maximal antichain. Jech [1973b] p 133 and Kurepa [1953].

105. There is a partially ordered set (A,\,\leq ) such that there is no set (B,\,\precsim ) (\precsim , the usual injective cardinal ordering) isomorphic to (A,\,\leq ). Forti/Honsell [1985] and Jech [1966c].
144. Every set is almost well orderable. Keisler [1970] and note 25.
217. Every infinite partially ordered set has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Pincus [1972a].

sec.title: TOPOLOGICAL FORMS (INCLUDING PROPERTIES OF \mathbb{R})

p.bold: I. Baire Category Type Theorems (See note 28.)

sec.p: [43 E] The Baire Category Theorem for Čech Complete-I Spaces: Every Čech complete space is Baire. Goldblatt [1985] and note 28.
[43 F] Baire Category Theorem for Sequentially Complete Metric Spaces: Every sequentially complete metric space is Baire. Blair [1977], Brunner [1983c], Goldblatt [1985], and note 28.
[43 J] Baire Category Theorem for Cantor Complete Metric Spaces: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. Brunner [1983c] and note 28.
[43 T] A sequentially complete metric space is not meager. Note 28.
[43 U] Baire Category Theorem for Filter Complete Metric Spaces: Every filter complete metric space is Baire, Morillon [1988] and note 28.
[43 V] Every convex-compact set in a Hausdorff topological vector space with a basis of convex open sets is Baire. Fossy/Morillon [1995] and note 23.
106. Baire Category Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: Every compact Hausdorff space is Baire. Goldblatt [1985], G. Moore [1982], and note 28.
[106 C] Every scattered compact space is a Baire space. Fossy/Morillon [1995] and note 28.
[\boldsymbol{0} B] If X is finite then X^{\omega } is compact. Brunner [1984b].
[\boldsymbol{0} D] Products of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b]

[\boldsymbol{0} E] The box product of a well ordered family of limited amorphous spaces is limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b] and note 52.

[1 AY] For each \lambda \in \Lambda let S_{\lambda } be a subset of some topological space X_{\lambda }. Then \mathrm{cl}( \prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }S_{\lambda })=\prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }\ \mathrm{cl}\ (S_{\lambda }), where the first “\mathrm{cl}” is closure in the product topology and the second “\mathrm{cl}” is closure in X_{\lambda }. Schechter [1992].

[1 AZ] For each \lambda \in \Lambda , let X_{\lambda } be a complete uniform space. Then, the product \prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }X_{\lambda } equipped with the product uniform structure, is also complete. (See, for example, Kelley [1955] pp 176ff for definitions.) Schechter [1992].
[10 B] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countable Families of Finite T_{2} Spaces: The product of a countable family of finite T_{2} spaces is compact. Krom [1981].

[14 J] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: The product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact. (For many compactness theorems T, it is clear that [14 J] implies T implies [14 K].) Łoś/Ryll-Nardzewski [1954] and Rubin/Scott [1954].

[14 K] Compactness of the Generalized Cantor Space: \{0,1\}^{I} is compact for any I. (For many compactness theorems T, it is clear that [14 J] implies T implies [14 K].) Jech [1973b] p 28, prob 17 and Mycielski [1964].

[14 Z] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Families of Finite Spaces: If \{X_{i}:i\in I\} is a family of finite topological spaces, then \prod _{i\in I}X_{i} is compact. (Cleary [14 Z] implies [14 K] and is implied by [14 J].) Jech [1973b] p 28 prob 17, A.A. Lewis [1983], and Wolk [1967].
[14 AB] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Sober Spaces: A product of compact, sober topological spaces is compact. Blass [1986], Johnstone [1984] and note 37.
[43 G] Form 106 + form 154. Brunner [1983c] [1984b].
[64 A] An amorphous power of a compact T_{2} space is compact. Brunner [1984b].
[64 B] Finite products of metric C spaces are C. (A space is C if each open covering has an amorphous refinement.) Brunner [1984b].
113. Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countably Many Spaces: The product of a countable set of compact spaces is compact. Brunner [1985a].
115. The product of weakly Loeb T_{2} spaces is weakly Loeb. (See form 114 for the definition of weakly Loeb.) Brunner [1985a].
127. An amorphous power of a compact T_{2} space, which as a set is well orderable, is well orderable. Brunner [1984b].
134. If X is an infinite T_{1} space and X^{Y} is T_{5}, then Y is countable. (T_{5} is “hereditarily T_{4}”.) A. H. Stone [1948].

135. If X is a T_{2} space with at least two points and X^{Y} is hereditarily metacompact then Y is countable. (A space is metacompact if every open cover has an open point finite refinement. If B and B^{\prime } are covers of a space X, then B^{\prime } is a refinement of B if (\forall x\in B^{\prime })(\exists y\in B)(x\subseteq y). B is point finite if (\forall t\in X) there are only finitely many x\in B such that t\in x.) van Douwen [1980].
139. Using the discrete topology on 2,\, 2^{\mathcal{P}(\omega )} is compact. Truss [1984].
154. Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countably Many T_{2} Spaces: The product of countably many T_{2} compact spaces is compact. Brunner [1983c].
177. An infinite box product of regular T_{1} spaces, each of cardinality greater than 1, is neither first countable nor connected. Brunner [1981a], Knight [1964], and note 52.
332. A product of non-empty compact sober topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.
343. A product of non-empty, compact T_{2} topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon [1988].
351. A countable product of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.
352. A countable product of second countable spaces is second countable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.
353. A countable product of first countable spaces is first countable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[1 P] A(P): (Depends on P for P\in \{W1,\,W2,\,B1,\,L1,\,L2, S,\,C,\,H1,\,A1\}) Every T_{2} topological space has property P. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[1 BP] For every dense in itself topological space (X,\,T) and every base B for X there exists a nest N included in B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.
[1 BQ] For every dense in itself topological space (X,\,T) and every base B for X there exists a tower R included in B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 CH] If a topological space is cwN, then it is cwH(B) for any basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[8 D] Every \sigma -compact, locally compact T_{2} space is weakly Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.
[8 I] A disjoint union of a countable set of Lindelöf T_{2} spaces is Lindelöf. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

DUCCC is “If X is a denumerable family of disjoint topological spaces each having the ccc property, then the disjoint union of the spaces in X has the ccc property.” (Y has the ccc property if every collection of disjoint open sets is countable.) [50 L] Form 301 + form 14. Bell [1988].

[67 C] A(P): (Depends on P\in \{D1,\,B2,\,B3,\,H2,\,A2\}.) Every T_{2} topological space has property P. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

eq j in I, the set E(i,\,j)=\{(x,\,y):x\,R\,y\ \mathrm{and}\ x\in T_{i}\ \mathrm{and}\ y\in T_{j}\} is closed in T_{i}	imes T_{j}. eq j in F. Then \exists f\in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in I\} such that f(i)\,R\,f(j) for all i
eq j in I. Rav [1977].

130. \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) is well orderable. Brunner [1984f].
[137 A(k)] For all X and Y\subseteq \mathbb{R} form 137(k) holds. Truss [1984].
142. \neg PB: There is a set of reals without the property of Baire. Jech [1973b] p 7 and note 28.
169. There is an uncountable subset of \mathbb{R} without a perfect subset. Banaschewski/Moore [1990], Bernstein [1908], and note 28.
[170 A] There is a function that assigns to each denumerable set D of reals a real number not in D. Sierpiński [1954].
[170 B] There is an uncountable, well orderable set of reals. Raisonnier [1982] and note 3.
197. \mathbb{R}^{2} is the union of three sets C with the property that for all x\in C there is a straight line L such that L\cap C=\{x\}. Davies [1978].
203. C(\mathrm{disjoint},\subseteq \mathbb{R}): Every partition of \mathcal{P}(w) into non-empty subsets has a choice function. Truss [1978].

211. DCR: Dependent Choice for Relations on \mathbb{R}: If R\subseteq \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} satisfies (\forall x\in \mathbb{R})(\exists y\in \mathbb{R})(x\ R\ y) then there is a sequence \langle x(n): n\in \omega \rangle of real numbers such that (\forall n\in \omega )(x(n)\,R\,x(n+1)). Mathias [1977a].

212. C(2^{\aleph _{0}},\,\subseteq \mathbb{R}): If R is a relation on \mathbb{R} such that for all x\in \mathbb{R}, there is a y\in \mathbb{R} such that x\,R\,y, then there is a function f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that for all x\in \mathbb{R},\,x\,R\,f(x). Mathias [1977a].

224. There is a partition of the real line into \aleph _{1} Borel sets \{B_{\alpha }:\alpha <\aleph _{1}\} such that for some \beta <\aleph _{1},\,\forall \alpha <\aleph _{1},\,B_{\alpha }\in G_{\beta }. (G_{\beta } for \beta <\aleph _{1} is defined by induction, G_{0}=\{A: A\ {is an open subset of}\ \mathbb{R}\} and for \beta >0,\,G_{\beta }=\{\bigcup _{i=0}^{\infty }A_{i}:(\forall i\in \omega )(\exists \xi <\beta )(A_{i}\in G_{\xi })\} if \beta is even and G_{\beta }=\{\bigcap _{i=0}^{\infty }A_{i}:(\forall i\in \omega )(\exists \xi <\beta )(A_{i}\in G_{\xi })\} if \beta is odd.) Stern [1979].
251. The additive groups (\mathbb{R},\,+) and (\mathbb{C},\,+) are isomorphic. Ash [1975].
252. The additive groups of \mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{R} and \mathbb{R} are isomorphic. Ash [1975].
272. There is an X\subseteq \mathbb{R} such that neither X nor \mathbb{R} -X has a perfect subset. Truss [1974b] and note 28.
273. There is a subset of \mathbb{R} which is not Borel. Truss [1974b].

305. There are 2^{\aleph _{0}} Vitali equivalence classes. (Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q).). Kanovei [1991].

306. The set of Vitali equivalence classes is linearly orderable. (Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q).). Kanovei [1991].

307. If m is the cardinality of the set of Vitali equivalence classes, then H(m)= H(2^{\aleph _{0}}), where H is Hartogs aleph function and the Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q). Kanovei [1991].

309. The Banach-Tarski Paradox: There are three finite partitions \{P_{1},\,\ldots ,\,P_{n}\},\,\{Q_{1},\, \ldots ,\,Q_{r}\} and \{S_{1},\,\ldots ,\,S_{n},\,T_{1},\,\ldots ,\,T_{r}\} of B^{3}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|\leq 1\} such that P_{i} is congruent to S_{i} for 1\leq i\leq n and Q_{i} is congruent to T_{i} for 1\leq i\leq r. Banach/Tarski [1924].
361. In \mathbb{R}, the union of a denumerable number of analytic sets is analytic. G. Moore [1982], pp 181 and 325.
362. In \mathbb{R}, every Borel set is analytic. G. Moore [1982], pp 181 and 325.
363. There are exactly 2^{\aleph _{0}} Borel sets in \mathbb{R}. G. Moore [1982], p 325.
364. In \mathbb{R}, there is a measurable set that is not Borel. G. Moore [1982], p 325.
366. There is a discontinuous function f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that for all real x and y,\,f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y). Hamel [1905].
367. There is a Hamel basis for \mathbb{R} as a vector space over \mathbb{Q}. Hamel [1905].
368. The set of all denumerable subsets of \mathbb{R} has power 2^{\aleph _{0}}. Sierpiński [1917].
369. If \mathbb{R} is partitioned into two sets, at least one of them has cardinality 2^{\aleph _{0}}. Luzin/Sierpiński [1917].

[\boldsymbol{0} L] Caristi’s Fixed Point Theorem: If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\, \rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)) every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Caristi [1976], Manka [1988a], and note 38.
[\boldsymbol{0} AK] Every separable metric space is second countable.
[1 I] In every metric space (X,\,d) there is an \epsilon -lattice for some \epsilon >0 which is not a strict upper bound of d. Brunner [1984e] and note 17.

[1 BK] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is pairwise disjoint. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997].

[1 CE] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is discrete. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[10 G] For all metric spaces X and Y and continuous functions f from X onto Y such that f^{-1}(y) is finite for all y\in Y, if X has a dense Dedekind finite subset, then so does Y. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.
[43 F] Baire Category Theorem for Sequentially Complete Metric Spaces: Every sequentially complete metric space is Baire. Blair [1977], Brunner [1983c], Goldblatt [1985] and note 28.
[43 J] Baire Category Theorem for Cantor Complete Metric Spaces: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. Brunner [1983c] and note 28.

[43 M] If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering, (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)), there is a maximal element. Brunner [1987a] and note 38.

[64 D] Metric C spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is C if every open covering has an amorphous refinement. A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is relatively compact.) Brunner [1984b].

[67 U] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[67 V] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X, d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
75. Every subspace of a separable metric space is separable. Jech [1973b] p 21.

[76 A] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is locally countable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[76 B] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is point countable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
173. MPL: Metric spaces are para-Lindelöf. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[173 A] MML: Metric spaces are meta-Lindelöf. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/ Stanley [1997] and note 141.
232. Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \sigma -point finite base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 A] Every metric space has a \gamma -point finite base, for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 B] Every metric space has a \sigma -locally finite base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 C] Every metric space has a \gamma -locally finite base, for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 D] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \sigma -discrete base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 E] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \gamma -discrete base, for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 F] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \sigma -disjoint base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[232 G] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \gamma -disjoint base for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
280. There is a complete separable metric space with a subset which does not have the Baire property. Wright [1973] and note 28.
337. Every separable metric space is Lindelöf. Good/Tree [1995].
338. Every second countable metric space is Lindelöf. Good/Tree [1995].
339. Every second countable metric space is separable. Good/Tree [1995].
340. Every Lindelöf metric space is separable. Good/Tree [1995].
341. Every Lindelöf metric space is second countable. Good/Tree [1995].
381. DUM: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b].
382. DUMN: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b].
383. MP: Every metric space is paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[383 A] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) has a refinement \mathcal{V} which covers X and which can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{V_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where each V_{\alpha } is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
[383 B] MM: Every metric space is metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[383 C] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X, d) has a refinement \mathcal{V} which covers X and which can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{V_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where each V_{\alpha } is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: We consider two types of models: Models of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, ZF, in section I and models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} in section II. These two versions of set theory are described in the introduction to the book. (In what follows, AC is the Axiom of Choice and GCH is the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis.) Our models of ZF are Cohen models (or some modern variation) which are obtained from models of ZFC = ZF +AC by using the method of forcing to construct an extension which is a model of ZF without AC. The models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} that we use are the permutation models of Fraenkel and Mostowski (FM models). We start with a model of \mathrm{ZF^{0}+ AC} which we refer to as the ground model and use a group of permutations of the atoms to construct a submodel in which AC is false. Details on the construction of models for ZF by the method of forcing can be found in Cohen [1966], Felgner [1971a], Jech [1973b], Kunen [1980], and Solovay [1970]. For more details on permutation models and the Fraenkel-Mostowski method we refer the reader to Felgner [1971a], Fraenkel [1922], Jech [1973b], and Levy [1963a].

We refer to the statements in the numerical list of forms both by their name (e.g. Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem or BPI) and by their number (e.g. BPI is form 14). Sometimes we refer to a form by a symbol. For example, C(\infty ,\,\infty ) is AC in the form: “Every set of non-empty sets has a choice function.” (form 1); C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}) is AC for a denumerable set of finite sets (10); C(WO,\,\infty ) is AC for a well ordered set of non-empty sets (40); UT(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}) is “The union of a denumerable number of denumerable sets is denumerable.” (The countable union theorem, 31); etc. These and other abbreviations are defined in both the numerical list of forms and the topical list of forms.

sec.title: Cohen Models, Models of ZF. (\mathcal{M})
sec.p: There are some weak forms of AC which are true in all Cohen models and some which are false in all Cohen models. These are described briefly below. More information can be found in the notes to which we refer.

Several of our weak forms of AC are known to imply AC in the theory ZF (but not in the theory \mathrm{ZF}^{0}). More detailed information can be found in notes 18 and 75. Since AC is false in all of our Cohen models of ZF all forms which imply AC in ZF must be false. In the theory \mathrm{ZF}^{0}, all of these forms are known to imply form 91. Therefore, in the description of each Cohen model, we will say “91 is false” and refer to note 75.

Secondly, there are several implications involving more than two forms that are known to hold in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. These are listed with references in note 120. Most are of the form A+B implies C, where A, B, and C are form numbers. When it follows from these implications that a certain form is true or false in a model we will, in the description of the model, assert that the form is true (or false) and give a reference to the part of note 120 from which the truth or falsity follows.

\mathcal{M}1: Cohen’s original model. Add a denumerable number of generic reals (subsets of \omega ), a_{1},\,a_{2},\, \cdots , along with the set b containing them. It follows from the work of Halpern and Levy that the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (BPI,14) and the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle (15) are true in this model. Cohen proved that in this model there is an infinite subset of the reals that has no denumerable subset (13 is false). Also, the Krein-Milman Theorem (KM, 65) is false because BPI + KM \rightarrow AC and Haddad and Morillon proved that in \mathcal{M}1 every orderable topological space is normal (118 is true). Jech has shown that the Axiom of Choice for a set of well orderable sets (C(\infty ,\,WO), 60) is true and the countable union theorem (UT(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}), 31) is true. Blass proved that Ramsey’s Theorem (17) is false. Brunner [1982a] has shown that every set that cannot be well ordered has an infinite Dedekind finite subset (163 is true), but the interval [0, 1] of real numbers is not well orderable and has no infinite subset with a Dedekind finite power set (164 is false). It is shown in note 102 that there is a set S consisting of finite unions of sets in b, the set of generic reals, that is closed with respect to chain unions, but has no \subseteq -maximal element (289 is false). Brunner [1984f] shows that in this model on every infinite set there is a Hausdorff topology with an infinite set of non-isolated points (128 is true). Blass [1979] has shown that in every symmetric model there is a set X such that for each set a, there is an ordinal \alpha and a function f mapping X\times \alpha onto a (191 is true). (See note 59.) Since BPI is true, it follows from Howard [1975] that Łos’ Theorem (253) is false. Monro proves that every cardinal that cannot be well ordered is decomposable (i.e. is the sum of two smaller positive cardinals), so 277 is true. In Jech [1973b] (prob 5.20), it is shown that the power set of an infinite set is Dedekind infinite (82 is true). David shows that no infinite subset of b is almost well orderable so 144 is false. See note 25 for definitions. By the results of Bell [1983], [1988] and Monro [1972a] the following three forms are false in \mathcal{M}1: Form 50 (Sikorski’s extension theorem on Boolean homomorphisms), form 299 (Any extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space is projective in the category of Boolean topological spaces.) and form 300 (Any continuous surjection between extremally disconnected Hausdorff spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain.) See notes 60 and 114 for definitions. Since 154 is true (14 implies 154) and 43 is false (43 implies 13), form 106 (the Baire Category Theorem for compact T_{2} spaces) is false because 106 + 154 implies 43. (See Brunner [1984b] and note 95.) In this model, \mathbb{R} with the order topology is a separable metric space that is not Lindelöf (337 is false). Also, there is a dense set K\subseteq \mathbb{R} which has no denumerable subset such that K is a second countable metric space that is neither Lindelöf nor separable (338 and 339 are false). (See Good/Tree [1995].)

\mathcal{M}1 \models 14, 15, 31, 60, 82, 118, 128, 163, 165, 191, and 277, but 13, 17, 50, 65, 106, 131, 144, 164, 253, 289, 299, 300, 337, 338, and 339 are false. References include Bell [1983], [1988], Blass [1979], [1977], Brunner [1982a], [1984b], [1984f], Cohen [1963], [1966], David [1980], Good/Tree [1995], Halpern/Levy [1971], Haddad/Morillon [1990], Howard [1975], Monro [1972a], [1973a], Sageev [1981], Shoenfield [1967], Smullyan [1994] and note 120(30 and 49). See, also, Felgner [1971a] (pp 100–103, 131–145), and Jech [1973b] (Chapt. 5, probs 20, 22).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 14, 15, 31, 60, 118, 128, 163, 165, 191, 277.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 13, 17, 50, 65, 131, 144, 253, 289, 299, 300, 337, 338, 339.

\mathcal{M}1(\langle (\omega _{1}\rangle ): Cohen/Pincus Model. Pincus extends the methods of Cohen and adds a generic \omega _{1}-sequence, \langle I_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \omega _{1}\rangle , of denumerable sets, where I_{0} is a denumerable set of generic reals, each I_{\alpha +1} is a generic set of enumerations of I_{\alpha }, and for a limit ordinal \lambda ,\,I_{\lambda } is a generic set of choice functions for \{I_{\alpha }:\alpha <\lambda \}. Pincus proves that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true, for each family of infinite sets x, there is a function f such that for each y\in x,\,f(y)\subseteq y and |f(y)|=\aleph _{0}(214), is true, every set can be linearly ordered (30) is true, there is a class of cardinal representatives, hence form 97 is true, but C(\aleph _{1},\,\aleph _{0}) is false because <I_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \omega _{1}> has no choice function. Therefore, forms 39 (C(\aleph _{1},\,\infty )) and 85 (C(\infty ,\,\aleph _{0})) are false. Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 163 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) is also false because 43 implies 8 and 8 + 163 implies AC (Brunner [1982a]). Since form 43 implies form 296 (Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets.) it follows from Pincus [1997] that form 295 (Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering.) is also true. (30 + 296 implies 295.) Form 62 (C(\infty ,\, <\aleph _{0})) is true because 295 implies 62 and form 60 (C(\infty ,\,WO)) is false because 60 implies 85. Therefore, form 329 (MC(\infty ,\,WO)) is false because 62 + 329 \rightarrow 60.

\mathcal{M}1(\langle \omega _{1}\rangle ) \models 30, 43, 97, 214, and 295, but 20, 39, 85, 91, 133, 151, 163, 328, and 329 are false. References Pincus [1977], [1997], Brunner [1982a], note 18, and note 120(32, 43, and 47).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 43, 97, 214, 295.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 39, 85, 91, 151, 163, 328, 329.

\mathcal{M}2: Feferman’s model. Add a denumerable number of generic reals to the base model, but do not collect them. Feferman has shown that in this model there is an infinite set of pairs with no choice function (88 is false), there is a partition of \mathcal{P}(\omega ) with no choice function (203 is false) and the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) is false. Truss [1978] has shown that in this model C(WO,\, \infty ) (40) is true. (He gives credit to Solovay for the proof.) In Truss [1978] it is also shown that \mathcal{P}(\omega ) does not have a non-trivial ultrafilter (70 is false), and for every infinite set x there is a mapping of x onto 2\times x (204) is true. (See note 65.) Pincus shows that there is a set of reals that does not have the property of Baire (142 is true), but \mathcal{P}(\omega ) has no nontrivial real valued measure which is 0 on finite sets (222 is false). (The proof of form 142 requires that the Continuum Hypothesis holds in the outer model.) Since 40 implies 8 (C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )), it follows from Brunner [1982a] that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Truss [1974b] proves that there is a sequence x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\cdots of cardinals such that for each n,\, x_{n}=\aleph _{n+1}+2^{\aleph _{0}} adj \aleph _{n+1}+\aleph _{2}\cdot 2^{\aleph _{0}} adj \aleph _{n+1}+\aleph _{3}\cdot 2^{\aleph _{0}} adj \cdots adj \aleph _{n+1}+\aleph _{n+1}\cdot 2^{\aleph _{0}}=x_{n}^{2}. (The symbol x adj y means x<y and there is nothing between x and y.) It follows that 274 is false.

\mathcal{M}2 \models 40, 142, 165, and 204, but 70, 88, 152, 163, 203, 222, and 274 are false. References Brunner [1982a], Feferman [1965], Pincus [1972], Truss [1978], [1974b], note 65, and note 120(34 and 46). (See also Felgner [1971a] pp 160-166 where credit for some of the proofs is given to D. Scott and R. Solovay.)
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 40, 142, 165, 204.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 88, 152, 163, 203, 222, 274.

\mathcal{M}2(\kappa ): Feferman/Pincus Model. This is an extension of \mathcal{M}2 in which there are \kappa generic sets, where \kappa is a regular cardinal. (\mathcal{M}2 is \mathcal{M}2(\aleph _{0}).) Pincus proves that the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) is false in this model. If \kappa is sufficiently large, then there is a non-trivial measure on \mathcal{P}(\omega ) which is 0 on finite sets (222 is true). \kappa has to be large enough so that form 222 is boundable in sets of rank \mu , where \mu is less than \kappa .
\mathcal{M}2(\kappa ) \models 222, but 52, and 91 are false. References Pincus [1972] and note 18.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 222.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 52, 91.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, 142, 222, 223, 280, (383).

\mathcal{M}2(\langle \omega _{2}\rangle ): Feferman/Truss Model. This is another extension of \mathcal{M}2. The set of all sequences of generic reals of length less than \omega _{2} are added to a countable transitive model of ZFC + V = L. Truss proves that C(|\mathbb{R}|,\,\infty ) (181) is true, but there is a partition of \mathcal{P}(\omega ) that has no choice function (203 is false). Since the Axiom of choice is false, it follows that all forms that imply AC in ZF are also false. In particular, C(LO,\,\infty ) (202), is false. (See the first paragraph of section I.) Form 163 (every set is either well orderable or has an infinite Dedekind finite subset) is also false because 181 implies 8 and 8 + 163 implies AC (Brunner [1982a]).
\mathcal{M}2(\langle \omega _{2}\rangle ) \models 181, but 163, 202, and 203 are false. References Truss [1978] and Brunner [1982a].
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 181.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 163, 203.

\mathcal{M}3: Mathias’ model. Mathias proves that the FM model \mathcal{N}4 can be transformed into a model of ZF, \mathcal{M}3. \mathcal{M}3 is an extension of \mathcal{M}1 in which a universal homogeneous partial ordering is defined on b, the set of generic reals. (See Jech [1973b] p 101 for definitions.) Mathias then proves that the partial ordering on b cannot be extended to a linear ordering (49 is false), but every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true). Also, in this model, every set of well orderable sets has a choice function (60) and the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle (15) are true. Form 60 implies 294 (Every linearly ordered W-set is well orderable.), and 30 + 294 + 144 (Every set is a W-set.) implies AC. It follows that 144 is false. (See note 25 for definitions.) Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (15 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false because 64 + 133 implies AC. The Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) is false because 14 implies 49, and C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) (62) is true because 15 implies 62. It was shown by Blass (see note 33) that 62 + 99 (Rado’s Selection Lemma) implies 14, so form 99 is false.

\mathcal{M}3 \models 15, 60, and 165, but 49, 91, 99, 144, 152, and 133 are false. References Mathias [1967], notes 25, 33 and 120(6, 34 and 43). Also, see Felgner [1971a] (pp 114–128) and Jech [1973b] (p 113, prob 8).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 15, 60, 165.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 49, 91, 99, 144, 152.

\mathcal{M}4: Pincus’ Model I. This model has many of the properties of the model given in Cohen [1966] (p 143). The ground model, \mathcal{M}, is a model of ZF + V = L. Forcing conditions are functions from countable subsets of \omega _{1} to \{0, 1\}. \mathcal{M}4 is a symmetric submodel of the corresponding generic extension of \mathcal{M}. Pincus proves that the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) is true, but there is an infinite set with no denumerable subset (9 is false), and there is a denumerable family of pairs that has no choice function. It follows that KW(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}) (358) and C(\infty ,\,2) (88) are false. Pincus also proves that the Krein-Milman Theorem (65) is false. (Since BPI (form 14) implies 358, BPI is also false.)
\mathcal{M}4 \models 52, but 65, 88, 91, and 358 are false. References Pincus [1972] and note 18.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 52.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 65, 88, 91, 358.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, 52, 93, 142, 221, 222, 223, 280, 287, 309, (383).

\mathcal{M}5(\aleph ): Solovay’s Model. An inaccessible cardinal \aleph is collapsed to \aleph _{1} in the outer model and then \mathcal{M}5(\aleph ) is the smallest model containing the ordinals and \mathbb{R}. (The method of collapsing cardinals that is used in the model and some of the proofs are due to A. Levy. An inaccessible cardinal is used to construct the model. See, for example, Drake [1974], Kanamori/Magador [1978] or Solovay/Reinhardt/Kanamori [1978] for information about large cardinals.) In this model, The Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true and every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable (93 is false). Moreover, if \aleph is a measurable cardinal, then so is \aleph _{1} (318 is false). (Also, see Jech [1972].) (It has been shown by Shelah [1984] and Raisonnier [1984] that if ZF + C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )(8)+\neg \ 93 is consistent (43 implies 8), then so is ZFC + “there exists an inaccessible cardinal”. Thus, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is necessary for this result.) Moreover, in \mathcal{M}5(\aleph ), every set of reals has the Baire property (142 is false) and the cardinal 2^{\aleph _{0}} is not well orderable and is not decomposable (the sum of two smaller positive cardinals) so 277 is false. Also, the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) and the Axiom of Choice for pairs (88) are false. Every uncountable set of reals contains a perfect subset (169 is false). The following two statements are also false in this model: There is a complete separable metric space with a non meager subset (280) and there is a Hilbert space H and an unbounded linear operator on H (281). (See also note 96.) Stern proves that in this model, every infinite sequence of Borel sets of the same rank is countable (224 is false). (Truss has shown that if the same construction is used with \aleph a limit cardinal then 169 is still false, but 43 is also false. See \mathcal{M}12(\aleph ).) Mathias has shown that there is no non-Ramsey set (234 is false). According to Kanovei [1991], if m is the cardinality of the set of Vitali equivalence classes, then, in \mathcal{M}5(\aleph ), H(m)=H(2^{\aleph _{0}}), where H is Hartogs’ function (307 is true). (H(x) is the smallest ordinal that is not similar to a subset of x and the Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q).) Since 43 implies 8 (C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )), it follows from Brunner [1982a] that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) In Wagon [1985], it is shown that \mathbb{Z} is not amenable in \mathcal{M}5(\aleph ) (313 is false) and that there is an amenable group with a non-amenable subgroup in \mathcal{M}5(\aleph ) (312 is false). (G is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure \mu on \mathcal{P}(G) such that \mu (G)=1 and \forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu (gA)=\mu (A).)

\mathcal{M}5(\aleph ) \models 43 and 307, but 88, 93, 142, 163, 169, 224, 234, 277, 280, 281, 312, 313, and 318 are false. References Solovay [1965], [1970], Brunner [1982a], Jech [1972], Kanovei [1991], Monro [1973a], Mathias [1968], Prikry [1976], Raisonnier [1984], Shelah [1984], Stern [1979], Truss [1974b], Wright [1973], Wagon [1985], and note 20.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 43, 307.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 93, 163, 169, 224, 234, 277, 280, 281, 312, 318.

\mathcal{M}6: Sageev’s Model I. Using iterated forcing, Sageev constructs \mathcal{M}6 by adding a denumerable number of generic tree-like structures to the ground model, a model of ZF + V = L. He proves that in \mathcal{M}6, every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true) and the 2m=m principle (3) holds, but the Axiom of Choice for a denumerable set of denumerable subsets of the reals (5) is false. Gonzalez has shown that every infinite set has a dense linear ordering in \mathcal{M}6 (295 is true). Form 3 implies form 10 (C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0})) and form 231 (UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO)) implies form 5. Thus, form 10 is true and form 231 is false. It is shown in note 123 that 10 + 163 (Every non well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) implies 231. Consequently, form 163 is false. (Halpern/Howard [1970] have shown using a permutation model that the 2m=m principle does not imply the Axiom of Choice in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} See \mathcal{N}9.) Form 165 (C(WO,\,WO)) is false because 165 implies 5 and form 122 (C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0})) is true because 295 implies 122. Therefore, form 330 (MC(WO,\,WO)) is false because 122 + 330 \rightarrow 165. In addition, 126 (MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )) is false because 30 is true and 5 is false. (8\,(C(\aleph _{0},\, \infty )) implies 5 and 30 + 126 implies 8.)
\mathcal{M}6 \models 3, 30, and 295, but 5, 126, 163, and 330 are false. References Sageev [1975], Gonzalez [1995a], notes 2(8), 120(9), and 123.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 3, 295.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 5, 126, 163, 330.

\mathcal{M}7: Cohen’s Second Model. In this model there are two denumerable sets U = \{U_{i}:i\in \omega \} and V=\{V_{i}:i\in \omega \} such that for each i\in \omega ,\,U_{i} and V_{i} cannot be distinguished. Therefore, in this model there is a denumerable set of pairs whose union has no denumerable subset, so form 18 is false, and KW(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}) (358) is also false. Blass [1979] has shown that in every symmetric model there is a set X such that for each set a, there is an ordinal \alpha and a function f mapping X\times \alpha onto a (191 is true). (See note 59.) It is shown in Good/Tree [1995] that in this model there is a Lindelöf metric space that is neither second countable nor separable (340 and 341 are false).
\mathcal{M}7 \models 191, but 18, 91, 340, 341, and 358 are false. References Blass [1979], Cohen [1965], [1963], [1966], Good/Tree [1995], Jech [1973b] (pp 68ff), and note 18.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 191.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 18, 91, 340, 341, 358.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, 182, 189, 190, 191, (383).

\mathcal{M}7(n): Generalization of \mathcal{M}7. Model \mathcal{M}7 can be generalized to n denumerable sets for 1<n\in \omega , then the Axiom of Choice for a denumerable number of n element sets, C(\aleph _{0},\,n), is false for 1<n<\omega . Therefore, C(WO,\,n)\ (47(n)) is also false for 1<n\in \omega .
In \mathcal{M}7(n), forms 47(n) and 91 are false. Reference note 18.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 0.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 47, 91.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, (383).

\mathcal{M}8: Apter’s Model. Suppose \mathcal{M} \models ZFC + “There are cardinals \kappa <\delta < \lambda such that \kappa is a supercompact limit of supercompact cardinals, \lambda is a measurable cardinal, and \delta is \lambda supercompact.” (See, for example, Drake [1974], Kanamori/Magador [1978], or Solovay/Reinhardt/Kanamori [1978] for information about large cardinals.) \mathcal{M}8 is constructed by first forcing over the ground model \mathcal{M}, constructing an inner model \mathcal{M}^{\prime }, doing an additional forcing argument over \mathcal{M}^{\prime }, and then constructing the final inner model \mathcal{M}8. In this model \aleph _{n}, for 3\leq n\leq \omega are singular cardinals so 25 (\aleph _{\alpha +1} is regular for all ordinals \alpha .) is false. Also, the Axiom of Choice for a denumerable number of sets, 8, is false. (Supercompact and measurable cardinals are used to construct the model.)
In \mathcal{M}8, forms 8, 25, and 91 are false. References Apter [1985a], notes 18 and 20.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 0.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 8, 25, 91.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, (383).

\mathcal{M}9: Feferman/Levy Model. Assume the ground model, \mathcal{M}, satisfies ZF + GCH (the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis). Let P, the set of forcing conditions, be the set of all finite sets p of triples (n,\,i,\, \alpha ) that satisfy: (i) n\in \omega ,\,i\in \omega , \alpha \in \omega _{n}; and (ii) (n,\,i,\,\alpha ), (n,\,i,\,\beta )\in p implies \alpha =\beta . Let G be a generic subset of P and let \mathcal{M}[G] be the corresponding generic extension of \mathcal{M}. \mathcal{M}9 is a symmetric submodel of \mathcal{M}[G]. In this model, \mathbb{R}\subseteq \bigcup \{R_{n}:n\in \omega \}, where |R_{n}|=\aleph _{n+1} for n\in \omega , and |\aleph _{n}|=|\aleph _{0}| for each n\in \omega . Therefore, the set of real numbers is a countable union of countable sets (38 is false).
In \mathcal{M}9, form 38 is false. References Feferman/Levy [1963], Cohen [1966] (p 143), Jech [1973b] (p 142).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 0.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 38.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, (383).

\mathcal{M}10: Derrick/Drake Model. Let \mathcal{M} be a model of ZF + GCH. Add to \mathcal{M} generic functions f_{n} for each n\in \omega , where f_{n}:\omega _{n}\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(w), but do not add \{f_{n}:n\in \omega \}. It is shown that in this model \aleph (2^{\aleph _{0}})=\aleph _{\omega } (56 is false). (\aleph (x) is the smallest ordinal that is not similar to a subset of x, Hartogs’ function.) (In fact, for every \alpha >0, it is consistent with ZF that \aleph (2^{\aleph _{0}})=\aleph _{\alpha }.) It is shown by Truss that in \mathcal{M}10 the sequence \{\aleph _{n}:n\in \omega \} has two distinct minimal upper bounds 2^{\aleph _{0}} and \aleph _{\omega }. (275 is false). Truss also proves that there is a well ordered set of sets that does not have a choice function (40 is false) and that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is false.
In \mathcal{M}10, forms 40, 43, 56, 91 and 275 are false. References Derrick/Drake [1967b], Mathias [1979] p 125, Truss [1974b], note 18.
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 0.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 43, 56, 91, 275.
A list of all forms known to be true in the model: 0, (383).

\mathcal{M}11: Forti/Honsell Model. Using a model of ZF + V = L for the ground model, the authors construct a generic extension, \mathcal{M}, using Easton forcing which adds \kappa generic subsets to each regular cardinal \kappa . (See Easton [1970].) Then, \mathcal{M}11 is a symmetric submodel of \mathcal{M}. In this model, the Kinna-Wagner Principle (15) and the Axiom of Choice for a family of well orderable sets (60) are true, but for any partially ordered set (X,\,\precsim ) there is a bijection f:X\rightarrow Y such that for all x,\, y\in X,\,x\precsim \ y\leftrightarrow |f(x)|\leq |f(y)| (105 is false). Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 163 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) is also false because 43 implies 8 and 8 + 163 implies AC (Brunner [1982a]). Form 15 implies the Ordering Principle (30) and form 60 implies that every linearly ordered set that is almost well orderable is well orderable (294). (See note 25 for definitions.) However, 30 + 144 (Every set is almost well orderable.) + 231 iff AC. Thus, form 144 is false.
\mathcal{M}11 \models 15, 60, and 165, but 91, 105, 133, 144, 152, and 163 are false. References Forti/Honsell [1985], Brunner [1982a], Easton [1970], notes 25 and 120(6, 34, and 43).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 15, 60, 165.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 91, 105, 144, 152, 163.

\mathcal{M}12(\aleph ): Truss’ Model I. This is a variation of Solovay’s model, \mathcal{M}5(\aleph ) in which \aleph is singular. (Truss uses the method of collapsing cardinal which is due to A. Levy, but, unlike \mathcal{M}5, \aleph is not an inaccessible cardinal.) Let \mathcal{M} be a countable model of ZF + V = L and let \aleph be a limit cardinal in \mathcal{M}. For each ordinal \alpha , the set of conditions Q^{\alpha } is the set of finite sets p of triples, (\beta ,\,n,\,\gamma ) where \gamma <\beta <\alpha and n\in \omega such that if (\beta ,\,n,\,\gamma _{1}), (\beta ,\,n,\,\gamma _{2})\in p, then \gamma _{1}=\gamma _{2}. Q_{\alpha } is the set of finite sets p of pairs of the form (n,\,\gamma ) where \gamma <\alpha and n\in \omega such that if (n,\,\gamma _{1}), (n,\, \gamma _{2})\in p then \gamma _{1}=\gamma _{2}. A function f: \omega \rightarrow \alpha is called an \mathcal{M}-generic collapsing map if the set of finite subsets of \{(n,\,\gamma ):f(n)=\gamma \} is an \mathcal{M}-generic subset of Q_{\alpha }. Let G be an \mathcal{M}-generic subset of Q^{\aleph } then, G_{\alpha }, the projection of G onto Q_{\alpha } is an \mathcal{M}-generic subset of Q_{\alpha }, for each \alpha < \aleph . Let f_{\alpha }=\bigcup G_{\alpha }. Then \mathcal{M}12(\aleph ) is the smallest model of ZF containing the same ordinals as \mathcal{M} and each \langle f_{\beta }:\beta <\alpha \rangle for \alpha <\aleph . In \mathcal{M}12(\aleph ), \aleph =\omega _{1}. If \aleph is singular, \omega _{1} is singular so 34 is false. On the other hand, the union of a denumerable set of denumerable sets of reals is denumerable (6 is true) and the union of a well ordered set of well orderable sets can be well ordered (231 is true). \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\omega )) cannot be linearly ordered, so 30 is false. Truss also proves that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is false, every set of reals is Borel (273 is false), and every uncountable set of reals has a perfect subset (169 is false). Form 40 (C(WO,\,\infty )) is false because 40 implies 31 and form 122 (C(WO,\, <\aleph _{0})) is true because 231 implies 122. Therefore, form 328 (MC(WO,\,\infty )) is false because 122 + 328 \rightarrow 40
\mathcal{M}12(\aleph )\models 6 and 231, but 30, 31, 34, 43, 106, 152, 169, 273, and 328 are false. References Truss [1974b] and note 43 and 120(43 and 55).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 6, 231.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 30, 34, 106, 152, 169, 273, 328.

\mathcal{M}13: Feferman/Solovay Model. This model is an extension of \mathcal{M}2 in which there are \omega _{1} generic real numbers, but no set to collect them. Solovay has shown that in this model, the Axiom of Choice for a well ordered family of sets (40) and the Principle of Dependent Choices (DC, 43) are true, while the extension of DC to \omega _{1} (44) is false. Since 40 implies 8 (C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )), it follows from Brunner [1982a] that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.)
\mathcal{M}13 \models 40, 43, and 165, but 44, 67, 91, 152 and 163 are false. References Felgner [1971a] p 166, Brunner [1982a], notes 18 and 120(41, 34 and 46).
(A minimal list of forms implying each form known to be true in the model: 40, 165.
A minimal list of forms at least one of which is implied by each form known to be false in the model: 44, 91, 152, 163.

\mathcal{M}14: Morris’ Model. This is an extension of Mathias’ model, \mathcal{M}3. Morris shows that the cofinal subsets of the partially ordered set b, the set of generic reals, can be systematically well ordered. He then proves that in this model, the Cofinality Principle (51) and the Ordering Principle (30) are true, but the Order Extension Principle (49) is false. Forms 30 and 294 (Every linearly ordered W-set is well orderable.) are both true in this model (51 implies 294). Since 30 + 294 + 144 (Every set is a W-set.) implies AC, it follows that 144 is false. (See note 25 for definitions.)
