sec.title: NOTE 4
sec.p: Form 73 \rightarrow [73 A]. (Form 73 is: For every A\subseteq \mathbb{R} and x\in \mathbb{R} the following definitions are equivalent:

def.p: x is in the closure of A iff every neighborhood of x intersects A.
x is in the closure of A if there is a sequence \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A such that \lim x_{n}=x.

sec.p: and form [73 A] is: For all A\subseteq \mathbb{R},\,x\in A and f: A\rightarrow \mathbb{R} the following are equivalent:

def.p: (\forall \epsilon )(\exists \delta )(\forall y\in A)(|y-x|<\delta implies |f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon )
Whenever \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A and \lim x_{n}=x then \lim f(x_{n})=f(x).)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Assume Form 73. Fix A\subseteq \mathbb{R} and x\in A. The fact that part (1) of [73 A] implies part (2) of [73 A] is clear. Assume (2) of [73 A] and \neg (1) of [73 A]. Then \exists \epsilon \,\forall \delta \,\exists y\in A such that |y-x|<\delta and |f(x)-f(y)|\geq \epsilon . Let B=\{y\in A:|f(x)-f(y)|\geq \epsilon \}. Every neighborhood of x intersects B. By form 73, x= \lim x_{n} for some sequence \{x_{n}\}\subseteq B(\subseteq A). But \lim f(x_{n})\neq f(x) contradicting part (2) of [73 A].

sec.title: NOTE 5
sec.p: [73 A] \rightarrow form 74. (See note 4 for a statement of [73 A]. Form 74 is: For every A\subseteq \mathbb{R} the following are equivalent:

def.p: A is closed and bounded.
Every sequence \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A has a convergent subsequence with limit in A.)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Assume [73 A]. The usual proof that part (1) of form 74 implies part (2) doesn’t require any choice. So assume A\subseteq \mathbb{R} and A satisfies (2) of 74 but not (1) of 74. Assume first that A is bounded. Then A is not closed so there is an x_{0}\not \in A such that every neighborhood of x_{0} intersects A. Define f: A\cup \{x_{0}\}\rightarrow \mathbb{R} by f(x)=1 if x\in A and f(x)=0 if x=x_{0}. Then (1) of [73 A] fails (with \epsilon =1) so there is a sequence \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A \cup \{x_{0}\} such that \lim f(x_{n})\neq f(x_{0}). This means we can assume \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A (replacing \{x_{n}\} by a subsequence if necessary). By (2) of form 74, \lim x_{n}\in A that is x_{0}\in A, a contradiction. Now assume that A is unbounded. Let f be a monotone, increasing function from the interval (-1,1) one to one, onto \mathbb{R} which satisfies (\forall a,\,b\in (-1,1))(|a-b|\leq |f(a)-f(b)|). (For example, f(x)=\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}} would work.) Then f^{-1}(A) is bounded and satisfies (2) of 74 because if \{x_{n}\} is a sequence in f^{-1}(A), then \{f(x_{n})\} is a sequence in A. Since A satisfies (2) of 74, \{f(x_{n})\} has a convergent subsequence with limit in A. Using the property which we required f to have we infer that f^{-1} applied to the convergent subsequence mentioned above gives a convergent subsequence of \{x_{n}\} with limit in f^{-1}(A). Since we have proved (2) of 74 implies (1) of 74 for bounded sets we conclude that f^{-1}(A) is closed. Hence there are numbers a and b such that -1<a<b<1 and (\forall x\in f^{-1}(A))(a<x<b). Since f is monotone increasing (\forall x\in A)(f(a)<x<f(b)). Hence A is bounded.

sec.title: NOTE 6
sec.p: [73 A] \rightarrow form 73. (See note 4 for a statements of forms 73 and [73 A].)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Assume [73 A] and assume A\subseteq \mathbb{R} and x_{0}\in \mathbb{R} satisfy part (1) of 73 but not (2) of 73 (This means x_{0}\not \in A). Then

Define f:A \cup \{x_{0}\}\rightarrow \mathbb{R} by f(x)=1 if x\in A and f(x)=0 if x=x_{0}. By (\ast ), if \{x_{n}\} converges to x_{0} and \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A \cup \{x_{0}\} then \{x_{n}\} is eventually constant and equal to x_{0}. Therefore, \lim f(x_{n})=f(x_{0}). Therefore, (2) of [73 A] holds (with A of [73 A] equal to A \cup \{x_{0}\} of the present proof). Hence (1) of [73 A] holds, which means (\exists \delta >0)(\forall x\in A\cup \{x_{0}\})(|x-x_{0}|<\delta \rightarrow |f(x)-f(x_{0})|<1). But by (1) of 73, the set B=\{x:|x-x_{0}|<\delta \}\cap A\neq \emptyset . Choose y\in B, then y\neq x_{0},\, y\in A and |1-0|=|f(y)-f(x)|<1, a contradiction.

sec.title: NOTE 7
sec.p: In this note we prove that form 43 (Dependent Choice) implies form 113 (A countable product of compact topological spaces is compact.) Our proof is based on the proof of theorem 6.1 in Good/Tree [1995]. Let \{X_{\alpha }:\alpha <\omega \} be a countable set of compact topological spaces. Let X=\prod _{\alpha \in \omega }X_{\alpha } and for \beta <\omega define p_{\beta }:X\rightarrow \prod _{\alpha \leq \beta }X_{\alpha } by p_{\beta } (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ) =(x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots ,\,x_{\beta }). To show that X is compact let \mathcal{C} be a collection of closed sets in X with the finite intersection property. We will use Dependent Choice to choose a sequence (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ) with the property that for all \alpha <\omega ,\,(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\, x_{\alpha })\in \bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}. Then we will prove, as in Good/Tree [1995], that (x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots ) \in \bigcap \mathcal{C}.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If x_{0}\in X_{0} and \alpha <\kappa we say x_{0} can be extended to level \alpha if there is a sequence (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\alpha }) such that (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\, x_{\alpha })\in \bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}. Similarly, if \alpha <\beta <\kappa and (x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots ,\,x_{\alpha })\in \bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\} then we say (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\alpha }) can be extended to level \beta if there is a sequence (y_{\alpha +1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{\beta }) such that (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\alpha },\,y_{\alpha +1},\,\ldots ,\, y_{\beta })\in \cap \{\overline{p_{\beta }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If \beta \leq \gamma <\kappa define
by

For every \alpha <\kappa , let X_{0,\alpha }=\{x\in X_{0}:x can be extended to level \alpha }. X_{0,\alpha } is closed in X_{0} because X_{0,\alpha }=p_{0,\alpha } (\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}) and

def.p: \prod _{0\leq \beta \leq \alpha }X_{\beta }=X_{0}\times \prod _{1\leq \beta \leq \alpha }X_{\beta } is compact.
\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\} is closed in \prod _{0\leq \beta \leq \alpha }X_{\beta }.
If Y and Z are compact topological spaces and D is closed in Y\times Z then the projection of D onto Y is closed.

statement.p: We also note that X_{0,\alpha }\neq \emptyset since \bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\} is non-empty (by the compactness of \prod _{0\leq \beta \leq \alpha }X_{\beta }). We can conclude that the family \{X_{0,\alpha }:\alpha <\kappa \} has the finite intersection property since X_{0,\alpha _{1}} \cap \ldots \cap X_{0,\alpha _{k}}=X_{0,\alpha } where \alpha =\max \{\alpha _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\alpha _{k}\}. Since X_{0} is compact \bigcap _{\alpha <\kappa }X_{0,\alpha }\neq \emptyset . Choose x_{0} \in \bigcap _{\alpha <\kappa }X_{0,\alpha }.

Assume that x_{0},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\beta } have been chosen so that (x_{0},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\beta }) is extendible to level \alpha for every \alpha such that \beta <\alpha <\kappa . For every such \alpha , let X_{\beta +1,\alpha }=\{x\in X_{\beta +1}:(x_{0},\, \ldots ,\,x_{\beta },\,x) is extendible to level \alpha }.

statement.label: Claim.
statement.p: X_{\beta +1,\alpha } is closed.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: First note that

\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\} is closed in \prod _{\gamma \leq \alpha }X_{\gamma }=\Big (\prod _{\gamma \leq \beta +1}X_{\gamma }\Big )\times \Big (\coprod _{\beta +1<\gamma \leq \alpha }X_{\gamma }\Big ). Therefore, by C. above, p_{\beta +1,\alpha } (\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}) is closed. Assume y\in X_{\beta +1} is in the closure of X_{\beta +1,\alpha }. We will complete the proof of the claim by showing that y\in X_{\beta +1,\alpha }. Let N be a neighborhood of (x_{0},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\beta },\,y) in \prod _{\gamma \leq \beta +1}X_{\gamma }. Then the projection of N onto X_{\beta +1} is a neighborhood of y. Therefore there is an x\in X_{\beta +1,\alpha } such that x is in this projection and therefore, the sequence (x_{0},\,\ldots ,\, x_{\beta },\,x) is in N. Also (x_{0},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\beta },\,x) is in p_{\beta +1,\alpha }(\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}). This shows that (x_{0},\,\ldots ,\, x_{\beta },\,y) is in the closure of p_{\beta +1,\alpha }(\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}) and hence (x_{0},\, \ldots ,\,x_{\beta },\,y) is in p_{\beta +1,\alpha }(\bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}). y is therefore in X_{\beta +1,\alpha }.

sec.p: As above, the family \{X_{\beta +1,\alpha }:\beta <\alpha <\kappa \} has the finite intersection property. Since X_{\beta +1} is compact, \bigcap _{\beta <\alpha <\kappa }X_{\beta +1,\alpha }\neq \emptyset . Choose x_{\beta +1}\in \bigcap _{\beta <\alpha <\kappa }X_{\beta +1,\alpha }.

The argument that (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ) is in \bigcap \mathcal{C} is by contradiction. Suppose the assertion is false. Then there is an open set U=\prod _{\alpha <\omega }U_{\alpha } and C\in \mathcal{C} such that (x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots ) \in U and U\cap C=\emptyset . Choose \gamma \in \omega so that U_{\alpha }=X_{\alpha } whenever \alpha >\gamma , and let V=\prod _{\alpha \leq \gamma }U_{\alpha }. V is open in \prod _{\alpha \leq \gamma }X_{\alpha }. Further (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\gamma })\in V hence V\cap p_{\gamma }(C)\neq \emptyset . This means that there is some sequence (y_{0},\,y_{1},\,\ldots ) \in C with (y_{0},\,y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{\gamma })\in V. Which (by definition of V) implies that (y_{0},\, y_{1},\,\ldots ) \in U. This contradicts U\cap C=\emptyset .

statement.p: Assume (\ast ) and suppose that x is a set which is infinite and not Dedekind infinite. Then by (\ast ), Y=\mathcal{P}(x) is infinite and Dedekind finite. Applying (\ast ) again, z=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(x)) is infinite and Dedekind finite. But \{A_{n}:n\in \omega \} is a denumerable subset of z where A_{n}=\{t\subseteq x:|t|=n\}, a contradiction. sec.title: NOTE 10
sec.p: [73 A] is equivalent to [73 B]. (See note 4 for a statement of [73 A]. Form [73 B] is: (\forall f:\mathbb{R}\,\rightarrow \mathbb{R})(\forall x\in \mathbb{R}) the following are equivalent:

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Clearly [73 A] implies [73 B]. Assume [73 B] and assume that [73 A] fails. Then \exists A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\, \exists x_{0}\in A and \exists f:A\rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that (2) of [73 A] holds but (1) of [73 A] fails. Define g:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} by g(x)=f(x) if x\in A and g(x)=f(x_{0}) if x\not \in A. Then (2) of [73 B] holds for g so (1) of [73 B] holds for g. This implies that (1) of [73 A] holds for f.

sec.title: NOTE 11
sec.p: Form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite) is equivalent to [9 C] (The image of a Dedekind finite set is Dedekind finite.)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Clearly form 9 implies [9 C]. By note 8 (above) to prove [9 C] implies 9, it suffices to prove [9 C] implies [9 A]. Assume [9 C] and that x is an infinite, Dedekind finite set and that \mathcal{P}(x) is Dedekind infinite. Then there is a one to one function f:\omega \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x).

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: We may assume that (\forall i,\,j\in \omega )(i\neq j implies f(i) \cap f(j)=\emptyset ).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: If g:\omega \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x) is one to one, then we define f:\omega \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x) by induction so that for each i\in \omega ,\,f(i)\cap f(j)=\emptyset for all j<i, and such that the set algebra generated by \{g(k)\cap (x-\bigcup _{j\leq i}f(j)):k>j\} is infinite, f(0) is defined as follows: Either the set algebra generated by \{g(k)\,\cap \,g(0):k>0\} is infinite or the set algebra generated by \{g(k)\,\cap \,(x-g(0)):k>0\} is infinite. If the latter is true then f(0)=g(0). If the latter is false then f(0)=x-g(0). Suppose that f(i) has been defined for every i<n satisfying the required conditions. Then for some k (and we take the least such) g(k) \cap (x-\bigcup _{j<n}f(j))\neq \emptyset (call this set A) and (x-\bigcup _{j<n}f(j))-g(k)\neq \emptyset (call this set B). Since A\cup B=(x-\bigcup _{j<n}f(j)), one of the two set algebras, either that generated by \{g(k)\,\cap \,A:k>n\} or that generated by \{g(k)\,\cap \, B:k>n\}, is infinite. If the latter is the case, let f(k)=A. If the latter fails, let f(k)=B. This completes the proof of the lemma.

sec.p: Form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite) and [9 D] (The union of a Dedekind finite family of finite sets is Dedekind finite) are equivalent.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: It is clear that form 9 implies [9 D]. Since 9 and [9 A] are equivalent (see note 8.) it suffices to show that [9 D] implies [9 A]. Assume [9 D] and that x is a set which is Dedekind finite such that \mathcal{P}(x) is Dedekind infinite. Then there is a one to one function f:\omega \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x) and, as in note 11, we may assume that (\forall i,\,j\in \omega )(i\neq j implies f(i) \cap f(j)=\emptyset ). sec.title: NOTE 13
sec.p: The fact that form 39 does not imply form 43 follows from the theorem of Jensen mentioned in Mathias [1979] p. 123 and proved in Felgner [1971a]:

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: If \alpha is an infinite cardinal in a countable standard model M of ZF+V=L then M can be extended to an model N of ZF with the same ordinals and (well ordered) cardinals as M in which C(\alpha ,\,\infty ) (form 39) is true and DC(\omega ) (form 43) is false.

sec.title: NOTE 14
sec.p: Form 40 does not imply form 44 by the following theorem which is proved in Jech [1966b]:

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Let M be a countable standard model for ZF+AC and \alpha a regular, infinite cardinal in M. Then there is a model N of ZF containing M with the same ordinals as M such that in N,\,\neg DC(\alpha ) (see form 87), \neg C(\alpha ,\,2) and there is a cardinal incomparable with \alpha . But for every \beta <\alpha ,\,DC(\beta ) and C(\beta ,\,\infty ) hold and \beta is comparable with every cardinal.

sec.title: NOTE 15
sec.p: Finite axioms of choice: C(\infty ,\,n),C(LO,\,n),C(WO,\,n),C(\infty ,\,\in Z),C(LO, \in Z),C(WO,\,\in Z) and C(\aleph _{0},\,n), (forms 45, 33, 47, 46, 120, 48, and 288 respectively) and generalizations have been studied extensively in Blass [1984b], Conway [1971], Gauntt [1970] and [1968], Mostowski [1958], Truss [1973a], Wiśniewski [1972a] and Zuckerman [1971]. Here is a summary of the results. (See Truss [1973a] for more details.)

Until further notice n\in \omega and Z is a finite subset of \omega . The first two of the following conditions on the pair (n,\,Z) were introduced by Mostowski in [1958] and the third by Gauntt in [1970].
D(n,\,Z). For any subgroup G of S_{n} (the symmetric group on n) without fixed points, there is a subgroup H of G and proper subgroups K_{1},\,\ldots ,\,K_{r}of H such that \Sigma |H:K_{i}|\in Z.

K(n,\,Z). For any subgroup G of S_{n} without fixed points, there is a subgroup H of G^{\omega } (the restricted direct product of countably many copies of G) and proper subgroups K_{1},\,\ldots ,\, K_{r} of H such that \Sigma |H:K_{i}|\in Z
L(n,\,Z). For any subgroup G of S_{n} without fixed points, there are proper subgroups K_{1},\, \ldots ,\,K_{r} of G such that \Sigma |G:K_{i}|\in Z.
Blass [1984b] has noticed that L(n,\,Z) is can be formulated as follows:
Every group that can act without fixed points on an n element set can also act without fixed points on a k element set for at least one k\in Z.
The equivalence of the two conditions is based on the following:

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Suppose that H is a group and A is a set of cardinality k then H acts without fixed points on A\Leftrightarrow there are proper subgroups J_{1},\,\ldots ,\, J_{r} of H (not necessarily distinct) such that \Sigma |H:J_{i}|=k.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: (Outline) (\Rightarrow ) If H acts without fixed points on A, let A_{1},\,\ldots ,\,A_{r} be the orbits of elements of A under the action. Then |A_{i}|\geq 2 and \Sigma |A_{i}|=k. If, for each i,\, 1\leq i\leq r we choose a_{i}\in A_{i} and let J_{i} be the subgroup of H consisting of those elements that fix a_{i} then J_{i} is proper and |H:J_{i}|=|A_{i}|.
(\Leftarrow ) Let A be the disjoint union of the left cosets of the J_{i},\,1\leq i\leq r. Then H acts on A without fixed points.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: D(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(\infty ,\,Z)\rightarrow C(\infty ,\,n). (\Leftarrow Gauntt [1970], \Rightarrow Mostowski [1958])

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: L(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(WO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n). (Gauntt [1968])

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: K(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(\infty ,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n). (\Rightarrow Truss [1973a], \Leftarrow Mostowski [1958])

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: L(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(LO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(LO,\,n). (Truss [1973a])

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: ZF\vdash C(LO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(WO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n). (Truss [1973a])

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: ZF\vdash C(\infty ,\,Z)\rightarrow C(LO,\,n)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(\infty ,\,Z)\rightarrow C(\infty ,\,n). (Truss [1973a])

The finite axioms of choice have been generalized in Conway [1971] as follows:

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let k be a natural number.

def.p: An ordered k-tuple (A,\,B,\,C,\,\ldots ) of disjoint finite sets of cardinalities a,\,b,\,\ldots respectively is called an (a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots ) set.
[a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots ] is the axiom: For every collection of (a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots ) sets there is a function f defined on the collection such that f(A,\,B,\,C,\,\ldots ) \in A\cup B \cup C \cup \cdots
\langle a,\, b,\,c,\,\ldots \rangle is the additive semi-group generated by a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots (I. e., the closure of \{a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots \} under addition.)

If S=\langle a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots \rangle then [S] denotes the axiom [a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots ]. (by result I below, if \langle a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots \rangle and \langle \alpha ,\,\beta ,\,\gamma \ldots \rangle are equal then [a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots ] and [\alpha ,\,\beta ,\,\gamma ,\,\ldots ] are equivalent.)
If G is any finite group, \langle G\rangle \subseteq \mathbb{N} is the semi-group generated by the indices in G of all proper subgroups of G.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (Some parts due to Mostowski)

def.p: If \langle \alpha ,\,\beta ,\,\gamma ,\,\ldots \rangle \subseteq \langle a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots \rangle then [\alpha ,\, \beta ,\,\gamma ,\,\ldots ]\Rightarrow [a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots ].
to hold it suffices that every group G with S\subseteq \langle G\rangle has some subgroup H for which S_{i}\subseteq \langle H\rangle for some i,\,1\leq i\leq N.
(Mostowski) For (\ast ) to hold it is necessary that every Abelian group G with S\subseteq \langle G\rangle have some subgroup H with S_{i}\subseteq \langle H\rangle for some i,\,1\leq i\leq N.

The condition of II is necessary and sufficient for effective implication, that is, for the existence of a formula F(f_{1},\,\ldots ,\,f_{N})=f which defines a choice function f for the class of all S sets whenever we substitute such choice functions for the classes of all S_{1} sets, S_{2} sets, \ldots , S_{N} sets for f_{1},\,f_{2},\ldots ,f_{N}.

sec.p: The following are proved in Wiśniewski [1972a]:

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Let P be the additive semi-group of positive integers generated by a set Z of prime numbers (P consists of sums of the form p_{1}+p_{2}+\cdots +p_{k} where p_{i},\, i=1,\,\ldots ,\,k are in Z.) Then there is a model \mathcal{N} of ZF^{0} in which C(\infty ,\,n) is true for all n\not \in P and C(\aleph _{0},\,n) is false for all n\in P.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Let G be a finite group, Q(G) the additive semi-group of positive integers generated by the indices of proper subgroups of G in G and R(G) the additive semi-group of positive integers generated by the orders of non-identity elements of G. Then there is a model \mathcal{N} of ZF^{0} in which C(LO,\,n) is true for all n\not \in Q(G), C(\infty ,\, n) is false for all n\not \in R(G) and C(\aleph _{0},\,n) is false for all n\in Q(G).

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Let p and q be primes such that p_{1}=(p^{q}-1)/(p-1) is prime. Then there is a model \mathcal{N} of ZF^{0} in which

def.p: C(LO,\,n) is true for n of the form kp_{1}+rp^{q}
C(\infty ,\,n) is false for n of the form kp+rq
C(\aleph _{0},\,n) is false for n of the form kp_{1}+rp^{q}.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: If for every prime p there are infinitely many primes of the form (p^{q}-1)/(p-1) then there is a model \mathcal{N} of ZF^{0} where C(\aleph _{0},\,n) is true for every n and C(\infty ,\,n) is false for every n>1.

sec.p: Note. The Mersenne Prime conjecture (there are infinitely many primes of the form 2^{n}-1) is a special case of the hypotheses of this theorem.
Along the same lines Zuckerman [1971] proves

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Let Z be any set of primes and P the additive semigroup of positive integers generated by Z. Then there is a model \mathcal{N} of ZF^{0} in which form 67 (the axiom of multiple choice, MC(\infty ,\,\infty )) is true and for every n\in \omega ,\,n>1,\,C(\infty ,\,n) is true if and only if n\in P.

sec.title: NOTE 16
sec.p: This note contains the definitions necessary to understand the forms in Brunner [1984d], that is, form 126.

def.p: A B-lattice is a vector lattice (see below for the definition of vector lattice) together with a Frechet-complete (Cauchy sequences are convergent) Riez-norm \Vert \cdot \Vert (i.e., (i) -y\leq x\leq y\rightarrow \Vert x\Vert \leq \Vert y\Vert (ii) if \Vert x\Vert \leq 1 there is a y\geq 0 such that -y\leq x\leq y and \Vert y\Vert \leq 1.)
A positive linear functional on X is a linear mapping f: X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that f(x)\geq 0 when x\geq 0.
A wedge W in a real linear space L is a convex set such that t\subseteq W for every t\geq 0\ (t\in \mathbb{R}). A cone is a wedge which contains no line through 0.

An ordered linear space (OSL) is a linear space L in which some wedge W, called the positive wedge has been, specified. The partial ordering \leq on L is defined by y\leq x iff x-y\in W. (Note that this differs from the definition of ordered vector space in note 31.)

(Facts: (a) \leq is reflexive & transitive (b) translation and multiplication by positive numbers preserves order, multiplication by negative numbers reverses order, (c) (x\geq y and y\geq x implies y=x) if and only if the wedge is a cone. (d) x\geq 0 iff x\in W. If a relation satisfies (a) and (b) then (d) defines a wedge.)

Let V be a partially ordered linear space with a positive wedge (defined). V is a vector lattice if the positive wedge in V is a cone and if each set \{x,\,x^{\prime }\} of two elements has a least upper bound x\vee x^{\prime }. These definitions are taken primarily from Day [1973].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: An \epsilon lattice in a metric space (X,dist) is a maximal subset L of X which satisfies (\forall x,\,y\in L)(\mathrm{dist}(x,\,y)\geq \epsilon for x\neq y). From Brunner [1984e]. See [1 I].
