sec.title: NOTE 19
sec.p: It is clear that König’s lemma, [10 F] implies [10 K] and using the usual proof that the Completeness Theorem implies the Compactness Theorem, it follows that [10 K] implies [10 L]. To show that [10 L] implies 10, C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}), let X=\{x_{i}: i\in \omega \} be a denumerable set of finite sets, where each x_{i}=\{x_{i,0},\,x_{i,1},\,\cdots x_{i,n_{i}}\}. Let \mathcal{L} be a first order language with a single function symbol f and constant symbols for each x_{i}\in X and each element x_{i,j} of \bigcup X. Let S be the following set of sentence in \mathcal{L}: For each i\in \omega , the conjunction of
\wedge (\{x_{i,j}\neq x_{i,k}:j,\,k\leq n_{i} and j\neq k\}) and
Each finite subset of S has a model, so [10 L] implies that the denumerable set of sentences has a model. In that model, f is a choice function on X.

sec.title: NOTE 20
sec.p: We give some definitions and properties of inaccessible cardinals. (Proofs of the results given below can be found in Drake [1974].)

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A cardinal \kappa is (strongly) inaccessible if \kappa is regular and for all \mu <\kappa ,\, 2^{\mu }<\kappa . (An inaccessible cardinal is also called a strong limit cardinal.)

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: No successor cardinal, \aleph _{\alpha +1}, is inaccessible. (This is form [0 AJ].)

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: \mu is called a 2-valued, \kappa -additive (complete) measure on x if \mu is a function from x to \{0,1\} such that

def.p: If y=\bigcup _{\alpha <\kappa }x_{\alpha }\subseteq x is a disjoint union, then \mu (y)=\sum \nolimits _{\alpha \in \kappa }\mu (x_{\alpha }).

statement.p: (The measure is called non-trivial if the measure of a one-element set is 0.)

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A cardinal \kappa is said to be measurable if \kappa >\aleph _{0} and \kappa has a 2-valued \kappa -additive non-trivial measure.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (ZFC) Every measurable cardinal is inaccessible. (Form 319.)

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A filter is \kappa -additive (complete) if the intersection of <\kappa members of the filter is in the filter.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: A cardinal \kappa is measurable iff there is a non-principal ultrafilter on \kappa which is \kappa -additive.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A measure \mu on \kappa is normal if \mu is a non-trivial \kappa -additive measure on \kappa such that for any function f:\kappa \rightarrow \kappa that is regressive (i.e., such that f(\alpha )<\alpha for all \alpha <\kappa ,\,\alpha \neq 0) there is a \beta <\kappa such that \mu (\{\alpha <\kappa :f(\alpha )=\beta \})=1 (i.e., every regressive function on \kappa is constant on a set of measure 1).

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If X=\langle X_{\alpha }:\alpha <\kappa \rangle is \kappa -sequence of subsets of \kappa , the diagonal intersection, D(X)=\bigcap _{\alpha <\kappa }(X_{\alpha }\cup \alpha +1)=\{\beta <\kappa :\forall \alpha <\beta (\beta \in X_{\alpha }\}.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: \mu is normal iff the diagonal intersection of any \kappa -sequence of sets of measure 1 is also of measure 1.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (ZFC) If \kappa is measurable then \kappa has a normal measure.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If \kappa and \lambda are cardinals, \mathcal{L}_{\kappa ,\lambda } is the language obtained by adding infinite conjunctions and disjunctions of cardinality less than \kappa and infinite quantifications of blocks of variables of cardinal less than \lambda . (The ordinary first-order language is equivalent to \mathcal{L}_{\omega ,\omega }.)

def.p: A cardinal \kappa >\aleph _{0} is weakly compact if the language \mathcal{L}_{\kappa ,\kappa } is (\kappa ,\,\kappa )-compact, i.e., if \Gamma is a set of sentences of \mathcal{L}_{\kappa ,\kappa } with cardinality \leq \kappa and every subset of \Gamma of cardinality <\kappa has a model, then \Gamma has a model.

A cardinal \kappa >\aleph _{0} is strongly compact if \mathcal{L}_{\kappa ,\kappa } is compact, i.e., if \Gamma is any set of formulas of \mathcal{L}_{\kappa ,\kappa } such that every subset of \Gamma of cardinality <\kappa has a model, then \Gamma has a model.
For n\in \omega ,\,[X]^{n} is the set of all n-element subsets of X, and [X]^{<\omega }, is the set of all finite subsets of X.

The partition relation \kappa \rightarrow (\kappa )^{n} holds iff for every function f:[\kappa ]^{n}\rightarrow 2 there is an unbounded subset X of \kappa such that f/[X]^{2} is constant. (The set X is called homogeneous for f.)

The partition relation \kappa \rightarrow (\kappa )^{<\omega } holds iff for every function f:[\kappa ]^{<\omega }\rightarrow 2 there is an unbounded subset X of \kappa such that f is constant on [X]^{n} for every n\in \omega .

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (ZFC) If \kappa is inaccessible, then \kappa is weakly compact iff \kappa \rightarrow (\kappa )^{2}.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: (ZFC) Every measurable cardinal is weakly compact.

sec.p: (Bull [1978] defines a measurable cardinal as a cardinal that has a normal measure. With this definition, ZF \vdash Every measurable cardinal is weakly compact.)

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (ZFC) If \kappa is a regular infinite cardinal, \kappa is strongly compact iff for any \kappa -complete filter J on a set X,\,J can be extended to a \kappa -complete ultrafilter on X.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: (ZFC) Every strongly compact cardinal is measurable.

def.p: \mathcal{P}_{\kappa }(\lambda ) is the set of all subsets of \lambda of cardinality <\kappa .

Let X=\mathcal{P}_{\kappa }(\lambda ),(i)
For each \xi <\lambda , let C_{\xi }=\{x\in X:\xi \,\in x\}. An ultrafilter extending the filter \{C_{\xi }:\xi \,<\lambda \} is called a regular ultrafilter. (The measure corresponding to the regular ultrafilter is called a regular measure.)(ii)
A measure \mu on X is called normal if it is \kappa -additive, regular and such that if f(x)\in x for each x\in X, then for some \xi <\lambda ,\,\mu (\{x\in X:f(x)=\xi \})=1.
If \kappa and \lambda are cardinals such that \aleph _{0}<\kappa \leq \lambda ,\,\kappa is \lambda -supercompact if there is a normal measure on \mathcal{P}_{\kappa }(\lambda ).
If \kappa >\aleph _{0},\,\kappa is supercompact if \kappa is \lambda -supercompact for every \lambda \geq \kappa .

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: (ZFC) Every supercompact cardinal is strongly compact.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Form 319 implies form 320. (Use [0 AJ].)

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: \kappa is a Ramsey cardinal iff \kappa \rightarrow (\kappa )^{<\omega }.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Every measurable cardinal is a Ramsey cardinal.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A cardinal \kappa is called a Rowbottom cardinal iff, whenever \mathfrak{A} = \langle A,\,U,\,\cdots \rangle is a structure of countable length, where |A|=\kappa ,\,U\subset A, and |U|<\kappa , then \mathfrak{A} has an elementary substructure \mathfrak{B} =\langle B,\,U^{\prime },\cdots \rangle with |\mathfrak{B}|=\kappa and |U^{\prime }|\leq \aleph _{0}.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Every Ramsey cardinal is a Rowbottom cardinal.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A cardinal \kappa is said to be almost huge iff there is an n\in \omega and a cardinal \lambda >\kappa , a \kappa -additive normal ultrafilter U on 2^{\lambda }, and a sequence \kappa =\lambda _{0}<\lambda _{1}<\cdots <\lambda _{n}=\lambda such that for each i<n,\,\{x\subseteq \lambda :x\cap \, \lambda _{i+1}=\lambda _{i}\}\in U.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Every almost huge cardinal is supercompact.

sec.p: In a series of papers (Apter [1985b], [1988], [1990], [1992] and Apter/Henle [1991]) various consistency results about large cardinals are obtained. We give some examples below.

def.p: Con(ZFC + There exists cardinals \kappa <\lambda such \kappa is \lambda -supercompact and \lambda is measurable) \rightarrow Con(ZF + \mathrm{cof}(\kappa )=\omega +\kappa is a Rowbottom cardinal +\ \kappa ^{+} is a measurable cardinal).
Con(ZFC + There exists an almost huge cardinal) \rightarrow Con(ZF + \aleph _{1} is measurable + All uncountable cardinals are singular).
Con(ZFC + There exists an almost huge cardinal) \rightarrow Con(ZF + \neg C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )\ + An uncountable cardinal is measurable iff it is the successor of a singular cardinal).
Con(ZFC + There exists an almost huge cardinal) \rightarrow Con(ZF +\neg C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )+ \forall \alpha \,\aleph _{\alpha } or \aleph _{\alpha +1} is measurable).
In Bull [1978], besides form 321, there are the following consistency results. Let S be the following statement:

sec.p: S. There are cardinals \aleph _{\alpha }<\aleph _{\beta }<\aleph _{\gamma } such that \aleph _{\alpha } is \aleph _{\gamma }-supercompact; \aleph _{\beta } is the first measurable cardinal greater than \aleph _{\alpha }; and \aleph _{\gamma }=|2^{\aleph _{\beta }}|.

def.p: Con(ZFC + S) \rightarrow Con(ZF + form 43 + \aleph _{1} is weakly compact + \aleph _{2} is measurable).

sec.p: S^{\prime }.: There are cardinals \aleph _{\alpha }<\aleph _{\beta } such that \aleph _{\beta } is the first weakly compact cardinal greater than \aleph _{\alpha } and \aleph _{\alpha } is \aleph _{\beta }-supercompact.

def.p: Con(ZFC + S^{\prime }) \rightarrow Con(ZF + C(\aleph _{\alpha },\,\infty )+\aleph _{\alpha } and \aleph _{\alpha +1} are both weakly compact. (In fact, 2 may be extended to a finite sequence of weakly compact cardinals.)

sec.title: NOTE 21
sec.p: Definitions for forms [10 F], [14 M], [14 N], [43 H], [106 A], 216, and 249.

def.p: A tree is a connected undirected graph without circuits one of whose vertices is designated as the origin.

Note that a tree may also be defined as a partially ordered set (P,\,\leq ) with a least element and with the property that for any element x\in P the set of predecessors of x is a finite set which is linearly ordered by \leq . Every tree in this sense is also a tree in the sense of definition 1 (under the obvious translation) and vice versa. Note also that the definition of tree for form [86 A(\alpha )] in note 119 differs from the definition given above.

The number of vertices on the unique path connecting a vertex v with the origin is the level of v,\,l(v). (Thus the set of vertices of a tree can be decomposed into an at most denumerable set of levels.)
A vertex v^{\prime } is a successor of a vertex v if v and v^{\prime } are connected by an edge and l(v^{\prime })=l(v)+1.
A tree is finite if its set of vertices is finite and locally finite if each vertex has only finitely many successors.
A branch in a tree is a maximal path beginning at the origin. If v and v^{\prime } are on the same branch, then v^{\prime } dominates v if l(v^{\prime })\geq l(v).
Konig’s lemma states that any infinite locally finite tree has an infinite branch.
An \omega -tree is a locally finite tree with at least one vertex of level n for each n\in \omega .
A subtree of a tree (P,\,\leq ) is a subset of P which is a tree under the induced ordering and which is closed under predecessor.

An antichain in a tree (P,\,\leq ) is a subset of P whose elements are pairwise incomparable. (Note that this differs from the definition of antichain used in form [86 A(\alpha )] and given in note 119.)
Let T be a collection of locally finite trees (not necessarily pairwise disjoint).
By a vertex or a level of T, we mean a vertex or a level of some tree in T.
If v and v^{\prime } are vertices of T, then v^{\prime } dominates v in T if v^{\prime } dominates v in some tree in T.
Let S be a set of vertices of T. S pierces a level l of T if |S\cap l|=1.
S is consistent if for every v,\,v^{\prime } in S there is a v^{\prime \prime } which dominates them both in T.

sec.title: NOTE 22
sec.p: Definitions for forms [1 L], [1 M], [1 N], [10 C] and [132 A]. A set mapping f is a function f:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(X) such that for all x\in X,\,x\not \in f(x). A free subset of X (relative to f) is a subset H of X such that for all x,\,y\in H,\,x\not \in f(y). A ramification system is a triple \langle X,\,E,\,S\rangle where X and E are sets and S\,:\,X^{\leq \theta }\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E) (where \theta is an ordinal and X^{\leq \theta } denotes all functions t:\alpha \rightarrow X where \alpha \leq \theta ) satisfies (i) S(\emptyset )=E (ii) If f,\, g\in \mathrm{dom}(S) and f\subseteq g, then S(g)\subseteq S(f) and (iii) If f\in \mathrm{dom}(S) and \eta =\mathrm{dom}(f) is a limit ordinal then S(f)=\bigcap _{\alpha <\eta }S(f/\alpha ).

sec.title: NOTE 23
sec.p: Definitions for forms [14 Q] and [52 E]: If E is a Banach space (complete, normed, linear space) then E^{\ast } (the dual of E) is the space of all bounded linear functionals on E. (That is, all f:E\rightarrow \,\mathbb{R} such that (\exists M)(\forall x\in E)(|f(x)|\leq \Vert x\Vert M). E^{\ast } is a Banach space if we define \Vert f\Vert =\sup _{x\neq 0}\Big (\frac{|f(x)|}{\Vert x\Vert }\Big ). Each x\in E can be thought of as a linear functional on E^{\ast } if we define x(f)=f(x) for all f in E^{\ast }. The weak^{\ast } topology on E^{\ast } is the weakest topology that makes all these linear functionals continuous. Sets of the form w_{x,\epsilon }=\{f\in E^{\ast }:|f(x)|<\epsilon \} form a basis for this topology. If X\subseteq E,\,X is convex-compact if whenever F_{i}, for i\in I, are closed convex subsets of X and \{X\,\cap \,F_{i}:i\in I\} has the finite intersection property, then \bigcap _{i\in I}(X\cap \,F_{i})\neq \emptyset . Note that the definition of convex-compact may be given in any topological vector space.

sec.title: NOTE 24
sec.p: This note contains some definitions from group theory that are used in \mathcal{M}22, and forms [62 C], [62 D], [67 D], 180, and 308.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let G be a group and let p be a prime.

def.p: The Frattini subgroup of G,\,\Phi (G), is the intersection of all maximal subgroups of G.
Let Z(G) be the center of G and G^{\prime }, the commutator subgroup of G.

G is said to be a p-group if for all x\in G there is an n\in \omega such that x^{p^{n}}=1. G is said to have exponent p if for every x\in G,\,x^{p}=1. An Abelian group is said to be elementary if there is a prime p such that every non-identity element has order p. \qquad G is said to be divisible if for each a\in G and for each integer m\neq 0 the equation x^{m}=a has a solution in G and G is called n-divisible if the equation x^{m}=a has a solution for all m<n.
A factor H/K of a series of G is said to be a central factor of G if K is normal in G and H/K is a subgroup of Z(G/K).
G is said to be nilpotent if it has a series all of whose factors are central factors of G.
The class of G is the least integer n such that Z_{n}(G)=G.
G is a special p-group if G is a p-group, G^{\prime }=Z(H)=\Phi (H), and G is either elementary Abelian or nilpotent of class 2.
G is an extra-special p-group if G is special and G^{\prime } is cyclic of order p.
A group is divisible if each element is divisible by each positive integer.
A group is torsion free if the only element of finite order is the identity element.

sec.title: NOTE 25
sec.p: For forms 144 and 179: Let W(0) be the class of well orderable sets and let W(\alpha +1)=\{\bigcup Q:Q\subseteq W(\alpha ) and Q\in W(0)\} and W(\lambda )=\bigcup \{W(\beta ):\beta <\lambda \} for limit ordinals \lambda . Then W (the class of almost well orderable sets) is defined to be \bigcup \{W(\alpha ):\alpha \in \, On\}. See Keisler [1970]. Blass [1977b] has shown that If P\subseteq W and P\in W, then \bigcup P\in W. Regarding the form(s) 179 (\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha )), R. David [1980] shows that for ordinals \alpha and \beta with 0<\alpha <\beta , the statement \forall x,\,x\in W(\beta ) does not imply \forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha ). (Clearly, \forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha ) implies \forall x,\,x\in W(\beta ).) It is clear that 30 + 294 (every linearly ordered W-set can be well ordered) implies that every W-set can be well ordered. Thus, 30 + 294 + 144 (every set is a W-set) implies AC.

sec.title: NOTE 26
sec.p: A summary of the definitions and results from Brunner [1983a]. Brunner considers 16 properties a topological space (X,\,\underline{X}) may have:

def.p: : \underline{X} is w.o. (well ordered);
: X is w.o.;
: X is covered by a w.o. family of closed, discrete sets.
: X is covered by a w.o. family of discrete sets;
: X has a w.o. base
: \exists f:X\times W\rightarrow \underline{X} such that W is w.o. and f^{\prime }\{x\}\times W) is a neighborhood base at x for each x\in X.
: \exists f:X\times W\rightarrow \underline{X} such that W is w.o. and \forall x\in X,\,\{x\}=\bigcap f^{\prime }\{x\}\times W)
: Each open cover of X has a w.o. subcover;
: Each open cover of X has a w.o. refinement;
: X has a dense, w.o. subset;
: Each family O\subseteq \underline{X} of pairwise disjoint sets is w.o.
: If O\subseteq \underline{X} covers X,\,\exists f:X\rightarrow O such that \forall x\in X,\, x\in f(x);
: If O\subseteq \underline{X} covers X,\,\exists f:X\rightarrow \underline{X} s.t. \forall x\in X,\,x\in f(x) and f^{\prime }X refines O;
: X is hereditarily A1;
: X is hereditarily A2;
: X is a continuous finite to one image of an A1 space.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If P is one of the above then A(P) is the statement: “Every topological space (X,\, \underline{X}) is P.” A(P,\,Q) is the statement: “If a topological space satisfies P then it satisfies Q.”

sec.p: All of the A(P)’s occur in the list of forms, but not all the A(P,\,Q)’s occur.

The table below, taken from Brunner [1983a], summarizes the results. In the table, 0 means that A(P,\, Q) (P the row heading and Q the column heading) is provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. N means A(P,\,Q) is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. AC (form 1), MC (form 67) and PW (form 91) mean respectively that A(P,\,Q) is equivalent to AC,\,MC or PW in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. And IMC or IPW mean that A(P,\,Q) implies MC or PW respectively in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

def.p: ZF\vdash A(P)\leftrightarrow AC for all P in the list.
ZF^{0}\vdash A(P)\leftrightarrow AC for P\in \{W1,\,W2,\,B1,\,L1,\,L2,\,S,\,C,\,H1,\,A1\}.
ZF^{0}\vdash A(P)\leftrightarrow MC (form 67) for P\in \{D1,\,B2,\,B3,\,H2,\, A2\}.
ZF^{0}\vdash AC\rightarrow A(F)\rightarrow MC (form 67) \rightarrow A(D2)\rightarrow PW (form 91).

sec.title: NOTE 27
sec.p: Notes on UT(WO,\,\kappa ,\,WO),C(WO,\,\kappa ) and D_{\kappa } from Brunner/Howard [1992].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: D_{\kappa } or D(\kappa ) is the sentence “Every non-well orderable set is the union of a disjoint, well orderable family of \kappa element sets.

sec.p: (Note that UT(WO,\,\kappa ,\,WO), C(WO,\,\kappa ), and D(\kappa ) all depend on the well ordered, infinite cardinal \kappa and that UT(WO,\,<\aleph _{0},\,WO), UT(WO,\,<\aleph _{1},\,WO), and D(\aleph _{0}) are forms [122 A], 151 and 152 respectively.)

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (ZF^{0}) UT(WO,\,\kappa ,\,WO) implies C(WO,\,\kappa ) but does not imply C(\aleph _{0},\, \kappa ^{+}) nor does it imply D(\kappa ^{+}).

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (ZF^{0}) D(\kappa ^{+}) does not imply D(\kappa ).

sec.title: NOTE 28
sec.p: In this note we give definitions for the various versions of the Baire category theorem and summarize the results from Brunner [1983b].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let (X,\,T) be a topological space.

def.p: A set Y\subseteq X is nowhere dense if the closure of Y has empty interior.
A set Y\subseteq X is meager or of the first category if Y is a countable union of nowhere dense sets.
A set Y\subseteq X is perfect if Y is closed, non-empty and has no isolated points.
A set Y\subseteq X has the Baire property if (Y\backslash U)\cup (U\backslash Y) is meager for some open set U.
(X,\,T) is Baire or is a Baire space if the intersection of each countable sequence of dense, open sets in X is dense in X.
(X,\,T) is sequentially complete if every sequence has a convergent subsequence.

(X,\,T) is Čech complete-I if it satisfies(i)
(X,\,T) is regular (every neighborhood of a point x\in S contains a closed neighborhood of x) and(ii)
there is a denumerable collection \{\mathcal{C}_{n}:n\in \omega \} of open covers of X such that for any collection F of closed subsets of X with the finite intersection property, if for each n,\,F contains a subset of diameter less than \mathcal{C}_{n} (that is, (\exists u\in F)(\exists c\in \mathcal{C}_{n})(u\subseteq c)), then F has a non-empty intersection.
(This is the definition of Čech complete used in form [43 E].)
(X,\,T) is Čech complete-II if (X,\, T) is homeomorphic to a G_{\delta } set in a compact, T_{2} space. ( G_{\delta }\equiv countable intersection of open sets.)
(This is the definition of Čech complete used in K9 below. K9 is equivalent to form 106.)

(X,\, T) is co-compact if \exists a family F of closed sets such that(i)
If G\subseteq F and G has the finite intersection property, then \bigcap G\neq \emptyset and(ii)
If x\in \mathcal{O}, with \mathcal{O} open, then \exists A\in F with x\in A^{\circ } (the interior of A) and A\subseteq closure (\mathcal{O}).)
(X,\,T) is scattered or Boolean if it is Hausdorff and has a basis of clopen sets.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let (X, d) be a metric space.

def.p: (X, d) is complete or Frechet complete if Cauchy sequences converge.

(X, d) is Cantor complete if \bigcap _{n\in \omega }A(n)\neq \emptyset for every sequence (A(n))_{n\in \omega } of non-empty closed sets satisfying(i)
(\forall n\in \omega )(A(n+1)\subseteq A(n)) and(ii)
\lim _{n\rightarrow \infty } diameter(A(n))=0.

(X, d) is Kuratowski complete if \bigcap _{n\in \omega }A(n)\neq \emptyset for each nested sequence (A(n))_{n\in \omega } of non-empty closed sets for which a(A(n))\rightarrow 0 where for A\subseteq X,\, a(A)=\inf \{\max \{\mathrm{diameter}(B):B\in Y\}:Y is a finite covering of A}.

(X, d) is filter complete if every Cauchy filter converges.K1
: Every Frechet Complete metric space is Baire. (This is what is usually known as the Baire Category Theorem and is [43 F] in the list of forms.)K2
: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. ([43 J])K3
: Every metric Kuratowski complete space is Baire.K4
: Every sequentially compact metric space is Baire.K5
: Every countably compact (Every countable open cover has a finite subcover.) metric space is Baire.K6
: Banach spaces (complete, normed, linear spaces) are Baire.K7
: Countably compact, regular spaces are Baire.K8
: Compact T_{2}-spaces are Baire. (This is form 106)K9
: Čech complete-II spaces are Baire.K10
: Co-compact, T_{2} spaces are Baire.K11
: Separable, Frechet complete, metric spaces are Baire.K12
: Separable, countably compact, regular spaces are Baire.

statement.p: The following results are proved in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}:K1 and K2 are equivalent to DC. DC (form 43) implies K9 and K10. K1 implies K6. DMC (Dependent Multiple choice, Form [106 A]) implies K3 implies K5. K4 for Cantor complete spaces implies DF=F (form 9). K11 is provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. DMC (form [106 A]) implies K7 implies K8. DMC implies K9 implies K8. DMC implies K10 implies K8. PW (form 91) implies K12.

The following independences are shown to hold in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}:MC
ot ightarrow K4,\, MC
ot ightarrow K6, BPI (Form 14) 
ot ightarrow K8 (Form 106), MC_{\mathrm{LO}} (form 112) 
ot ightarrow K7,\,C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) 
ot ightarrow K8 and none of the following are provable in ZF: Ki,\,i=1,2,4,6,7,8,9,10.
The following questions are asked:
Are the following provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}?: K3,\,K5,\,K12.
Are Ki,\,7\leq i\leq 10, equivalent to DMC (form [106 A]).
In Fossy/Morillon [1995] it is shown that K8 implies DMC from which it follows that Ki,\,7\leq i\leq 10 are all equivalent to DMC.

sec.title: NOTE 29
sec.p: Definitions for forms [14 R] through [14 U], [14 BH] through [14 BL], and [86 B]. See Banaschewski [1981], [1983], [1997], Paseka [1989], and Vickers [1989].

def.p: A local lattice (or frame or complete Heyting algebra) is a complete lattice L satisfying the distribution law: x\bigvee _{i\in I}x_{i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}(x\wedge x_{i}), for all x,\,x_{i}\in L and \{x_{i}:i\in I\}\subseteq L. (Example: \mathcal{D}X - the open sets of a topological space)

A lattice L is spatial if for some topological space X,\,L is isomorphic to \mathcal{D}X. (Theorem. Every complete Boolean algebra is a local lattice. A complete Boolean algebra is a spatial iff it is atomic.)
c\in L (L a local lattice) is compact if and only if c\leq \bigvee _{i\in I}x_{i} implies c\leq x_{i_{1}}\vee \ldots \vee x_{i_{n}}, for some indices i_{1},\,\ldots ,\,i_{n}.
L is compact iff its top element e is compact.
L is coherent iff (i) Each element of L is the join of compact elements and (ii) the meet of any finite set, including the empty set, of compact elements is compact.
L is regular iff for each x\in L,\,x is the join of all y\ll x, where y\ll x means (\exists z\in L)(y\wedge z=0 and x\vee z=e).
L is 0 dimensional iff for each x\in L,\,x=\bigvee \{y\in L:y^{\ast }\vee y=e and y\leq x\}. (y^{\ast } is the pseudo-complement of y,\,y^{\ast }=\bigvee \{c\in L\,:\,c\wedge a=0\}.)
L is conjunctive iff \forall a,\,b\in L, such that a<b,\,\exists c\in L such that a\vee c<e and b\vee c=e.
A closed set F of a topological space X is irreducible iff whenever G_{i},\,1\leq i\leq n, are closed sets with F\subseteq \bigcup _{i=1}^{n}G_{i}, then F\subseteq G_{i} for some i.
If F is a closed set in a topological space X, then x\in X is a generic point for F iff F is the closure of \{x\}.
A topological space is sober iff every irreducible closed set has a unique generic point.
The sum of two frames L_{1} and L_{2} is the lattice whose set is the Cartesian product of the two frames with operations done componentwise.
A ring R is regular iff (\forall a)(\exists b)(aba=a). (It is known that every prime ideal in a commutative regular ring is maximal.)
A Gelfand algebra is a commutative Banach algebra A with unit 1 over the real numbers \mathbb{R} such that \Vert a^{2}\Vert =\Vert a\Vert ^{2} and 1+a^{2} is invertible for all a\in A.

A \aleph _{\alpha }-frame is a partially ordered set A with zero (0) and unit (e) in which every pair of elements has a meet and every subset of cardinality \leq \aleph _{\alpha } has a join and which satisfies the distributive law: a\wedge \bigvee S=\bigvee \{a\wedge t:t\in S\} for any a\in A and subset S of A of cardinality \leq \aleph _{\alpha }.
A cover of a lattice L is a subset S of L such that \bigvee S=e where e is the unit in the lattice. A subcover of S is a subset of S which is still a cover.
A lattice L is \aleph _{\alpha }-Lindelöf if every cover of L has a subcover of cardinality \leq \aleph _{\alpha }.

For any \aleph _{\alpha }-frame A and ideal J of A, let k_{0}(A)=\{\bigvee S:S\subseteq A\wedge |S|\leq \aleph _{\alpha }\}. Then {J:J is an ideal in A and k_{0}(J)=J} ordered by \subseteq is a frame and is called the frame envelope of A.

sec.title: NOTE 30
sec.p: This note contains the proof that forms 14 (The Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem), [14 BM], [14 BN], and [14 BO] are equivalent. ([14 BM]: A system of equations over a finite ring R has a solution in R if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in R. [14 BN]: A system of equations over a finite field F has a solution in F if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in F. [14 BO]: A system of equations over a finite structure (A,\,+,\,\cdot ) has a solution in A, if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in A.) First, it is clear that [14 BO] implies [14 BM] implies [14 BN]. We shall show that [14 J] implies [14 BO] and that [14 BN] implies 14.

statement.label: Theorem 1.
statement.p: [14 J] implies [14 BO].

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let A be a finite set with two operations + and \cdot defined on it. Suppose \Sigma is a set of equations over A such that every finite subset of \Sigma has a solution. Let V be the set of variables which occur in \Sigma . Since A is finite the discrete topology on A is compact. By [14 J], the product P=\prod _{i\in V} A is compact. For each finite subset \sigma of \Sigma , let x_{\sigma }=\{f\in P:f is a solution for \sigma }. Let B=\{x_{\sigma }:\sigma is a finite subset of \Sigma }. The set B is a set of closed subsets of P with the finite intersection property. Since P is compact, the intersection of B is non-empty. Any element of the intersection is a solution of the system \Sigma .

statement.label: Theorem 2.
statement.p: [14 BN] implies 14.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let B be a Boolean algebra and for each b\in B, let x_{b} be a variable. For b\in B, let b^{\prime } be the complement of b. For each b,\,c\in B, consider the following set of equations \Sigma over the two element field \{0,1\}:
It is easy to see that each finite subset of \Sigma has a solution. [14 BN] implies that \Sigma has a solution. Therefore, the set \{b\in B:x_{b}=1\} is an ultrafilter.

sec.title: NOTE 31
sec.p: Definitions for forms [14 W], [70 A], [52 H] through [52 L], 372 and [372 A] through [372 D]. These are modifications of definitions from Schechter [1996a] and [1996b].

def.p: A pre-order is a reflexive, transitive relation.
A directed set (\mathbb{D},\,\leq ) is a non-empty, preordered set in which each finite subset has an upper bound.
A net in a set X is any function from a directed set into X. (x:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow X, usually denoted (x(\delta ):\delta \in \mathbb{D}) or (x_{\delta })).

If x:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow X is a net and S is any set we say x is eventually in S if (\exists \delta _{o}\in \mathbb{D})(\forall \delta \in \mathbb{D})(\delta \geq \delta _{o}\rightarrow x(\delta )\in S) and we say x is frequently in S if (\forall \delta \in \mathbb{D})(\exists \delta ^{\prime }\in \mathbb{D})(\delta ^{\prime }\geq \delta and x(\delta ^{\prime })\in S)
x is frequently constant if for some c,\,x is frequently in \{c\}.

Assume (x(\alpha ):\alpha \in \mathbb{A}) and (y(\beta ):\beta \in \mathbb{B}) are two nets in X, then (y(\beta )) is a subnet of (x(\alpha )) (in the sense of Aarnes and Andenees - (This is not the usual definition of subnet.)) if (\forall S\subseteq X)(If (x(\alpha )) is eventually in S, then (y(\beta )) is eventually in S). (Which is equivalent to (\forall S\subseteq X)( If (y(\beta )) is frequently in S then (x(\alpha )) is frequently in S). )
A universal net (or ultranet) on a set X is a net (x(\delta ):\delta \in \mathbb{D}) with the property that (\forall S\subseteq X) (x is eventually in S or x is eventually in X\backslash S).
A partially ordered set is Dedekind complete if each subset that has an upper bound has a least upper bound. (Equivalently, if each subset that has a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.)

An ordered vector space is a real vector space Z equipped with a partial ordering \preccurlyeq which also satisfies:
x\preccurlyeq y implies x+z\preccurlyeq y+z
x\succcurlyeq 0 and r\geq 0 imply rx\succcurlyeq 0.
(Note: This differs from the definition of ordered linear space in note 16.)
In definitions 10 through 13, X is a vector space, (Z,\preccurlyeq ) is an ordered vector space and p:X\rightarrow Z.
p is sublinear if p(x+y)\preccurlyeq p(x)+p(y) and for all c\in [0,\,+\infty ), p(cx)=cp(x).
p is convex if p(cx+(1-c)y)\preccurlyeq cp(x)+(1-c)p(y) for all c\in [0,1].
p is concave if p(cx+(1-c)y)\succcurlyeq cp(x)+(1-c)p(y) for all c\in [0,1].
p is affine if p(cx+(1-c)y)=cp(x)+(1-c)p(y) for all c\in [0,1].

Let (\Delta ,\,\sqsubseteq ) be a directed set and (Z,\preccurlyeq ) be a Dedekind complete ordered vector space. Let B(\Delta ,\,Z) be the set of functions f from \Delta to Z such that the range of f has both an upper bound and a lower bound. For f\in B(\Delta ,\,Z) let
\liminf (f)=\sup _{\alpha \in \Delta }\inf _{\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta }f(\beta ) and
\limsup (f)=\inf _{\alpha \in \Delta }\sup _{\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta }f(\beta )

sec.title: NOTE 32
sec.p: Notes for forms [159 A] and [159 B] from Blass [1983a].

A similarity type \tau is a set J of operation symbols and for each j\in J, an arity I_{j} (I_{j} indexes the argument places of j). An algebra of type \tau is a set A and for each j\in J, an operation j_{A} from A^{I_{j}} into A. The following is a theorem of ZF. (See Blass [1983a].)

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: For any similarity type \tau and set V there is an algebra F(V) of type \tau (called the \tau free algebra generated by V) with the property that V\subseteq F(V) and for any A of type \tau and any \eta :V\rightarrow A there is a unique homomorphism \alpha :F(V)\rightarrow A with \alpha (v)=v for all v\in V.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A \tau identity is a triple (V,\,w,\,w^{\prime }) where V is a set (of variables) and w and w^{\prime } are words in the free \tau algebra F(V).

Given a similarity type \tau and a set of identities E, the variety determined by \tau and E is the class of all algebras of type \tau where all the identities in E are true. ((V,\,w,\,w^{\prime }) is true in A if for every function \eta :V\rightarrow A,\,\alpha (w)=\alpha (w^{\prime }) where \alpha is the unique homomorphism extending \eta .)

If V is a variety and X is a set then a free algebra in the variety on X is an algebra A and a function \eta :X\rightarrow A such that for any A^{\prime } in the variety, and \eta ^{\prime }:X\rightarrow A^{\prime }, there is a unique homomorphism \alpha :A\rightarrow A^{\prime } with \eta ^{\prime }=\alpha \eta .
If X=\emptyset then A is called an initial algebra in the variety.

sec.title: NOTE 33
sec.p: The following proof that form 99 (Rado’s selection lemma) and form 62 (C(\infty , < \aleph _{0})) imply the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14) is due to A. Blass.

Assume Rado’s lemma and C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) and let B be a Boolean algebra. Let X=\{\{x,\overline{x}\}:x\in B\} where \overline{x} denotes the complement of x in B. For each finite subset A of X, let f_{A} be a choice function on A chosen so that \{f_{A}(Y):Y\in A\} can be extended to a proper ideal in the subalgebra of B generated by \bigcup A. (Choosing f_{A} for each finite A\subseteq X uses C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}).) By Rado’s lemma there is a choice function f for X such that for each finite A\subseteq X there is a finite B\subseteq X such that A\subseteq B and f_{B} agrees with f on A. Let I=\{f(Y):Y\in X\}. It is reasonably easy to show that I is a maximal proper ideal in B.

sec.title: NOTE 34
sec.p: A proof that Alexander’s subbase lemma [14 AA] (A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase S for the topology such that every cover by elements of S has a finite subcover.) implies [14 Z] (Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for families of finite spaces.)

Let \{X_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of non-empty finite sets and let X=\prod _{i\in I}X_{i}. If X is empty we are done otherwise let g\in X and for each j\in I and a\in X_{j} let B_{j,a}=\{f\in X:f(j)\in X_{j}\backslash \{a\}\}. \mathcal{B} =\{B_{a,j}:j\in I and a\in X_{j}\} is a subbase for the topology on X. We show every cover of X by elements of \mathcal{B} has a finite subcover. Let \mathcal{C} be such a cover. If for some j\in I,\,B_{a,j} and B_{a^{\prime },j} are in \mathcal{C} with a\neq a^{\prime }, then these two sets are the required finite subcover. If not then we can define an element of X that is not covered by \mathcal{C} as follows: f(j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} a, & \mathrm{if}\ B_{j,a}\in C\\g(j), & \mathrm{otherwise} \end{array}\right. .

sec.title: NOTE 35
sec.p: Form 10 (C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0})) is equivalent to [10 F] (Every \omega -tree has an infinite chain.) The proof that 10 implies [10 F] uses the fact that form 10 is equivalent to UT(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}) which implies an \omega -tree is denumerable. For the argument that [10 F] implies form 10, let A be a denumerable set of finite sets and T be the set of all choice functions on initial segments of A. Define < on T by f<g iff f is a proper subset of g. T is an \omega tree and an infinite chain in T induces a choice function on A. This proof is due to Arthur and Jean Rubin. A proof of the equivalence of form 10 and [10 F] also occurs in Pelc [1978].

sec.title: NOTE 36
sec.p: In this note we prove that form 284 (Every finitely solvable system of linear equations over a field has a solution in the field.) implies \forall n\in \omega ,\,n\geq 2,\,C(\infty ,\,n) (form 61). The proof is by mathematical induction on n, starting with the case n=1 which is clear. Assume that C(\infty ,\,k) is true for every k<n and let X be a collection of pairwise disjoint n element sets. By the induction hypothesis there is a choice function h for the set Y=\{z:(\exists x\in X)(z\subseteq x)\wedge 1\leq |z|<n\}. Let p be the smallest prime that divides n, say n=r\cdot p. We define a system of linear equations over the field \mathbb{Z}_{p} (the integers \mod \,p) as follows: We have one variable t_{a} for each a\in \bigcup X and for each x=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}\in X we include the equation t_{a_{1}}+\cdots +t_{a_{n}}=1. This system of equations is clearly finitely satisfiable hence by form 284 it has a solution S:\{t_{a}:a\in \bigcup \,X\}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{p}. We now define a choice function f on X. Let x=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} be an element of X. The solution S determines a partition of x into the sets z_{m}=\{a\in x:S(t_{a})=m\},\,0\leq m\leq p-1, some of which may be empty. However, there is no m,\,0\leq m\leq p-1, for which x=z_{m} because the existence of such an m would mean that S(t_{a_{1}})=\cdots =S(t_{a_{n}})=m. Hence S(t_{a_{1}})+\cdots +S(t_{a_{n}})=m\cdot n=m\cdot (r\cdot p)=0, which is a contradiction since S is a solution to the equation t_{a_{1}}+\cdots +t_{a_{n}}=1.
Let m_{0} be the least element of \mathbb{Z}_{p} for which z_{m_{0}}\neq \emptyset . Since z_{m_{0}}\neq x,\, |z_{m_{0}}|<n and we may therefore define f(x)=h(z_{m_{0}}).

sec.title: NOTE 37
sec.p: Definitions for form [14 AB] (Tychonoff theorem for sober spaces).

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A topological space is sober if every closed set C\neq \emptyset that is not the union of two proper closed (not necessarily disjoint) subsets (such a C is called irreducible) is the closure of a unique singleton.

sec.p: In Hausdorff spaces, irreducible closed sets are singletons and therefore

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Hausdorff implies sober implies T_{0}.

sec.p: See Blass [1986] and Johnstone [1984].

sec.title: NOTE 38
sec.p: Definitions from Manka [1988] and [1988].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Suppose that (X,\,\leq ) is a partial ordering

def.p:
A set \mathcal{A}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X) is supremal in (X,\,\leq ) if(a)
\forall S\in \mathcal{A} and for every upper bound y of S,\,S\cup \{y\}\in \mathcal{A} and(b)
\forall S\in \mathcal{A} every initial segment of S is in \mathcal{L}.

If \mathcal{A} is supremal in (X,\,\leq ) and \sigma :\mathcal{A}\rightarrow X then \sigma is a sup function iff(a)
\forall S\in \mathcal{A},\,\sigma (S) is an upper bound for S and(b)
\forall S\in \mathcal{A},\,\sigma (S) is the greatest element of S if there is one.
(X,\,\leq ) is directed if each two element subset of X has an upper bound.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If (X, \rho ) is a metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}, then \phi is upper semi-continuous iff for every convergent sequence \{x_{n}\} in (X,\,\rho ) and for all r\in \mathbb{R}, the inequality \phi (x_{n})\geq r for all n\in \omega implies \phi (\lim x_{n})\geq r.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If (X,\,\leq ) is a directed, partially ordered set and \tau is a topology on X, then (X,\,\leq ) is upper-semi continuous with respect to \tau if for every x_{0} in X,\,\{y\in X:x_{0}\leq y\} is closed.

sec.title: NOTE 39
sec.p: In this note the results of Harper/Rubin [1976] are summarized.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Suppose that R is a relation on X.

def.p: R is connected on X if (\forall u,\,v\in X)(u\neq v\rightarrow uRv or vRu).
An element u\in X is R-maximal in X if (\forall v\in X)(uRv\rightarrow vRu). R-minimal is defined similarly.
If Y\subseteq X,\,u\in X is an (R) upper bound for Y if (\forall v\in Y)(v\neq u\rightarrow vRu). Lower bound is defined similarly.
X is directed (upwards) by R iff R partially orders X and every finite subset of X has an upper bound.
If y\in X, the initial segment generated by y is y^{\ast }=\{u\in X:uRy\}.
X is ramified by R if R partially orders X and for every y\in X,\,y^{\ast } is linearly ordered by R.
(X,\,R) is a forest if R is a partial ordering and y^{\ast } is well ordered by R for every y\in X.
(X,\,R) is a tree if (X,\,R) is a forest and is directed downward by R.
Q\subseteq X is quasi-cofinal in X if Q has no strict upper bound in S. (“Strict” = “not in Q”.)
Q\subseteq X is cofinal in X if Q is linearly ordered by R and (\forall y\in X)(\exists z\in Q)(y\,R\,z).
A\subseteq X is an antichain if \forall x,\,y\in A, neither xRy nor yRx holds.
In Harper/Rubin [1976], the following weak forms of AC are studied:
Z(Q,\,U): Every non-empty Q-ordered set in which every U-ordered subset has an upper bound, has a maximal element.
C(Q,\,U): Every Q-ordered set contains a quasi-cofinal U-ordered subset.
H(Q,\,U): Every Q-ordered set contains a \subseteq -maximal, U-ordered subset.
H^{\prime }(Q,\,U): Every Q-ordered set has the property that each U-ordered subset can be extended to a \subseteq -maximal U-ordered subset.

statement.p: where Q and U range over the following properties: A: arbitrary (binary) relation, TR: transitive, AS: antisymmetric, C: connected, P: partially ordered, W: well ordered, L: linearly ordered, D: directed, R: ramified, F: forest, T: tree, AS & C and, TR & C.
In particular:
Form 51 is equivalent to Z(L,\,U) where U=W,\,F or T and to Z(R,\,F) and to Z(R,\,T).
Form 143 is equivalent to H(C,\,TR) and H(C,\,TR&C),
Form 202 ([202 A]) is equivalent to H(TR\& C,\,U) where U=AS,\,AS&C,\,P,\,L,\,D, or R.
Form 255 is equivalent to Z(P,\,R)
Form 256 is equivalent to Z(Q,\,U) where Q\in \{P,\,D\} and U\in \{F,\,T\}.
Form 257 is equivalent to Z(TR,\,AS) and Z(TR,\,P).
Form 258 is equivalent to Z(D,\,U) where U\in \{C,\,AS\& C,\,TR\& C,\,L\}.
Form 259 is equivalent to Z(TR\& C,\,U) where U\in \{W,\,F,\,T\}.
Form 260 is equivalent to Z(TR\& C,\,U) where U\in \{AS,\,AS\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}.
Form 261 is equivalent to Z(TR,\,F) and Z(TR,\,T).
Form 263 is equivalent to H(AS\& C,\,U) where U\in \{TR,\,TR\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}.
Form 264 is equivalent to H(C,\,U) where U\in \{P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}.
Form 266 is equivalent to H(AS,\,TR) and H(AS,\,P) and \{AS,\,AS\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}.
Form 261 is equivalent to Z(TR,\,F) and Z(TR,\,T).
Form 263 is equivalent to H(AS\& C,\,U) where U\in \{TR,\,TR\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}.
Form 264 is equivalent to H(C,\,U) where U\in \{P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}.
Form 202 ([202 A]) is equivalent to H(TR\& C,U) where U=AS,\,AS\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D, or R.
Form 266 is equivalent to H(AS,\,TR) and H(AS,\,P).

sec.title: NOTE 40
sec.p: Notes on [94 A] and [94 B]. Brunner [1982d] proves that [94 B] implies form 13 (lemma 6, p. 164) by showing that the negation of form 13 implies the negation of [94 A] which implies the negation of [94 B]. Since [94 A] clearly implies [94 B], it only remains to prove that [94 A] implies 94 (to complete the argument for the equivalence of 94, [94 A] and [94 B]). (Form 94: C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ,\, \mathbb{R}); [94 A]: The discrete topology on \omega is Lindelöf; and [94 B]: There is a Lindelöf space with a closed, discrete infinite subset.)

Assume [94 A] and let \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a denumerable family where for all i\in \omega ,\, A_{i}\neq \emptyset and A_{i}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\omega ). It suffices to find a choice function for the family \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} (identifying reals with sets of natural numbers).
Now using the family \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} we define a second family of sets of sets of natural numbers \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \} so that

More specifically, for each i\in \omega , let m(i) be the least element of \bigcup A_{i}. Define f_{i}:\{k\in \omega :k\geq m(i)\}\rightarrow \omega by f_{i}(k)=[2(k-m(i))+1]2^{i} and let B_{i}=\{f_{i}^{\prime \prime }x:x\in A_{i}\}. It is clear that \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \} satisfies (\ast ) and that it suffices to find a choice function for \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}. Further \bigcup _{i\in \omega }B_{i}\cup \big \{\{k\in \omega :k\not \in \bigcup _{i\in \omega }(\bigcup \,B_{i})\}\big \} is an open cover for \omega (using the discrete topology). Since the topology is Lindelöf there is a countable subcover \{x_{j}:j\in \omega \}. Defining, for each i\in \omega ,\,F(B_{i})=x_{j} where j is the least element of \omega such that 2^{i}\in x_{j} provides a choice function for \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}.

sec.title: NOTE 41
sec.p: The following proof that form 233 is true in \mathcal{N}1 is due to David Pincus. Form 233 is “Algebraic closures of fields, if they exist, are unique.”

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: If K is an algebraically closed field, if \pi is a non-trivial automorphism of K satisfying \pi ^{2}=1_{K} (the identity on K), and if i\in K is a square root of -1, then \pi (i)=-i\neq i.

sec.p: (H. Läuchli has given a proof of this lemma with the additional hypothesis that the characteristic of K is not equal to 2. See Jech [1973b], p. 147.)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let L=\{x\in K:\pi (x)=x\}. The order of the group of automorphisms generated by \pi is 2. Therefore by Artin’s theorem (theorem 1.8 on page 264 of Lang [1993]) the index of L in K is 2. By corollary 9.3, page 299 of Lang [1993] (If L is a field and K is the algebraic closure of L and is of finite degree over L, then K=L(i) where i^{2}=-1 and L has characteristic 0.) K=L(i), where i^{2}=-1 and L has characteristic 0, and hence K has characteristic 0.

Choose x\in K such that \pi (x)
eq x. Let y=\pi (x)-x so that y
eq 0 and \pi (y)=-y. Let z be a square root of y. Then \pi (z) is a square root of \pi (y)=-y hence \pi (z)=iz for some square root i of –1. Since y
eq 0,\,z
eq 0. We can therefore compute
The last inequality is a consequence of the fact that the characteristic of K is not 2. Since \pi has order 2, and \pi (-i)=i. This completes the proof of the lemma.

sec.p: Now let (K,\,+,\,\cdot ,\,0,1) be a field in \mathcal{N}1 with finite support E\subseteq A where A is the set of atoms. Assume that K is algebraically closed. We will show that every element of K has support E. This implies that all algebraically closed fields are well orderable in \mathcal{N}1 and therefore the standard proof of the uniqueness of algebraic closures (using AC) is valid in \mathcal{N}1.

The proof is by contradiction. Assume that x\in K does not have support E. We will arrive at a contradiction in two steps. The first is to show that for some permutation \pi of A which fixes E pointwise, \pi (x)\neq x and \pi ^{2} is the identity. The permutation \pi induces an automorphism of (K,\,+,\cdot ,\,0,1) and we can therefore apply the lemma to conclude that \pi (i)=-i\neq i for some square root i of -1 in K. The second step is to show that for every permutation \pi of A that fixes E pointwise, \pi (i)=i for every square root i of -1 in K.

For step one, suppose that x has support E\cup F where E\cap F=\emptyset . Let F^{\prime } be a subset of A for which |F^{\prime }|=|F| and F^{\prime }\cap (E\cup F)=\emptyset . Let \pi be a permutation of A which interchanges the elements of F and F^{\prime }, that is, \pi is a product of cycles of length 2, \pi =(a_{1},\,b_{1})(a_{2},\, b_{2})\cdots (a_{n},\,b_{n}) where F=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} and F^{\prime }=\{b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{n}\}. Clearly \pi ^{2} is the identity and \pi fixes E pointwise. The proof that \pi (x)\neq x is a standard permutation model argument and depends on the fact that x does not have support E.

For step two, we note that if i is a square root of –1 in K, then i is a solution to the equation x^{2}+1=0 all of whose coefficients are fixed by any permutation that fixes E pointwise. Therefore if \eta is a permutation of A that fixes E pointwise, \eta (i) is also a solution to x^{2}+1=0. Suppose that i does not have support E. Let E\cup F be a support of i where E\cap F=\emptyset . By a standard permutation model argument, we can show that if \pi and \pi ^{\prime } are any two permutations of A that fix E pointwise and \pi (F) \cap \pi ^{\prime }(F)=\emptyset then \pi (x)\neq \pi ^{\prime }(x). It follows that the equation x^{2}+1=0 has infinitely many solutions in K which is a contradiction and the proof is complete.

sec.title: NOTE 42
sec.p: In Brunner [1982a] is a study, in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} without AC, of conditions under which a topological space is well orderable. These conditions are summarized below.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (2.4 from Brunner [1982a]) Assume X is a T_{2} topological space

def.p: Assuming form 163, X is well orderable if (a) X is hereditarily separable or (b) X is hereditarily Lindelöf and linearly orderable.

Assuming form 164, X is well orderable if (a) X is hereditarily Lindelöf or (b) X is first countable and Lindelöf or (c) X is first countable and hereditarily Souslin or (d) X is second countable or (e) X is separable.

Assuming form 133, X is well orderable if (a) X is hereditarily Souslin or (b) X is linearly orderable. (Note: X is linearly orderable means that the topology on X is the order topology of some linear order, X is well orderable means that the set X is well orderable but the topology need not be the order topology of the well ordering.)
X is first countable if every point has a countable neighborhood base.
X is second countable is X has a countable basis.
X is Souslin if every family of disjoint open sets is countable.
X is metacompact if every open cover has a point finite refinement. (See form 135 for a definition of point finite.)

statement.label: Corollary.
statement.p: (2.5 in Brunner [1982a]) Assuming form 164, the following are equivalent for a metric space X: (1) X is separable, (2) X is second countable, (3) X is Souslin and (4) X is Lindelöf.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (2.6) Under the assumption of form 133 and form 17 (Ramsey’ s Theorem) a regular, Lindelöf, Souslin and hereditarily metacompact space is well orderable.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (2.7) Assuming form 133, a T_{2} topological space X is well orderable if X^{2} is hereditarily normal and X is Lindelöf.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: (2.8) Assuming form 164, a T_{2} space is well orderable if X^{2} is hereditarily locally Lindelöf and X is hereditarily Souslin.

sec.p: Finally some counter examples: In the model \mathcal{M}1 (The basic Cohen model) X=[0,1] (the closed interval in \mathbb{R}) with the order topology is compact, metric, separable, second countable, hereditarily Souslin and linearly ordered, but X is not well orderable.

In the model \mathcal{N}3 (The ordered Mostowski model of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}): Let X=[a,\,b] be an interval in the set of atoms with the order topology. X is compact, hereditarily normal (that is T_{5}) and T_{2}. Further, each finite power of X is compact, T_{4} and hereditarily Souslin, but X is not well orderable.

In the model \mathcal{N}1 (The basic Fraenkel model with a denumerable set of atoms, using the group of all permutations of the atoms and finite supports): Let X= [A]^{<\omega } (all finite subsets of the set of atoms) with a basis for the topology all set of the form \{x:E\subseteq x and x\cap F=\emptyset \} where E and F range over the finite subsets of U. The space X is Souslin, perfectly regular and not well orderable.

sec.title: NOTE 43
sec.p: These are definitions from Brunner [1982b] and results similar to the equivalence of [8 C] and [8 D] to form 8 and [10 H] to form 10. We also include some results from Brunner [1987b].

def.p: A topological space is \sigma -compact if it can be covered by a countable set of compact sets.

A space is weakly Lindelöf if every open cover has a countable refinement. If C is an open cover of a space X a refinement of C is an open cover C^{\prime } of X such that for all y\in C^{\prime }, there is a z in C such that y\subseteq z.

A space X is paracompact if X is Hausdorff and every open covering of X has an open, locally finite refinement. (An open covering C of X is locally finite if for all x\in X, there is an open set containing x that intersects only finitely many elements of C. In general, a family of subsets S of X is called locally finite if each point in X has a neighborhood meeting a finite number of sets in S.)
The results from Brunner [1982b] are:
It is not possible to prove, without AC, that every weakly Lindelöf space is Lindelöf since in the basic Cohen model \mathcal{M}1,\,\mathbb{R} is weakly Lindelöf but not Lindelöf.
The assertion that every \sigma -compact, locally compact space with countable neighborhood bases is Lindelöf implies form 32 (C(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0})).
In the basic Cohen model, \mathcal{M}1,\,C(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}) holds and there is a \sigma -compact locally compact space with countable neighborhood bases which is not Lindelöf.
C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}) is implied by “Every \sigma -compact, ultra metric group without isolated points is Lindelöf.”
The assertion “Every \sigma -compact, regular space without isolated points is Lindelöf” implies form 9 (Dedekind finite = Finite).
The results from Brunner [1987b] are:

In \mathcal{N}3,\,L is a paracompact and weakly Lindelöf topological space which is not Lindelöf. (In \mathcal{N}3,\,L=(A\times \mathbb{Z})\cup \mathbb{Z}, where the ordering on L is defined as follows: for a,\, b\in A and m,\,n\in \mathbb{Z},\,(a,\,n)<(b,\,n) if a<b and (a,\,n)<m<(b,\,m) if n<m. The topology on L is the order topology.)
In \mathcal{M}1, every T_{1} Lindelöf space is compact.
In \mathcal{M}17, every countably compact space is compact.

sec.title: NOTE 44
sec.p: Sageev [1981] shows that the implication form 62 (C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}))\ + form 57 (Any two Dedekind cardinals are comparable.) implies form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite) is not provable in ZF. Ellentuck [1974] shows that \mathrm{ZF}\vdash (62+57\rightarrow \langle \omega , \cdot , +\rangle is an elementary submodel of \langle \Delta ,\,\cdot , +\rangle ) where \Delta is the set of Dedekind finite cardinals (\omega \subseteq \Delta ) and \cdot and + are the usual cardinal operations.

sec.title: NOTE 45
sec.p: For research on set theory without AC the following references may be consulted:
A. Results on Dedekind finite, infinite fields in set theory without AC see Hickman [1978a], [1980a], and [1982].
B. The Dedekind cardinals without AC see Ellentuck [1970], [1973], [1976] and Monro [1975].
C. Order types of linearly ordered Dedekind finite sets without AC see Hickman [1979a].
D. Ordered sets satisfying “there is no infinite descending sequence”, see Hickman [1975].
E. Possible properties of rings see Hodges [1974] where the negation of form 278 is shown to be consistent with ZF.

F. Estimates of the sizes of \aleph (x) and \aleph ^{\ast }(x) in set theory without AC. \aleph (x) is the smallest ordinal \alpha such that \neg (|\alpha |\leq |x|) and \aleph ^{\ast }(x) is the smallest ordinal \alpha such that \neg (|\alpha |\leq \ast |x|) where \leq \ast is the surjective cardinal ordering. See Kruse [1974].
G. Possible cardinality of the set of Dedekind finite cardinals in a Fraenkel-Mostowski model see A. Rubin/J. Rubin [1974].
H. Amorphous sets X for which \mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}(X) is large see Monro [1973]. (X is amorphous if X is infinite and \forall Y\subseteq X,\,Y is finite or X-Y is finite.)
I. Topology without the axiom of choice see Chandler [1972a].
J. Possible order types of convex sets of cardinal numbers see Truss [1973].
K. Large cardinals in set theory without the axiom of choice see Spector [1991] and Apter [1992].
L. Logic without AC see Malitz [1992].
M. Posets and lattices without AC see Hickman [1977].

sec.title: NOTE 46
sec.p: With regard to form 325 (Ramsey’s Theorem II), all the arguments given in Blass [1977] can be modified slightly to show that all the properties of form 17 (Ramsey’s Theorem I) proved by Blass also hold of 325. In particular

def.p: Form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite) implies form 325.
Form 325 is true in \mathcal{N}1.
Form 325 is injectively boundable.

sec.title: NOTE 47
sec.p: Definitions from Shannon [1990].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume that (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order (reflexive and transitive).

def.p: x and y in P are compatible if \exists z\in P such that z\leq x and z\leq \mathrm{y}.
Incompatible means not compatible.
I\subseteq P is an antichain if each pair of elements of I are incompatible.
D\subseteq P is dense if \forall x\in P,\,\exists y\in D such that y\leq x.

F\subseteq P is a filter ifa)
\forall x,\,y\in F\,\exists z\in F such that z\leq x and z\leq y andb)
\forall x\in F\, \forall y\in P,\,x\leq y implies y\in F.
If \mathcal{D}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(P), a filter F is \mathcal{D} generic if F\cap D\neq \emptyset for all D in \mathcal{D}. F is P generic if F\cap D\neq \emptyset for all dense subsets D of P.
A chain C of (P,\,\leq ) is a covering chain iff for all x\in C, if x is not maximal in C, then \exists y\in C such that y covers x in P (i.e., y>x and there is no z\in P such that y>z>x).

If Q\subseteq P and x\in P, the depth of x (relative to Q) is the order type of the smallest well ordered (under the quasi-order) covering chain C which begins at x and ends at an element of Q. (The depth of x is only defined if such a chain exists.)
Two elements x and y of P are Q strongly incompatible if x and y are incompatible and the depth of x is different from the depth of y.
I\subseteq P is a Q strong antichain if any two elements are Q strongly incompatible.

statement.p: Shannon [1990] proves that the following are equivalent for each ordinal \alpha :
(i) C(\aleph _{\alpha },\, <\aleph _{0})
(ii) If (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order such that P\neq \emptyset and P is a union of \aleph _{\alpha } finite sets and every antichain is finite, then there is a well orderable, P generic filter.

(iii) For some ordinal \beta \geq \alpha , for every quasi-order (P,\,\leq ) such that P\neq \emptyset and such that P is the union of \aleph _{\alpha } finite sets and such that every antichain is finite then for every family \mathcal{D} of \aleph _{\beta } dense sets there is a well orderable \mathcal{D} generic filter.

sec.title: NOTE 48
sec.p: Jech [1982] shows that [34 A] implies form 34. The proof that 34 implies [34 A] uses the fact that if \aleph _{1} is regular then no set of rank \omega _{1} can be countable.

sec.title: NOTE 49
sec.p: In von Rimscha [1982] three transitivity conditions are considered:
Tr.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f such that u is transitive and f is a function from f one to one and onto u. This is form 175.
Tr^{\prime }.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f such that u is transitive and u\subseteq TC(x) and f is a one to one function from x onto u.
Tr^{\prime \prime }.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f such that u is transitive and f is a one to one function from x onto u and \forall s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s).

It is shown that in ZF, AC implies Tr^{\prime \prime } and that Tr^{\prime \prime } implies Tr^{\prime } implies Tr. All proofs can be done in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} with minor modifications. It is also shown that \mathrm{ZF} \vdash Tr\rightarrow form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite). This could be reformulated as \mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash Tr\rightarrow all pure Dedekind finite sets are finite. We can therefore conclude that Tr (form 175) implies Dedekind finite sets of reals are finite (form 13).

It is however possible to prove in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} that Tr^{\prime \prime } (form 174) implies Dedekind finite = finite (form 9). We proceed as follows: Assume Tr^{\prime \prime }. We first show that every infinite subset of the atoms A is Dedekind infinite. Assume B\subseteq A and that B is infinite. We will use Tr^{\prime \prime } to get a choice function for \mathcal{P}(B) from which it follows that B has a denumerable subset. Let \kappa be the least well ordered cardinal which is not \leq |\mathcal{P}(B)|. For each a\in B and ordinal \alpha , define a_{\alpha } by induction: a_{0}=a,\,a_{\lambda }=\bigcup _{\alpha <\lambda }a_{\alpha } for limit ordinals \lambda and a_{\alpha +1}=a_{\alpha }\cup \{a_{\alpha }\}. (a_{\alpha } is the ordinal \alpha with every occurrence of \emptyset replaced by a.) Then for each \alpha ,\, |a_{\alpha }|=|\alpha |. Let B^{\prime }=\{a_{\kappa }:a\in B\} and let x=\mathcal{P}(B^{\prime }). By Tr^{\prime \prime } there is a transitive set u and a function f:x\rightarrow u which is one to one and onto and such that for each s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s). Suppose that C\subseteq B and let s=\{a_{\kappa }:a\in C\}\in x. Then

since |TC(s)|\geq \kappa ,\,s\not \in u. (|u|=|\mathcal{P}(B)| which is not \geq \kappa .). So f(s)\in \bigcup _{a\in C}a_{\kappa }. Since a\neq b implies a_{\kappa }\cap b_{\kappa }=\emptyset ,\, f(s) determines a unique element of C.

Now let x be any infinite set. By Tr^{\prime \prime } there is a transitive u and a one to one function f from x onto u. If u contains only finitely many atoms, then the von Rimscha proof can be modified to show that x has a denumerable subset. If u contains an infinite set of atoms B, then by the first argument B and therefore x contains a denumerable subset.
Problem (from von Rimscha [1982]): Are any of the implications Tr\rightarrow Tr^{\prime }\rightarrow Tr^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow AC provable in ZF?

sec.title: NOTE 50
sec.p: Definitions from Andreka/Nemeti [1981] and Höft/Howard [1981].

An algebra is a pair (A,\,F) where A is a set and F is a function from an index set I such that for each i\in I, there is a k_{i}\in \omega such that F(i) is a function from A^{k_{i}} into A. The function \Delta with domain I defined by \Delta (i)=k_{i} is called the type of the algebra (A,\,F). Two algebras of the same type are similar.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let K be any class of similar algebras

def.p: S(K)= the class of subalgebras of algebras in K
H(K)= homomorphic images of algebras in K
P(K)= direct products of non-empty families of algebras in K
HSP\ K=H(S(P(K))).
Mod\,Eq\,K= the class of all algebras which are models of the set of equations which hold in every member of K.

statement.p: The fact that [0 U] is equivalent to form 0 answers problem 31 in Grätzer [1979].

A multi-algebra is a pair (A,\,F) where A is a set and F is a function from an index set I such that for each i\in I, there is a k_{i}\in \omega such that F(i) is a function from A^{k_{i}} into \mathcal{P}(A)-\{\emptyset \}. We will denote F(i) by f_{i}. The function \Delta with domain I defined by \Delta (i)=k_{i} is called the type of the algebra. Note that this doesn’t require that constants, i. e., 0-ary operations, have to be singleton sets.

If (A,\,F) and (B,\,G) are algebras or multi-algebras of the same type then a function \phi :A\rightarrow B is a homomorphism if for every i\in I and \mathbf{a}= (a_{1},\,\ldots a_{k_{i}})\in A^{k_{i}},\,\phi (f_{i}(a_{1},\,\ldots a_{k_{i}}))=g_{i}(\phi (a_{1}),\,\ldots \phi (a_{k_{i}})). The function \phi is an isomorphism between multi-algebras if \phi and \phi ^{-1} are bijective homomorphisms.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Suppose that (A,\,F) is a multi-algebra of type \Delta and (B,\,G) is an algebra of type \Delta . Let E be an equivalence relation on B and let C/E be the set of equivalence classes, (C/E,\,G/E) is the multi-algebra of type \Delta defined by
Here we have used [a] to denote the E equivalence class of a\in C.

sec.title: NOTE 51
sec.p: In Drake [1974], p.203 there is a proof of Ramsey’s theorem (form 17) which uses König’s lemma (form [10 F]). However this proof also uses the well ordering theorem and hence does not show that [10 F] implies form 17. (Which is in fact false. See Blass [1977].) Therefore the proof in Lolli [1977] that Ramsey’s theorem implies form 10 is invalid because it uses “[10 F] implies 17”

sec.title: NOTE 52
sec.p: In Brunner [1981a] it is shown that there is a model of ZF in which \mathbb{R}^{A} is metrizable and connected, where A is a suitably chosen set and the box topology is used on the product. (If for each i\in I,\,X_{i} is a topological space, then the box product is the topological space whose underlying set is the Cartesian product \prod _{i\in I}X_{i} and whose topology has as a basis, sets of the form \prod _{i\in I}U_{i}, where U_{i} is open in X_{i}.)

sec.title: NOTE 53
sec.p: In Zuckerman [1969a] and [1981] the relationship between versions of form 178(n,\,N) are considered. (Form 178(n,\,N): If n\in \omega ,\,n\geq 2 and N\subseteq \{1,2,\,\ldots ,\,n-1\},\, N\neq \emptyset ,\, MC(\infty ,\,n,\,N): If X is any set of n-element sets then there is a function f with domain X such that \forall A\in X,\,f(A)\subseteq A and |f(A)|\in N.) A sample of the results follows. Using the notation of Zuckerman [1981], S(n,\,\ell ) is MC(\infty ,\,n,\,\{\ell \}) and T(n,\,\ell ) is MC(\infty ,\, n,\,\{1,2,\,\ldots ,\,\ell \}).

statement.p: If m\leq n and n-\ell <m then S(n,\,\ell )\rightarrow T(m,\,\ell ).

b) for \ell not of the form jn for any j\leq k,\,S(kn,\,\ell )\rightarrow T(n,\,l).

a) \ell <n,\,T(kn,\,\ell )\rightarrow T(n,\ell ).
b) for \ell not of the form jn for any j\leq k,\,S(kn,\,\ell )\rightarrow T(n,\, l).

sec.title: NOTE 54
sec.p: Spector [1980] proves that form 43 (dependent choice) implies [43 P] which implies [43 R] and [43 R] clearly implies [43 L]. Diener [1994] shows that if forms 43 and [43 S] are altered by restricting them to relations which are partial orderings, the resulting forms remain equivalent to form 43. In addition, if [43 R] is altered by removing the restriction to partial orderings the resulting form remains equivalent to form 43.

sec.title: NOTE 55
sec.p: The following results are from Gitik [1980]. Let \Omega =\{\alpha \in On: (\forall \beta \leq \alpha )(\beta = 0\vee (\exists \gamma )(\beta =\gamma +1)\vee (\forall n\in \omega )(\exists \gamma _{n}\leq \beta )(\beta =\bigcup _{n\in \omega }\gamma _{n})\}. Gitik shows, by making small changes in \mathcal{M}17, that each of the following are consistent:

def.p: ZF + \Omega = On.
ZF + \Omega =\omega _{\Omega }.
ZF + \Omega =\omega _{\alpha +1}, for any \alpha .

sec.p: In fact, item 1 holds in \mathcal{M}17 itself. It is clear that ZFC \vdash \Omega =\omega _{1} (form 315).

In Gitik [1985], the following theorem is given: Suppose M is a countable model of ZFC and \kappa is an almost huge cardinal in M. (See note 20 for the definition of various types of inaccessible cardinals.) If S is any subset of \kappa consisting of nonlimit cardinals, then there is a model \mathcal{M}(S) of ZF such that the regular cardinals are exactly \{\aleph _{\alpha }:\alpha \in S\cup \{0\}\}. In the case that S=\emptyset , then all uncountable \aleph _{\alpha }’s are singular. Note, however, that in \mathcal{M}17 all uncountable \aleph _{\alpha }’s are singular. Further, the construction of \mathcal{M}17 requires only the existence of a strongly compact cardinal which is weaker than the existence of an almost huge cardinal.

sec.title: NOTE 56
sec.p: Hickman [1980b] generalizes the notion of amorphous as follows:

def.p: X is an \aleph _{\alpha } set if |X| is incomparable with \aleph _{\alpha } and for all \beta <\alpha ,\,\aleph _{\beta }<|X|.
X is \aleph _{\alpha } minimal if X is an \aleph _{\alpha } set and for all Y\subseteq X, either |Y|<\aleph _{\alpha } or |X-Y|<\aleph _{\alpha }, (abbreviated X is \alpha -m).
X is weakly \aleph _{\alpha } minimal if X is an \aleph _{\alpha } set and for all Y\subseteq X at most one of Y and X-Y is an \aleph _{\alpha } set, (X is \alpha -wm).
X is pseudo \aleph _{\alpha } minimal if X is an \aleph _{\alpha } set and for all Y\subseteq X, exactly one of Y and Y-X is an \aleph _{\alpha } set, (X is \alpha -pm).

sec.p: The following are proved:

statement.label: Theorem 1.
statement.p: X is 0-m iff X is 0-wm iff X is 0-pm.

statement.label: Theorem 2.
statement.p: (a) For all \alpha ,\,X is (\alpha +1)-pm implies X is (\alpha +1)-wm and (b) X is (\alpha +1)-wm iff X is (\alpha +1)-m.

statement.label: Theorem 3.
statement.p: If \alpha is a limit ordinal (\alpha \neq 0), then
(a) X is \alpha -m implies X is \alpha -wm.
(b) X is \alpha -wm iff X is \alpha -pm.

statement.label: Theorem 4.
statement.p: For all ordinals \alpha ,\,Con(ZF+\exists X(X is \alpha -m)).

statement.label: Theorem 5.
statement.p: (a) For all ordinals \alpha , the following is not theorem of ZF:
(b) For all limit ordinals \alpha , it is not a theorem of ZF that

statement.label: Theorem 6.
statement.p: If \aleph _{\alpha } is regular, then Con(ZF + there is a linearly ordered (\alpha +1)-pm set).

statement.label: Theorem 7.
statement.p: For any \alpha , Con(ZF + there is a linearly ordered (\alpha +1)-m set).

statement.label: Theorem 8.
statement.p: If \alpha is a limit ordinal there are no linearly ordered \alpha -wm sets.

sec.p: Open Problem. The consistency of the existence of linearly ordered (\alpha +1)-pm set where \aleph _{\alpha } is not regular.

sec.title: NOTE 57
sec.p: Truss [1995] studies the various structures an amorphous set can carry. (A set is amorphous if it is infinite but is not the disjoint union of two infinite sets.) If \pi is a partition of an amorphous set U into infinitely many parts, then each part must be finite. (Otherwise, if X were an infinite part, then U=X\cup (U-X), contradicting the fact that U is amorphous.) Define a map f from U into \omega such that for each x\in U,\,f(x)=n where x\in \xi \in \pi and |\xi |=n. Since U is amorphous, the range of f must be finite. Since U=\bigcup \{f^{-1}(n): n\in range of f}, there is a unique n such that f^{-1}(n) is infinite. Let n(\pi ) be this unique n, then \{\xi \in \pi :|\xi |=n(\pi )\} is infinite.
Let \Pi (U) be the set of finitary partitions of U and let n(U)= \sup \{n(\pi ):\pi \in \Pi (U)\}. If n(U) is finite, U is called bounded, and if n(U) infinite, U is called unbounded.
Two interesting results that Truss obtains are:

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: The following are consistent with ZF:

def.p: There is an amorphous set and all amorphous sets are bounded.
There is an amorphous set and all amorphous sets are unbounded.

sec.p: See Truss [1995] for additional results.

sec.title: NOTE 58
sec.p: J. L. Hickman [1979b] shows that if \Gamma and \Delta are Dedekind finite cardinals then the following are equivalent: (1) lub\{\Gamma ,\,\Delta \} exists, (2) \Gamma and \Delta are comparable and (3) gib \{\Gamma ,\,\Delta \} exists.

sec.title: NOTE 59
sec.p: Form 191 is the statement: There is a set S such that for every set a, there is an ordinal \alpha and a function from S\times \alpha onto a and form 182 is: There is an aleph whose cofinality is greater than \aleph _{0}. In Blass [1979] it is proved, assuming form 191, that \forall A there is a limit ordinal \alpha such that A cannot be mapped cofinally onto \alpha . If A cannot be mapped cofinally onto \alpha , then A cannot be mapped cofinally onto \aleph _{\alpha }. Therefore form 191 implies form 182.

Blass also shows that if 191 holds with a set S then form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) holds if and only if there is an ultrafilter U on S^{<\omega } that is regular in the sense that \{p\in S^{<\omega }: s\in range p\} is in U for every s\in S.
With regard to (191,n), Blass shows that 191 holds in most known models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} or ZF. In particular,

def.p: Every permutation model whose class of atoms forms a set satisfies 191.

Every symmetric model satisfies 191. (A symmetric model is a model constructed from a ground model M of ZFC by taking a complete Boolean algebra B in M, an M generic filter G in B, a group \mathcal{G} of automorphisms of B and a normal filter of subgroups of \mathcal{G}. The model consists of members of M[G] that have hereditarily symmetric names.)
If V is any model of ZFC and A\in V, then the submodel HOD(A) of sets hereditarily ordinal definable over A satisfies 191.

sec.title: NOTE 60
sec.p: Definitions from category theory, in particular for forms 188, 189, 190, 192 and 193 from Blass [1979].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume \mathbf{C} is a category

def.p: An object p in \mathbf{C} is projective (in \mathbf{C}) if for all objects a and b in \mathbf{C}, if f\in \mathrm{hom}(a,\, b) is an epimorphism and g\in \mathrm{hom}(p,\,b), then there is an h\in \mathrm{hom}(p,\,a) such that f\circ h=g.
p is injective if for all objects a and b in \mathbf{C}, if f\in \mathrm{hom}(b,\,a) is a monomorphism and g\in \mathrm{hom}(b,p) then there is an h\in \mathrm{hom}(a,p) such that h\circ f=g.

An Abelian group G is projective if for all Abelian groups A and B if f:A\rightarrow B is a homomorphism from A onto B and g:G\rightarrow B is a homomorphism then there is a homomorphism h:G\rightarrow A such that f\circ h=g.

An Abelian group G is injective if for all Abelian groups A and B, if f:B\rightarrow A is a one to one homomorphism and g:B\rightarrow G is a homomorphism then there is a homomorphism h:A\rightarrow G such that h\circ f=g.

A set X is projective if for all sets A and B, for all f from A onto B and for all g from X into B there is a function h from X into A such that f\circ h=g, (i.e., For any X-indexed family \{y_{t}:t\in X\} of non-empty sets there is a choice function.)

sec.title: NOTE 61
sec.p: Kanovei [1979] studies the relationships between AC(K) and DC(K) where K is either in the analytic or projective hierarchy. We give definitions and summarize some of the results from Kanovei [1979]. AC(K) is: For any P\subseteq \omega \times {^{\omega }}\omega with domain \omega , if P\in K, then there is a sequence \langle x_{k}: k\in \omega \rangle of elements of {^{\omega }}\omega with \langle k,\,x_{k}\rangle \in P for all k\in \omega . And

DC(K) is: For every P\subseteq {^{\omega }}\omega \times {^{\omega }}\omega with domain ^{\omega }\omega , if P\in K then for any y\in {^{\omega }}\omega there is a sequence \langle x_{k}: k\in \omega \rangle with x_{0}=y and for all k\in \omega , \langle x_{k},\,x_{k+1}\rangle \in P. The sets in the analytic hierarchy (\varSigma _{n}^{1},\, \varPi _{n}^{1} and \varDelta _{n}^{1} for n\in \omega ) and the sets in the projective hierarchy (\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{n}^{1},\, \boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1} and \boldsymbol{\Delta }_{n}^{1} for n\in \omega ) are defined as follows: For purposes of these definitions ^{k,\ell }\omega is {^{k}}\omega \times {^{\ell }}(^{\omega }\omega ) and a relation R\subseteq {^{k,\ell }}\omega is of rank (k,\,\ell ).

def.p: R of rank (k,\,\ell ) is arithmetic if for all \mathbf{m}\in {^{k}} \omega and all \boldsymbol{\alpha }\in {^{\ell }}(^{\omega }\omega ), R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }) iff Q_{1}x_{1}\ldots Q_{r}x_{r}P(\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },) where P\subseteq ^{r+k,\ell }\omega is recursive, and each Q_{i} is either \exists or \forall .

R of rank (k,\,\ell ) is analytic if R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }) iff Q_{1}\beta _{1}\ldots Q_{r}\beta _{r}P(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\beta _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\beta _{r}) where P is of rank (k,\,\ell +r) and is arithmetic.

(The analytic hierarchy)(i)
\varSigma _{0}^{1}=\varPi _{0}^{1}= the arithmetic relations.(ii)
\varSigma _{r+1}^{1}=\{\exists \beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta ,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }):P\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}\wedge P has rank (k,\, \ell +1)\}(ii)
\varPi _{n+1}^{1}=\{\forall \beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta ,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }):P\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}\wedge P has rank (k,\, \ell +1)\}(iv)
\varDelta _{r}^{1}=\varSigma _{r}^{1}\cap \varPi _{r}^{1}.

R of rank (k,\,\ell ) is recursive in \boldsymbol{\beta } iff the characteristic function K_{R}(\mathbf{m},\, \boldsymbol{\alpha }) of R is G(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\boldsymbol{\beta }) for some partial recursive G.

Assume \boldsymbol{\beta } has rank (0,\,\ell ) then \varSigma _{r}^{1}[\beta ] and \varPi _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }] are defined by R\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }] iff R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha })\leftrightarrow S(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\boldsymbol{\beta }) for some S\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}. \varPi _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }] is defined similarly.

(The projective hierarchy)(i)
\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{r}^{1}=\bigcup \{\varSigma _{r}^{1}[\beta ]:b\in {^{\omega }}\omega \}(ii)
\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{r}^{1}=\bigcup \{\varPi _{r}^{1}[\beta ]:b\in {^{\omega }}\omega \}(iii)
\boldsymbol{\Delta }_{r}^{1}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{r}^{1}\cap \boldsymbol{\Pi } 1_{r}.

sec.p: In Kanovei [1979], it is shown for any n\geq 2 that, AC(\varPi _{n+1}^{1}) does not follow, in ZF from DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}), that DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}) implies AC(\varPi _{n}^{1}) and that AC(\varPi _{n}^{1}) does not imply DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}). Kanovei [1976] has further results on AC and the projective hierarchy. See forms [0 X], 194 and 199.

sec.title: NOTE 63
sec.p: Since most class forms of AC are not consequences of form 1 (AC) we are not including class forms of AC in this project. A summary of what is known about class forms of AC can be found in H. sec.p: Form 200 is studied in Dawson/Howard [1976] where it is shown that

def.p:
Each of(a)
\exists infinite x such that 2^{x}<x!(b)

\exists infinite x such that 2^{x} and x! are incomparable
are consistent with ZF. (x! is the cardinality of the set of all one to one functions from x onto x.).
for all x,\,2x=x implies 2^{x}\leq x!.

sec.p: In Pincus [1978] a model of ZF is constructed in which AC (form 1) is false, \forall infinite x,\, 2x=x (form 3) is false and \forall infinite x,\,2^{x}=x! is true. Also true in this mod el are \forall infinite x,\,2^{x}=|x^{x}| and \forall infinite x,\,2^{x}=|x^{x}-x!|.

sec.title: NOTE 65
sec.p: Truss [1978] shows that in Feferman’s model, \mathcal{M}2 (Feferman [1965]), the following hold:

def.p: \forall ordinals \alpha ,\,2^{\aleph _{\alpha }}=\aleph _{\alpha +1} \cdot 2^{\aleph _{0}}
For all X, if [X]^{2} has a choice function, then \exists \alpha such that |X|\leq 2^{\aleph _{\alpha }}.
Form 40 (C(WO,\,\infty )).
