sec.title: NOTE 66
sec.p: In this note we prove that form 322 (KW(WO,\,\infty )) is true in \mathcal{N}1. (Brunner [1982a], (Proposition 4.5) also has a proof of this result.)

Assume that X is a well ordered set in \mathcal{N}1 and that \forall y\in X,\,|y|\geq 2. Let E be a (finite) support of a well ordering of X and let fix(E) be the group of permutations of A (the set of atoms) which fix E pointwise. Then for all \phi \in fix(E), \phi fixes X pointwise. Choose an atom a\in A-E. We will show that for every y\in X,\,E\cup \{a\} is a support of a non-empty proper subset y^{\prime } of y. This will suffice since it follows that the function y\mapsto y^{\prime } is in \mathcal{N}1.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: If \beta and \gamma are in fix(E) and \beta (F)\neq \gamma (F) then \beta (t)\neq \gamma (t).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p:
Assume b\in  eta (F)-\gamma (F). Since F is minimal, there is no proper subset B of  eta (F) for which E\cup B is a support of  eta (t). Hence there is a \psi \in fix((E\cup  eta (F))-\{b\}) such that \psi ( eta (t))
eq  eta (t). We can find such a \psi for which \psi (b)
ot \in \gamma (F). (If \psi (b)\in \gamma (F) then we choose d\in A-(\gamma (F)\cup  eta (F)\cup E). Since \psi ( eta )
ot \in  eta (F) the cycle ho =(d,\,\psi (b)) of length two fixes E\cup  eta (F) pointwise so that ho ( eta (t))= eta (t). If we let \psi ^{\prime }=ho \circ \psi then \psi ^{\prime } fixes (E\cup  eta (F))-\{b\} pointwise. Further, since ho ( eta (t))= eta (t) and \psi ( eta (t))
eq  eta (t), we conclude that \psi ^{\prime }( eta (t))=ho (\psi ( eta (t)))
eq  eta (t). We can therefore replace \psi by \psi ^{\prime }.)

Let \sigma be the cycle (b,\,\psi (b)). Since \sigma agrees with \psi on a support of \beta (t), \sigma (\beta (t))=\psi (\beta (t))\neq \beta (t). Since \sigma fixes \gamma (F) pointwise, \sigma (\gamma (t))=\gamma (t). Therefore \beta (t)\neq \gamma (t). This completes the proof of the lemma.

sec.p: Choose an \eta \in fix(E) so that \eta (F) \cap F=\emptyset . Then for every \phi \in fix(E\cup \{a\}), \eta (F)\neq \phi (F). It follows from the lemma that for all such \phi ,\,\eta (t)\neq \phi (t). Therefore \eta (t)\in (y-y^{\prime }).

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Form 203 (Every partition of \mathcal{P}(\omega ) into non-empty subsets has a choice function) implies form 94 (C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ,\,\mathbb{R})).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Form 203 implies that every partition of \mathcal{P}(\omega )\times \omega into non-empty subsets has a choice function. Assume \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} is a denumerable set of sets of reals. (We identify \mathbb{R} with \mathcal{P}(\omega ).) For each i\in \omega , let B_{i}=A_{i}\times \{i\}. Then the family \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \} is a disjoint family from \mathcal{P}(\omega )\times \omega and therefore, by 203, has a choice function. This induces a choice function on \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \}.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: form 3 (2m =m for infinite cardinals m) implies form 53 (m^{2}\leq 2^{m} for infinite cardinals m).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Assume that for all infinite cardinals m,\,2m=m and that X is an infinite set. Then f(x,\, y)=\{(0,\,x),\,(1,\,y)\} is a 1-1 function from X\times X into \mathcal{P}(2\times X).

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: |x|\leq ^{\ast }|y| (or x\precsim ^{\ast } y) if y can be mapped onto x.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Form [40 B] implies form 208.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: [40 B] is “For all ordinals \alpha and all sets x if \aleph _{\alpha }\leq ^{\ast }|x|, then \aleph _{\alpha }\leq |x|.” and 208 is “2^{\aleph _{\alpha }}\geq \aleph _{\alpha +1}” (Form 208 depends on the ordinal \alpha ).) Assume [40 B]. As is shown in Kunen [1980], chapter 1, |\aleph _{\alpha }\times \aleph _{\alpha }|=\aleph _{\alpha } and therefore, |\mathcal{P}(\aleph _{\alpha }\times \aleph _{\alpha })|= |\mathcal{P}(\aleph _{\alpha })|. The function f from \mathcal{P}(\aleph _{\alpha }\times \aleph _{\alpha }) defined by f(R)= the order type of R, if R is a well ordering and f(R)=0 otherwise is onto \aleph _{\alpha +1}. It follows that \aleph _{\alpha +1}\leq ^{\ast }|\mathcal{P}(\aleph _{\alpha })| and therefore by [40 B], \aleph _{\alpha +1}\leq |\mathcal{P}(\aleph _{\alpha })|.

sec.title: NOTE 70
sec.p: We give a proof that form [62 E] (KW(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0})) implies form 62 (C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0})). Let x be a set of finite sets and let y=\{u:(\exists v\in x)u\subseteq v\}. By [62 E], there is a Kinna-Wagner selection function, f, on y. We define a choice function g on x as follows: Let u\in x be such that |u|=n. There exists an m\in \omega ,\,m<n, such that f^{m}(u) is a singleton. Define g(u) to be the single element of f^{m}(u). (Form 323, KW(WO,\,\infty ), clearly implies [62 E].)

sec.title: NOTE 71
sec.p: In this note we give definitions from Morillon [1988] for forms [14 L], [14 BP] through [14 BX], [14 CC] through [14 CH], [118 I] through [118 T], 331, 332, 343, 344, and [345 C] through [345 E].
Let X be a topological space, let E=\{(A,\,B):A and B are closed in X and A \cap B=\emptyset \} and let F=\{(U,\,V):U and V are open in X and U\cap V=\emptyset }.

def.p: f:E\rightarrow F is a normality operator on X if \forall (A,\,B)\in E,\,f(A,\, B)=(U,\,V) where A\subseteq U and B\subseteq V.
X is effectively normal if X is T_{2} and there is a normality operator on X.
X is hereditarily normal (or completely normal) if all subspaces of X are normal.
X is hereditarily effectively normal if all subspaces of X are effectively normal.
A set I\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X) is discrete if \forall x\in X,\,\exists a neighborhood N of x such that N\cap A\neq \emptyset for at most one element A\in I.

X is collectionwise normal if X is T_{2} and for every discrete I\subseteq \{U:U is closed in S\} there is a set J of pairwise disjoint open subsets of X such that for every F\in I,\,\exists U\in J such that F\subseteq U.

Let D={ I:I is a discrete collection of closed subsets of X} and O=\{J:J is a collection of pairwise disjoint open subsets of X}. Then f:D\rightarrow O is a collectionwise normality operator on X if \forall I\in D, if f(I)=J then \forall F\in I,\,\exists U\in J such that F\subseteq U. N_{c}(X) denotes the set of collectionwise normality operators on X.
X is effectively collectionwise normal if X is T_{2} and N_{c}(X)\neq \emptyset .
X is highly separated if X is T_{2} and \{N_{c}(F):F\subseteq X\} has a choice function.
X is functionally separated if for all pairs (A,\,B) of closed disjoint subsets of X there is a function f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] such that A\subseteq f^{-1}(0) and B\subseteq f^{-1}(1).
X is Tietze-Urysohn if for every closed F\subseteq X and every continuous function f:F\rightarrow [0,\,1] there is a continuous function g:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] which extends f.

Let C={ g:g:X\rightarrow [0, 1] and g is continuous}. A function f:E\rightarrow C is a Urysohn operator on X if \forall (A,\,B)\in E, if U=f(A,\,B) then A\subseteq U^{-1}(0) and B\subseteq U^{-1}(1). U(X) denotes the set of Urysohn operators on X.
Let B=\{(F,\,U):F is a closed subset of X and U:F\rightarrow [0, 1] is continuous}. A function f:B\rightarrow C is a Tietze-Urysohn operator if \forall (F,\,U)\in B, if f(F,\, U)=V then V extends U.
X is effectively functionally separated if U(X)\neq \emptyset . X is effectively Tietze-Urysohn if T-U(X) \neq \emptyset . (Where T-U(X) is the set of all Tietze-Urysohn operators on X.)
X is highly functionally separated if \{U(A):A\subseteq X\} has a choice function.
X is highly Tietze-Urysohn if {T-U(A):A\subseteq X\} has a choice function.

X is collectionwise separated (or collectionwise Hausdorff) if it is T_{2} and for every discrete set I of singletons from X there is a set J of open subsets of X such that for every F\in I, there is a unique O\in J containing (the singleton) F.
Assume that (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order.
A\subseteq X is convex if \forall (x,\,y)\in A^{2},\,\forall u\in X, if x<u<y then u\in A.
(X, \leq ) is conditionally complete if each non-empty subset with an upper bound has a least upper bound and each non-empty subset with a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.
(X,\,\leq ) is complete if X=\emptyset or every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.

Let X be a topological space, let E be defined as above and let \Omega (X) be the set of open subsets of X. A function f:E\rightarrow \Omega (X) is a monotone normality operator on X if for every (F,\,G)\in E the following conditions hold(i)
F\subseteq f(F,\,G)\subseteq \overline{f(F,\,G)}\subseteq X-G.(ii)
If (F^{\prime },\,G^{\prime })\in E,\,F\subseteq F^{\prime } and G^{\prime }\subseteq G then f(F,\,G)\subseteq f(F^{\prime },\,G^{\prime }).
A topological space X is monotonely normal if it is T_{1} and there is a monotone normality operator on X.

Let (X,\,\leq ) be a complete linear order and let E be the set of non-empty open intervals of X. An increasing choice function on (X,\,\leq ) is a function \ast :E\rightarrow X such that(i)
\forall I\in E,\,\ast (I)\in I.(ii)
If (a,\,b)\in E and (b,\,c)\in E then \ast ((a,\,b))\leq \ast ((a,\,c))\leq \ast ((b,\,c)).
A topological space X is completely regular if for all open U\subseteq X and all p\in U, there is a continuous f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] such that f(p)=0 and \forall x\in X-U,\,f(x)=1.
An ordered set (T,\,\leq ) is a lattice if any two elements have a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. A lattice is bounded is it has a smallest and largest element.
An ideal I in a lattice (T,\,\leq ) is prime if \forall x,\,y\in T, if x\wedge y\in I then either x\in I or y\in I.
If T is a bounded distributive lattice a function f is a prime ideal choice function on T if for each proper ideal I of T,\,f(I) is a prime ideal containing I.

Assume that T is a bounded distributive lattice in which every subset has a least upper bound then T is \vee -compact if for all F\subseteq T such that \bigvee F=1, there is a finite F^{\prime }\subseteq F such that \bigvee F^{\prime }=1. (If (\Omega ,\,\subseteq ) is the lattice of open sets of a topological space X then X is compact if and only if (\Omega ,\,\subseteq ) is \vee -compact.)
Let E be a set. An ultra filter choice function f on E is a function such that for all proper filters I in \mathcal{P}(E), f(I) is an ultra filter containing I.
Let E be a set and U an ultra filter on a set I. U is E-adequate if for every filter F in \mathcal{P}(E) there is a function g:I\rightarrow E such that g(U) contains F.
A topological space is irreducible if it is not empty and is not the union of two proper closed subsets.
A topological space X is sober if every closed irreducible subset of X is the closure of a unique singleton.
A Banach algebra is a normed algebra in which every Cauchy filter converges.

Let (I,\,\leq ) be a preorder (reflexive and transitive), let (E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I} be a family of sets and for each (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I\times I let f_{\alpha ,\beta } be a function from E_{\beta } to E_{\alpha }. Assume that the f_{\alpha ,\beta } satisfy the following conditions:
(LP_{I})\ \alpha \leq \beta \leq \gamma \Rightarrow f_{\alpha ,\gamma }=f_{\alpha ,\beta }\circ f_{\beta ,\gamma }.
(LP_{II}) For all \alpha \in I,\,f_{\alpha ,\alpha } is the identity on E_{\alpha }.

Then ((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is called a projective system relative to the preorder (I,\,\leq ). Let E=\prod _{\alpha \in I}E_{\alpha } and for each pair (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I\times I such that \alpha \leq \beta , let E_{\alpha ,\beta }=\{x\in E:f_{\alpha ,\beta }(x_{\beta })=x_{\alpha }\}. Then the set Y=\bigcap _{\alpha <\beta }E_{\alpha ,\beta } is called the projective limit of the projective system ((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}). Y is denoted \lim _{\leftarrow }(E_{\alpha },\,f_{\alpha ,\beta }). In case the preorder (I,\,\leq ) is directed to the right (that is, \forall (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I^{2},\,\exists \gamma \in I such that \alpha \leq \gamma and \beta \leq \gamma .) we say that the projective system ((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\, (f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is directed.

If ((X_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is a projective system relative to the preorder (I, \leq ) and if each X_{\alpha } has a topology C_{\alpha } such that f_{\alpha ,\beta } is continuous relative to the topologies C_{\alpha } and C_{\beta } then the system ((X_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is called a projective system of topological spaces. In this case the projective limit of the system with the topology induced by the product topology on \prod _{\alpha \in I}X_{\alpha } is called the the projective limit of the projective system of topological spaces.
If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded, distributive lattice, X is a subset of A and F is a filter in A, then F respects X if X\subseteq F and \bigwedge X exists implies \bigwedge X\in F.

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded, distributive lattice, X is a subset of A and F is a filter in A, then F strongly respects X if X\subseteq F implies \exists y\in F such that \forall x\in X,\,y\leq x.

If X is a subset of a bounded, distributive lattice (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) then X is of Boolean type if for all b\in A,\,[(\forall x\in X,\,b\vee x=1) and (\forall y\leq X,\,y\leq b)] implies b=1. (y\leq X means (\forall x\in X)(y\leq x).)

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded, distributive lattice we say that A has the Rasiowa-Sikorski property (respectively the strong Rasiowa-Sikorski property) if for all a,\,b\in A such that a\not \leq b and all sequences (X_{n})_{n\in \omega } of subsets of A of Boolean type there is a prime filter containing a, not containing b and respecting (respectively strongly respecting) each X_{n}.

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded distributive lattice then an element a\in A is \vee -compact if for every subset I\subseteq A,\,\bigvee I=a implies (\exists J\subseteq I) (J finite and \bigvee J=a).

sec.title: NOTE 72
sec.p: We prove that form 207(\beta ) implies 209 for any ordinal \beta . (form 207(\beta ) is UT(\aleph _{\beta },\,\aleph _{\beta },\,<2^{\aleph _{\beta }}) and 209 is (\exists an ordinal \alpha ) (\forall X) (If X is a denumerable union of denumerable sets then \mathcal{P}(X) cannot be partitioned into \aleph _{\alpha } non-empty sets.)) Assume form 207(\beta ) is true. Then for any set X, if X is a denumerable union of denumerable sets, then |X|<2^{\aleph _{\beta }}. Choose an ordinal \alpha so that \neg (\aleph _{\alpha }\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph _{\beta }}))|). For any X which is the denumerable union of denumerable sets we have |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph _{\beta }}))|. A partition of \mathcal{P}(X) into \aleph _{\alpha } non-empty sets would give \aleph _{\alpha }\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|.
Similarly, form 26 implies form 209 and form 31 implies form 209.

sec.title: NOTE 73
sec.p: In Pincus [1977] a general method for adding Dependent Choice (43) to models of ZF is described and the following models of ZF are constructed with the properties indicated:
Model A (\mathcal{M}43). Form 62 (C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0})) and form 43 (DC) are true and form 30 (OP) is false.
Model B (\mathcal{M}44). Forms 30 and 43 are true and form 15 (Kinna-Wagner Principle) is false.
Model C (\mathcal{M}45). Forms 30 and 43 are true and form 49 (the order extension principle) is false.
Model D (\mathcal{M}46(n,\,M)). For each finite set Z of positive natural numbers and natural number n>1, for which the following is false

def.p: S(Z,\,n): For every decomposition n=p_{1}+\ldots +p_{s} of n into a sum of primes at least one p_{i} divides and element of Z, (See Mostowski [1945]. Also see note 15. Condition S implies condition D of note 15.)

sec.p: there is a model in which form 46 (C(\infty ,\,Z)) and form 43 are true and form 45 (C(\infty ,\,n)) is false.
Model E (\mathcal{M}47(n,\,M)). For every finite set Z of positive integers and integer n>1, for which the following condition is false

def.p: M(Z,\,n): For any decomposition n=p_{1}+\ldots +p_{s} of n into a sum of primes there are non-negative q_{1},\,\ldots , q_{s} such that q_{1}p_{1}+\ldots +q_{s}p_{s}\in Z.

sec.p: There is a model in which form 46 (C(\infty ,\,Z)) and form 43 are true and form 47 (C(WO,\,n)) is false. (See Mostowski [1945]. Also, condition K of note 15 implies condition M.)

sec.title: NOTE 74
sec.p: In Pincus [1977] it is shown that C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{\alpha })\rightarrow C(\infty ,\,\aleph _{\alpha }) is not a theorem of ZF for regular \aleph _{\alpha }. For singular \aleph _{\alpha } the question is open.

sec.title: NOTE 75
sec.p: Several weak forms of AC are known to be equivalent to AC in ZF. These include:

def.p: MC: The Axiom of Multiple Choice, form 67;
LW: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered, form 90;
PW: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered, form 91;
VB: Every vector space has a basis, form 66;
A: The Antichain Principle, form 89; and
C(LO,\,\infty ): Every linearly ordered family of non-empty sets has a choice function, form 202.

sec.p: Consequently everything that implies one of these six forms is equivalent to AC in ZF. That is, 95, 109, 112, 114, 133, 147, 149, 164, 218, 264, 292, 333, 334, and 335(n) for n\geq 2, also imply AC in ZF. In fact in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} the following two chains of implications are provable: AC \rightarrow VB \rightarrow MC \rightarrow A \rightarrow LW \rightarrow PW, and AC \rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty )\rightarrow LW. With regard to the reverse implications, VB \rightarrow AC, MC \rightarrow VB and LW \rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty ) are open questions. The other reverse implications are known to be unprovable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. (See Jech [1973b], page 134, Felgner/Jech [1973], Blass [1984a], H. Rubin [1960], H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], Part I, 5, Brunner [1983a],[1984b],[1985a], Howard/Rubin [1977], Truss [1978], Keremedis [1996a],[1996], and note 18.) It follows from the two chains of implications that each of the twenty forms mentioned above implies PW, form 91, in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

In Pincus [1972], page 740, it is shown that if \neg \Phi is boundable (see Pincus [1972], p. 722 for the definition of boundable) and \Phi \rightarrow AC is a theorem of ZF, then \Phi \rightarrow form 91 (PW) is a theorem of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

sec.title: NOTE 76
sec.p: In this note we prove that form 126 (MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )) implies forms 82 (If a set is infinite then its power set is Dedekind infinite.) and 185 (Every Dedekind finite, linearly ordered set is finite.)

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) implies that for every infinite set X there is a sequence (Y_{n})_{n\in \omega } of finite subsets of X such that \forall n\in \omega ,\,Y_{n}\subsetneq Y_{n+1}.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let X be an infinite set and for each n\in \omega , let X_{n}=\{Y\subseteq X:|Y|=n\}. By MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) there is a function f such that \forall n\in \omega ,\,f(X_{n}) is a finite non-empty subset of X_{n}. We define the sequence (Y_{n})_{n\in \omega } by induction as follows: Y_{0}=\emptyset . Assume that Y_{n} is defined and let k be the least natural number such that |Y_{n}|<k. We let Y_{n+1}=(\bigcup f(X_{k}))\cup Y_{n}. Since \mathrm{f}(X_{k}) is a set of k element sets |Y_{n}|<k\leq |\bigcup f(X_{k})|\leq |Y_{n+1}|.

sec.p: It is clear from the lemma that MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) implies that the power set of an infinite set is Dedekind infinite. To show that MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) implies form 185, let X be a Dedekind finite set which is linearly ordered by \leq . The assumption that X is infinite leads to a contradiction as follows: By the lemma we get a sequence (Y_{n})_{n\in \omega } of finite subsets of X such that Y_{n}\subsetneq Y_{n+1} for all n\in \omega . If we define t_{n} to be the \leq -least element of Y_{n+1}-Y_{n} then (t_{n})_{n\in \omega } is an infinite sequence of distinct elements of X and therefore X is Dedekind infinite.

sec.title: NOTE 77
sec.p: In this note we include definitions from Keremedis [1996b] for forms [1 BL] through [1 BR], [1CB], and [67 G].
In what follows (X,\,T) is a topological space and P\subset \mathcal{P}(X).

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A non-empty set \mathcal{F}\subseteq P-\{\emptyset \} is called a P-filter iff

def.p: F_{1},\,F_{2}\in \mathcal{F} implies F_{1}\cap F_{2}\in \mathcal{F}.
F\in \mathcal{F},\,F\subset F^{\prime } and F^{\prime }\in P implies F^{\prime }\in \mathcal{F}.

statement.p: A T-filter is called an open filter. \mathcal{F} is called a filter base if it just satisfies (1) above.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A non-empty set \mathcal{I}\subseteq P-\{X\} is called a P-ideal iff

def.p: I_{1},\,I_{2}\in \mathcal{I} implies I_{1}\cup I_{2}\in \mathcal{I}.
I\in \mathcal{I},\,I^{\prime }\subset I and I^{\prime }\in P implies I^{\prime }\in \mathcal{I}.

statement.p: If F is the set of closed subsets of X, then a F-ideal is called a closed ideal. \mathcal{I} is called complete if \bigcup C\in \mathcal{I} for every C\subseteq \mathcal{I}.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A disjoint set C\subseteq T-\{\emptyset \} is called a cellular family of X.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A nest of (X,\,T) is a maximal linearly ordered subset of the partially ordered set (T-\{\emptyset \},\,\subseteq ).

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A tower \mathcal{T} of (X,\,T) is a linearly ordered subset of the partially ordered set (T-\{\emptyset \},\,\subseteq ) such that either the interior of \bigcap \mathcal{T} is empty or the interior of \bigcap \mathcal{T} does not properly contain any non-empty open set.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If \{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\} is a family of topological spaces, then the box topology on \prod _{i\in k}X_{i} is the topology having a base of all sets of the form \prod _{i\in k}O_{i} where O_{i}\in T_{i} for all i\in k.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: If \{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\} is a family of disjoint topological spaces, then the free union is the set X=\bigcup \{X_{i}:i\in k\} together with the topology T containing all sets O\subseteq X such that O\cap X_{i}\in T_{i} for all i\in k.

sec.title: NOTE 78
sec.p: In Rav [1977], it is shown that under the assumption of RL (form 99) and certain conditions on a set X and filter \mathcal{F} in \mathcal{P}(X), \mathcal{F} can be extended to an ultrafilter. Either of the following conditions suffices:

def.p: \{A:A\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)\wedge A finite \wedge \forall x,\,y\in A(x\neq y\rightarrow x\cap y =\emptyset )\} has a choice function.
\mathcal{F} has a choice function.

sec.title: NOTE 79
sec.p: Definitions for forms 227 and 228.

def.p: A partially ordered group is a triple (G,\,\circ ,\,\leq ) such that (G,\,\circ ) is a group and (G,\,\leq ) is a partially ordered set satisfying for all x,\,y,\,a and b in G if x\leq y, then axb\leq ayb.
P=\{a\in G:a\geq e\} is the positive cone (where e is the identity in G).
If P\cup P^{-1}=G then G is fully ordered. (This is equivalent to saying that \leq is a linear ordering.)
A group is torsion free if the only element of finite order is the identity element.

sec.title: NOTE 80
sec.p: In Rav [1977] forms [14 AL], [14 AM], [14 AO] and [14 AP] are shown to follow from form 14 (BPI). The arguments that they imply form 14 are fairly straightforward. ([14 AL]: The radical of a proper ideal A in a commutative ring R with identity (The radical of A=\{x\in R: for some m\in \omega ,\,x^{m}\in A\}.) is the intersection of all prime ideals in R containing A; [14 AM]: Let A be a subring of a commutative ring R and p a prime ideal in A such that p=Rp\cap A. Then there is a prime ideal J in R such that p=J\cap A; [14 AO]: Suppose R is a commutative ring, A is a proper ideal in R, and S is a multiplicative semigroup in R not meeting A. Then there is a prime ideal p in R such that A\subseteq p and p\cap S=\emptyset ; and [14 AP]: Suppose to each finite subset F of a set I there corresponds a set \Phi (F) of functions whose domains are subsets of I including F and such that (a) F_{1}\subseteq F_{2} implies \Phi (F_{2})\subseteq \Phi (F_{2}) and (b) \forall i\in I,\,\{\phi (i):\phi \in \bigcup { \Phi (F):F finite and F\subseteq I\}\} is finite. Then there is a function f with domain I such that for all finite F\subseteq I,\,\exists \phi \in \Phi (F) such that \phi and f coincide on F.)

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: [14 AL] implies BPI.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Suppose B is a Boolean algebra with more than two elements. Choose b\in B with b\neq 0 and b\neq 1. Let A be the ideal generated by b and apply [14 AL] to get a prime ideal in B.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: [14 AM] implies BPI.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let B be a Boolean algebra and let r be a proper ideal in B. Let A=\{x:x\in r or \overline{x}\in r\}. A,\,B and r satisfy the hypotheses of [14 AM]. The conclusion of [14 AM] gives a prime ideal J in B containing r.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: [14 AO] implies BPI.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: If B is a Boolean algebra and A is a proper ideal in B let S=\{1\}\subseteq B. S is a multiplicative sub-semi-group of B and therefore the hypotheses of [14 AO] are satisfied. The conclusion of [14 AO] gives a prime ideal in B.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: [14 AP] implies BPI.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Since it is shown in Cowen [1973] (see Rav [1977], Corollary 2.3) that [14 AP] implies Rado’s lemma (form 99) and it is known that Rado’s lemma together with C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) (form 62) imply BPI (see form [14 Y]), it suffices to prove that [14 AP] implies C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}). Let \{x_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of pairwise disjoint finite sets. For each finite subset F of I, let

\Phi and I satisfy the hypotheses of [14 AP] and therefore by [14 AP] there is a function f with domain I such that \forall finite F\subseteq I,\,\exists \phi in \Phi (F) such that \phi and f agree on F. Therefore, for all i\in I,\,f(i)\in x_{i} and we have a choice function for \{x_{i}:i\in I\}.

sec.title: NOTE 81
sec.p: We argue that form 30 (the ordering principle) implies form 83 (If every subset of \mathcal{P}(X) which is linearly ordered by \subseteq has a maximum element then X is finite.)

Assume X is infinite and let \leq be a linear ordering of X. There must be either a non-empty subset Y of X with no least element (under \leq ) or a non-empty subset with no greatest element. (If every non-empty subset of X has a least element then let x_{1} be the least element of X,\,x_{2} be the least element of X-\{x_{1}\}, etc. This produces a subset \{x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots \} with no greatest element.) If Y is an infinite subset of X with no greatest element, we get a linearly ordered subset A of \mathcal{P}(X) with no maximum by letting A=\{\{x:x\in Y\wedge x\leq y\}:y\in Y\}. We can proceed similarly if Y is an infinite subset of X with no smallest element.

sec.title: NOTE 82
sec.p: We give the definitions for form 230 (L^{1}=HOD) from Myhill/Scott [1971].

def.p: DF^{0}(A) is the set of all subsets of A definable by first order formulas in \langle A, \in _{A}\rangle using parameters from A, i.e., DF^{0}(A) is all sets of the form \{x\in A:\Phi ^{(A)} (x,\,a_{0},\,\ldots a_{n-1})\} where \Phi is a formula of the type described above, a_{0},\,\ldots ,\, a_{n-1} are in A and \Phi ^{(A)} means all variables range over A.
Gödel’s constructible sets are defined by L_{\alpha }^{0}=\bigcup _{\beta <\alpha }DF^{0}(L_{\beta }^{0}) and L^{0}= \bigcup _{\alpha \in \mathrm{On}}L_{\alpha }^{0}.
DF^{1}(A) consists of all sets of the form \{x\in A:\Phi (x,\,a_{0},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n-1})\} where a_{0},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n-1} are in A and the quantifiers are restricted to A or \mathcal{P}(A).
L_{\alpha }^{1}=\bigcup _{\beta <\alpha }DF^{1}(L_{\beta }^{1}) and L^{1}=\bigcup _{\alpha \in \mathrm{On}}L_{\alpha }^{1}.
HOD is the class of hereditarily ordinal definable sets.

sec.title: NOTE 83
sec.p: In Hickin/Plotkin [1976] it is shown that form 14 (BPI) implies [14 AR]. Since [14 AQ] follows from [14 AR] we get the equivalence of [14 AR] and 14.

sec.title: NOTE 84
sec.p: This note contains (standard) algebraic definitions for forms 241 through 244.

def.p: If F is a subfield of E,\,\alpha \in E is algebraic over F if \exists a_{0},\,a_{1},\, \ldots ,\,a_{n}\in F not all zero such that a_{0}+a_{1}\alpha \ldots +a_{n}\alpha ^{n}=0.
E is algebraic over F if every element of E is algebraic over F.
A field L is algebraically closed if every polynomial of degree \geq 1 with coefficients in L has a root in L.
If K is a field, an algebraic closure of K is an algebraically closed algebraic extension of K.
A field K is real if –1 is not the sum of squares in K.
A field is real closed if it is real and any real, algebraic extension of K equals K.
A principal ideal domain is an integral domain (commutative ring with identity and no zero divisors) in which every ideal is principal.

A unique factorization domain is an integral domain in which(i)
every non-zero, non-unit element (unit \equiv invertible) can be written a= c_{1}c_{2}\ldots c_{n} with c_{1},\,c_{2},\,\ldots ,\,c_{n} irreducible. (That is, each c_{i} is non-zero and non-unit and if c_{i}=ab then either a or b is a unit.)(ii)
If a=c_{1}c_{2}\ldots c_{n}=d_{1}d_{2}\ldots d_{m} where c_{i} and d_{i} are irreducible then n=m and there is a permutation \sigma of \{1, 2, \ldots ,\,n\} such that c_{i}=r_{i}d_{\sigma (i)} where r_{i} is a unit, i=1,\,\ldots ,\,n.

sec.title: NOTE 85
sec.p: The monadic theory MT(\omega _{1},\,<) mentioned in form 246 is defined as follows: The language has a countable set x,\,y,\,\ldots of variables ranging over \omega _{1}, a countable set of variables X,\,Y,\, \ldots ranging over subsets of \omega _{1}, a relation < on \omega _{1} and a relation \in between individual variables and set variables. The formulas are built up with the usual logical connectives and quantifiers \forall and \exists on both types of variables. MT(\omega _{1},\,<) is the set of all sentences true in (\omega _{1},\,<)

sec.title: NOTE 86
sec.p: In Plotkin [1976], it is shown that several properties of Boolean algebras provable in ZFC are not provable in ZF alone. Forms 247 and 248 are examples.

sec.title: NOTE 87
sec.p: In Truss [1975] the following weakenings of König’s lemma are considered: For any subset Z\subseteq \omega ,\,KL(Z) is the formula “If T is an infinite tree such that for every element a of T, the number of immediate successors of a is in Z, then T has an infinite branch.” Form 249 is KL(\{2\}). Here is a summary of the results:

def.p: Form 250 ((\forall n\in \omega )(C(WO,\,n))\rightarrow KL(\{k\}) is not a theorem of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} for any k>1.
Form 80 (C(\aleph _{0},2))\rightarrow KL(\{2\}) is not a theorem of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

The following conditions are equivalent:(i)
\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash KL(Z)\rightarrow KL(\{n\})(ii)
\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash KL(Z)\rightarrow C(\aleph _{0},\,n)(iii)
\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash (\forall m\in Z)(KL(\{m\})))\rightarrow C(\aleph _{0},\,n)(iv)
Gauntt’s condition L(n,\,Z), see note 15.

sec.title: NOTE 88
sec.p: Either \mathcal{N}1 or \mathcal{N}3 may be used to prove that form 31 (UT(\aleph ^{0},\,\aleph ^{0},\,\aleph ^{0})) does not imply form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite). Form 9 is known to be false in these models and a proof that form 31 holds is given below. The result is transferable to ZF by Pincus [1972].

Let \mathcal{N} be either \mathcal{N}1 or \mathcal{N}3 with set of atoms A and \mathcal{G} the group of permutations used in defining the model. Assume that in \mathcal{N},\,B is a denumerable set of denumerable sets. Let e\subseteq A be a finite support for every b\in B. Such an e exists since B is well orderable in \mathcal{N}. Assume b\in B and x\in b. The proof will be completed by showing that e is a support of x. We argue by contradiction. Assume that e is not a support of x. We will show that under this assumption b has a subset of the same cardinality as an infinite subset of A which contradicts the countability of b.

Let e^{\prime }\supseteq e be a support of x. Then there is a t\in e^{\prime }\backslash e and a \phi \in \mathcal{G} which fixes e^{\prime }\backslash \{t\} pointwise and such that \phi (x)\neq x. (It follows that \phi (t)\neq t.) It can be verified that
is a one to one function from an infinite subset of A into b which is in \mathcal{N}.

sec.title: NOTE 89
sec.p: Definitions for form 267 and [0 Y].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A free complete Boolean algebra over a set D is a complete Boolean algebra B together with a mapping f:D\rightarrow B such that range(f) generates B as a complete Boolean algebra and for every complete Boolean algebra C and function g:D\rightarrow C, there is a complete homomorphism h:B\rightarrow C such that g=h\circ f

sec.title: NOTE 90
sec.p: Monro [1972a] shows that for all n\in \omega ,\,\neg (\mathrm{ZF}\vdash K(n+1)\rightarrow K(n)). K(n) is form 81(n): For every set S there is an ordinal \alpha and a one to one function f:S\rightarrow \mathcal{P}^{n}(\alpha ). (\mathcal{P}^{0}(X)=X and \mathcal{P}^{n+1}(X)=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}^{n}(X)). K(0) is form [1 E] and K(1) is form [15 A]. Monro [1972a] also says that in an unpublished model due to H. Stewart K(2) holds, form 85 (C(\infty ,\, \aleph _{0})) fails and form 64 (there is no amorphous set) fails. (A is amorphous if A is infinite and is not the union of two non-empty, disjoint infinite sets.)

sec.title: NOTE 91
sec.p:
In this note we argue that form 269 is false in the first Fraenkel model \mathcal{N}1 of ZF^{0}. Form 269 is: “For every cardinal m, there is a set A such that 2^{|A|^{2}}\geq m and there is a choice function on the collection of 2 element subsets of A.” It suffices to show that for any set A in \mathcal{N}1 if the set [A]^{2} of two element subset of A has a choice function, then A is well orderable in \mathcal{N}1. Assume that A is such a set and assume that E is a (finite) support of A and a choice function f on [A]^{2}. Assume x\in A. We show by contradiction that E must be a support of x. Suppose not and let F be a support of x containing E. We claim there is a permutation \psi in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E) and an element y\in A such that x
eq y,\,\psi (x)=y and \psi (y)=x. This would contradict our choice of E as a support for a choice function on [A]^{2} since \psi fixes \{x,\,y\} but moves both of its elements. To get such a \psi , let \phi \in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E) satisfy \phi (x)
eq x and \phi moves only finitely many atoms. Assume F-E=\{t_{1},\,\ldots ,\,t_{n}\} and choose a set of atoms \{s_{1},\,\ldots ,\, s_{n}\} disjoint from F\cup \{t\in U:\phi (t)
eq t\}. Let \psi be the product of transpositions \prod _{i=1}^{n}(t_{i},\,s_{i}). The element \psi (x) is different from x since \phi (x)
eq x and \phi (\psi (x))=\psi (x). It is also clear that if y=\psi (x), then \psi (y)=x.

sec.title: NOTE 92
sec.p: In Kolany/Wojtylak [1991] some relationships between forms 271(m) and 45(n) are given. (271(n) is CT_{n}: The for the propositional calculus restricted to sets of formulas where each variable occurs in at most n formulas, and 45(n) is C(\infty ,\,n).) For example, CT_{m} implies C(\infty ,\,n) if m\geq n!+n(n-1). Also considered are forms CT_{m}^{\ast }\ (CT_{m} restricted to formulas which are disjunctions of formulas of the form p or (\neg p) where p is a propositional variable). For example, it is shown that CT_{3}^{\ast } implies C(\infty ,\,2).

sec.title: NOTE 93
sec.p: We give proofs due to A. Rubin that MC(\infty ,\,\infty , even) (334) is true in \mathcal{N}2 and MC(\infty ,\, \infty , odd) (333) is true in \mathcal{N}2^{\ast }(3).

statement.label: Theorem 1.
statement.p: MC(\infty ,\,\infty ,\,even) is true in \mathcal{N}2.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let M be a non-empty set in \mathcal{N}2, each of whose elements has at least two elements. The group \mathcal{G} in \mathcal{N}2 is Abelian and each of its elements has order two. Let \mathcal{F} be the filter determined by S, the set of finite subsets of the set of atoms, A. (\mathcal{F} is generated by the set of all subgroups H of \mathcal{G} such that there is an E\in S such that H fixes E pointwise.) The filter \mathcal{F} is in the model because each element in \mathcal{G} has order two so \mathcal{F} has null support. In fact,

Define a linear ordering \leq on \mathcal{F} which extends \supseteq , that is, if H_{1},\,H_{2}\in \mathcal{F} and H_{1}\supseteq H_{2}, then H_{1}\leq H_{2}. The relation \leq is in the model because of (1). (In fact, \leq is a well ordering, but we do not need this.) Let W be the set of all sets in the model that have null support. Every permutation in \mathcal{G} leaves W pointwise fixed so W can be well ordered by a relation R.

Suppose X\in M. We shall give an algorithm to construct a subset of X whose cardinality is a power of two. Let Y=\{\mathcal{G}^{\prime \prime }\{x\}:x\in X\}. Each element of Y has null support so Y can be well ordered by R. Moreover, each element of Y is finite. (In fact, the cardinality of each element of Y is a power of two because |\mathcal{G}^{\prime \prime }\{x\}|=|\mathcal{G}/\mathrm{sym}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)|, where \mathrm{sym}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)=\{\sigma \in \mathcal{G}:\sigma (x)=x\}.) Let y be the R-first element of Y and let x=y\cap X. Let \mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}}(x) be the group of all \sigma \in \mathcal{G} that fixes x pointwise and let

Since \mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)\in J,\, J\neq \emptyset . Moreover, J is finite and is linearly ordered by \leq . Let H_{0} be the \leq -first element of J. We claim that if z,\,w\in x and, H_{0}^{\prime \prime }\{z\} and H_{0}^{\prime \prime }\{w\} are both subsets of x, then H^{\prime \prime }_{0}\{z\}=H^{\prime \prime }_{0}\{w\}. The reason for this is as follows. By the definition of y(x\subseteq y), there is a \sigma \in \mathcal{G} such that \sigma (z)=w. Let K=H_{0}\cup H_{0}\sigma . Then K^{\prime \prime }\{z\}=H_{0}^{\prime \prime }\{z\}\cup H^{\prime \prime }_{0}\{w\}\subseteq x. We have \mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}} (x)\subseteq H_{0}\subseteq K so K\in J, and K\leq H_{0}. However, H_{0} is the \leq -first element of J, so K=H_{0}. Consequently, H^{\prime \prime }_{0}\{z\}=H_{0}^{\prime \prime }\{w\}.

Then, for each X\in M, we choose the unique H_{0}^{\prime \prime }\{z\} which is a subset of x\subseteq X. H_{0}^{\prime \prime }\{z\} has the same cardinality as the factor group, H_{0}/\mathrm{sym}_{H_{0}}(z), which is a power of two.

Let Z=\{u\subseteq X:X\in M\} and let f be a multiple choice function on Z such that for each u\in Z,\,|f(u)| is a power of 2. We define a multiple choice function g on M satisfying MC(\infty ,\, \infty , even) as follows. Suppose X\in M. If |f(X)|>1, then g(X)=f(X). If |f(X)|=1, consider u=f(X-\{f(X)\}). If |u|=1, then define g(X)=\{f(X),\,u\}; and if |u|>1, define g(X)=u.

statement.label: Theorem 2.
statement.p: MC(\infty ,\,\infty ,\,odd) is true in \mathcal{N}2^{\ast }(3).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: In this model the group \mathcal{G} is Abelian and each element has order three. Let M be a set of non-empty sets. We shall show that there is a multiple choice function f on M such that for each X\in M,\,|f(X)| is a power of three. The proof is the same as the proof of MC(\infty ,\,\infty , even) in Theorem 1 above up to and including the definition of x=y\cap X. Then we proceed as follows. For each u\in x, let Q(u)=\{\sigma \in \mathcal{G}:\sigma (u)\in x\}. Each Q(u) has null support and is therefore in W. Let Q_{0} be the R-first element of \{Q(u):u\in x\} and let z=\{u\in x:Q(u)=Q_{0}\}. We claim that the cardinality of z is a power of three. Fix u\in z and let K=\{\sigma \in \mathcal{G}:\sigma (u)\in z\}.\,K is a subgroup of \mathcal{G} because K=\{\sigma \in \mathcal{G}:(\sigma ^{-1})^{\prime \prime }Q_{0}=Q_{0}\}. Therefore, |z|=|\mathcal{G}/fix_\mathcal{G}(u)| which is a power of three.

sec.title: NOTE 94
sec.p: In this note we summarize what is known about the relationships between possible definitions of “finite”.

Several authors have studied this topic they include Diel [1974], Howard/Yorke [1989], Levy [1958], Spis̆iak [1993], Spis̆iak/Vojtás̆ [1988], Tarski [1938b] and [1954a], Truss [1974a] and Hickman [1972a]. The first eight definitions and their names are due to Tarski [1954a]

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: . A set A is said to be

def.p: decomposable if there are two pairwise disjoint non-empty sets x and y such that x\prec A,\, y\prec A, and A=x\cup y. (Similarly, a cardinal number m is said to be decomposable, if there exist two non-zero cardinal number p and q such that p<m,\,q<m, and m=p+q.)
Dedekind finite if it is not equivalent to a proper subset of itself. Otherwise, A is Dedekind infinite.
T-finite if every non-empty, monotone X\subseteq \mathcal{P}(A) has a \subseteq -maximal element.
I-finite if every non-void family of subsets of A has an \subseteq -maximal element. (This is (equivalent to) the usual definition of finite.)
Ia-finite if it is not the union of two disjoint sets neither of which is I-finite.
II-finite if every non-empty \subseteq -monotone family of subsets of A has a \subseteq -maximal element.
III-finite if the power set of A is Dedekind finite.
IV-finite if A is Dedekind finite.
V-finite if |A|=0 or 2 \cdot |A|>|A|.
VI-finite if |A|=0 or |A|=1 or |A|^{2}>|A|.
VII-finite if A is I-finite or not well orderable.

statement.p: In Tarski [1954a] and Levy [1958] it is shown that if a set is finite according to any definition in the above list then it is finite according to any following definition and none of the reverse implications hold.
In Tarski [1938b] the following definitions are considered:

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: For each n\in \omega , A set A is T(n)-finite if for every S\subseteq \mathcal{P}(A), if every collection of n non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets of A contains an element of S, then there are 2n+1 elements x(i), 1\leq i\leq 2n+1 of S such that A\subseteq \bigcup \{x(i):1 \leq i\leq 2n+1\}.

sec.p: In Howard/Yorke [1989] the following definition is introduced:

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A set A is D finite if |A|=0 or |A|=1 or A=C\cup D with |C|<|A| and |D|<|A|. (Note that A is D finite if and only if |A|=0 or |A|=1 or A is decomposable.

sec.p: It is shown there that IV \rightarrow D and D\rightarrow VII. Further, V \not \rightarrow D and D\not \rightarrow VI.
In Truss [1974a] the following classes of Dedekind finite cardinals are considered:

statement.label: Definition.

def.p: \Delta _{1}=\{x:x=y+z\rightarrow y or z is finite}. (We will say A is \Delta _{1} finite if |A|\in \Delta _{1}.
\Delta _{1}-finite is equivalent to Ia-finite.)
\Delta _{2}=\{|A|: any linearly ordered partition of A is finite}. (\Delta _{2}-finite is equivalent to II-finite.)
\Delta _{3}=\{|A|: any linearly ordered subset of A is finite}.
\Delta _{4}=\{x:\neg (\aleph _{0}\leq ^{\ast }x)\}. (\Delta _{4}-finite is equivalent to III-finite.)
\Delta _{5}=\{x:\neg (x+1\leq ^{\ast }x)\}.

statement.p: It is shown that I-finite \rightarrow \Delta _{1}\rightarrow \Delta _{2}\rightarrow \Delta _{4}\rightarrow \Delta _{5}\rightarrow IV-finite and \Delta _{2}\rightarrow \Delta _{3}\rightarrow IV-finite and that none of the implications are reversible. It is also shown that various combinations of equality and inequality between these classes are consistent. For example, it is shown that
is consistent.
In Diel [1974] two definitions are finite are considered: “Almost finite” which is equivalent to III-finite and “strongly Dedekind finite” which is equivalent to \Delta _{5}-finite.
Finally in Howard/Spis̆iak [1994], Spis̆iak [1993] and Spis̆iak/Vojtás̆ [1988] the following forms are considered:

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let F be one of I, Ia, II, III, IV, V, VI or VII. Then a set A is F^{\prime \prime }-finite if \mathcal{P}(A) is F-finite.

sec.p: It is shown that each of \mathrm{I}^{\prime \prime }, \mathrm{Ia}^{\prime \prime }, \mathrm{II}^{\prime \prime } and \mathrm{III}^{\prime \prime } are equivalent to I and that the following implications hold: III \rightarrow \mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow \mathrm{IV},\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime \prime } \rightarrow \mathrm{V}, and \mathrm{VII}\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime \prime }. Further it is consistent (with \mathrm{ZF}) that there exists a set with any combination of the properties \mathrm{III},\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime },\mathrm{VI}^{\prime \prime }, \mathrm{IV} and \mathrm{V} not excluded by the known implications described so far in this note. Finally, it is shown that form 88 (C(\infty ,\,2)) implies that \mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime } and III are equivalent.

In addition, in Howard/Yorke [1989], if J and K are two possible definitions of finite then the assertion that J and K are equivalent is denoted by E(J,\,K) and the strength of these weak forms of AC is investigated. Several of these appear in the list of forms: E(I,\,IV) is form 9, E(I,\,Ia) is form 64, E(I,\,III) is form 82, E(I,\,II) is form 83, E(II,\,III) is form 84, E(II,\,IV) is form [9 B], E(IV,\,V) is form [3 E], E(V,\,VI) is form [1 AH], E(VI,\,VII) is form [1 AI], E(V^{\prime \prime },\,III) is form 276 and E(D,\,VII) is form 277.
We note that E(I,\,D) which is equivalent to “every infinite set is decomposable” is equivalent to the axiom of choice since it is form CN 4F in H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], p. 139.
The known relationships between the various definitions of finite are summarized in the following diagram:
This leaves several problems open. For example, what is the relationship between \Delta _{3} and III or between \Delta _{5} and \mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime }?

sec.p: Form [154 A] appears in Brunner [1984b] as T_{\omega } and there Brunner refers to Brunner [1983b] for the result that form [154 A] is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. In Brunner [1983b] (p 437 Satz 2.2 (5)), the result (tych_{2}(\omega ) + form 106) \Leftrightarrow DC appears, that is,
Also in Brunner [1983b] (p 437 Satz 2.2 (1)) is the result
