sec.title: NOTE 96
sec.p: In Wright [1973] it is shown that form 0\not \Rightarrow form 281 by showing that every linear operator on a Hilbert space is bounded in Solovay’s model \mathcal{M}5. In this note we give the definitions for forms 279 and 281 and related results from Wright [1973].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Suppose X is a topological vector space

def.p: X is locally convex if there is a neighborhood base at \overset{\rightarrow }{0} consisting of convex sets.
A metric d on X is invariant if for all x,\,y and z in X,\,d(x+z,\,y+z)=d(x,\,y).
X is a Fréchet space if X is locally convex and the topology on X is induced by a complete, invariant metric.

statement.p: In the model \mathcal{M}5 (Solovay[1970]) form 43 (DC) and the negation of form 280 hold (the negation of 280 is “Every subset of a complete, separable metric space has the Baire property.”). Wright [1973] shows that the following are consistent by showing that they are theorems of \mathrm{ZF}+DC+\neg \mathrm{form}\,280:

def.p: If X and Y are separable, metrizable topological groups and X is complete and H:X\rightarrow Y is a group homomorphism, then H is continuous.
If X is a Fréchet space and Y is a separable, metrizable topological vector space and T:X\rightarrow Y is linear, then T is continuous.
Every linear functional on a Fréchet space is continuous.
If X and Y are Fréchet spaces, T:X\rightarrow Y is linear and there are enough linear functionals on Y to separate the points of Y then T is continuous.
If H is a Hilbert space and T:H\rightarrow H is linear, then T is bounded.

sec.title: NOTE 97
sec.p: Definitions for forms 282 and [0 AD] and related results from Kleinberg/Seiferas [1973].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume \kappa \geq \omega and \gamma \geq 1 are well ordered cardinals and \alpha and \beta are ordinals. Then \kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{\alpha } denotes the partition relation “For every function F mapping the set of \alpha -sequences from \kappa into \gamma there exists a subset X of \kappa of order type \beta such that the range of F on the set of \alpha sequences from X has cardinality 1.” If \gamma =2 we write \kappa \rightarrow (\beta )^{\alpha }. (An \alpha -sequence from Y\subseteq On is an order preserving map from \alpha to Y.) \kappa \not \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{\alpha } denotes the negation of \kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{\alpha }.

sec.p: Form [0 AD] is: For any finite n, for all ordinals \beta and well ordered cardinals \gamma , there is a well ordered cardinal \kappa such that \kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{n} and form 282 is \omega \not \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }. The axiom of choice implies for any \alpha \geq \omega , given any well ordered cardinal \gamma >1 and ordinal \beta there is no \kappa \geq \omega for which \kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{\alpha }. Also proved in Kleinberg/Seiferas [1973] are the following:

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Assume \gamma >1 is a well ordered cardinals and \alpha and \beta are ordinals with \alpha \leq \beta then

def.p: If (\ast ) fails then \exists \kappa (\kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{\alpha })\Leftrightarrow \omega \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }.
Assume C(WO,\,\infty ) and “\mathbb{R} can be well ordered” then for all \alpha ,\,\beta and \gamma ,\,\neg \exists \kappa (\kappa \rightarrow (\beta )_{\gamma }^{\alpha })
C(\aleph _{\alpha },\,\infty ) (which is form 86) implies \aleph _{\alpha }\not \rightarrow (\omega +\omega )^{\omega +\omega }.
C(\aleph _{\alpha },\,\infty )\Rightarrow \aleph _{\alpha }\not \rightarrow (\omega +\omega )^{\omega }.
C(\aleph _{\alpha },\,\infty )\Rightarrow \aleph _{\alpha }\not \rightarrow (\omega )_{\omega }^{\omega }. (So form 8 (C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )) implies form 282.

sec.title: NOTE 98
sec.p: Definitions for forms [1 AK], [1 AL] and [1 AM] from Truss [1973a].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume x and y are cardinal numbers

def.p: \aleph (x) is the least well ordered cardinal \aleph such that \aleph \not \leq x.

\alpha (x,\,y) is the least ordinal \alpha such that whenever \{z_{\gamma }:\gamma <\beta \} is a sequence of cardinals satisfying x<z_{\gamma }<y for all \gamma <\beta and \gamma <\delta \rightarrow z_{\gamma }<z_{\delta } then \beta <\alpha .

sec.title: NOTE 99
sec.p: Form 65 (Krein-Milman Theorem) does not imply form 14 (BPI) in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. The argument is as follows: By results of Bell/Jellett [1971], form 14 + form 65 implies form 1 (AC). By Pincus [1972] and [1972], 65 is true and 1 is false in \mathcal{N}2 hence form 14 is false in \mathcal{N}2. Similarly, form 52 does not imply form 286 in ZF since form 52 + form 286 implies form 1 (Bell/Jellett [1971]) and by Pincus [1972], form 52 does not imply form 14 in ZF.

sec.title: NOTE 100
sec.p: In this note we show that in \mathcal{N}23\,C(\infty ,\,2) (form 88) is false and C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 126) is true. The proof that C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) is true is due to A. Rubin.

First we shall show that C(\infty ,\,2) is false. Let B be the set of subsets x of A such that the order type of x with respect to < is \omega . Let D be the set of equivalence classes of elements of B under the relation xRy iff the symmetric difference, (x-y) \cup (y-x) is finite. (Denote the equivalence class of x by [x].) Let P be the set of pairs of elements of D. P has no choice function in the model because if f is such a choice function and E\subseteq A is a support of f it follows that for all order preserving permutations \phi of A such that \phi fixes E pointwise and for all [x],\, [y] in D, if \phi fixes \{[x],\,[y]\} then \phi fixes both [x] and [y]. We can construct a \phi ,\,x and y for which this is false as follows: Since E is well ordered there are elements a,\,b\in A such that the interval (a,\,b) contains no points of E. Let \phi be an order preserving permutation of A that fixes E pointwise, fixes a and b but moves at least one element t of (a,\,b). We may assume (by replacing \phi with \phi ^{-1} if necessary) that t<\phi (t). Let x=\{\phi ^{2n}(t):n\in \omega \} and y=\{\phi ^{2n+1}(t):n\in \omega \}. Then \phi ([x])=[y] and \phi ([y])=[x] (and [x]\neq [y]).

Next, we shall show that C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) is true in \mathcal{N}23. Let X=\{Y_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a denumerable set of non-empty sets in the model. Let B be a common support for X and the Y_{i}’s, i\in \omega . Let the open intervals of A-B be denoted by I_{\beta }, for \beta <\alpha . For each i\in \omega , choose (in the outer model) z_{i}\in Y_{i} and let B_{i} be a support of z_{i}. Let J_{\beta i}=I_{\beta }\cap B_{i}. (Note: Whenever we choose a sequence of elements in A, we choose them in increasing order. Also, \beta will range over \alpha , and i and j will range over \omega .)

We then define K_{\beta ji} as follows: For each \beta and i, choose E_{\beta i}=\{e_{\beta ji}:j\in \omega \} cofinal in I_{\beta } such that each e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i} and E_{\beta i}\cap \mathrm{cl}(B_{i})=\emptyset . Then define K_{\beta ji}= B_{i}\cap (e_{\beta ji},\,e_{\beta j+1i}). (If J_{\beta i} is not cofinal in I_{\beta }, choose E_{\beta i} such that e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i}<e_{\beta 1i} so there is only one non-empty K_{\beta ji}.)

For each \beta , choose \{c_{\beta i}:i\in \omega \} cofinal in I_{\beta } and choose \{d_{\beta ji}:i\in \omega \} in the interval (c_{\beta j},\,c_{\beta j+1}). For each \beta ,\,j, and i, let f_{\beta ji} be a function mapping K_{\beta ji} into the interval (d_{\beta ji},\,d_{\beta ji+1}) and let L_{\beta ji} be the range of f_{\beta ji}. Next, let f_{i} be an extension of \bigcup _{\beta ,j}f_{\beta ji} to a complete isomorphism of A fixing B. We claim that F=\{<Y_{i},\,f_{i}(z_{i})>:i\in \omega \} is a choice function for X that is in the model. Since f_{i} preserves B, we must have that f_{i}(z_{i})\in f(Y_{i})=Y_{i}. A support of F is \bigcup _{\beta ,j,i}L_{\beta ji} which is a well ordered union of the well ordered sets L_{\beta ji} and, therefore, can be well ordered.

sec.title: NOTE 101
sec.p: The argument that form 43 (DC) implies [43 S] (If S is a relation on A such that (\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A)(x\,S\,y) and x_{0} is any element of A, then there is a sequence a(1),a(2),\ldots of elements of A such that a(n)\,S\,a(n+1) for all n\in \omega and such that a(0)=x_{0}.) is as follows: Let S be a relation on a set A satisfying the hypotheses of [43 S] and assume that x_{0}\in A. Let B be the set of finite sequences y=\langle y(i)\rangle _{i=0}^{n} of distinct elements of A such that y(0)=x_{0} and y(i)\,S\,y(i+1) for i=0 to n-1. Define R on B by y\,R\,z\Leftrightarrow y is a proper initial segment of z. Then the relation R on B satisfies the hypotheses of form 43. The conclusion of form 43 gives a sequence y_{0}\,R\,y_{1}\,R\,y_{2}\,\ldots which gives an infinite sequence of elements of A satisfying the conclusion of [43 S].

sec.title: NOTE 102
sec.p: Form 289 (If S is a set of subsets of a countable set and S is closed under chain unions, then S has a \subseteq -maximal element.) is false in \mathcal{M}1. Let b be the generic set of generic reals in \mathcal{M}1, let E(b) be the set of all finite subsets of b, and let S=\{\cup x:x\in E(b)\}. Since b is generic, for any finite subset \{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} of b,\,a_{0}\not \subseteq \cup \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} It follows that if x,\,y\in E(b), then \cup x\subseteq \cup y iff x\subseteq y. Hence, any chain in S corresponds to a chain in E(b) and a \subseteq -maximal element of S corresponds to a \subseteq -maximal element of E(b). We claim that there is no infinite chain in E(b). For suppose x_{0}\subset x_{1}\subset x_{2}\cdots is an infinite chain in E(b). Let a_{n} be the smallest element in x_{n+1}-x_{n} for n\in \omega . Then \{a_{n}:n\in \omega \} is a denumerable subset of b, which is impossible because b is Dedekind finite. Thus, all chains in E(b) are finite so E(b) is closed under chain unions. Consequently, S is closed under chain unions. Since b is infinite, E(b) has no \subseteq -maximal element and, therefore, S has no \subseteq -maximal element.

sec.title: NOTE 103
sec.p: The results of Jech/Sochor [1966a] and [1966b] and Pincus [1971], [1972], and [1977] show that many independence results in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} will transfer automatically to ZF. These transfer theorems are given in this note. We use the notation of Pincus.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume x is a set, A is a class and \Phi (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) is a formula in the language of \mathrm{ZF} with variables among x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}.

def.p: |x| is the least ordinal \alpha such that there is a one to one function from x onto \alpha . (Note that this definition of |x| is for this note only and differs from the definition of |x| used elsewhere in this document. Also note that |x| is defined only for well ordered sets x.)
|x|^{-}=\sup \{|y| : there is a surjection from x onto y}.
|x|_{-}=\sup \{|y| : there is an injection from y to x}.

R_{\beta }(x) is defined for ordinals \beta by induction: R_{0}(x)=x,\, R_{\alpha +1}(x)=R_{\alpha }(x)\cup \mathcal{P}(R_{\alpha }(x)) and for limit ordinals \lambda ,\, R_{\lambda }(x)=\bigcup _{\gamma <\lambda }R_{\gamma }(x).

\Phi ^{A}(x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) is \Phi with quantifiers restricted to A. Similarly, if \sigma is a term in \mathrm{ZF} then \sigma ^{A} is the term defined by the same formula that defines \sigma but with its quantifiers restricted to A.

Assume that V is a model of \mathrm{ZF} and V_{0}\subseteq V is a substructure of V which is a model of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} such that every element of a V_{0} set is an element of V_{0}. (But elements of V_{0} atoms are not in V_{0}.) Assume also that V and V_{0} have the same ordinals, the same cofinality function, the same surjective cardinal function |x|^{-} (on V_{0} sets), the same injective cardinal function |x|_{-} (on V_{0} sets) and the same cardinality function |x| (on V_{0} sets.) Then the formula \Phi (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) is absolute if for all x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n} in V_{0},\, \Phi ^{V_{0}} (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n})\leftrightarrow \Phi (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}). (This is sometimes called absolute for V_{0},\,V.)
A term \sigma (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) is ordinal valued if \mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash \sigma (x_{1},\, \ldots ,\,x_{n})\in On.
A sentence is boundable if it is the existential closure of a boundable formula.

statement.p: The theorem of Jech/Sochor [1966b] is

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: A boundable sentence is transferable.

sec.p: Many applications of the theorem use the following corollary:

statement.label: Corollary.
statement.p: If \Phi is a sentence such that there is an ordinal \alpha such that ZF^{0}\vdash \Phi \leftrightarrow \Phi ^{R_{\alpha }(A)} where A is the set of atoms, then \Phi is transferable. (Note that \alpha must be a constant absolute ordinal valued term.)

sec.p: For example, form 5, C(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0},\,\mathbb{R}) is the statement “If D is a denumerable collection of denumerable subsets of \mathbb{R} then \exists f: D\rightarrow \bigcup D such that \forall d\in D,\,f(d)\in D. This is equivalent to (C(\aleph _{0},\, \aleph _{0)}\mathbb{R}))^{R_{\omega _{2}}(A)}. Similarly, the following forms are boundable and therefore transferable: 6, 11, 12, 13, 35, 36, 37, 38, 70, 73, 74, 79, 92, 93, 94, 130, 142, 169, 170, 194, 197, 199, 203, 206, 211, 212, 222, 223, 251, 252, 272, 273, 280, 289, 305, 306, 307, 309, 313, 361, 362, 363, 364, 366, 367, 368, and 369. In addition all of these forms are true in all Fraenkel-Mostowski models since they make assertions about the standard part of the model only.
Pincus has strengthened the theorem of Jech/Sochor by the following:

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A formula \Phi (y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{k}) is surjectively boundable if it is a con junction of formulas of the form

where \sigma (y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{k}) and \Psi (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n},\,y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{k}) are boundable. A sentence is surjectively boundable if it is the existential closure of a surjectively boundable formula.

A formula is injectively boundable if it is a conjunction of formulas of the form (\ast ) but with \bigcup _{j=1}^{n} x_{j}|^{-} replaced by \bigcup _{j=1}^{n}x_{j}|_{-} and a sentence is injectively boundable if it is the existential closure of an injectively boundable formula.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: An injectively boundable statement is transferable.

sec.p: Note that boundable statements are surjectively boundable and surjectively boundable statements are injectively boundable.
In many cases the following corollary suffices:

statement.label: Corollary.
statement.p: A formula \Phi is transferable if \Phi is a conjunction of sentences of the form
where \sigma _{i} is a boundable constant term and \Psi is boundable.

sec.p: For example, form 9, Dedekind finite \cong finite, is injectively boundable since it is equivalent to \forall x (|x|_{-}\leq \omega \rightarrow x is finite). Similarly, 18 and 128 are injectively boundable. Form 166 (PC(\infty ,\,2,\,\infty )) is injectively boundable since it is equivalent to (\forall x)(|x|_{-}\leq \omega \rightarrow every infinite family of pairs whose union is x has an infinite subfamily with a choice function). Similarly, 132, 336, 342, 376, 377, and 378 are injectively boundable. Other injectively boundable forms are 10, 31, 32, 80, 119, 350, 357, 358, 373, and 374 (all using Howard/Solski [1993], lemma 3.5), 17 (Blass [1977]), 64 (Pincus [1972], 2B3), 71, 82, 83 (Pincus [1972], 2B4), 98, 163, 216, (Pincus [1972], 2B5), 217 (Pincus [1972] 2B6), and 325 (note 46).
In Pincus [1972] the following transfer theorem also appears.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: A formula \Psi (x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\,w_{n}) is an onto property if it is provable that

def.p: If there is a function f from x onto y and \Psi (x, w_{1},\,\ldots ,\, w_{n}) then \Psi (y, w_{1},\,\ldots w_{n}).
x\in V_{0}\rightarrow (\Psi (x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\,w_{n})\leftrightarrow \Psi ^{V_{0}}(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\, w_{n})).
A term \sigma (x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots w_{n}) is invariant if
\sigma (x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\,w_{n})=\{z\in R_{\alpha }(x):\Phi ^{R_{\alpha }(x)}(z,\,x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\, w_{n})\} for some \Phi .
\sigma (x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\,w_{n})\neq \emptyset if x is infinite
There is a definable operator \hat{\ } such that if f:y\rightarrow x is one to one then \hat{f}:\sigma (y,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\,w_{n})\rightarrow \sigma (x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots ,\,w_{n}) is one to one.

statement.p: A formula Z(\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta }) with ordinal parameters \overset{\rightarrow }{\beta } is a term-choice formula if it is equivalent to a formula in the form
where \Psi (y,\,\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta }) is onto and \sigma (y,\,\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta }) is invariant.

A sentence is a term-choice sentence if it is equivalent to a statement in the form \forall \overset{\rightarrow }{\beta }[\Omega (\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta })\wedge Z(\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta })] where Z(\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta }) is term choice and \Omega (\overset{\rightarrow }{\beta }) is absolute.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: Class 2 statements are transferable where a class 2 statement is a finite conjunction of
(a) surjectively boundable statements,
(b) “every set can be linearly ordered”,
(c) term-choice statements.

sec.p: The following forms are class 2 statements: forms 30, 45, 46, 47, 48, 60 and 165 (all from Pincus [1972], pp 736–737), 61, 85, 88, 122, 178, 185, 213, 250, and 295.
Another transfer theorem from Pincus [1972]:

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: If \Phi is a class 2 statement which is true in the Mostowski linear order model (\mathcal{N}3) then \Phi is ZF consistent with the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14).

sec.p: Finally a transfer theorem from Pincus [1977].

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: If \Phi is a conjunction of any of the following seven kinds of statements and \Phi has a Fraenkel-Mostowski model, then \Phi has a ZF model:

def.p: Injectively boundable statements.
For any ordinal number \alpha ,\,C(<\aleph _{\alpha },\,\infty ). (This includes, for any ordinal \alpha ,\,C(\aleph _{\alpha },\,\infty ) which is equivalent to C(<\aleph _{\alpha +1},\, \infty ).)
For every ordinal \eta ,\, DC^{<\eta }. See the note below for definitions.
The ordering principle, OP (form 30)
Term choice statements
The Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14).
The Hahn-Banach theorem (form 52).

sec.p: Note. DC^{<\eta } is the statement \forall \lambda <\eta ,\,DC^{\lambda } and DC^{\lambda } is “If for every \alpha <\lambda every R-admissible \alpha sequence extends to an R-admissible \alpha +1 sequence then there is an R-admissible \lambda sequence.” (An \alpha sequence is a function with domain \alpha and an \alpha sequence \sigma is R-admissible if for all \beta <\alpha ,\,\sigma |\beta \, R\,\sigma (\beta ).
Note also that DC^{\aleph _{\alpha }} is equivalent to form 87 (DC(\aleph _{\alpha })).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: We show that DC(\aleph _{\alpha }) implies DC^{\aleph _{\alpha }}. The proof of the other impli cation is easier. Assume R is a binary relation such that for every \beta <\aleph _{\alpha } every R-admissible \beta sequence of elements of X extends to an R-admissible \beta +1 sequence of elements of X. Define the relation R^{\prime } by \sigma \, R^{\prime }\,t iff (\sigma is an R-admissible \beta sequence for some \beta <\aleph _{\alpha } and the \beta +1 sequence \sigma ^{\prime } which extends \sigma for which \sigma ^{\prime }(\beta )=t is R-admissible) or (\sigma is not R-admissible). R^{\prime } satisfies the hypotheses of DC(\aleph _{\alpha }) and therefore there is an R^{\prime }-admissible \aleph _{\alpha } sequence f. f is R-admissible for if not let \beta be the least ordinal <\aleph _{\alpha } for which \neg (f|\beta \, R\,f(\beta )). Since f|\beta \, R^{\prime }\, f(\beta ) it must be the case that f|\beta is not R-admissible. Hence for some \gamma <\beta ,\,\neg ((f|\beta )|\gamma \, R\,f(\gamma )). Since (f|\beta )|\gamma =f|\gamma , this contradicts the definition of \beta .

sec.p: Forms that can be transferred using this theorem and which have not been mentioned in this note include 8, 14, 39, 40, 43, 44, 52, 86, and 87,
In Pincus [1974], Postscript 3, it is shown that 123 is transferable and according to Pincus [1976], 120 and 121 are transferable.

sec.title: NOTE 104
sec.p: If N=N(A,\,\mathcal{G},\,S) is a permutation model, then the 2m=m principle (form 3) is false in N if the following holds in N:

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p:
Suppose there is a 1-1 function f in N mapping 2	imes A into A. Let E be a support of f and let a\in A-E. Then, since f is 1-1, f(i,\,a)
eq a for i=0 or i=1. Suppose that f(i,\, a)=b
eq a. It follows from (\ast ) that there is a \sigma \in \mathcal{G} that leaves E pointwise fixed (so \sigma (f)=f) and \sigma (a)=c
eq a. If \sigma (b)=b, then f(i,\,a)=b and f(i,\,c)=b, contradicting the fact that f is 1- 1. If \sigma (a)=b and \sigma (b)=a, then f(i,\,a)=b and f(i,\, b)=a. If j\in \{0,1\} and j
eq i, then f(j,\,a)=c, where c
eq a and c
eq b. Consequently, f(j,\,b)=c again contradicting the fact that f is 1-1.

sec.p: Examples of models that satisfy (\ast ) are \mathcal{N}1,\,\mathcal{N}2,\,\mathcal{N}2(\aleph _{\alpha }), and \mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{\alpha }).

sec.title: NOTE 105
sec.p: Proofs for the models given in 2B3–2B6 of Pincus [1972].

statement.label: Theorem 1.
statement.p: \mathcal{N}4\models 64, but 83 is false (2B3)

sec.p: (Form 64 is “There are no amorphous sets. (Every infinite set is the union of two disjoint infinite sets.)” and form 83 is “T-finite is equivalent to finite.” (A set S is T-finite if every non-empty, monotone X\subseteq \mathcal{P}(S) has a \subseteq -maximal element.).)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: First we shall show that in \mathcal{N}4 there is no infinite \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(A). Suppose C=\{S_{i}:i\in I\} is such a chain with support E. Then for all \phi \in \mathrm{fix}(E)(=\{\psi \in \mathcal{G}:(\forall a\in A)\psi (a)=a\}), for all i\in I,\,\phi (S_{i})\in C, and for all i,\,j\in I,\,S_{i}\subseteq S_{j} iff \phi (S_{i})\subseteq \phi (S_{j}). There must be an S_{j}\in C and a \phi \in fix(E) such that \phi (S_{j})\neq S_{j}. Otherwise, C can be well ordered, which contradicts the fact that in \mathcal{N}4,\, \mathcal{P}(A) is Dedekind finite. Suppose \phi (S_{j})=S_{k}. We may assume without loss of generality that S_{j}\subset S_{k}. It follows that S_{k} is Dedekind infinite, contradicting the fact that A is Dedekind finite.

Next, we shall show that every infinite set is the union of two disjoint infinite sets (64 is true). Let x be an infinite set with support E. Suppose there is a t\in x and a \phi \in fix(E) such that \phi (t)\neq t. (If no such t exists, x can be well ordered and is therefore the union of two disjoint infinite sets.) Let F be a support of t, then \phi (F) is a support of \phi (t) and F-E\neq \emptyset . Let a\in F-E. Since \precsim is a homogeneous universal partial ordering there are infinitely many elements b\in A-(E\cup F) such that a\prec b and infinitely many c\in A-(E\cup F) such that c\prec a. Let B=\{b\in A-(E\cup F):a\prec b\} and C=\{c\in A-(E\cup F):c\prec a\}. Since a\in F-E, for each b\in B and c\in C there are \phi ,\,\psi \in \mathrm{fix}(E) such that \phi (a)=b and \psi (a)=c. It follows that both of the following subsets of x are infinite: \{\phi (t):\phi \in fix(E)\wedge (\exists b\in B)(\phi (a)=b)\} and \{\psi (t):\psi \in fix(E)\wedge (\exists c\in C)(\psi (a)=c)\}. Thus, x can be partitioned into two infinite sets.

statement.label: Theorem 2.
statement.p: \mathcal{N}2\models 83, but 215 is false (2B4).

sec.p: (Form 83 is given in theorem 1 and form 215 is “If (\forall y\subseteq X)(y can be linearly ordered implies y is finite), then X is finite.”)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: First we note that the set of atoms, A, has the property that no infinite x\subseteq A can be linearly ordered so 215 is false. We shall show that for all infinite x in \mathcal{N}2,\,\mathcal{P}(x) has an infinite \subseteq -chain. Suppose x is an infinite set with support E. Suppose t\in x with support F, then y=\{\phi (F):\phi \in fix(E)\} is finite. Consequently, z_{t}=\{\phi (t):\phi \in fix(E)\} is finite. Hence, since x is infinite, Z=\{z_{t}:t\in x\} is infinite and it can be well ordered because each element has support E. Let u_{0},\,u_{1},\,u_{2},\,\cdots be an infinite sequence of elements of Z. We can construct an infinite \subseteq -chain \{U_{n}:n\in \omega \} in \mathcal{P}(x) as follows: U_{0}=u_{0} and U_{n+1}=\bigcup _{i=0}^{n}u_{i}.

statement.label: Theorem 3.
statement.p: \mathcal{N}34\models 216, but 217 is false (2B5).

sec.p: (Form 216 is “Every infinite tree has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain.” and form 217 is “Every infinite partially ordered set has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain.”.)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: First we note that the relation R on the atoms defined by c\, R\, d if and only if (\exists q,\,r\in \mathbb{Q})(q<r\wedge c\in C_{q}\wedge d\in C_{r})\vee c=d is a partial ordering in the model with no infinite chain and no infinite antichain in the model (217 is false). We shall prove that Every infinite tree (X,\,\precsim ) in the model has either an infinite chain (in the model) or an infinite antichain (in the model).

If H is a subgroup of \mathcal{G} and E\subset A, we will use the notation \mathrm{fix}_{H}(E) to denote the subgroup \{\phi \in H:(\forall x\in E)(\phi (x)=x)\} of H. H will usually be \mathcal{G} or G_{1}. One useful fact is that if \phi \in G_{1} and \psi \in G_{2} then there is a \psi ^{\prime }\in G_{2} such that \phi \circ \psi =\psi ^{\prime }\circ \phi .
We will call a finite subset D of \mathcal{C} a \ast -support of x if \bigcup D is a support of x. The following lemma about dense linear orderings and their automorphisms will be useful.

statement.label: Lemma A.
statement.p: Assume a,\,b\in \mathbb{Q},\,a<b and that E and F are finite subsets of the interval (a,\,b). Also assume that \phi is an order automorphism of (a,\,b) which fixes E pointwise. Then there is a finite set \{\phi _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\phi _{n}\} of automorphisms of (a,\,b) each of which fixes E pointwise and such that

def.p: For i=1,\,\ldots ,\,n,\,\phi _{i} moves at most one element of F and
(\forall z\in F)(\phi _{1}\circ \cdots \circ \phi _{n}(z)=\phi (z)).

sec.p: (Although we won’t prove this lemma, the first step would be the case where E=\emptyset ,\,F=\{y,\,z\} with y<z and z<\phi (y). In this case we would choose \phi _{2} so that \phi _{2}(z)=z and y<\phi _{2}(y)<z. Then \phi _{1} could be chosen so that \phi _{1}(y)=y,\, \phi _{1}\circ \phi _{2}(y)=\phi (y) and \phi _{1}(z)=\phi (z).)

Assume (X,\,\precsim ) is a tree in \mathcal{N}34 with \ast -support E. If every element of X has \ast -support E then X is well ordered in the model and therefore applying the axiom of choice in the ground model will give either an infinite chain or infinite antichain in the model. We therefore may assume that (\exists t\in X)(\exists \eta \in \mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}}(\bigcup E))(\eta (t)\neq t). Assume that t has \ast -support E\cup F where E\cap F=\emptyset . By a previous remark \eta can be written \psi \circ \phi where \phi \in G_{1} and \psi \in G_{2} and by Lemma A there are permutations \phi _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\phi _{n} in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(E) such that each \phi _{i} moves at most one element of F and \forall z\in F,\, \phi _{1}\circ \cdots \circ \phi _{n}(z)=\phi (z).

statement.label: Claim.
statement.p: There is a \gamma in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(E) that moves at most one element of F such that \gamma (t)\neq t.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p:
If \phi (t)
eq t then for at least one i,\,1\leq i\leq n,\,\phi _{i}(t)
eq t and the proof is finished by letting \gamma =\phi _{i}. Otherwise \phi (t)=t and therefore \psi (t)=\psi \circ \phi (t)=\eta (t)
eq t. The permutation \psi is a product of transpositions one of which, say 	au _{q}=(a_{q},\,b_{q}) moves t. Further C_{q}=\{a_{q},\,b_{q}\}\in F otherwise 	au _{q} fixes  igcup F pointwise and hence 	au _{q}(t)=t. Choose \gamma \in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}( igcup [(E\cup F)-\{C_{q}\}]) so that \gamma (C_{q})
eq C_{q}. Then \gamma (t) has \ast -support [(E\cup F)-\{C_{q}\}]\cup \{\gamma (C_{q})\} hence 	au _{q}(\gamma (t))=\gamma (t) since 	au _{q} fixes a support of \gamma (t) pointwise. But 	au _{q}(t)
eq t therefore \gamma (t)
eq t. This completes the proof of the claim.

sec.p: Using the notation of the claim, let D=(E\cup F)-\{C_{q}\}. And assume, as in the claim, that \gamma \in G_{1} fixes D pointwise and that \gamma (t)\neq t. We will show that the set W=\{\beta (t):\beta \in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(\bigcup D)\} (which is clearly in the model) is an infinite antichain in (X,\,\precsim ).

The first step is to argue by contradiction that \{t,\,\gamma (t)\} is not a (two element) chain in (X,\,\precsim ). Assume \{t,\,\gamma (t)\} is a chain and assume that \gamma (t)\prec t. (The argument is similar is t\prec \gamma (t).) We also assume that \gamma (C_{q})\prec C_{q} in the ordered set (\mathcal{C},\, \preceq ) (Again, an argument similar to the one we will give here will work if C_{q}\prec \gamma (C_{q}).) The set S={ \phi (C_{q}):\phi \in G_{1} and \phi fixes D pointwise} is an interval in (\mathcal{C},\, \preceq ). We will argue that, under the above assumptions, that T=\{\phi (t):\phi \in G_{1} and \phi fixes D pointwise} under the ordering \precsim is order isomorphic to S. The isomorphism f is defined by f(\phi (t))=\phi (C_{q}). (The details of the proof that f is an isomorphism will be left to the reader.) This is a contradiction since a tree cannot have dense linearly ordered subset.

Therefore \{t,\,\gamma (t)\} is an antichain. There is only one element of \mathrm{fix}_{G_{2}}(\bigcup D) that could move t, namely the transposition \tau _{q}=(a_{q},\,b_{q}). If \tau _{q}(t)\neq t then \{t,\, \tau _{q}(t)\} is also an antichain since \tau _{q}^{2} is the identity permutation. In addition \{\tau _{q}(t),\,\gamma (t)\}= \tau (\{t,\,\gamma (t)\} is an antichain because \tau fixes \precsim . Similarly \{t,\,\gamma (\tau _{q}(t))\} is an antichain.

Now assume \beta _{1}(t) and \beta _{2}(t) are in W. We first argue that if \beta _{1}(t)\neq \beta _{2}(t) then \{\beta _{1}(t),\,\beta _{2}(t)\} is an antichain. Since \beta _{1}\in G,\,\beta _{1}=\phi _{1}\circ \psi _{1} where \phi _{1}\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(\bigcup D) and \psi _{1}\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{2}}(\bigcup D). Since the only transposition in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{2}} that can possibly move t is the transposition \tau _{q}=(a_{q},\,b_{q}) we can assume that \psi _{1} is either \tau _{q} or the identity. Therefore \beta _{1}(t)=\phi _{1}(t)\circ \psi _{1}(t) where \phi _{1}\in G_{1} and fixes \bigcup D pointwise and \psi _{1} is either \tau _{q} or the identity. Similarly \beta _{2}(t)=\phi _{2}(t)\circ \psi _{2}(t) where \phi _{2}\in G_{1} and fixes \bigcup D pointwise and \psi _{2} is either \tau _{q} or the identity. The proof now proceeds by cases.
Case 1. \beta _{1}(t)=\phi _{1}(t) and \beta _{2}(t)=\phi _{2}(t).

Since \beta _{1}(t)\neq \beta _{2}(t) we have \phi _{1}(C_{q})\neq \phi _{2}(C_{q}). Therefore there is an \alpha \in G_{1} which fixes D pointwise and for which \alpha (\{C_{q},\, \gamma (C_{q})\})=\{\phi _{1}(C_{q}),\,\phi _{2}(C_{q})\}. Hence \alpha (\{t,\,\gamma (t)\})=\{\phi _{1}(t),\, \phi _{2}(t)\} and therefore, since \alpha fixes \precsim ,\,\{\beta _{1}(t),\,\beta _{2}(t)\} is an antichain.
Case 2. \beta _{1}(t)=\phi _{1}\circ \tau _{q}(t) and \beta _{2}(t)=\phi _{2}(t) where \tau _{q}(t)\neq t.

Assume that \phi _{1}(C_{q})\prec \phi _{2}(C_{q}) and that C_{q}\prec \gamma (C_{q}). (The arguments in the other possible cases are similar.) Then there is an \alpha \in G_{1} which fixes D pointwise and for which \alpha (C_{q})=\phi _{1}(C_{q}) and \alpha (\gamma (C_{q}))=\phi _{2}(C_{q}). Hence \alpha (\tau _{q}(t))= \phi _{1}(\tau _{q}(t) and \alpha (\gamma (t))=\phi _{2}(t). Therefore \alpha (\{\tau _{q}(t), \gamma (t)\})=\{\beta _{1}(t),\,\beta _{2}(t)\}. which must therefore be an antichain.
The other cases are similar. Since every two element subset of W is an antichain, W is an antichain.

It remains to show that W is infinite. This can be done by showing that for all \phi _{1},\,\phi _{2}\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(\bigcup D), \phi _{1}(t)=\phi _{2}(t)\leftrightarrow \phi _{1}(C_{q})=\phi _{2}(C_{q})

statement.label: Theorem 4.
statement.p: \mathcal{N}1\models 217, but 9 is false (2B6).

sec.p: (Form 217 is given in theorem 3 and form 9 is “Every Dedekind finite set is finite.”.)

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: The set of atoms is an infinite Dedekind finite set so 9 is false. We shall show that every infinite partially ordered set (poset) in \mathcal{N}1 either has an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Let (X,\, \leq ) be a poset with support E. If every element of X has support E, then X can be well ordered and we are done. Assume there is a t\in X and a \psi \in \mathrm{fix}(E) such that \psi (t)\neq t. We may assume that \psi moves only finitely many atoms. Let F=E\cup K be a support of t, where E\cap K=\emptyset .

sec.p:
We first argue that there is a k\in K and \phi \in \mathcal{G} which fixes F-\{k\} pointwise and \phi (t)
eq t. Choose \eta \in \mathrm{fix}(E) such that \eta (K) is disjoint from K\cup \{a\in A:\psi (a)
eq a\}. We have that \eta (t)
eq t because \psi (t)
eq t but \psi (\eta (t))=t. Assume K=\{k_{1},\,k_{2},\,\cdots ,\,k_{n}\} and for i=1,2,\,\cdots ,\,n, let f_{i} be the permutation of A that interchanges k_{i} and \eta (k_{i}). Then \prod _{i=1}^{n}f_{i} agrees with \eta on a support of t, so \gamma (t)= \eta (t)
eq t. Therefore, for at least one of the f_{i}’s, f_{i}(t)
eq t.

Now, for \gamma ,\,\sigma \in \mathrm{fix}(F-\{k\}), \gamma (t)=\sigma (t) iff \gamma (k)=\sigma (k). It follows that y=\{\gamma (t):\gamma \in \mathrm{fix}(F-\{k\})\} is an infinite subset of x that is in \mathcal{N}1. Moreover, y is an antichain, for suppose \gamma (t)<\sigma (t), where \gamma (t),\sigma (t)\in y. Let \rho \in \mathrm{fix}(F-\{k\}) be a permutation that interchanges \gamma (t) and \sigma (t). Then \sigma (t)<\gamma (t) which is a contradiction.

sec.title: NOTE 106
sec.p: This note contains results from McCarten [1988] and Schnare [1968] relating to forms [1 BF] (DT_{0}), [1 BG] (CT_{0}), [1 BH] (TT_{0}), and [1 BI] (MT_{0}).

def.p: [1 BF] (DT_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is dense in X. (Y is dense in X if there is no non-empty open subset O\subseteq X such that O\cap Y=\emptyset .)
[1 BG] (CT_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is codense in X. (Y is codense in X if there is no non-empty closed subset C\subseteq X such that C\cap Y=\emptyset .)

[1 BH] (TT_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is thick in X. (Y is thick in X if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset H\subseteq X such that H\cap Y=\emptyset .)
[1 BI] (MT_{0}): Every topological space has a maximal T_{0} subspace.

Forms \mathrm{D}T_{0} and \mathrm{C}T_{0} are false if “T_{0}” is replaced by “T_{1}”. (A counter example is the topological space (\mathbb{R},\,\tau ), where \tau =\{G\subseteq \mathbb{R}:G=(a,\,\infty ), a\in \mathbb{R} \vee G= \emptyset \vee G=\mathbb{R}\}.) McCarten [1988].
Form \mathrm{T}T_{0} remains equivalent to \mathrm{AC} if T_{0} is replaced by T_{n}, for any n such that T_{n} implies T_{0}. McCarten [1988].
\mathrm{M}T_{0} is equivalent to \mathrm{M}T_{1}. Schnare [1968].

Schnare [1968] shows that the statement \mathrm{MP} is false if \mathrm{P}=T_{2},\,T_{3},\,T_{4}, regular, completely regular, normal, paracompact, metrizable, linearly disconnected or discrete. (It follows from the lemma that if P is a property that is possessed by every finite discrete space, but not by a countably infinite minimal T_{1} space, then MP is false.)

sec.title: NOTE 107
sec.p: Good/Tree [1995] proves that each of [34 B] through [34 E] implies 34. In this note we supply the details of the converses.

In Kelley [1955], pages 173–2 there is an outline of a proof that form [34 B] (\omega _{1} with the order topology is not paracompact.) follows from \mathrm{AC}. We note that the proof requires only form 34 (\omega _{1} is regular.) and therefore 34 implies [34 B].

Let \mathcal{C} be the open cover of \omega _{1} from Kelley’s hint. That is, \mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta :\beta <\alpha \}:\alpha <\omega _{1}\}. We show that \mathcal{C} has no open, locally finite refinement by contradiction. Assume that \mathcal{A} is an open, locally finite refinement of \mathcal{C}. We define an increasing function f:\omega \rightarrow \omega _{1} by induction: f(0)=0. Assume that f(n) is defined. For each \beta \leq f(n), the set D_{\beta }=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:\beta \in x\} is finite since \mathcal{A} is locally finite. It’s also true that for each x\in D_{\beta },\, \sup \{\gamma :\gamma \in x\} is less that \omega _{1} since x is a subset of one of the elements of \mathcal{C}. Let g(\beta ) be the maximum of \{\sup (x):x\in D_{\beta }\}. g(\beta ) is also less than \omega _{1}. Now apply form 34 to the set W=\{g(\beta ):\beta \leq f(n)\}. This is a countable set of ordinals each <\omega _{1} and therefore \sup W<\omega _{1}. Let f(n+1) be the least ordinal greater than \sup W. The important property of the function f is that

The sequence \langle f(n)angle _{n\in \omega } is strictly increasing so its \sup (call the \sup \,  eta ) is a limit ordinal. Further, by form 34,  eta <\omega _{1}. Since \mathcal{A} is locally finite, there is an (open) neighborhood y of  eta such that \{x\in \mathcal{A}:x\cap \,y
eq \emptyset \} is finite. Since y is open and  eta is a limit ordinal, there is an ordinal \gamma < eta such that the interval (\gamma ,\, eta +1)\subseteq y. For some natural number k, this interval must contain f(n) for all n\geq k. For each n\geq k we consider the sets D_{f(n)}=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:f(n)\in x\}. These sets are pairwise disjoint (by (\ast )), each is non-empty and for each element x\in D_{f(n)},\, x\cap (\gamma ,\,  eta +1)
eq \emptyset . Therefore \{x\in \mathcal{C}:x\cap \,y
eq \emptyset \} is infinite, a contradiction.

To show that 34 implies [34 C] (\omega _{1} with the order topology has the property that every infinite subset has a limit point in \omega _{1}.), let X be an infinite subset of \omega _{1}. Since X is well ordered and infinite, it must have an initial segment of order type \omega . Form 34 implies that each such initial segment must be bounded, so the least upper bound of this set is a limit point of X in \omega _{1}.

If \omega _{1} is regular and contains a denumerable discrete family of open sets, then the set of smallest elements in each set would be an infinite set with no limit point, contradicting [34 C]. Thus, 34 implies [34 D] (\omega _{1} with the order topology does not contain a countable discrete family of open subsets.).

The uncountable open cover of \omega ,\,\mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta :\beta <\alpha \}:\alpha <\omega _{1} \}, described above does not contain a countable subcover. If it did we could construct a countable cofinal sequence in \omega _{1}, contradicting 34. Therefore, 34 implies [34 E] (\omega _{1} with the order topology is not Lindelöf.).

sec.title: NOTE 108
sec.p: We give the proof that each pair of cardinal numbers has a greatest lower bound (glb) (form 187) is true in \mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{1}). (The proof is due to A. Rubin.)

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: \mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{1})\models every pair of cardinals has a greatest lower bound (187).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let A^{[\omega ]} be the set of all 1-1 functions from \omega to A, the set of atoms. Let Q_{0} be the set of all partitions of A^{[\omega ]} that have the empty set as a support. (Thus, for all q\in Q_{0} if u,\,v\in q, then |u|=|v|.) Since Q_{0} can be well ordered, we can construct a subset Q\subseteq Q_{0} such that for each q\in Q_{0} there is exactly one q^{\prime }\in Q such that |q'|=|q|. Let D:Q_{0}\longrightarrow Q be such that for each q\in Q_{0},\,D(q) is the unique member q^{\prime }\in Q such that |q'|=|q|. Then, define J on Q_{0} such that for each q\in Q_{0},\, J(q):q\approx D(q). Both D and J are in the model. (Clearly D has empty support. The set F={ \{f:f is a 1–1 function from q onto D(q)\}:q\in Q_{0}} is a well ordered family of sets and, therefore, has a choice function in \mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{1}). The function J is a choice function on F.)

Suppose X is a set with support E. Let B and C be pairwise disjoint denumerable sets of atoms that are disjoint from E. Let H= \mathrm{fix}(E\cup B) and let T_{X}=\{\{\sigma (x):\sigma \in H\}:x\in X\}. T_{X} can be well ordered because H leaves T_{X} pointwise fixed. Since the axiom of choice for a well ordered family of sets is true in this model, we can construct a choice function ch for T_{X} with support E\cup B\cup C. Define functions g and h such that g:\omega \approx C and h:A\approx A-E\cup B. Let t\in T_{X} and s\in A^{[\omega ]}. Let \sigma _{s} be a permutation in H such that for all c\in C,\, \sigma _{s}(c)=h\circ s \circ g^{-1}(c). For each x\in t\in T, define j_{t}^{\prime }(x)=\{s\in A^{[\omega ]}:x=\sigma _{s}(ch(t))\}, then \{j_{t}^{\prime }(x):x\in t\in T\}=q^{\prime }\in Q_{0} and j_{t}^{\prime }:t\approx q^{\prime }. Define the function j_{t} so that j_{t}=J(q^{\prime })\circ j_{t}^{\prime }, then j_{t}(t)=D(q^{\prime })\in Q. Suppose F: T\approx \alpha , where \alpha is an ordinal. For each x\in X, where x\in t\in T, define f(x)=\langle F(t), j_{t}(x)\rangle , then f:X \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}A_{q}\times q, where A_{q} is a set of ordinal numbers. Suppose for each q\in Q,\,|A_{q}|=\alpha _{q}, then X \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\alpha _{q}\times q. This construction is independent of the choice of E,\,B and C. Now that we have this representation for each set in the model, we are ready to prove that form 187 is true.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Suppose, using the construction above, X \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\alpha _{q}\times q and Y\approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\beta _{q}\times q. Then, X\precsim Y iff for all q,\,\alpha _{q}\leq \beta _{q}.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Suppose f:X\precsim Y. Let E be a support for X and choose B\subseteq A disjoint from E such that E\cup B is a support for X,\,Y, and f. It follows that for each t_{X}\in T_{X},\, f(t_{X})=t_{Y}\in T_{Y} and f:t_{X}\approx t_{Y}. Thus, for each q\in Q,\,f induces a 1-1 map from \alpha _{q} into \beta _{q}. The converse is clear.

sec.p: Finally, if X \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\alpha _{q}\times q and Y \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\beta _{q}\times q are the representations of X and Y, we claim that Z= \bigcup _{q\in Q}\min (\alpha _{q},\,\beta _{q})\,\times \, q has the property that |Z|= \mathrm{glb}(|X|,\,|Y|). Clearly, |Z|\leq |X| and |Z|\leq |Y|. Suppose, |Z_{0}|\leq |X| and |Z_{0}|\leq |Y|. Also, suppose Z_{0} \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\gamma _{q}\times q is the representation of Z_{0}. By the lemma, \gamma _{q}\leq \alpha _{q} and \gamma _{q}\leq \beta _{q} for all q. Thus, \gamma _{q}\leq \min (\alpha _{q},\,\beta _{q}) for all q so it follows that |Z_{0}|\leq |Z|.

sec.title: NOTE 109
sec.p: Below are some definitions for forms involving conditional choice and variations of Rado’s lemma.

def.p: M is a binary mess on a set S if M is a set of functions from finite subsets of S to \{0,1\} such that for all finite P\subseteq S, there is a t\in M with domain P and for all t\in M, and for all finite P\subseteq S,\,t|P\in M.
If M is a binary mess on S, a function f:S\rightarrow \{0,\,1\} is consistent with M if f|P\in M for all finite P\subseteq S.
If f is a function and R a symmetric binary relation, f is R-consistent if for all x and y in the domain of f,\,f(x)Rf(y).

sec.title: NOTE 110
sec.p: In this note we prove the result from G. Moore [1982] that form 36 (If A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} and A \bigcap B is countable for every bounded B then A is countable.) implies form 38 (\mathbb{R} is not the union of a countable family of countable sets.)

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that form 38 is false and therefore that \mathbb{R} = \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n} where each A_{n} is countable. Let f be any bijection between \mathbb{R} and the interval (0,1). For each n\in \omega let A_{n}^{\prime }=f^{\prime \prime }A_{n}+n (where for any set X of reals and any real t,\,X+t=\{x+t:x\in X\}). Then

def.p: |A_{n}^{\prime }|=|A_{n}| and therefore each A_{n} is countable.
There is an injection from \mathbb{R}= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n} to \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}^{\prime }(x\mapsto f(x)+n where n is the least natural number such that x\in A_{n}).

sec.p: Let A= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}^{\prime }. It follows from (a) that every bounded subset of A is contained in some finite union \bigcup _{n<N}A_{n}^{\prime }. Hence, by (b), every bounded subset of A is countable. By (c), A is uncountable hence form 36 is false.

sec.title: NOTE 111
sec.p: The relationships between the forms 336(n) and 342(n) were discussed by C. Montenegro in a talk at the Latin American Logic Symposium in Bogota, 1995. (336(n) is: If X is infinite then there is an infinite Y\subseteq X such that \{t\subseteq Y:|t|=n\} has a choice function and 342(n) is PC(\infty ,\,n,\, \infty ).) He noted that for n=2 or 3, 336(n) clearly implies 342(n). He proved that 336(4) implies 342(4). The question of whether or not 336(5) implies 342(5) is open.

sec.title: NOTE 112
sec.p: In this note we prove that in \mathcal{N}41, form 9 (Dedekind finite and finite are equivalent) is true and form 122 (C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0})) is true.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: Assume that \psi is an order automorphism of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) with the property that \forall a\in \mathbb{Q},\, \lim _{n\rightarrow \infty }\psi ^{n}(a)=\infty . (That is, (\forall a\in \mathbb{Q})(\forall b\in \mathbb{Q})(\exists n\in \omega )(\psi ^{n}(a)\geq b).) Then there is an order automorphism \eta of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) such that for all a\in \mathbb{Q},\,\eta \psi \eta ^{-1}(a)=a+1.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: It follows from the hypotheses that \psi ^{n}(0)<\psi ^{n+1}(0) for each n\in \omega and that \mathbb{Q} is the disjoint union \mathbb{Q} = \bigcup _{n\in \mathbb{Z}}[\psi ^{n}(0),\, \psi ^{n+1}(0)). Let \sigma be an order isomorphism from the interval [0,\,\psi (0)) onto the interval [0,1). We define the function \eta on \mathbb{Q} as follows: Assume a\in [\psi ^{n}(0),\,\psi ^{n+1}(0)), then \eta (a)=\sigma (\psi ^{-n}(a))+ n.

A straightforward argument shows that \eta \ |\ [\psi ^{n}(0),\,\psi ^{n+1}(0)) is an order automorphism from [\psi ^{n}(0),\,\psi ^{n+1}(0)) onto [n,\,n+1) for all n\in \mathbb{Z} and that for b\in [n,\,n+1), \eta ^{-1}(b)=\psi ^{n}\sigma ^{-1}(b-n). It follows from the first assertion that \eta is an order automorphism of \mathbb{Q} and from the second we can calculate for b\in [n,\,n+1):
This completes the proof of the lemma.

statement.label: Corollary.
statement.p: Any order automorphism \psi of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) satisfying
has an n^{th} root for every n\in \omega -\{0\}. That is, there is an order automorphism \psi ^{\prime } of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) such that (\psi ^{\prime })^{n}=\psi .

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: With \eta as in the lemma, \psi =\eta ^{-1}\pi \eta where \pi (a)=a+1. Assume n\in \omega -\{0\} and let \pi _{n}(a)=a+\frac{1}{n}. If we let \psi ^{\prime }=\eta ^{-1}\pi _{n}\eta , then (\psi ^{\prime })^{n}=\psi .

statement.label: Corollary.
statement.p: Any order automorphism \psi of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) which satisfies (\forall a\in \mathbb{Q})(\forall b\in \mathbb{Q})(\exists n\in \omega )(\psi ^{n}(a)\leq b) has an n^{th} root for all n\in \omega -\{0\}.

statement.label: Corollary.
statement.p: Every order automorphism of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) has an n^{th} root for all n\in \omega -\{0\}.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let \phi be an order automorphism of (\mathbb{Q},\,\leq ) and for each a\in \mathbb{Q} let [a]={ b\in \mathbb{Q}:\exists n\in \mathbb{Z} such that b is between a and \phi ^{n}(a) }. If a is a fixed point of \phi then [a]=\{a\} otherwise [a] is an open interval in the sense that if c<d<e and c and e are in [a], then d\in [a] and [a] has no first or last element. Further the set \{[a]:a\in \mathbb{Q}\} is a partition of \mathbb{Q}. If a is not a fixed point of \phi , then it is also the case that \phi |[a] is an order automorphism of [a] and either (\forall b\in [a])(\forall c\in [a])(\exists n\in \omega )(c\leq \phi ^{n}(b)) (if \phi (a)>a) or (\forall b\in [a])(\forall c\in [a])(\exists n\in \omega )(\phi ^{n}(b)\leq c) (if \phi (a)<a). Therefore, by the previous two corollaries \phi \ |\ [a] has an n^{th} root which we denote by (\phi |[a])^{\frac{1}{n}}. Then \psi ^{\prime } defined by \psi ^{\prime }(a)=(\phi \ |\ [a])^{\frac{1}{n}}(a) is an n^{th} root of \psi .

sec.p: It will follow from the lemma below that form 9 (DF=F) and form 122 (C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0})) are true in \mathcal{N}41.

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: If x\in \mathcal{N}41 has support E=B_{0}\cup \cdots \cup B_{k} and there is some \phi \in G which fixes E pointwise but does not fix x pointwise, then x has a well orderable, infinite subset.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Assume the hypotheses. Then there is some y\in x and \phi \in G such that \phi fixes E pointwise and \phi (y)\neq y. If we assume that y has support E^{\prime }= (B_{0}\cup \cdots B_{k})\cup (B_{k+1}\cup \cdots \cup B_{r}) then we may also assume without loss of generality that for some i with k+1\leq i\leq r,\,\phi fixes A-B_{i} pointwise.

We note that if z is any element of \mathcal{N}41 of the form z=\psi (y) where \psi \in G and \psi fixes A-B_{i} pointwise, then z has support E^{\prime } (because \psi (E^{\prime })=E^{\prime }) and z\in X (since \psi fixes E pointwise). We intend to show that there are infinitely many such elements z. Assume not. Let W be the set of all such z and assume |W|=q\in \omega . By the last corollary, the permutation \phi has an n^{th} root for every positive integer n and we choose an n which is divisible by all of the integers 1,2,\ldots ,q+1. Let \eta \in G satisfy \eta ^{n}=\phi (and we may assume that \eta fixes A-B_{i} pointwise). Clearly, for any j,\,1\leq j\leq q+1,\,\eta ^{j}(y)\neq y (otherwise \eta ^{n}(y)=\phi (y)=y). It follows that for 1\leq j<m\leq q+1,\,\eta ^{j}(y)\neq \eta ^{m}(y) because equality would imply that y=\eta ^{m-j}(y). Therefore, |W|\geq q+1 a contradiction and W is infinite. Since each z\in W has support E^{\prime },\,W can be well ordered. This complete the proof of the lemma.

sec.p: To show that C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0}) is true in \mathcal{N}41 let Y be a well ordered set of finite sets in \mathcal{N}41. Suppose that E is a support of a well ordering of Y. Then for each x in Y,\,E is a support of x. By the lemma, since x is finite, E is a support of every element of x. It follows that if f is any choice function for Y (in the ground model) then E is a support of f.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: C(\infty ,\,2) (form 88) is false in \mathcal{N}10.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let C be the set of all order preserving functions f:\omega \rightarrow A such that rng(f) has an upper bound in A but no least upper bound in A. This means that rng(f) is a support and therefore f is in \mathcal{N}10. C is in \mathcal{N}10 since it has empty support. Now define an equivalence relation \sim on C by f\sim g\leftrightarrow (\exists n\in \omega )(f(k)= g(k+n) for all k\in \omega or g(k)=f(k+n) for all k\in \omega . Let [f]_{\sim } denote the \sim equivalence class of f and let X be the set of all pairs of elements of \{[f]_{\sim }:f\in C\}. The set X has no choice function in \mathcal{N}10 for suppose that E is a support of such a choice function. Choose a sequence \langle a_{n}\rangle _{n\in \omega } which has order type \omega in the ordering on A and which lies in one of the intervals determined by E in the ordering on A. There is a permutation \psi \in \mathcal{G} which fixes E pointwise and which satisfies (\forall n\in \omega )(\psi (a_{n})=a_{n+1}). Therefore, if we define f:\omega \rightarrow A by f(n)=a_{2n} and g:\omega \rightarrow A by g(n)=a_{2n+1}, then \psi ([f]_{\sim })=[g]_{\sim } and \psi ([g]_{\sim })=[f]_{\sim }. Therefore, no choice function with support E for a set containing \{[f]_{\sim },\,[g]_{\sim }\} exists.

sec.title: NOTE 114
sec.p: Definitions from Bell [1988].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume that X and Y are topological spaces.

def.p: If f is a continuous surjection from X onto Y,\,f is irreducible if the image of a proper closed subset of X is a proper subset of Y.
X is 0-dimensional if X has a base of clopen sets.
X is Boolean if X is compact, Hausdorff and 0-dimensional.
X is extremally disconnected if the closure of any open set is open.
X is \sigma -extremally disconnected if X is 0-dimensional and the algebra of clopen subsets of X is \sigma -complete (that is, countably complete). (From Morillon [1993])
If X is compact Hausdorff, a Gleason cover of X is a pair (E,\,\pi ) where E is an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space and \pi is an irreducible continuous surjection \pi :E\rightarrow X.

sec.title: NOTE 115
sec.p: Definitions from Diener [1989].

def.p: A type \tau is a function \tau =(K_{i})_{i\in I} where for each i\in I,\,K_{i} is a set (not necessarily finite). If I=\{i\} and K_{i}=M we write \tau =(M).
An algebra of type \tau is an ordered pair \mathbf{A}=(A,\,(f_{i})_{i\in I}) such that (\forall i\in I)(f_{i}:A^{K_{i}}\rightarrow A).
A homomorphism from an algebra A of type \tau to an algebra B of type \tau is closed if the image of every subalgebra of A is a subalgebra of B.

An algebra is a Peano algebra ifa.
The ranges of the operations are pairwise disjoint.b.
All of the operations are injective.c.
The elements which are not values of any operation form a generating set.
\mathfrak{P}(\tau ;Z) is the Peano algebra of type \tau with generating set Z.

sec.p: In Diener [1989] it is shown that for any set M, if \tau =(M), then the axiom of choice for families of cardinality |M| (that is, C(|M|,\,\infty )) is equivalent to the the statement “Every homomorphism of \tau algebras is closed.” See also forms [1 AP], [1 AQ], [1 AR], [67 E] and [67 F].

sec.title: NOTE 116
sec.p: A proof that form 304 (There does not exist a T_{2} topological space X such that every infinite subset of X contains an infinite compact subset.) is true in \mathcal{N}1.

Let X be an infinite \mathrm{T}_{2} topological space in \mathcal{N}1. We need to show that there is an infinite Y\subseteq X\ (Y\in \mathcal{N}1) such that Y has no infinite compact subsets (in \mathcal{N}1). If X is well orderable then it is clear that such a Y exists. Assume that X is not well orderable in \mathcal{N}1.
Choose an x\in X, a support E, an element a\in A, and a permutation \phi \in G which fixes E pointwise so that

def.p: E is a support of X and its topology.
E\cup \{a\} is a support of x and
\phi (x)\neq x. (And therefore by (b) \phi (a)\neq a.)

statement.label: Lemma.
statement.p: For all \psi ,\,\eta \in G such that \psi and \eta fix E pointwise, \psi (x)=\eta (x) if and only if \psi (a)=\eta (a).

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p:
If \psi (a)=\eta (a), then \psi and \eta agree on a support of x and therefore \psi (x)=\eta (x). Conversely, if \psi (a)
eq \eta (a), then the permutation  eta , defined to be the product of the two transpositions  eta =(a,\,\psi (a))(\phi (a),\,\eta (a))\in G, fixes E pointwise, agrees with \psi on a support of x, and agrees with \eta \phi ^{-1} on a support of \phi (x). It follows that  eta (x)=\psi (x) and that  eta (\phi (x))=\eta \phi ^{-1}(\phi (x))=\eta (x). Since x
eq \phi (x) we conclude that  eta (x)
eq  eta (\phi (x)), that is \psi (x)
eq \eta (x).

sec.p: By the lemma, the set of pairs F=\{(\psi (x),\,\psi (a)):\psi \in G and \psi fixes E pointwise} is a one to one function (in the model \mathcal{N}1) from Y=_{\mathrm{def}}\{\psi (x):\psi \in G and \psi fixes E pointwise} onto A-E.

Since the topology on X is \mathrm{T}_{2} we can choose open sets C and D so that x\in C,\,\phi (x)\in D and C\cap D=\emptyset . Since Y can be put in a one to one correspondence with a subset of the atoms in the model, every subset of Y in the model must be finite or cofinite. This means that at least one of Y\cap C or Y\cap D is finite. We may assume that Y\cap C is finite by replacing C by C\cap \phi ^{-1}(D) if necessary. Under this assumption we can conclude that \mathcal{C}=\{\psi (C):\psi \in G and \psi fixes E pointwise} is an open cover for Y. Further each element of \mathcal{C} is finite. It follows that for any infinite subset Z of Y,\,\mathcal{C} is an open cover for Z without a finite subcover.

sec.title: NOTE 117
sec.p: Definitions from Cowen [1990] for forms [14 BD] through [14 BG]. A hypergraph is a pair H=\langle V,\, E\rangle where V is a set (of vertices) and E is a set of non-empty finite subsets of V. E is called the set of edges. H is finite if V is finite. K=\langle W,\, F\rangle is a subhypergraph of H=\langle V,\, E\rangle if W\subseteq V and F\subseteq E. W\subseteq V is independent in H=\langle V,\, E\rangle if no two elements of W belong to the same edge of H. W\subseteq V is a vertex cover of H=\langle V,\, E\rangle if each element of \mathrm{E} contains at least one element of W. An n-coloring of H=\langle V,\, E\rangle is a function f:V\rightarrow \{0,\,1,\,\ldots ,\,n-1\} such that |f^{\prime \prime }e|>1 for all e\in E with |e|>1.

sec.title: NOTE 118
sec.p: Definitions from Galvin/Komjáth [1991] for forms [1 AT] through [1 AW].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume that G=(V,\,E) is a graph.

def.p: S\subseteq V is dependent if \{x,\,y\}\in S for some \{x,\,y\}\in E. Otherwise S is independent.
f:V\rightarrow C is a good coloring if f^{-1}(c) is independent for each c\in C.
Let \kappa =|C|, then G is \kappa colorable if there is a good coloring f:V\rightarrow C. (C need not be well orderable.)
The least \kappa for which G is \kappa colorable (if it exists) is the chromatic number of G.
A good coloring f:G\rightarrow C is irreducible if f^{-1}(c_{1})\cup f^{-1}(c_{2}) is dependent whenever c_{1},\,c_{2}\in C and c_{1}\neq c_{2}.
(So a graph admits an irreducible good coloring just in case its vertex set can be partitioned into independent sets such that the union of any two is dependent.)
For any two sets A and B define the graph G(A,\,B) with vertex set A\times B by (a_{1},\,b_{1})\neq (a_{2},\,b_{2}) are adjacent if a_{1}=a_{2} or b_{1}=b_{2}.

sec.title: NOTE 119
sec.p: Definitions from Shannon [1992] for form [86(\alpha ) A].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order (i.e., reflexive and transitive).

def.p: x,\,y\in P are incompatible if there is no z\in P such that z\leq x and z\leq y.
I\subseteq P is an antichain if any two different elements of I are incompatible.
A partially ordered set (P,\,\leq ) is a tree iff \forall x\in P,\,\{y\in P:y\leq x\} is well ordered by \leq and (P,\,\leq ) has a unique minimal element.

statement.p: Assume (P,\,\leq ) is a tree.

def.p: If x\in P then ht(x) (the height of x) is the order type of \{y\in P:y<x\}.
\mathrm{lev}_{\alpha }(P)=\{x\in P:ht(x)=\alpha \}.
The height of P is the least \alpha such that \mathrm{lev}_{\alpha }(P)=\emptyset .
A branch in (P,\,\leq ) is a maximal chain.
If (P,\,\geq ) is an upside down tree then a strong antichain in (P,\,\geq ) is an antichain that has at most one element from each level of (P,\,\leq ).
