sec.title: NOTE 121
sec.p: This note contains an argument that the order extension principle (form 49) together with “Every linear ordering has a cofinal well ordered subset.” (form 51) implies AC (form 1). This result was announced in Morris [1969].
Assume that Y is a set of non-empty sets. Let P be the set of choice functions f such that the domain of f is a subset of Y. We define the following partial ordering on P:

Extend \preceq _{0} to a linear ordering \preceq on P. Let \{f_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \beta \} be a cofinal subset of the linear ordering (P,\,\preceq ) where f_{\alpha }\prec f_{\gamma }\leftrightarrow \alpha \in \gamma . (\in is the usual well ordering on the ordinals.) The set W= \bigcup _{\alpha \in \beta } \mathrm{dom}(f_{\alpha }) has a choice function F defined by F(x)=f_{\alpha }(x) where \alpha is the least ordinal for which x\in \mathrm{dom}(f_{\alpha }). We complete the proof by showing that W=Y. If not, then there is some x\in Y-W. Let t be any element of x, then G=F\cup \{(x,\,t)\} is in P and has the property that \forall \alpha \in \beta ,\,f_{\alpha }\prec _{0}G and hence, since \preceq extends \preceq _{0},\,f_{\alpha }\prec G. This contradicts the cofinality of \{f_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \beta \}.

sec.title: NOTE 122
sec.p: In \mathcal{N}43, both C(\aleph _{0},2) (form 80) and the Multiple Choice Axiom (MC(\infty ,\,\infty ), form 67) are false.

C(\aleph _{0},2) is false in \mathcal{N}43: For each n\in \omega , let w_{n}=(a_{0}^{n},\,a_{1}^{n},\,\ldots ,\, a_{n}^{n}) be a fixed well ordering of P_{n}. (The function choosing these well orderings will not be in the model.) Let C_{0}^{n}={\phi (w_{n}):\phi is an even permutation of P_{n}} and C_{1}^{n}=\{\phi (w_{n}):\phi is an odd permutation of P_{n}}. Then for every n\in \omega , \{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\} is in \mathcal{N}43 and has empty support. In fact if \psi |P_{n} is even then \psi fixes \{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\} pointwise and if \psi |P_{n} is odd then \psi interchanges C_{0}^{n} and C_{1}^{n}.

If E is any support, then there is a \psi \in G that fixes E pointwise and an n\in \omega such that \psi |P_{n} is odd. Since such a \psi fixes \{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\} but moves both its elements, E is not a support of a choice function on \{\{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\}:n\in \omega \}.

MC(\infty ,\,\infty ) is false in \mathcal{N}43: Let F be the set of all choice functions f:\omega \rightarrow A such that \forall n\in \omega ,\,f(n)\in P_{n}. Suppose that E is a support of a multiple choice function H on \mathcal{P}(F)-\{\emptyset \} in \mathcal{N}43. Let k= \sup \{|E\cap P_{n}|:n\in \omega \} and define T\subseteq F by T=\{f\in F:(\forall i>k)(f(i)\in P_{n}-E)\}. Since E is a support of T and of H,\, E is a support of H(T) which must be a finite, non-empty subset of T. Fix f in H(T) then for every g\in T for which g(i)=f(i) for i\leq k, there is a \phi \in G which fixes E pointwise such that \phi (f)=g. Therefore g\in H(T). Since there are infinitely many such g’s, H(T) is infinite. This is a contradiction.

sec.title: NOTE 123
sec.p: We shall prove that form 10 (C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}))\ + form 163 (Every non-well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) implies form 231 (UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO)) and also that form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous set.) implies form 231. (It is shown in Brunner [1982a] that 10 + 163 implies 165 (C(WO,\,WO)).)

Suppose X is a well ordered set of pairwise disjoint well orderable sets. Assume Y=\bigcup X cannot be well ordered. Form 163 implies that Y has an infinite Dedekind finite set Z. Let T=\{w\cap \,z:w\in X\wedge w\cap z\neq \emptyset \} For each w\in Z,\,w\cap Z is a well ordered Dedekind finite set so it must be finite. If T is finite, then Z is a finite union of finite sets and is therefore finite. This contradicts the definition of Z. If T is infinite, then T is well ordered because X is well ordered. Therefore T must have a denumerable subset, U. U is a denumerable set of finite sets, so by 10, U has a choice set. This choice set is a denumerable subset of Z. This contradicts the definition of Z. Thus, the union of X can be well ordered.
Since form 133 (every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset) implies form 10 (Brunner [1984b]) and 133 implies 163 (clear), it follows that 133 implies 231.

sec.title: NOTE 124
sec.p: A proof that form 314 (Every permutation on a non-empty set can be expressed as a product of two reflections.) implies form 119 (C(\aleph _{0},uniformly orderable with order type of the integers)).

Assume that B=\{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} is a denumerable set of denumerable sets and f is a function defined on \omega such that \forall i\in \omega ,\,f(i) is an ordering of A_{i} with order type that of the integers. We want to construct a choice function g for B so we may assume that the elements of B are pairwise disjoint.

Let \eta be the permutation of \bigcup B defined by \eta (a)= the immediate successor of a under the ordering f(A_{i}) where A_{i} is the unique element of B such that a\in A_{i}. By form 314, \eta is the product of two reflections: \eta =\phi \circ \psi .

Fix an i\in \omega and for each permutation \beta of \bigcup B, let \beta ^{\prime }=\beta \ |\ A_{i}. Then \eta ^{\prime }=\phi ^{\prime }\circ \psi ^{\prime } and \phi ^{\prime } and \psi ^{\prime } are reflections. We complete the proof by showing that exactly one of \phi ^{\prime } or \psi ^{\prime } has exactly one fixed point. (This fixed point will be g(A_{i}).)

Since \phi ^{\prime } and \psi ^{\prime } are both reflections, \phi ^{\prime } and \psi ^{\prime } can both be written as a product of disjoint cycles, \phi '=\prod _{i\in I}(s_{i},\,t_{i}) and \psi ^{\prime }=\prod _{j\in J}(c_{j},\,d_{j}). Assume that A_{i}=\{\ldots ,\,a_{-1},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots \} where the elements are listed in the order determined by the ordering f(A_{i}). Then \eta ^{\prime } is the infinite cycle \eta ^{\prime }= (\ldots ,\,a_{-1},\, a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots ). Let r be the smallest positive integer such that for some integer k the transposition (a_{k},\,a_{k+r}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}) or one of the (c_{j},\,d_{j})

We first show that r=1. Assume that r>1 and that (a_{k},\,a_{k+r}) is one of the (c_{j},\,b_{j}). (The argument is similar if (a_{k},\,a_{k+r}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}).) This means that \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+r}. Since \eta ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+1} (and r\neq 1), \phi ^{\prime }(a_{k+r}) must be a_{k+1}, hence the transposition (a_{k+1},\,a_{k+r}) must be one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}). This contradicts the definition of r.

Assume that (a_{k},\,a_{k+1}) is one of the (c_{j},\,d_{j}). (The argument is similar if (a_{k},\, a_{k+1}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}).) This means that \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+1}. Since \eta ^{\prime }(a_{k})= a_{k+1} we conclude that a_{k+1} must be a fixed point of \phi ^{\prime }. Further, since \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k+1})=a_{k} and \eta ^{\prime }(a_{k+1})=a_{k+2} we conclude that \phi ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+2}, that is, (a_{k},\,a_{k+2}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}). By this last conclusion, \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k+2})=a_{k}. It follows that \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k-1})=a_{k+2}, that is (a_{k-1},\, a_{k+2}) is one of the (c_{j},\,d_{j}). Continuing in this way, we see that for every natural number j,\,\psi ^{\prime } interchanges a_{k-j} and a_{k+j+1} and \phi ^{\prime } interchanges a_{k-j} and a_{k+j+2}. Therefore, \psi ^{\prime } has no fixed points and \phi ^{\prime } has exactly one fixed point.

sec.title: NOTE 125
sec.p: In this note we survey forms of the Hahn-Banach Theorem discussed in Buskes [1993].

statement.label: Definition 1.
statement.p: Let E be a vector space over \mathbb{R}, and let p be a mapping from E to \mathbb{R}.

def.p: p is called sublinear if p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y), for all x,\,y\in E, and p(rx)=rp(x), for all x\in E and all r\in \mathbb{R}^{+}.
p is called a seminorm if p is sublinear and p(rx)=|r|p(x), for all x\in E and all r\in \mathbb{R}.
p is called a norm if p is a seminorm and p(x)=0 iff x=0, for all x\in E.
p is called superlinear if p(x)+p(y)\leq p(x+y) for all x,\,y\in E, and p(rx)=rp(x), for all x\in E and all r\in \mathbb{R}^{+}.

statement.label: H-B 1.
statement.p: (Form 52) Assume E is a vector space over \mathbb{R} and p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is a sublinear function. Suppose E_{0} is a subspace of E and f_{0} is a linear function from E_{0} to \mathbb{R} such that f_{0}(x)\leq p(x), for all x\in E_{0}. Then there is a linear function f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} that extends f_{0} and f(x)\leq p(x), for all x\in E.

statement.label: H-B 2.
statement.p: Assume E is a vector space over \mathbb{R} and p is a norm on E. Suppose E_{0} is a subspace of E and f_{0} is a continuous linear function from E_{0} to \mathbb{R}. Then there is a continuous linear function f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} that extends f_{0} and \Vert f_{0}\Vert =\Vert f\Vert . (For any subspace E_{0}\subseteq E and any linear function f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R},

statement.label: H-B 3.
statement.p: Assume E is a vector space over \mathbb{R},\,p a sublinear function on E, and q a superlinear function on E. If q(x)\leq p(x) for all x\in E, then there exists a linear function f: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that q(x)\leq f(x)\leq p(x) for all x\in E.

statement.label: H-B 4.
statement.p: (Complex form of \mathbf{H{-}B\ 1}) Assume E is a vector space over \mathbb{C} and p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} a seminorm (a sublinear function for which p(\alpha x)=|\alpha |p(x) for all x\in E and all \alpha \in \mathbb{C}). Let E_{0} be a subspace of E and f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{C} be linear such that |f_{0}(x)|\leq p(x) for all x\in E. Then there is a linear function f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{C} such that |f(x)|\leq p(x) for all x\in E.

statement.label: H-B 5.
statement.p: (Complex form of \mathbf{H{-}B\ 2}) (Change “\mathbb{R}” in \mathbf{H}{-}\mathbf{B\ 2} to “\mathbb{C}”. \mathbf{H{-}B\ 5} is equivalent to \mathbf{H{-}B\ 2}. Let f_{0}=f_{1}+if_{2}, where f_{1} and f_{2} are real continuous function from E_{0} to \mathbb{R}. Let f_{1}^{\ast } be an extension of f_{1} to E so that \Vert f_{1}^{\ast }\Vert \leq \Vert f_{0}\Vert . Then the desired extension f of f_{0} can be defined as f(x)=f_{1}^{\ast }(x)-if_{1}^{\ast }(x) for all x\in E.)

statement.label: Definition 2.
statement.p: A metric space E is spherically complete if the set of its closed balls has the binary intersection property (if the intersection of each pair of balls is non-empty, the intersection of the whole set is non-empty).

statement.label: H-B 6.
statement.p: (Ingleton’ s Theorem) Assume K is a spherically complete, non-Archimedean valued field. Let E be a normed vector space over K and let E_{0} be a subspace of E.
Let f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow K be a continuous linear function. Then there exists a continuous linear function f:E\rightarrow K that extends f_{0} and for which \Vert f\Vert =\Vert f_{0}\Vert .

statement.label: Definition 3.
statement.p: Let (E,\,\Vert \ \Vert ) be a normed vector space.

def.p: exists.

(E,\,\Vert \ \Vert ) is said to be uniformly convex if for every \epsilon >0 there is a \delta >0 such that for all x,\,y\in E with \Vert x\Vert =\Vert y\Vert =1,\,\Vert x-y\Vert \geq \epsilon implies \frac{1}{2}\Vert x+y\Vert \leq 1-\delta .

statement.label: H-B 7.
statement.p: (Ishihara’s Theorem) Let E_{0} be a subspace of a uniformly convex Banach space E with a Gateaux differentiable norm. Let f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R} be a non-zero continuous linear function. Then there is a unique linear continuous extension f from E to \mathbb{R} such that \Vert f\Vert =\Vert f_{0}\Vert .

statement.label: H-B 8.
statement.p: Suppose E is a normed vector space in which the unit ball is weakly compact and the norm in E is Gateaux differentiable. Let E_{0} be a subspace of E. Then every continuous linear function f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R} can be uniquely extended to a continuous linear function f: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that \Vert f\Vert =\Vert f_{0}\Vert .

statement.label: H-B 9.
statement.p: (Mazur-Orlicz Theorem) Assume E is a vector space over \mathbb{R} and p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is a sublinear function. Let T be a set and let \phi and \alpha be functions such that \phi :T\rightarrow E and \alpha :T\rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Then the following are equivalent.

def.p:
There exists a linear f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that(i)
f\leq p and(ii)
\alpha (t)\leq f(\phi (t)) for all t\in T.

sec.p: The last three forms are examples of Hahn-Banach theorems in which the range of the function that is to be extended may not be commutative.

statement.label: H-B 10.
statement.p: (Kantorovich) Suppose E is an ordered vector space and E_{0} a cofinal subspace. Let F be an order complete vector space. Then each positive linear map from E_{0} to F can be extended to a positive linear map from E to F.

statement.label: H-B 11.
statement.p: (Lipecki-Plachky-Thomsen, Luxemburg-Schep) Suppose E is a vector lattice and E_{0} is a cofinal vector sublattice. Let F be an order complete vector lattice. Then each vector lattice homomorphism from E_{0} to F can be extended to a vector lattice homomorphism from E to F.

def.p: A Banach algebra is a complex algebra together with a complete norm satisfying the condition \Vert xy\Vert \leq \Vert x\Vert \Vert y\Vert , for all x and y. If the algebra contains an identity element e,\,\Vert e\Vert =1.

A C^{\ast }-algebra is a Banach algebra with an involution x\mapsto x^{\ast } on it satisfying(i)
x^{\ast \ast }=x for all vectors x.(ii)
(ax+bx)^{\ast }=\overline{a}x^{\ast }+\overline{b}y^{\ast } for all vectors x and y and all complex numbers a and b.(iii)
(xy)^{\ast }=y^{\ast }x^{\ast } for all vectors x and y.(iv)
\Vert x^{\ast }x\Vert =\Vert x\Vert ^{2} for all vectors x.

statement.label: H-B 12.
statement.p: (Arveson) Suppose E is a C^{\ast }-algebra and E_{0} is a cofinal \ast -invariant subspace of E. Let H be a Hilbert space and B(H) the space of all bounded operators on H. Then each completely positive linear map from E_{0} to B(H) extends to a completely positive linear map from E to B(H).

sec.p: For additional results see Buskes [1993] and his references.

sec.title: NOTE 126
sec.p: We give definitions for form [43 B] from Goldblatt [1985].
Let \Phi be a class of formulas in a language that includes the language of the sentential calculus and suppose the deducibility relation, \vdash , satisfies the following:

def.p: \emptyset \vdash \phi , for every tautology \phi .
\Gamma \cup \{\phi \}\vdash \psi iff \Gamma \vdash \phi \rightarrow \psi , where \Gamma \subseteq \Phi .
If \Gamma \vdash \phi and \Gamma \subseteq \Delta , then \Delta \vdash \phi , where \Gamma ,\, \Delta \subseteq \Phi .

statement.label: Definition 5.
statement.p: \Gamma \subseteq \Phi is finitely consistent if every finite subset of \Gamma is consistent.

statement.label: Definition 6.
statement.p: An ordered pair (\Pi ,\,\psi ) is called an inference if \Pi \subseteq \Phi and \psi \in \Phi .

statement.label: Definition 7.
statement.p: If \Gamma \subseteq \Phi ,\,\Gamma respects the inference (\Pi ,\,\psi ) if

statement.label: Definition 8.
statement.p: If \Gamma \subseteq \Phi ,\,\Gamma decides the inference (\Pi ,\,\psi ) if
(We say \Gamma respects (decides) a set of inferences I if \Gamma respects (decides) each inference in I.)

def.p: Countable Henkin Principle: Let \Phi be the class of formulas in a language that includes the language of the sentential calculus. Let I be a countable set of inferences, and \Gamma a consistent subset of \Phi such that \Gamma \cup \{\psi \} respects I for each \psi \in \Phi . Then for any \phi \in \Phi , if \phi is consistent with \Gamma then \Gamma has a finitely consistent extension that contains \phi and decides I.

statement.p: Goldblatt [1985] proves that [43 B] is equivalent to the principle of dependent choices (form 43) and Goldblatt [1984] shows how [43 B] may be used to prove completeness and omitting-types theorems for countable first-order languages.

sec.title: NOTE 127
sec.p: Forms [1 BZ] (Vector space multiple choice) and 346 (Vector space Kinna-Wagner principle) were suggested by K. Keremedis. It is clear that [1 BZ] implies 346. In this note we prove that 346 implies the Kinna-Wagner principle KW(\infty , < \aleph _{0}) (form [62 E]). Since the axiom of choice is implied by the conjunction of forms 62 and 67, we obtain a proof that 346+67 implies the axiom of choice. (Form 62 is C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) and 67 is the axiom of multiple choice.) Similarly, since [1 BZ] implies form 67, we obtain the result: [1 BZ] implies the axiom of choice.

Let X=\{y_{i}:i\in K\} be a family of finite sets. For each y_{i} let U_{i} be the real vector space \mathbb{R}^{y_{i}} with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. (If y_{i}= \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\, a_{n}\} we could think of U_{i} as being the set of all formal sums k_{1}a_{1}+\cdots +k_{n}a_{n} where the k_{i}’s are real.) Let S_{i} be the subspace { g\in U_{i}:g is constant}. (Or in terms of formal sums, S_{i} is all formal sums ka_{1}+\cdots +ka_{n}.) Let V_{i} be the quotient space V_{i}=U_{i}/S_{i}. That is, V_{i} consists of all equivalence classes [g] of elements of U_{i} under the relation g\sim f\Leftrightarrow g-f\in S_{i}. By form 346 there is a family \{F_{i}:i\in K\} such that for each i\in K,\,F_{i} is an independent subset of V_{i}. Since U_{i} is finite dimensional F_{i} must be finite. Say F_{i}=\{b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{r}\} then since F_{i} is independent, the element w_{i}=b_{1}+\cdots +b_{r} is not zero. The vector w_{i}=[g] for some g\in U_{i}. Assume f\in [g]. Then if a,\,a^{\prime }\in y_{i} and g(a)\leq g(a^{\prime }) it follows from the fact that f-g is constant that f(a)\leq f(a^{\prime }). Therefore the set K_{i}=\{a\in y_{i}:g(a) is minimum among the numbers g(a^{\prime }) for a^{\prime }\in y_{i}} is independent of the choice of g\in w_{i}. It is also true that K_{i}\neq y_{i}. This follows from the fact that w_{i}\neq 0 which implies that g is not constant. The family \{K_{i}:i\in K\} is therefore a Kinna-Wagner function for X.

sec.title: NOTE 128
sec.p: In this note we prove that in \mathcal{N}51, form 64 (There are no amorphous sets.) and form 90 (Every linearly orderable set is well orderable.) are true and form 221 (Every infinite set has a non-principal measure.) is false. The Hahn-Banach Theorem (form 52) implies 221, so it is also false. (See Brunner/Howard/Rubin [1996].)

We first note that for each finite ordered partition P= (B_{1},\,\ldots ,\,B_{n}) of A,\,G_{P}\in \mathcal{F}, where G_{P}=\{\psi \in G:\psi (P)=P\} and \mathcal{F} is the filter of subgroups which determine \mathcal{N}51. Further, if H\in \mathcal{F} then there is a finite ordered partition P of A such that G_{P}\subseteq H. Therefore for each x\in \mathcal{N}51, there is a finite ordered partition P of A such that (\forall \psi \in G_{P})(\psi (x)=x). We will refer to such a partition P as a support of x.
In order to prove that form 221 is false we shall give a proof that in \mathcal{N}51 there is no non-principal measure on A, the set of atoms.

Suppose, m is a non-principal measure on A supported by the partition P= (B_{1},\,\ldots ,\,B_{n}) of A. Since m is finitely additive on disjoint sets, m(A)=1, and m(\{a\})=0, for all a\in A. It follows that there must be an i\leq n such that B_{i} is infinite and m(B_{i})\neq 0. There exist pairwise disjoint infinite subsets, S_{1},\,S_{2}, and S_{3}, of B_{i} such that B_{i}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cup S_{3}. Suppose \sigma _{1},\,\sigma _{2}\in G_{P} are such that
Consequently, m(S_{1})=2m(S_{1}), which implies that m(S_{1})=0. Thus, by (b), m(B_{i})=0, which is a contradiction.

In order to prove that forms 90 and 64 are true, we need the following lemma which is a slight strengthening of form 314 (from Degen [1988]). The proof requires the axiom of choice but we intend to use the lemma in the ground model where AC holds.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: In \mathcal{N}51 every linearly orderable set is well orderable.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Let X be linearly orderable in \mathcal{N}51 and assume that the ordered partition P= (B_{1},\,\ldots ,\, B_{k}) is a support of a linear ordering < on X. We shall show that if \psi \in G_{P}, then \psi fixes X pointwise and hence P is a support of a well ordering of X. Assume \psi \in G_{P}. By the lemma, \psi =\rho _{2}\circ \rho _{1} where \rho _{1} and \rho _{2} are reflections and (by part (ii)) \rho _{1} and \rho _{2} are in G_{P}. The permutations \rho _{1} and \rho _{2} are therefore order automorphisms of (X,\,<). Since no order automorphism of a linearly ordered set can have a finite cycle of length greater than 1, we conclude that for all x\in X,\,\rho _{1}(x)=x and \rho _{2}(x)=x hence \forall x\in X,\,\psi (x)=x.

statement.label: Theorem.
statement.p: In \mathcal{N}51 there are no infinite amorphous sets.

statement.title: Proof.
statement.p: Assume that X\in \mathcal{N}51 is infinite and that the ordered partition P= (B_{1},\,\ldots ,\,B_{k}) of A is a support of X. We will show that there is an infinite set R\in \mathcal{N}51 such that R\subset X and X-R is infinite.
If every element of X has support P then X is well orderable in \mathcal{N}51 and the proof is easy. We therefore assume that y\in X and there is a \phi \in G_{P} such that \phi (y)\neq y.
Step 1. We show that we may assume that y has a support

sec.title: NOTE 129
sec.p: In this note we give definitions concerning free groups for forms [1 BB], [1 CA], 68 and 348.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume that (G,\,\circ ) is a group freely generated by X, that A\subseteq G, and that a,\,b and c are in G.

def.p: The subgroup of G generated by A is denoted \langle A\rangle .

The length of a with respect to X (denoted by L_{X}(a) or L(a)) is the unique natural number n such that there are elements a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n} of X\cup X^{-1} such that a_{j}\neq a_{j+1}^{-1} and a=a_{1}\circ \cdots \circ a_{n}.
The subset A is level with respect to X if \langle A\rangle is freely generated by A and for each b\in \langle A\rangle ,\,b\in \langle \{a:a\in A\wedge L(a)\leq L(b)\}.

A subset A of G has the Nielsen property with respect to X ifa.
A\cap A^{-1}=\emptyset .b.
If a,\,b\in A\cup A^{-1} and L(a\circ b)<L(a) then b=a^{-1}, andc.
If a,\,b and c\in A\cup A^{-1} and L(abc)\leq L(a)-L(b)+L(c) then either b=a^{-1} or c=b^{-1}.

statement.p: In Federer/Jonsson [1950] it is shown that a set with the Nielsen property is level.

sec.title: NOTE 130
sec.p: In this note we prove that form [30 G] (Every \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(X) is contained in a maximal \subseteq -chain) is equivalent to form 30 (The ordering principle). Form [30 G] was suggested by Adam Kolany.

Assume [30 G]. Let X be a set and let Y be a maximal \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(X). Define \leq on X by a\leq b iff (\exists A\in Y)(a\in A\wedge b
ot \in A). \leq is linear because if not there are a,\,b\in X such that a
ot \leq b and b
ot \leq a. If this happens then Y\cup \{A_{0}\} (where A_{0}=( igcup \{A\in Y:a
ot \in A\})\cup \{b\}) is a chain in \mathcal{P}(X) which properly extends Y.

Assume form 30. Let X be a set and Y a \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(X). Let \leq be a linear ordering of X. Define another linear ordering R on X by a\, R\,b iff [(\exists A\in Y)(a\in A\wedge b\not \in A)] or [(\forall A\in Y)(a\in A\leftrightarrow b\in A)\wedge a\leq b]. Then Y^{\prime }=\{A\subseteq X:(\forall a\in A)(\forall x\,R\,a)(x\in A)\} is a maximal \subseteq -chain containing Y.

sec.title: NOTE 131
sec.p: In this note we give a proof of form [ 0 AL] (For every set A, there is an \aleph which cannot be covered by fewer than |A| sets each of cardinality <|A|.) in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. Form [0 AL] was suggested by K. Keremedis.

Let A be a set and suppose that K is an aleph which is covered by fewer than |A| sets of cardinality <|A|. Let \leq be the usual ordering on K and let \bigcup _{b\in B}C_{b}=K where |B|<|A| and for each b\in B,\,|C_{b}|<|A|. Since each C_{b} is well orderable, |C_{b}|<H(A). (The function H is Hartogs’ aleph function, H(A) is the least aleph that is not \leq |A|.) Therefore the ordering (C_{b},\,\leq ) has order type that of an ordinal \alpha _{b}<H(A). Let f_{b} be the unique order automorphism from \alpha _{b} onto C_{b}. Let \gamma be a fixed element of K and define F:A\times H(A)\rightarrow K by F(b,\,\beta )=f_{b}(\beta ) if b\in B and \beta \in \alpha _{b} and F(b,\,\beta )=\gamma otherwise. F is onto and |K|=|\mathcal{E}| where \mathcal{E} is the set of equivalence classes \subseteq A\times H(A) under the relation q\sim r\Leftrightarrow F(q)=F(r). Therefore |K|=\aleph _{\sigma } where A\times H(A) has a partition of cardinality \aleph _{\sigma }. Therefore, if we let \aleph _{\rho } be the smallest well ordered cardinal greater than every cardinal in the set \{\aleph _{\sigma }:A\times H(A) has a partition of cardinality \aleph _{\sigma }}, then \aleph _{\rho } cannot be covered by fewer than |A| sets each of cardinality |A|.

sec.title: NOTE 132
sec.p: The following definitions and results for forms [8 M], [8 N], [43 Q], [126 B] through [126 F] are from Keremedis [1996].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let (X,\,T) be a topological space. B\subseteq T-\{\emptyset \} is said to be a \pi -base for X if every non-empty element of T includes an element of B.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let (P,\,\leq ) be a partially ordered set (poset).

def.p: A subset D\subseteq P is set to be dense if every element of P has a lower bound in D. D is said to be open if it is open in the order topology.
An element a\in P is said to be an atom if every pair of lower bounds of a are compatible (have a common lower bound).
If P has no atoms it is called atomless. A pairwise incompatible subset of P is called an antichain.
Let D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a denumerable family of dense open sets in P. C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega \},\,\bigcup C=\omega is called a matrix for D if the following three conditions are satisfied:
\forall i\in \omega \, C_{i} is a countable antichain in P.
\forall i\in \omega ,\,\forall j>i,\,\forall c\in C_{i} there exist infinitely many t\in C_{j} such that t\leq c.
\forall i\in \omega ,\,\forall j\in \omega , all but finitely many element of C_{j} belong to D_{i}.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let A=\{A_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of non-empty sets.

def.p: A has the strong finite intersection property, sfip if for each finite Q\subseteq A,\,|\bigcap Q|\geq \omega .
An infinite subset S of A is a pseudo-intersection if |S-A_{i}|<\omega for all i\in I.

statement.p: The following statements are considered:
MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ): For every denumerable family A of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets, there exists a set C such that for all a\in A,\,0<|C\cap a|\leq \omega .
pseudo(w)([126\ \mathrm{F}]): Every denumerable family of sets having the sfip also has a pseudo-intersection.

DP: If (X,\,T) is a topological space having a countable \pi -base, then for every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open sets of X, there is a countable dense set S\subseteq X such that for all i\in \omega and for all but finitely many s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}. (DP is form [8 N]).

DP^{\ast }\ ([126\ \mathrm{E}]): If (X,\,T) is a topological space, then for every family D=\{D_{i}: i\in \omega \} of dense open sets of X, there is a countable dense set S\subseteq X such that for all i\in \omega and for all but finitely many s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}.
WCMC\ ([126\ \mathrm{D}]): For every denumerable family A of disjoint non-empty sets there is a set C\subset \bigcup A such that for every a\in A,\, 0\leq |C\cap a|<\omega .
FSCB: Every separable first countable space (X,\,T) has a countable \pi -base.

Matrix(\omega ): For every atomless poset (P,\,\leq ) and every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open subsets of P, there exists a matrix C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega \},\, |\bigcup C|=\omega of P for D. (Matrix(\omega ) is form [43 Q].)
Results:

def.p: MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 126) \leftrightarrow MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )+MC(\aleph _{0},\, \aleph _{0}) (form 350). (The conjunction MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )+MC(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}) is form [126 B].)

C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 8) \leftrightarrow MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )+C(\aleph _{0},\, \aleph _{0}) (form 32). (The conjunction MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )+C(\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}) is form [8 M].)
C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 8) \leftrightarrow DP (form [8 N]).
MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 126) \leftrightarrow WCMC ([126 D]).

(Clearly, MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )\rightarrow WCMC. Let X=\{A_{n}:n\in \omega \} be a denumerable set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets. For each n\in \omega , let B_{n}=A_{0}\times A_{1}\times \cdots \times A_{n} and let B=\{B_{n}:n\in \omega \}. Let C=\{B_{n_{i}}:n_{i}\in \omega \} be a denumerable subset of B which has a multiple choice function f. The function f can be used to construct a choice function on A. This result was noted by K. Keremedis.)
WCMC ([126 D])\leftrightarrow DP^{\ast } ([126 E]) \leftrightarrow pseudo(\omega ) ([126 F]).
MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 126) \leftrightarrow FSCB\, +\, MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ). (The conjunction FSCB+ MC_{\omega }(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) is form [126 C].)
DC(\omega ) (the Principle of Dependent Choices (43)) \leftrightarrow Matrix(\omega ) (form [43 Q]).

sec.title: NOTE 133
sec.p: In this note we prove that forms [1 F] and [1 CC] are equivalent to form 1.

Form [1 F] is “For all ordinals \alpha ,\,DC(\aleph _{\alpha }): Given a relation R such that for every subset Y of a set X with |Y|<\aleph _{\alpha }, there is and x\in X with Y\,R\,x, then there is a function f:\aleph _{\alpha }\rightarrow X such that \forall \beta <\aleph _{\alpha },\, \{f(\gamma ):\gamma <\beta \}\ R\ f(\beta ).)”. It is clear that form 1 implies [1 F]. To prove the converse, well order X by using Y\,R\,x\Leftrightarrow x\not \in Y and use DC(\aleph _{\alpha }) for sufficiently large \aleph _{\alpha }.

The question of the equivalence of [1 CC] and 1 was first raised by K. Keremedis. Form [1 CC] is the conjunction of PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty ): “Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.” and MC_{\omega ^{+}}: “For every natural number n\geq 1 and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function f such that for each u\in x,\,f(u) is a non-empty finite subset of u such that |f(u)| and n are relatively prime.” We first prove that PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty ) implies “every denumerable family of odd sized sets has a choice function”. Let X=\{x_{n}:n\in \omega \} be a denumerable family of odd sized sets. For each n\in \omega , let y_{n}=\{f:f is a choice function for \{x_{i}:i\leq n\}}. |y_{n}|=|x_{1}|\cdots |x_{n}| and is therefore odd. Applying PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty ) to Y=\{y_{n}:n\in \omega \} gives an infinite subset Y^{\prime } of Y with a choice function F. Then defining G by G(x_{n})=F(y_{k})(x_{n}) where k is the least natural number \geq n for which y_{k}\in \mathrm{dom}(F) gives a choice function for X.

To prove that PC(\aleph _{0}, \mathrm{odd},\infty ) and MC_{\omega ^{+}} imply AC. It suffices to show that \forall n\in \omega ,\,C(\infty ,\,n)(form 61)+MC(form 67)+MC_{\omega ^{+}}+ “Every denumerable family of odd sized sets has a choice function” implies AC. This is because MC_{\omega ^{+}} is equivalent to \forall n\in \omega ,\, C(\infty ,\,n)+MC (by lemma 3 of Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin [1997]) and because PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\, \infty ) is equivalent to “Every denumerable of odd sized sets has a choice function”

Let X be a set of pairwise disjoint, non-empty sets. By MC there is an f:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\bigcup X) such that \forall x\in X,\,\emptyset \neq f(x)\subseteq x and |f(x)| is finite. For each n\in \omega , let Y_{n}=\{x\in X:|f(x)|=n\}. By C(\infty ,\,n), Y_{n} has a choice function (even if Y_{n} happens to be empty, but it might be clearer to exclude n for which Y_{n} is empty). Therefore the set C_{n}=\{g:g is a choice function for Y_{n}} is non-empty. By MC_{\omega ^{+}} there is a function F defined on \omega such that F(n) is an odd sized subset of C_{n} for each n\in \omega . Since every denumerable of odd sized sets has a choice function, there is a function G defined on \omega such that for every n\in \omega ,\,G(n)\in F(n). We can now define a choice function Ch for X by Ch(x)=G(n)(x) where |f(x)|=n.

sec.title: NOTE 134
sec.p: In this note we prove the result from Luzin/Sierpiński [1917] that form 100 (If n and m are cardinal numbers, then m\leq ^{\ast }n\rightarrow \neg (n<m).) implies form 369 (If \mathbb{R} is partitioned into two sets, at least one has cardinality 2^{\aleph _{0}}.). We give a proof here because Luzin/Sierpiński [1917] is not readily available.

Since 2^{\aleph _{0}}=|\mathcal{P}(\omega )|=|2^{\omega }| it suffices to show that for any partition \{A,\,B\} of \mathcal{P}(\omega ), either |A|=|2^{\omega }| or |B|=|2^{\omega }|. Since |A|\leq |2^{\omega }| and |B|\leq |2^{\omega }|, by 100 it suffices to show that there is either a function from A onto 2^{\omega } or a function from B onto 2^{\omega }. Define f:\mathcal{P}(\omega )\rightarrow 2^{\omega } by the following: Assume X=\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots \}\in \mathcal{P}(\omega ) where a_{0}<a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots . Then

Assume that f|B is not onto 2^{\omega }. Then for some \gamma in 2^{\omega }, the non-empty set C= \{X\in \mathcal{P}(\omega ):f(X)=\gamma \}\subseteq A. Then we can define a function g from C onto 2^{\omega } as follows: Assume X=\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots \} \in C where a_{0}<a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots and assume n\in \omega . If \gamma (n)=0, then a_{n+1}-a_{n} is even or |X|\leq n+1, and we define
If \gamma (n)=1, then a_{n+1}-a_{n} is odd and we define

The proof that g is onto 2^{\omega } could be done by induction, that is, given any \beta \in 2^{\omega } we could define by induction a sequence \langle a_{n}\rangle _{n\in \omega } so that X=\{a_{1},\,a_{2},\, \ldots \}\in C and g(X)=\beta .

sec.title: NOTE 135
sec.p: In this note we prove that form 18 (PUT(\aleph _{0},2,\,\aleph _{0})) and [18 B] (The union of a denumerable family of pairs has a denumerable subset.) are equivalent. It suffices to show that [18 A] (PC(\aleph _{0},2,\,\infty )) implies [18 B].

Let X be a denumerable family of pairs. By [18 A] there is a denumerable subset Y\subseteq X and a choice function f for Y. If the range of f is infinite then it is a denumerable subset of \bigcup X. If the range of f is finite, then for some t\in \bigcup X there are infinitely many elements y\in Y such that f(y)=t. Each such y has the form y=\{a_{y},\,t\}. In this case the set \{a_{y}:f(y)=t\} is a denumerable subset of \bigcup X.

sec.title: NOTE 136
sec.p: In this note we prove that the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14) is true in \mathcal{N}19. We shall use Blass’ theorem (Blass [1986], Theorem 2) which characterizes Fraenkel-Mostowski models in which BPI is true. According to this theorem BPI holds in a Fraenkel-Mostowski model if and only if the model is determined by a filter of subgroups \Gamma with the Ramsey property described below.

statement.label: Definition.

def.p: A subgroup H of a group G is a Ramsey subgroup if for every finite F\subseteq G/H (the set of left cosets of H in G) there is a finite Y\subseteq G/H such that whenever Y is partitioned into two pieces there is a g\in G such that gF is included in one of the pieces.
A filter \Gamma of subgroups of G has the Ramsey property if it has a basis consisting of Ramsey subgroups of G.

statement.p: Let E be a support. By Blass’ theorem it suffices to show that \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E) is a Ramsey subgroup of G. We shall argue that this follows from Rado’s corollary which is given in Halpern [1964], page 61. Rado’s corollary is

sec.p: Rado’s Corollary. Assume that n,p\in \omega and that \langle m_{i}\rangle _{i\in n}\in \omega ^{n}. Then there is a q\in \omega such that for all sequences \langle X_{i}\rangle _{i\in n} of disjoint sets such that |X_{i}|\geq q for every i\in n, if \Delta is a partition of \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}X_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap \,X_{i}|=m_{i})\} into two pieces there then is a sequence \langle Y_{i}\rangle _{i\in n} such that for all i\in n,\,Y_{i}\subset X_{i} and |Y_{i}|=p and \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}Y_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap \,Y_{i}|=m_{i})\} is a subset of one of the pieces.

Let F=\{\phi _{1}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E),\ldots ,\,\phi _{k}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\} be a finite subset of G/\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E). We will find a Y satisfying the condition from definition 1 above. We first note that it is easy to verify that

Let E^{\prime }=\phi _{1}(E)\cup \cdots \cup \phi _{k}(E). E and E^{\prime } are finite and therefore there are natural numbers j_{0},\,\ldots ,\,j_{n-1} such that E\cup E^{\prime }\subseteq B_{j_{0}}\cup \cdots \cup B_{j_{n-1}}. For i\in n, define E_{i}=B_{j_{i}}\cap E,\,E_{i}^{\prime }=B_{j_{i}}\cap E^{\prime },\,m_{i}=|E_{i}| and let p= \max \{|E_{i}^{\prime }|:i\in n\}. The integers n,\,p and the sequence \langle m_{i}\rangle _{i\in n}\in \omega ^{n} satisfy the hypothesis of Rado’s corollary. Therefore there is a q\in \omega satisfying the conclusion. For i\in n, choose a set X_{i}\subseteq B_{j_{i}} so that |X_{i}|=q. Let Y= \{\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E):\phi (E)\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}X_{i}\}. We now show that this Y satisfies the condition of definition 1.

Let \Delta =\{\Delta _{1},\,\Delta _{2}\} be a partition of Y into two pieces. Let \Gamma _{1}=\{\phi (E):\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in \Delta _{1}\} and \Gamma _{2}=\{\phi (E):\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in \Delta _{2}\}. By (1), \Gamma =\{\Gamma _{1},\,\Gamma _{2}\} is a partition of \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}X_{i}:(\forall i\in n)\,|Z\cap \,X_{i}|=m_{i}\}. By Rado’s corollary, there is a sequence \langle Y_{i}\rangle _{i\in n} such that |Y_{i}|=p for i\in n and W= \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}Y_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap Y_{i}| =m_{i}\} is either a subset of \Gamma _{1} or a subset of \Gamma _{2}. We assume without loss of generality that W\subseteq \Gamma _{1}. Let \eta \in G be a permutation such that \eta (E_{i}^{\prime })\subseteq Y_{i} for i\in n. (This is possible since |Y_{i}|=p\geq |E_{i}^{\prime }|.) Then (since \phi _{t}(E_{i})\subseteq E_{i}^{\prime } for 1\leq t\leq k) \eta \phi _{t}(E_{i})\subseteq Y_{i} for i\in n and 1\leq t\leq k. Therefore, for 1\leq t\leq k,\, \eta \phi _{t}(E)\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}Y_{i}. Using this and the fact that |\eta \phi _{t}(E)\cap Y_{i}|=|\eta \phi _{t}(E_{i})|=|E_{i}|=m_{i} for 1\leq t\leq k and i\in n we conclude that \eta \phi _{t}(E)\in \Gamma _{1}. Hence \eta \phi _{t}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in \Delta _{1}.

sec.title: NOTE 137
sec.p: We shall give a proof that [1 BU] (In every vector space over \mathbb{Q}, every generating set includes a basis.) implies 1, AC. Bleicher [1964] has shown that
[1 BU]implies C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) (62), so it is sufficient to prove that [1 BU] implies MC (67). (The proof is due to K. Keremedis.)

Let X=\{x_{i}:i\in I\} be a set of pairwise disjoint infinite sets. For each i\in I, let V_{i} be the set of all functions from x_{i} to \mathbb{Q} such that for all f\in V_{i},\,\exists r\in \mathbb{Q} such that \{u\in x_{i}:f(u)\neq r\} is finite. Then V_{i} is a vector space. Let V be the weak direct product of the V_{i}’s. For each i\in I, define
Let G=\bigcup \{G_{i}:i\in I\}. Then G is a generating set for V. Let B\subseteq G be a basis for V. For each i\in I, let H^{i} be the function in V such that \forall u\in x_{j},

For each i\in I,\,H^{i} can be uniquely represented as a linear combination of a finite number of basis elements. It follows from the definition of G_{i} that each basis element uniquely specifies an element in x_{i}. Thus, each H^{i} uniquely specifies a finite subset of x_{i}.

sec.title: NOTE 138
sec.p: In this note we include a proof due to K. Keremedis that form 375 (Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem) implies form 119 (C(\aleph _{0},uniformly orderable with order type of the integers).

sec.title: NOTE 139
sec.p: We give a proof that form 67 (MC, Multiple Choice Axiom) implies form 375 (Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem). To the best of our knowledge, this result is due to David Pincus.

Suppose X is a normal topological space. Then, if A and B are disjoint closed sets, there exist disjoint open sets C and D such that A\subseteq C and B\subseteq D. MC gives us a rule for choosing a finite number of pairs (C,\,D) with the above property. Since the intersection of a finite number of open sets is open, MC implies that there is a function F such that for each pair of disjoint closed sets (A,\,B), F(A,\,B)=(C,\,D), where C and D are disjoint open sets such that A\subseteq C and B\subseteq D. Thus, using the standard proof of Urysohn’s lemma (see, for example, Kelley [1955], p 115), there is a rule for choosing a function f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] which is zero on A and one on B. Given this rule for choosing Urysohn’s function, the standard proof of the Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem can be given in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} (See, for example, Kelley [1955], p 242.).

sec.title: NOTE 140
sec.p: In this note we give a proof that form 214 (For every family A of infinite sets, there is a function f such that \forall y\in A,\,f(y)\subseteq y and |f(y)|=\aleph _{0}.) implies form 152 (Every non-well orderable set is the union of a pairwise disjoint, well orderable family of denumerable sets.)

Let X be a set which cannot be well ordered and let Y be the set of all infinite subsets of X. Form 214 implies that there is a function f such that for each y\in Y,\,f(y)\subseteq y and |f(y)|=\aleph _{0}. We define a function g on the ordinals so that g(0)=f(X) and g( \alpha )=f(X\,\backslash \, \bigcup _{\beta <\alpha }g(\beta )). Since X is a set, there is an ordinal \gamma such that X\, \backslash \, \bigcup _{\beta <\gamma }g(\beta ) is finite. We can use this function g to cover X with a well ordered family of pairwise disjoint denumerable sets.

sec.title: NOTE 141
sec.p: In this note we give the definitions for forms [1 CE] through [1 CH], [67 K] through [67 T], [126 G] through [126 K], 173, [173 A], 232, [232 A] through [232 G], 383, and [383 A] through [383 C].

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Let (X,\,T) be a topological space.

def.p: X is normal if for every pair of disjoint closed sets A and B, there exist disjoint open sets C and D such that A\subseteq C and B\subseteq D.

X satisfies Urysohn’s lemma iff it satisfies: If A,\,B are closed and disjoint in X then there exists a continuous function f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] separating A and B. i.e., A\subseteq f^{-1}(0) and B\subseteq f^{-1}(1). (In the remainder of this note we shall refer to a space that satisfies Urysohn’s lemma as a U space.)

X satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem iff it satisfies: If A is closed in X and f:A\rightarrow [0,\,1] is a continuous function, then there exists a continuous extension \bar{f} of f to all of X taking values in [0,1]. (We shall refer to a space satisfying the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem as a T space.)

The disjoint union of the disjoint family \{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\} of topological spaces is the set X=\bigcup \{X_{i}:i\in k\} such that O is open in X iff O\cap X_{i} is open in X_{i} for all i\in k.

A family \mathcal{K} of subsets of a topological space (X,\,T) is locally finite (respectively locally countable) iff each point of X has a neighborhood meeting only a finite number (respectively countable number) of elements of \mathcal{K}.

X is paracompact (respectively para-Lindelöf) iff X is \mathrm{T}_{2} and every open cover \mathcal{U} of X has a locally finite (respectively locally countable › open refinement \mathcal{V}, (that is, \mathcal{V} is a locally finite open cover of X and every member of \mathcal{V} is included in a member of \mathcal{U}).
A family \mathcal{K} of subsets of X is point finite (respectively point countable) iff each element of X belongs to only finitely many (respectively countably many) members of \mathcal{K}.
X is metacompact (respectively meta-Lindelöf) iff each open cover \mathcal{U} of X has an open point finite (respectively point countable) refinement.

A set C\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X) is \sigma -locally finite (respectively \sigma -point finite, \sigma -disjoint, \sigma -discrete) if C= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }C_{n} where each C_{n} is locally finite (respectively, point finite, pairwise disjoint, discrete).

Assume that \gamma is a well ordered cardinal number, that is, \gamma is an initial ordinal. A set C\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X) is \gamma -locally finite (respectively \gamma -point finite, \gamma -disjoint, \gamma -discrete) if C= \bigcup _{\alpha \in \gamma }C_{\alpha } where each C_{\alpha } is locally finite (respectively, point finite, pairwise disjoint, discrete).

An open cover \mathcal{U} =\{U_{i}:i\in k\} of X is shrinkable iff there exists an open cover \mathcal{V}=\{V_{i}:i\in k\} of non-empty sets such that \bar{V}_{i}\subseteq U_{i} for all i\in k. \mathcal{V} is also called a shrinking of \mathcal{U}.
X is a PFCS space iff every point finite open cover of X is shrinkable.

D\subseteq X is discrete if every x\in X has a neighborhood U such that |U\,\cap \, D|=1. A set C\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X) is discrete if \forall x\in X, there is a neighborhood U of x such that U\cap A\neq \emptyset for at most one element A\in C. (Thus, D\subseteq X is discrete iff \{\{d\}:d\in D\} is discrete.)

X is cwH (collectionwise Hausdorff) iff if X is \mathrm{T}_{2} and for every closed and discrete subset D of X there exists a family U=\{U_{d}:d\in D\} of disjoint open sets such that d\in U_{d} for all d\in D.

X is cwH(B) (collectionwise Hausdorff with respect to the base B) iff if X is \mathrm{T}_{2} and for every closed and discrete subset D of X there exists a family U=\{U_{d}:d\in D\} of disjoint open sets such that U\subseteq B and d\in U_{d} for all d\in D.

X is cwN (collectionwise normal) if X is T_{2} and for every discrete C of pairwise disjoint closed subsets of X, there exists a family U=\{U_{A}:A\in C\} of disjoint open sets such that A\subseteq U_{A} for all A\in C. (cwN(B) is defined similarly to cwH(B) in 15.)

sec.title: NOTE 142
sec.p: In this note we prove that form 234 (There is a non-Ramsey set.) implies form 282 (w\not \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }).

Assume that there is a non-Ramsey set A. The proof will be by contradiction. We therefore assume that \omega \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }. Then (using the definitions in note 97) for every F:\omega ^{\omega }\rightarrow \{0,1\} there is an infinite subset X of \omega such that either

def.p: (\forall g\in X^{\omega })(F(g)=0) or
(\forall g\in X^{\omega })(F(g)=1).

sec.p: Using A we define a function F:\omega ^{\omega }\rightarrow \{0,1\} by

Let X be the infinite subset of \omega guaranteed by \omega \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }. For each infinite subset Y of \omega , let g_{Y}\in \omega ^{\omega } be the unique strictly increasing function whose range is Y. Then F(g_{Y})=0 if and only if Y\in A. Either (i) or (ii) must be true of X and F. If (i) holds then for every infinite Y\subseteq X,\,g_{Y}\in X^{\omega } so F(g_{Y})=0 and hence Y\in A. On the other hand, if (ii) holds then for every infinite Y\subseteq X,\,g_{Y}\in X^{\omega } so F(g_{Y})=1 and hence Y\not \in A. This contradicts the assumption that A is non-Ramsey.

sec.title: NOTE 143
sec.p: Form [0 AM] is a form of the Hahn-Banach Theorem for separable vector spaces. We shall prove by induction that it is provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

Assume V is a separable vector space, D=\{d_{0},\,d_{1},\,\cdots \} is a countable dense subset of V, and p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R} satisfies p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y), and (\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x)). Also assume that p satisfies the following condition:

Let S be a subspace of V and let f be a linear function from S to \mathbb{R} such that for all x\in S,\,f(x)\leq p(x). We shall define by induction a countable set of linear functions G=\{g_{n}:n\in \omega \} such that g_{n}\subseteq g_{n+1} and such that the linear extension of f,\,f^{\ast }=\bigcup \, G, can be extended to all of V by using the condition (\ast ).

We define g_{0}=f. Suppose g_{n} has been defined and S_{n} is the domain of G_{n}. In what follows, we shall let d=d_{n+1} and g=g_{n+1}. If d is in the domain of g_{n}, then define g=g_{n}. Suppose that d is not in the domain of g_{n}. We would like to define g so that for any t\in \mathbb{R} and any x\in S_{n},\ g(td+x)=tg(d)+g(x)\leq p(td+x). Then tg(d)\leq p(td+x)-g(x). If t=1,\, g(d)\leq p(d+x)-g(x) and if t=-1,\,g(d)\geq g(x)-p(x-d). Let s= \sup _{x\in S}(g(x)-p(x-d)) and let i= \inf _{x\in S}(p(d+x)-g(x)). Then s\leq g(d)\leq i. Define g(d) to be the mid-point of the interval [s,\,i]. For any x\in S_{n}, We define g(x)=g_{n}(x) and, for each t\in \mathbb{R}, we define g(td+x)=tg(d)+g(x). Let f^{\ast }=\bigcup \{g_{n}:n\in \omega \}. It is clear that f^{\ast } is a linear function, f^{\ast }(x)\leq p(x) for all x in the domain of f^{\ast }, and D is a subset of the domain of f^{\ast }.

Let \epsilon >0 and x\in V. Then, by (\ast ), there is a y\in D such that p(x-y)<\epsilon and p(y-x)<\epsilon . If f^{\ast }(x-y)\geq 0, then 0\leq f^{\ast }(x-y)\leq p(x-y)<\epsilon . If f^{\ast }(x-y)<0, then 0<-f^{\ast }(x-y)=f^{\ast }(y-x)\leq p(y-x)<\epsilon . Consequently, |f^{\ast }(x-y)|<\epsilon and f^{\ast } can be extended to all of V.

sec.title: NOTE 144
sec.p: A proof that dependent choice (form 43) holds in FM models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} in which the set of supports S is closed under countable unions. This includes models where S consists of all countable subsets of the set A of atoms.

Assume that \mathcal{N} is such a model and that R is a relation in \mathcal{N} such that for all x\in \mathrm{dom}(R) there is a y such that x\ R\ y. Then, in the ground model (where AC holds) there is a sequence (x_{n})_{n\in \omega } such that (\forall n\in \omega )(x_{n}\ R\ x_{n+1}). If for each n\in \omega ,\,x_{n} has support E_{n}, then \bigcup _{n\in \omega }E_{n} is a support for (x_{n})_{n\in \omega }. Hence, this sequence is in \mathcal{N}.

sec.title: NOTE 145
sec.p: A proof that form 287 (the Hahn-Banach theorem for separable normed linear spaces) implies form 222 (there is a non-principal measure on \omega ). This result and its proof are due to M. Morillon.

Let E be the vector space of bounded sequences of reals. Let M be a norm on E such that the normed vector space (E,\,M) is separable: for example, if x= (x_{k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}\in E let M(x)= \sum \nolimits _{k\in \mathbb{N}}\frac{|x_{k}|}{(k+1)^{2}}. Here, the normed vector space (E,\,M) is separable because the set of sequences in \mathbb{Q}^{(\mathbb{N})} which end in an infinite sequence of zeros is dense in E.

For every x=(x_{k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}\in E, let p(x)=\varlimsup \{x_{k};k\in \mathbb{N}\}. Hence, we obtain a sublinear functional p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Using form 287, let g:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} be a linear functional such that g\leq p. We have p(1)=1 and p(-1)=-1. Hence, g(1)=1. For every finite subset A\subseteq \mathbb{N} we have p(1_{A})=p(-1_{A})=0, hence, g(1_{A})=0. Here 1_{A} denotes the characteristic function of the set A.
For every A\subseteq \mathbb{N}, lf m(A)=g(1_{A}), then m:\mathcal{P}(\omega )\rightarrow [0,\,1] is a non-principal measure on \omega .

sec.title: NOTE 146
sec.p: Form [43 W] is due to Claus-Peter Wirth. In this note we prove that it is equivalent to form 43. Form [43 W] is: Let M be a non-empty set partially ordered by < without <-minimal elements. Then there is a subset C of M which is linearly ordered by < such that C has no <-minimal element. Form 43 is the principle of dependent choice, DC. To prove [43 W] from DC let X=M and define R by x\,R\,y if and only if y<x. Then the sequence (x_{n})_{n\in \omega } which is guaranteed by DC is a linearly ordered subset of M with no <-minimal elements.

To prove [43 W] implies DC, let R be a relation on a set X such that \forall x\in X,\,\exists y\in X such that x\,R\,y. Let M be the set of all finite sequences (x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) of elements of X such that x_{1}\ R\ x_{2}\ R\ \ldots \ R\ x_{n} and define a relation < on M by (x_{1},\, \ldots ,\,x_{n})<(y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{m}) if and only if (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) is a proper extension of (y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{m}). M has no <-minimal elements so by (ii) there is a < chain C in M with no minimal element. From C an infinite sequence (x_{n})_{n\in \omega } can be constructed with the property that x_{n}\ R\,x_{n+1} for all n\in \omega .

sec.title: NOTE 147
sec.p: Definitions for measures on Boolean algebras.

statement.label: Definition.
statement.p: Assume that \mathcal{B} =(B,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ,\,\mathbf{1,\,0}) is a Boolean algebra.

def.p: A measure or additive real valued measure on \mathcal{B} is a function m:\mathcal{B} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that m(\mathbf{1})=1,\,(\forall x\in B)(m(x)\geq 0), and (\forall x,\,y\in B)(x\wedge y=\mathbf{0}\rightarrow m(x\vee y)= m(x)+m(y)). (It follows that m(\mathbf{0})=0.)
A two valued measure on \mathcal{B} is a measure on \mathcal{B} whose range is \{0,1\}.
If \mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{P}(X),\,\cap ,\,\cup ,\,X,\,\emptyset ) then a measure m on \mathcal{B} is non-principal if m(\{x\})=0 for every x\in X.

sec.title: NOTE 148
sec.p: We give a proof that forms 154 and [154 A] are equivalent. First, it is clear that 154 implies [154 A]. To prove the converse, assume [154 A] holds. Let \{X_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a countable family of pairwise disjoint compact \mathrm{T}_{2} spaces and let Y be the one point compactification of \bigcup _{i\in \omega }X_{i}. Form [154 A] implies that Y^{\omega } is compact. Since \prod _{i\in \omega }X_{i} is a closed subspace of Y^{\omega }, it is also compact.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: To explain this part of the book, it is helpful to consider some examples. Five typical lines are below.

The first two numbers are form numbers. The third number which occurs in parentheses is a code number for the status of the implication. For example, in the first line above, the number 3 means that the implication “form 43 implies form 63” is not provable in Zermelo-Fraenkel (ZF) set theory. The other code numbers that we use are

def.p: for “The status of the implication is unknown.”
for “The implication is provable.”
for “The implication is provable and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1.”
for “The implication is not provable in ZF.”
for “The implication is not provable in ZF and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1 or 3.”
for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.”
for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are odd.”
for “The status of the implication is unknown and we have found the question asked somewhere in the literature.”

sec.p: (See the introduction for the definition of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.)

The implication codes are odd numbers for the most part. In a typical line following the code number, is a reference to a bibliography item and possibly a note and, in the case of a non-implication, a model number. (We normally only list one model even if there are several models with this property.) In the first example above, Felgner [1971a] refers to the Bibliography and M2 refers to the model \mathcal{M}2 of ZF from our models section. (\mathcal{M}2 is a model in which form 43 is true and form 63 is false.)

In the second example above we see that form 85 implies form 78 is not provable in ZF set theory; the reference is Brunner [1980]; and the model is the permutation model \mathcal{N}3. \mathcal{N}3 is a model of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. However, many of the results obtained for permutation models can be transferred to ZF models because of the work of Jech/Sochor [1966a], [1966b], and Pincus [1971], [1972a], [1974c], [1977a]. If a result is transferable, the numeral 3 will occur in the line to mean that the implication is not provable in ZF set theory. Following the reference, we give the permutation model with a “\mathrm{T}” following its number to indicate the result is transferable. (See note 18 for a list of forms that are transferable and note 103 for a summary of the transfer results of Jech/Sochor [1966a] and [1966b] and Pincus [1971], [1972a], and [1977a].)

The letters “IC” following a model number indicate that an inaccessible cardinal was used to construct the model. In some cases, the reference is just a model. In these cases it is clear from the model itself why the implication does not hold. (See, for example, the line at position (317,3) and model \mathcal{N}38.)

It follows from example 3 above that form 67 implies form 80 is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}, the references are Fraenkel [1922] and Jech [1973b], and the permutation model is \mathcal{N}2. The last example above tells us that form 87 implies form 86 in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. The references are Jech [1973b] (p 120 theorem 8.1), Levy [1964], and additional information can be found in note 9 in the notes section of the book. When note 120 is the reference, we state which part of the note applies. For example, at position (152,67) the reference is note 120(41). This means that we are using item 41 in note 120 (67+122\leftrightarrow 1, where form 1 is AC) to obtain the independence result. Form 122 is true in \mathcal{N}15, so by note 120 part 41, form 67 must be false. (AC is false in all our models.) In addition, form 152 is true in this model. Consequently, there is a 5 at position (152,67) below.

If the reference is note 18, we mean that either the first form listed is true in every permutation (FM) model, the second form is false in each such model, or the second form is false in every Cohen model. We have several forms that depend on parameters. (See note 18 for a list of these forms.) Sometimes the relationships between such forms depend on the value of the parameters. For example, we have the following line below:

Both forms 120 and 33 depend upon parameters. The notation means that for certain values of the parameters, form 120 is true in the model M47(n, M) and form 33 is false. The reader should look at the model to determine when this holds.
Each of our weak forms of the Axiom of Choice is implied by AC (form 1), but for some of our forms, it is unknown whether they imply AC. Each one of these forms, n, is listed below in the form:
Similarly, for some forms, it is unknown whether they are provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. Each one of these forms, m, is listed below as:
In these two cases, for those forms for which we have not found a reference in the literature we use “This project” as the reference.
